definitions.definition: The 'unbroken' metre of Marathi devotional song and the song composed in it — the form of the Vārkarī saints' poetry, sung in bhajan and kīrtan.
The reflection of consciousness in the intellect, compared to the sky reflected in a pond; unreal, a product of ignorance; the jīva as agent (Rāma-hṛdaya, Rāma Gītā).

An appearance manifested by consciousness within itself as if external (ĪPK 1.5.1); the world is ābhāsa, real as manifestation; the individual too manifests (ābhāsana) as the first of his five acts (PH 11).
Semblance: the jīva as a mere appearance of consciousness in the intellect (Sureśvara); in BS 2.3.50 'reflection'.

notes: Contrasted by the tradition with Advaita's vivarta (see dsp:causation, dsp:world-real-or-appearance).

definitions.definition: A dependent reality of three kinds: prior non-existence, destruction and constant (absolute) non-existence; mutual non-existence (difference) is not a fourth, being the nature of things. Known by inference and by perception.
The seventh category, of four kinds (prior, posterior, absolute, mutual); not listed by Praśastapāda because determined through its counterpositive, not because unreal (Udayana).
Proposed as a means of knowledge (in the sense of non-apprehension); reduced to inference (NS 2.2.2).
Where the five positive means of knowledge do not arise, the non-apprehension itself is the means of knowing non-existence (ŚV abhāva 1; the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Not a separate means: the Prakaraṇapañcikā counts five means only; absence is grasped as the bare locus (as the Kāśikā on the Ślokavārttika reports the Prābhākara view).
A soul that by its inherent nature will never attain liberation (TS 2.7).
The safety the renouncer gives to all beings on going forth (MDh 6.39–40).
Fearlessness: 'brahman is fearlessness' (BAU 4.4.25); Janaka has reached fearlessness (4.2.4); fear arises from a second (1.4.2); the knower of bliss is never afraid (TU 2.4, 2.9).
The renouncer's gift: 'fearlessness to all beings from me'.
Non-discrimination, non-difference: seeing no division of pure and impure, high and low, since Śiva is in all.
The non-dual conduct (advaitācāra) of the Kaula (KJN 11.3–4).
Hostile sorcery; one class of Atharvavedic rites.
Denotation, the primary power of a word to convey its conventional meaning; the first of the three powers (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā).
The primary power (śakti) of words; for the grammarians grounded in the eternal relation of word and meaning.

In the true sense, stainless wisdom with its retinue; conventionally, also the wisdom and treatises that lead to it — for the Vaibhāṣikas the seven canonical books, word of the Buddha arranged by disciples.
For the Sautrāntikas, not a separate basket of treatises but the sūtras in which the characteristics of dharmas are taught (e.g. the Arthaviniścaya).
The first daily period: purification and approaching the Lord (going to the temple).

A secret resolve limiting the conditions under which a mendicant will accept alms — like Mahāvīra's vow, fulfilled by the shackled Candanā, to accept food only from a captive princess with shaven head, one foot inside the threshold, weeping.

Words first express their own meanings and cease; the expressed meanings then connect to yield the sentence-meaning, as the flame is an intermediate stage in cooking with wood (Śabara on MS 1.1.25; ŚV vākya 342–343).

(As reported) One of six classes — black, blue, red, yellow, white, supremely white — through which beings pass; the supremely white are the three Ājīvika leaders (AN 6.57, ascribed to Pūraṇa); in the Tamil report, black, dark blue, green, red, golden, white, with release in the supremely white birth.
The Buddha's six: dark or bright birth yielding a dark result, a bright result, or nibbāna.

equivalents.note: the Jain six colour-classes of soul (leśyā) are also six and colour-named; the texts draw no link

definitions.definition: Lunar mansion abhijit: presiding deity Brahmā (Vidhi) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord — (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class swift (kṣipra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). 28th asterism, used in muhūrta (MC 2.1, 2.6) but absent from the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa list and from the Viṃśottarī scheme.

Superknowledge; six — magical power, divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of former lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, destruction of outflows; the last three are the 'knowledges' (vidyā).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The devotee's affectionate reproach of the Mother for neglecting her child, a hallmark of the Śākta songs.
The nature of ahaṃkāra (SK 24); also the misidentification by which puruṣa seems colored (SS 6.28).
Self-regard, 'I-ness': for Bhoja the one true rasa, called śṛṅgāra, of which the named rasas are developments.
The sixth of the ten bodhisattva grounds in the Daśabhūmika.
Acting, 'carrying towards' the spectators: fourfold — bodily (āṅgika), verbal (vācika), costume and make-up (āhārya) and involuntary states (sāttvika) (NŚ 6.23).
Sumedha's aspiration to Buddhahood, which succeeds by the combination of eight conditions (Bv 2.59).
Clinging to life, flowing by its own momentum, present even in the wise (2.9); the wish 'may I not cease, may I be', a fear of death that shows former births (YBh 2.9).
Six direct knowledges: psychic power, divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye, destruction of the effluents (DN 2; MN 119).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Penetration of the truths; the Theravāda holds that each path penetrates all four truths at once.
Clear realization of the truths: gradual (anupūrva), in sixteen moments.
Realization of the four truths in a single moment (ekābhisamaya) — attributed to the Mahāsāṃghika and Vibhajyavādin side in the doxographies (low confidence).
The heroine's going out to meet her lover at night; Rādhā's going to the bower (GG 11).
Consecration conferring the office of teacher (ācāryābhiṣeka) or of power-seeker (sādhakābhiṣeka).
Bathing of the installed image; in Kerala, kalaśa-abhiṣeka rites renew the deity's power.
Production understood as the manifestation of what already exists, as a pot is manifested by a lamp (SS 5.59; cf. 1.120).
Mica, the seed of Gaurī (the Goddess), joined with mercury (Śiva's seed) to make the divine body (SDS Raseśvara 9-10).

notes: Restricted subject.

definitions.definition: That which was covered by the void before That One was born by tapas (RV 10.129.3); its sense (life-force, emptiness, the germ) is debated by commentators.

checks.note: Located: 'tucchyenābhv apihitaṃ yad āsīt' (RV 10.129.3).

definitions.definition: What the conventional standpoint describes — not false, but not the thing's own nature (Samayasāra 11).
Daily oil-massage of body, head, ears and feet, which makes the body firm, calms vāta and delays ageing (Ca Sū 5.81-92; AHS Sū 2.8-9).
The six inner austerities culminating in meditation (TS 9.20).
Practice: effort toward the mind's stability (1.13), firmly grounded when long, uninterrupted and devoted (1.14); with dispassion the means of stilling (1.12).
Practice, which together with dispassion restrains the restless mind (BhG 6.35); a step of the devotional ladder (12.9).
Practice, with dispassion a support of meditation (SS 3.36) and of the cessation of coloring (SS 6.29).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Practice: together with dispassion (vairāgya) the means by which the restless mind is held (6.35); the 'former practice' (pūrva-abhyāsa) of a previous life carries the fallen yogin onward (6.44).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Repetition of an injunction, which would be pointless unless it marks a distinct rite (MS 2.2.2); in Vedānta usage one of the six marks of purport.

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from abhyāsa 'practice' in Yoga.

definitions.definition: Repeated practice of bringing the mind back to the Lord; the second step of the ladder of BhG 12.9, and the 'yoga of practice' of 8.8.
The first result of dharma (VS 1.1.2); sought through visible means where the visible result is absent, and through pure food with restraint (VS 6.1.8, 6.2.1, 6.2.9 C).
Neither wholesome nor unwholesome: resultants, functionals, all matter and nibbāna.
The eighth of the ten bodhisattva grounds in the Daśabhūmika.
The seven modes: Veda, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Siddhānta and Kaula, each higher than the last (Kulārṇava 2.7-8).
The practice of the good (sadācāra) as a source of dharma (MDh 2.6); without it the Vedas do not purify (VDh 6.3).

The name later given to Caraka's teaching that the truthful, non-angry, non-violent, calm, generous, devout and self-controlled person 'enjoys constant rasāyana' and alone gains the full benefits of rasāyana (Ca Ci 1.4.30-35; AHS Utt 39.179-181: 'nityarasāyana').

notes: The compound ācāra-rasāyana is the later name; the texts say 'nitya-rasāyana'.

definitions.definition: One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the bhakta stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The Tathāgata has no closed fist of a teacher holding back teachings (DN 16).
The teacher who, initiating the student, bears him three nights as an embryo (AVŚ 11.5.3).
The true teacher (sadācārya) of the unbroken lineage, who imparts the five sacraments and the secret mantras out of compassion.
The teacher who initiates and teaches the Veda with its ritual and secret parts, 'from whom one gathers the dharmas' (ĀpDh 1.1.1.14); ten times more venerable than a sub-teacher (MDh 2.145).
Teacher: knowledge learned from a teacher leads most surely to the goal (ChU 4.9.3); 'a person who has a teacher knows' (ChU 6.14.2); 'let your teacher be a god to you' (TU 1.11.2).
In Jainism the head of an order, third of the five supreme beings, who receives the Sūrimantra at installation.
The consecrated teacher (also deśika, guru) empowered to initiate and to perform installations.
In the Vinaya: a teacher — the officiant of the legal act, the instructor of the candidate, or the teacher of a monk in dependence.

notes: Buddhist Vinaya sense only; other lineages' definitions of ācārya are other units'.

definitions.definition: Being held as one's own by a true teacher, which the Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam teaches is itself sufficient for salvation for one who can do nothing else.
Steadfast devotion to the teacher as sufficient refuge — Madhurakavi's way: 'I know no other god' than Nammāḻvār.

equivalents.note: ācārya-abhimāna is the teacher's saving regard (the teacher's side); ācārya-niṣṭhā the disciple's sole reliance on him

definitions.definition: Consecration of an initiate as ācārya, entitled to initiate others and teach.
The five receptacles among the ninety-six principles (stomach, intestine, rectum, bladder, seminal receptacle).

One of the ten extraordinary events of this descending half-cycle that ordinarily should not happen (a woman Tīrthaṅkara, the embryo transfer, an attack on a Jina, a fruitless first sermon, and others).
Nakedness, the first of the Digambara monk's special root qualities; required for full renunciation and liberation.
Either nakedness (the Jinakalpa mode, followed by Mahāvīra and early ascetics) or wearing few, poor garments; one of the twenty-two hardships; not required now.
Naked monasticism kept as the rule, with clothing allowed by exception (apavāda-liṅga) and for women.

cross_language.note: the term in Tattvārthasūtra 9.9

definitions.definition: Insentient reality: eternal (the Vedas), eternal-and-non-eternal (Purāṇas etc., time, prakṛti), and non-eternal products, uncompounded and compounded.
The 'unknown bird' that comes and goes in the cage of the body — the soul or the Man of the Heart.
The four unthinkables: the Buddhas' domain, jhāna's domain, the results of kamma, speculation about the world (AN 4.77).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self: it cannot be an object of thought (2.25, with 'unmanifest' and 'unchangeable').
Inconceivable: what cannot be established or refuted by reasoning and is known only from revelation — used of the Lord's powers.
Inconceivable simultaneous difference and non-difference of the Lord and his powers (souls, world); inconceivable because his powers are beyond reason.
The bodhisattva liberation by which Sumeru fits in a mustard seed without change to either.

cross_language.form: bukesiyi jietuo 不可思議解脫

definitions.definition: Insentient reality in three kinds: pure sattva, mixed sattva (prakṛti) and that devoid of sattva (time); the body of the Lord together with the souls.
The non-conscious reality, of three kinds: aprākṛta, prākṛta and time.
The sun's northern course (late winter to summer) which takes away the earth's moisture and men's strength; fiery (Ca Sū 6.4-6; AHS Sū 3.2-4).
Name of the base-consciousness as appropriating the body; not taught to the foolish lest they take it for a self.

cross_language.form: len pa'i rnam par shes pa

definitions.definition: The Nāth greeting and response ('ādeś, ādeś'), acknowledging the command/presence of the Lord in the other.
Instruction, teaching formula: 'now the instruction: not so, not so' (BAU 2.3.6); the teaching about brahman in lightning and in the mind (Kena 4.4-5); the teaching of 'I' and of the self (ChU 7.25).
The 'uncatchable Man', the Man of the Heart as he comes and goes in the body and slips from grasp; in coded songs he appears at a certain time 'with the tide'.

(1) The root centre (GŚ 10). (2) The sixteen supports of the body on which breath and attention are fixed; jālandhara 'binds the sixteen ādhāras' (HYP 3.73); the Haṭhatattvakaumudī devotes a chapter to them.
A support-point of attention in the body (sixteen in the Yogacūḍāmaṇi); the base centre.

literal: non-dharma, what is contrary to dharma

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, the disorder that overpowers a family once its family dharmas perish, leading to the corruption of its women and varṇa-mixture (1.40–41).
The tāmasa opposite of virtue (SK 23), leading to downward movement (SK 44).
A quality of the self produced by forbidden acts (Tarkasaṅgraha).
What is made known by prohibition as leading to harm (anartha), e.g. the violence aimed at in the Śyena rite; also the demerit (pāpa) that results.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The counter-order whose rise, together with the decline of dharma, is the occasion on which the Lord sends himself forth (4.7).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A single, formless, world-pervading substance that assists the rest of moving things, as shade assists a traveller (TS 5.17).
Suffering caused by humans, animals, birds, reptiles, insects and plants (commentaries on SK 1).
Perishable existence (BhG 8.4).
Two grounds for holding self and world arisen without cause: recollection from the non-percipient gods, and reasoning.
The training of the higher mind (the jhānas) (AN 3.89); pursued by removing distracting thoughts (MN 20) and gross to subtle impurities (AN 3.101).
The Puruṣa (BhG 8.4).
With respect to the gods (the cosmos), paired with adhyātma (ChU 3.18; Kena 4.4).
Suffering from supernatural or cosmic agencies: cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning (Gauḍapāda) or possession by yakṣas, rākṣasas and planets (Vācaspati).
Right view arising through instruction or study (TS 1.3); also 'understanding' of the realities through pramāṇa and naya (TS 1.6).
Realization, the Dharma as attained (the wings of awakening), the second aspect of the true Dharma.
The intercalary lunar month in which no solar ingress occurs; also called mala-māsa, it is unfit for sacraments and many rites, though prized for devotion (Kālamādhava; Nirṇayasindhu).

Eligibility for knowledge and scripture, in three grades (low, middle, highest) by birth and by qualities; the highest is the dispassionate renunciant devoted to Viṣṇu. Eligibility to Veda, Tantra or the Name is distinguished by class and gender.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.47: one's right or proper claim, which extends to action alone and never to its fruits.

The qualification of the agent entitled to perform a rite and enjoy its fruit: a human (MS 6.1.4–5), man or woman — husband and wife jointly (MS 6.1.8, 6.1.17) — of the three higher varṇas, with Vedic learning (MS 6.1.25–38); the subject of adhyāya 6.

Fitness for a practice: the Śiva Saṃhitā assigns the four yogas to four grades of aspirant (5.10–14); the Jyotsnā holds the dispassionate alone properly eligible though Purāṇic verses grant yoga to all beings; the HYP and DYŚ say anyone who practises succeeds.
An injunction that conveys ownership (enjoyership) of the fruit of the act, e.g. 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice'.
A topic-section of the sūtras treated in five steps: subject, doubt, prima facie view, conclusion and connection.
The unit of Mīmāṃsā discussion, with five members: subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view and conclusion (Nyāyamālā).
Seven procedures for settling disputes.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The eligible agent of a rite, the one to whom the fruit belongs ('one desiring heaven').
The qualified student: purified by prescribed duties and endowed with the four means.
Decision about the object; an occasional factor; as an imperfection of insight, strong resolve (faith).
Confidence in the supreme vehicle, the 'seed' of the buddha's children.
The training in higher wisdom: knowing the four truths as they are (AN 3.89).
The training in higher virtue: restraint by the Pātimokkha, seeing danger in the slightest fault (AN 3.89).
The need for a controller, a proof of puruṣa (SK 17); in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, governance by mere proximity, like a magnet (SS 1.96).
Substratum: the real on which something unreal is superimposed (the rope for the snake; Brahman for the world).
The eighth perfection, unshakeable like a rocky mountain (Bv 2); the four foundations of MN 140 (wisdom, truth, relinquishment, peace).
The Lord himself in the body (BhG 8.4).
The seven hellish earths (TS 3.1).
The three time-paths (past, present, future) in which properties stand; past and future exist in their own form because of this difference (4.12).
The six 'paths' of the cosmos — letters, words, mantras, kalās, principles and worlds — purified in nirvāṇa-dīkṣā.
The six paths - letters, mantras, words; kalās, tattvas, worlds - contemplated from gross to supreme (VBT 56-57; TĀ 6-12).
Time-period (past, present, future); conditioned dharmas are themselves 'the times'; the times are distinguished by activity.

notes: Parallels the Sarvāstivāda term adhvan (see brw:sarvastivada-yoga-time-and-transformation).

definitions.definition: The priest who performs the ritual actions speaking the Yajus formulas.
Deliberate superimposition by scripture and teacher (creation, sheaths, attributes) as a provisional teaching device.

Superimposition: 'the appearance, of the nature of memory, of something previously seen in something else' — the mutual superimposition of self and not-self that is the basis of all empirical life, called avidyā.

Superimposition: the appearance of one thing as another through error, like a snake in a rope; ego is the first superimposition on the Self; jīva and witness appear mutually superimposed like fire and iron.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In the compound adhyātma-cetas (3.30): the mind directed to the self, with which one resigns all actions to Kṛṣṇa; commentators gloss it variously.
The own nature (svabhāva) of the Imperishable (BhG 8.3); the knowledge of the self is the best of sciences (10.32).
With respect to the self/body, as opposed to adhidaivata, with respect to the gods: the two registers in which the Upaniṣads state correspondences (ChU 3.18; Kena 4.4-5).

(1) In Haribhadra's Yogabindu the first yoga: study and contemplation of reality with friendliness etc. by one with vows; (2) in Yaśovijaya, pure activity centred on the self by one free of delusion (Adhyātmasāra 1.2); (3) the name of the seventeenth-century movement centred on the Samayasāra.
The study and direct experience of the pure self (śuddhātman) by the ultimate standpoint, as taught in the Samayasāra and its Hindi renderings.
Inner clarity in the lucidity of nirvicārā coalescence (1.47): a clear light of insight grasping things as they are, without sequence (YBh 1.47).
The yoga of the inner self, by which the wise one realizes the hidden god and leaves joy and sorrow (KU 1.2.12).
Learned from the Yoga śāstra: austerity, breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, fixation (NBh 4.2.46).
Knowledge of the self as in the Upaniṣads; Nyāya is more than this because of its separate categories, though in it knowledge of truth is knowledge of the self (NBh 1.1.1).
A member of the seventeenth-century Adhyātma movement.
Internal suffering, bodily (from imbalance of wind, bile and phlegm) and mental (from desire, anger, separation from the dear, etc.) (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati on SK 1).
The nature of buddhi (SK 23); perception is determination concerning each object (SK 5), explained by Vācaspati as a predominance of sattva in buddhi.
The accomplishment of gaining knowledge of the twenty-five principles by studying texts (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).
The danger in sensual pleasures — toil, loss, conflict, bad destiny (MN 13).
The hereditary Śaiva priests (Śivācāryas, gurukkaḷ) of South Indian temples, entitled to parārtha worship.
Mother of the Ādityas, before whom one prays to be sinless (RV 1.24.15); born of Dakṣa, and Dakṣa of her (10.72.4).
The sons of Aditi (Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman and others), who stand by ṛta (RV 10.85.1).
Kapila as the first knower who, assuming a created mind, taught the doctrine to Āsuri out of compassion (saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.25, ascribed to Pañcaśikha).
The unseen cause of motions without visible cause and of the mind's passage at death and birth; its absence is liberation (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.14, 5.2.19–20 C).
The residue of past action that brings about the body (NS 3.2.60); set in motion by the Lord (NBh 4.1.21).
Unseen force; used by Śāstradīpikā for what awakens impressions in dreams, and generally for the unseen results of acts, of which apūrva is the Mīmāṃsā form.
(As reported) Denied: there is no unseen cause; the variety of things is from own-nature.

equivalents.note: Mīmāṃsā's apūrva is the unseen potency produced by a rite; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika's adṛṣṭa is merit/demerit as qualities of the self — both link act to later result.

literal: to be experienced in an unseen birth

definitions.definition: Karma ripening in a future life; none remains for one whose afflictions are exhausted (YBh 2.12).

Rejected as a practice for the worshipper at the māheśvara stage, since worship rests on difference (SSM 10.37–43), and affirmed at the aikya stage, where difference is seen to be imagined by māyā (14.8–14).
Without a second, non-dual: 'he becomes the ocean, the one seer without duality' (BAU 4.3.32); the fourth is 'peaceful, auspicious, non-dual' (MāU 7, 12).

notes: The adjective of the Upaniṣads; the school-name Advaita Vedānta is later.

definitions.definition: The inclination toward non-duality, which arises only by the grace of the Lord.
That paired concepts — saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, defiled and pure, self and no-self — are not two; entry into non-duality is beyond words, shown by Vimalakīrti's silence.

equivalents.note: Both deny duality; the Mahāyāna sūtras deny a single substantial reality, while Advaita affirms Brahman; related by later polemics (dsp:advaita-crypto-buddhism)

definitions.definition: Kālī as the primordial Śakti and giver of nirvāṇa (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.41; Mahānirvāṇa 4.32).
Toxicology: signs and treatment of bites of snakes, insects, spiders, rodents and of combined poisons (Su Sū 1.8); 'daṃṣṭrā' in AHS Sū 1.5.
Faultless speech; above all the authorless Veda and the other true scriptures, the only means by which Viṣṇu is known.
Testimony: the activity arising in a hearer from the words of a reliable speaker who has seen or inferred the matter (YBh 1.7); it too reaches only the general (1.49).
The teaching that has come down through the succession of teachers from Maheśvara.

Revealed Śaiva scripture spoken by Śiva/Sadāśiva, the 'higher knowledge' as against the lower knowledge beginning with the Veda; in South Indian usage especially the 28 Siddhānta scriptures and their upāgamas.
The Pāñcarātra saṃhitās as scripture spoken by Bhagavān himself (Bhagavacchāstra).
In Buddhist usage: the transmitted scripture (the sūtra collections — Dīrgha, Madhyama, Saṃyukta, Ekottarika); one of the two aspects of the true Dharma.
Scripture and unbroken tradition, without which dharma cannot be established by reasoning (VP 1.30).

notes: A widely quoted etymology (ā-gata from Śiva's mouth, gata to Girijā, mata by Vāsudeva) is of uncertain source and not recorded as a definition here.
alt_notes: Buddhist sense only; the Śaiva/Pāñcarātra Āgamas are other units' definitions.

definitions.definition: The canonical scripture: the words of the Tīrthaṅkara as composed by the gaṇadharas and elders, fixed at Valabhī — forty-five texts for Mūrtipūjakas, thirty-two for Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs.

The Digambaras hold the original āgama (the Aṅgas and Pūrvas) lost; the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa preserve parts of it and are called 'āgama', and the works of later ācāryas in the four anuyogas serve as scripture.

cross_language.note: Śvetāmbara synonym for the canon
common name for canonical texts

definitions.definition: Bengali songs of Umā's homecoming from Kailāsa to her mother Menakā at the autumn Durgā festival; with the vijayā songs of farewell, composed by Rāmprasād, Kamalākānta and others.
Karma done after knowledge, which does not cling to the knower, as water to a lotus leaf.
Defilements that are not the mind's nature but come to it like dust or clouds, separable from the tathāgatagarbha and removable.
An offence, especially against the gods' ordinances, which the worshipper asks Varuṇa to loosen like a rope (RV 2.28.5).
The four biases by which evil is done: desire, hatred, delusion, fear (DN 31).
'Not terrible' (a-ghora): the benign-terrible face of Śiva, name of one of the five Brahma-mantras; the lineage takes it as its name, holding that nothing is to be feared or shunned as impure.

notes: The Aghora Brahma-mantra is in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka's tenth book (chapter-level ref; not checked).

definitions.definition: An ascetic of the Aghora lineage.
Visualising fire rising from the syllable 'arhaṃ' and burning the lotus of the eight karmas and the body (YŚ 7).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the digestive-metabolic fire; no fire in the body exists apart from pitta (Su Sū 21.9); life, complexion, strength, health, ojas, tejas and the prāṇas depend on it — extinguished one dies, balanced one lives long, disturbed one falls ill; 'agni is the root' (Ca Ci 15.3-4); its states are balanced, irregular (vāta), sharp (pitta) and weak (kapha) (AHS Sū 1.8); later counted as thirteen: the belly-fire, the five element-fires and the seven tissue-fires (Ca Ci 15.13-15).
Fire and the god of fire: household priest and messenger between men and gods, carrier of oblations, present in all fires, guardian of ṛta (RV 1.1).

The year-long building of the great brick fire-altar (often in the shape of a falcon) in five layers, explained in ŚB 6–10 as the rebuilding of Prajāpati who fell apart, so that the sacrificer builds and becomes an immortal self.

The twice-daily milk offering into the sacred fires by one who has set them up; the Brāhmaṇas explain it as healing the junction of day and night (ŚB 1.6.3.36), as an offering of 'truth in faith' when nothing else exists (ŚB 11.3.1.4), and as a cycle through the worlds and the body (ŚB 11.6.2).
Interiorized as the offering into the breaths at meals (ChU 5.19–24) and as the continuous 'inner Agnihotra' of speech and breath (KU 2.5).
Offerings into the consecrated fire in a kuṇḍa, part of daily and occasional worship.
The formless (amūrta) worship of Viṣṇu through fire offerings.
The supreme vehicle for which the Vajracchedikā is taught, not hearable by those of low resolve.
Devotion without motive and without interruption to the Supreme Person, flowing to him like the Gaṅgā to the sea (Kapila); also 'animittā'.
Devotion without any motive of gain, which does not even seek liberation.

equivalents.note: both name the highest, desireless devotion beyond the guṇa-graded forms; the Kapila Gītā's devotee refuses oneness, whereas the Devī Gītā's supreme devotion ends in non-dual knowledge

definitions.definition: The 'I': the fusion of the first letter 'a' and the last 'ha', the union of Śiva and Śakti that holds the universe (KKV 5).
The supreme 'I', spanning the letters from A (Śiva) to HA (Śakti) joined by the bindu (PTV).
The self as what the word and awareness 'I' refer to; not the ego-evolute of prakṛti but the soul itself, which persists as 'I' in deep sleep and liberation.
'I am Brahman' (BĀU 1.4.10): the realization sentence (anubhava-vākya), mahāvākya of the Yajurveda and of Śṛṅgeri.

The evolute of mahat whose nature is self-assertion (abhimāna); from it proceed the eleven organs (from its vaikṛta, sāttvika form) and the five subtle elements (from its bhūtādi, tāmasa form), both with its taijasa form (SK 24–25). It, not puruṣa, is the agent (SS 6.54).

Ego, one of the eight constituents of the lower nature (BhG 7.4); the deluded by ego think 'I am the doer' (3.27); free of 'mine' and ego one attains peace (2.71); in the Nārāyaṇīya, Aniruddha is called ahaṃkāra (12.327.26).

The I-maker: the 'teaching of I' (ahaṃkārādeśa) precedes the teaching of the self (ChU 7.25.1); listed among the faculties resting in the self (PrU 4.8); the jīva is endowed with intention and ahaṃkāra (ŚU 5.8).
The notion 'I' and 'mine', at whose arising the mind is to go to the supportless (VBT 131); in the Krama it is dissolved in the phases of Kālāgnirudra and Mahākāla (TĀ 4.161-168).

cross_language.note: also renders asmimāna; as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Meditation on the object as oneself ('I am Brahman'), as opposed to symbol-meditation (BS 4.1.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sense of 'I' by which one whose self is deluded thinks 'I am the doer', though actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); the one who attains peace is without it (nirahaṃkāra, 2.71).
The ego, the I-maker: the inner organ as appropriating ('I', 'mine'), the knot of superimposition of consciousness and the insentient.
The false notion of 'I' regarding body and the like, which ceases through knowledge of the truth about the causes of the faults (NS 4.2.1) and through contemplation of the body within (NBh 4.2.2).
An evolute of prakṛti; distinct from the true 'I' (aham-artha), which is the self; the false identification of body as self is the obstacle.

notes: Not the Sāṃkhya evolute; here a mistaken cognition.

definitions.definition: The making of 'I' and 'mine' and the underlying tendency to conceit, absent in the liberated one (AN 3.33).

equivalents.note: same word ahaṃkāra; in Sāṃkhya a cosmic evolute, here the mental act of I-making

definitions.definition: The first support of life; wholesome food alone makes the person grow and unwholesome food causes disease (Ca Sū 25.31); its rule has eight factors (Vi 1.21); food is the root of living beings, of strength, complexion and ojas (Su Sū 1.28).
Food, which is threefold by the guṇas: life-giving, savoury and wholesome for the sāttvic; bitter, sour and burning for the rājasic; stale and impure for the tāmasic (BhG 17.7–10).

The four nutriments that maintain beings: edible food, contact, mental volition and consciousness (MN 9; SN 12.63); also the conditions that feed or starve the hindrances and awakening factors (SN 46.51).
Purity of food (or of what is taken in): from it purity of mind, firm memory and the loosening of all knots (ChU 7.26.2).
A subtle auspicious body projected by an advanced ascetic in the sixth stage to consult an omniscient (TS 2.36, 2.49).
The count of civil days elapsed from an epoch (the start of the kalpa or of the Kali age), from which mean positions are computed.
Struck sound, produced by contact (voice, instrument); in music the means that delights people and breaks worldly bondage (ŚR 1.2.3, 1.2.167).
The eastern fire into which oblations are offered.
Consciousness without any of the six roots: the eighteen rootless types.
(As reported) That beings are defiled and purified without cause or condition; ascribed to Makkhali (DN 2) and to Pūraṇa (SN 22.60, SN 46.56).
One of the three sectarian tenets that end in inaction.
Not injuring any being in any way at any time; the root of the other restraints and observances (YBh 2.30); when established, hostility is abandoned in one's presence (2.35).

Non-violence, 'the highest dharma for all beings that breathe' (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116); a mark of knowledge (BhG 13.7) and of the divine endowment (16.2); the eternal dharma taught by Tulādhāra (12.253–256); yet the meat-seller teaches that no one lives without some harm (3.199).
The ekāntins are non-violent; worship without animal slaughter (MBh 12.336.58; 12.323–324).
Non-injury, first of the common duties of all classes (MDh 10.63; YS 1.122; Arthaśāstra 1.3.13); the Veda-prescribed injury is declared to be non-injury (MDh 5.44).

The first and chief vow: not severing the vitalities of any being through careless (passion-driven) activity (TS 7.13); inwardly, the non-arising of attachment and other passions (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 44); called the supreme Brahman (Svayambhūstotra).
Violence is prohibited; hence the Śyena rite, whose aim is violence, is harmful (anartha) though the Veda states it as a means for one who wishes to harm (Śabara on MS 1.1.2).
Tamil kollāmai: the Siddhar poets condemn killing and flesh-eating (Paṭṭiṉattār; Pattirakiriyār 14; Kaṭuveḷi 25, 29).
Strict non-harming, down to the smallest creature, required of the renunciant.

cross_language.note: first Jain vow

definitions.definition: Lack of moral shame; one of the four universal unwholesome factors.
The two qualities seen means lack (SK 1) and final isolation has (SK 68): certain (invariable) and final (without recurrence).
The doctrine that the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā (on ritual) and the Uttara Mīmāṃsā (on Brahman), with the Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa, form one continuous science.
The sixth sthala: free of longing for the droplets of sense-pleasure, pure of intent, immersed in the ocean of Śiva's bliss (SSM 14.2; 14.4); in common usage also the devotee's death (liṅgaikya).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) giving non-obstruction (SK 45); the commentaries list eight powers — becoming minute (aṇimā), great, light, reaching, irresistible will, lordship, control and going wherever one wishes. In Sāṃkhya these powers are aiśvarya, not 'siddhi'; attachment to them is the error called moha.

The eight lordly powers — minuteness, lightness, greatness, reach, irresistible will, control, lordship, and settling things at will (YBh 3.45); Īśvara's lordship, which has no equal or superior (YBh 1.24).
Proposed as a means of knowledge; not different from verbal testimony (NS 2.2.2).
'The five' — the senses, pictured as a band of thieves or tormentors that must be put under guard.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self: unborn, eternal, everlasting, primeval (2.20); knowing it as unborn one sees that it neither slays nor is slain (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Said by Kṛṣṇa of himself: though unborn and of imperishable self, and lord of beings, he comes into being through his own māyā (4.6).
The unborn (she-goat): one unborn female, red, white and black, producing many like herself, and two unborn males who enjoy and leave her (ŚU 4.5; cf. 1.9).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

literal: the unborn part (or: the goat as portion)

definitions.definition: What Agni is asked to heat and carry to the world of the well-doers at cremation (RV 10.16.4); read either as the dead man's unborn part or as the goat offered as Agni's portion.
The python's way of living: accepting whatever food comes unsought, lying still if none comes.
Living like a python on whatever comes unsought, without striving (MBh 12.172).
Non-exclusive implication, which retains the direct meaning and adds to it ('the red runs' = the red horse); rejected for 'tat tvam asi'.
The 'unrepeated' repetition — the haṃsa mantra made by the breath itself (Yogaviṣaya 28–29; KJN 13.2).
The mantra 'recited' by the breath without effort (ajapā-gāyatrī).
The spontaneous japa of the breath, 21,600 per day and night, the Goddess's japa (VBT 156).
'Unrepeated repetition': the Name going on by itself with the breath, without tongue or beads (Dādū, Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants).
Unageing and deathless — the Nāth ideal of the perfected yogī (GŚ 56 'ajarāmara').
'There is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned'; were there not, no escape from the born would be known (Ud 8.3; Iti 43).
The doctrine of non-origination: nothing whatever is ever born; creation-teachings are only means; the highest truth of Gauḍapāda.
Livelihood; its purity is the third purity of virtue, violated by scheming, talking, hinting, belittling and seeking gain with gain.
Everything without consciousness: matter, the media of motion and rest, space and time (TS 5.1–3, 5.39).

literal: one who lives (by a rule of) livelihood

definitions.definition: A member of the naked ascetic order of Gosāla and his predecessors; the name appears in the Pali and Jain canons, the Arthaśāstra, Aśoka's edicts and inscriptions, and Tamil works.

notes: The etymology 'one who follows his profession / keeps the livelihood rule' is debated; Buddhist texts pun on ājīva (livelihood).

definitions.definition: The two-petalled centre between the brows, of mind, with the praṇava (ṢCN); HYP 4.48 calls the place between the brows the place of Śiva.
The centre in the head, between the brows.
The power of command that comes from firm contemplation (PKS 1.13).
Contemplating reality as taught by the Jina (TS 9.36).
The tāmasa opposite of knowledge (SK 23); from it (viparyaya) comes bondage (SK 44).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Ignorance, which covers knowledge and so deludes creatures (5.15); destroyed by knowledge of the self, after which knowledge illumines the highest (5.16); the source of the doubt lodged in the heart (4.42); the ignorant one (ajña) perishes (4.40).
Ignorance, synonym of avidyā: 'something positive, indescribable as being or non-being, made of the three guṇas, opposed to knowledge' (Vedāntasāra).
Not the absence of knowledge but incomplete manifestation of the knowable (TĀ 1.25-26); twofold, in the intellect and in the person, the latter the root of saṃsāra (Tantrasāra 1).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A stage of ignorance; seven are taught: seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep, each branching a hundredfold.
(Jain report) The fourth 'assembly': 67 kinds; its adherents hold ignorance better than knowledge — 'who knows whether the soul exists, and what use is knowing it?'.
The ignorant cannot settle their inquiry in ignorance or instruct others.
Death before the exhaustion of life's measure through wrong conduct, as an axle breaks midway (Ca Vi 3.38; Śā 6.28).
The 'interior' genre of Tamil poetry — love in union and separation, with landscapes and conventional voices (heroine, mother, friend); the Āḻvārs use it to voice the soul's love for the Lord.
The mutual need of the parts of a sentence, which makes them one sentence (MS 2.1.46).
A word's inability to produce a connected cognition without another word (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The first letter, in which the whole perfection of wisdom is contained (Ekākṣarī PP).
(Jain report) That the self neither acts nor causes action.
The letter 'a', ground and root of all letters and of all things; in the Tirumūla ñāṉam the Supreme itself (taṟparam).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Inaction: one should not be attached to it (2.47); action is better than inaction, and without action even the body cannot be maintained (3.8).
Inaction, which the wise see in action and whose presence in inaction they also see (BhG 4.18); attachment to inaction is forbidden (2.47).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of the three things to be understood along with action (karma) and vikarma (4.17); even sages are bewildered about it (4.16); the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction (4.18); the unattached one 'does nothing at all' though engaged in action (4.20).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The Gītā returns to action and inaction at 4.16–18 (outside this chunk).

definitions.definition: Puruṣa is non-agent (SK 19); agency belongs to the guṇas and puruṣa only appears as agent (SK 20); ahaṃkāra is the agent (SS 6.54).
One, all-pervading, eternal substance whose quality is sound.

Space: the final support from which all beings arise and into which they return (ChU 1.9.1); the accomplisher of name and form (ChU 8.14.1); the first element to arise from the self (TU 2.1); the space within the heart (ChU 8.1.3); 'kha' is brahman (ChU 4.10.4; BAU 5.1.1).
The substance that gives room to all others; divided into world-space (lokākāśa), where the other substances are, and infinite empty non-world space (alokākāśa) (TS 5.9, 5.12, 5.18).
Space as an unconditioned dharma, whose nature is non-obstruction; distinct from the space-element (a cavity), which is conditioned matter.
Mere absence of tangible resistance.
The first formless attainment, reached by passing beyond perceptions of form (MN 121; MN 111).

literal: mode in the form of the undivided

definitions.definition: The mental mode in the form of the partless Brahman arising from the mahāvākya; it destroys ignorance and then subsides, like a clearing-nut in water.
Partless meaning: a sentence that conveys a single non-relational entity, as the mahāvākya conveys the one self.
The Bāul hermitage or gathering place of a guru and disciples, where songs are sung and practice taught (e.g. Lalon's ākhṛā at Cheuṛiyā).

cross_language.note: among North Indian ascetics the word names an armed order or its seat

definitions.definition: The verb, whose chief meaning is becoming (bhāva) as a sequence (Nirukta 1.1).
Error is not the appearance of an unreal object but the non-apprehension of the difference between a perception ('this') and a memory ('silver'); ignorance itself is non-apprehension.
The third formless attainment, taught to the bodhisatta by Āḷāra Kālāma (MN 26); Upasīva is told to cross the flood relying on nothingness (Snp 5.7).
Destitution of any means of one's own — no ritual merit, self-knowledge or devotion — the qualification for surrender.
Having nothing: 'your servant with no other refuge' (TVM 6.10.10); the girls 'a clan without knowledge' (TP 28); 'I have nothing' (Tirumālai 25).
The ninth virtue: the attitude 'nothing is mine' (TS 9.6).
(As reported) Pūraṇa's doctrine that the doer does no evil and the giver gains no merit.
One of the four 'assemblies' of disputants: those who deny action; 84 kinds; they hold the world barren and fixed.

notes: The Pali and Jain uses overlap but are not identical: the Jain class is wider (it includes denial of the categories of soul etc.).

definitions.definition: Said of activities that have discernment as their object and oppose the operation of the guṇas (YBh 1.5).

literal: receiving (the fruit of) what was not done

definitions.definition: The absurdity of reaping results of acts one did not do — used to refute rival accounts of embodiment and of the agent (NS 3.2.38, 3.2.72 DCS).
The universal, which is what a word means, because Vedic action is directed to it (MS 1.3.33).
What is called the mark of the universal (NS 2.2.70 DCS).
Form, universal: Vājapyāyana held that words denote the ākṛti (Mahābhāṣya on P 1.2.64).
Rosary into whose beads the fifty letters a–kṣa are invoked.
The rosary for counting japa; also the 'garland of letters' a to kṣa (akṣa-mālā) with which mental japa is counted.
Lakṣmī, whose body is imperishable; beyond her is Hari (Puruṣottama).

The imperishable: that on which space is woven, described by negations (BAU 3.8.8), by whose command sun and moon stand apart (3.8.9); the object of the higher knowledge (MuU 1.1.5); also 'syllable', especially Om (ChU 1.1.1; KU 1.2.16; MāU 1).
The syllable in the highest heaven on which the verses rest and the gods sit (RV 1.164.39); the thousand-syllabled cow of speech (1.164.41).

The imperishable supreme Brahman (BhG 8.3), the goal entered by ascetics (8.11); the unchanging (kūṭastha) imperishable puruṣa (15.16), surpassed by the highest person (15.18); also the syllable (Oṃ, 'the one syllable', 8.13, 10.25).
A syllable or phoneme (akṣarasamāmnāya, the list of phonemes, PŚ 57).
The imperishable syllable Oṃ, which is Brahman and Prajāpati, while all rites pass away (MDh 2.84).
The imperishable Word-Brahman (VP 1.1) and the syllable/letter.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.15 the imperishable from which brahman arises (in the chain: action from brahman, brahman from the imperishable); its identification is disputed among commentators.
The imperishable Brahman, Puruṣottama's abode and 'feet', the goal of knowers; lower than Puruṣottama.
Śiva (in contrast with kula, Śakti); the Goddess is 'akulā', beyond kula (LSN 37).
What is beyond the Kula, Śiva's own abode, where Bhairava abides at the end of aeons (KJN 16.41); the nectar is 'beyond Akula and Kula' (14.97).
Śiva, beyond the totality of powers (Kulārṇava 17.27).
Śiva as beyond the kula; the Akula abode into which full consciousness finally dissolves (TĀ 4.170).
'The hero beyond the Kula': the single reality beyond all distinctions, the same in all, in which all dharmas dissolve (Akulavīra A.3–41).

equivalents.note: the Akulavīra is the Akula as realised 'hero'; the text does not itself equate the words

definitions.definition: Unwholesome: consciousness rooted in greed, hatred or delusion, blameworthy and producing painful results; twelve types.
Class of mental factors (two): shamelessness, lack of dread of blame.
Taking no interest (seeking no gain) even in the highest reflection (4.29, YBh 4.29).
Failure to attain a stage of samādhi (YBh 1.30).
The 'unmarked, invisible' — a Nāth name for the supreme, called out in the begging cry 'alakh!' and joined with nirañjan ('alakh nirañjan').
'The unseen, unmarked' — a name of the ultimate shared with Nāth usage ('alakh nirañjan'); in Sant Mat, Alakh Lok is a region above Sach Khand.

equivalents.note: joined as one epithet in the Nāth cry 'alakh nirañjan'

definitions.definition: The support or object on which the mind rests (1.10, 1.38); samādhis with a support are samprajñāta (YBh 1.17).
In the Yogaviṃśikā the fourth yoga: meditation with an external support such as the Jina's image.
Figure of speech ('ornament') of sound or sense; for Bhāmaha and Daṇḍin the essence of poetic beauty, for Ānandavardhana subordinate to rasa.
Laziness: inactivity from heaviness of body and mind (YBh 1.30).

Perception through an extraordinary contact: through the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇā — grasping all smoke via smoke-hood, which grounds pervasion), through a prior cognition (jñānalakṣaṇā — e.g. 'fragrant sandal' seen), and yogic (yogaja).
Supernatural capacity to relish the Lord's bliss, the highest fruit of service.
The consciousness that holds all seeds and the body, from which the other consciousnesses arise like waves from the ocean; in the Laṅkāvatāra identified with the tathāgatagarbha.

cross_language.form: kun gzhi rnam par shes pa
alaiye shi 阿賴耶識 / zangshi 藏識

definitions.definition: The fourth level: the unmanifest pradhāna, subtlest of objects, beyond which nothing is subtler (1.45, 2.19).
The pitta in the eye that makes sight possible (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.14).
The function of the sense capacities: mere awareness of sound and the rest (SK 28).
The initial non-conceptual awareness (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
Disclosing one's faults to the teacher without concealment (TS 9.22).
Infinite empty space beyond the universe, into which nothing can move since the medium of motion is absent (TS 10.8).
Title of the twelve Tamil saint-poets of Viṣṇu: 'one who is immersed' — sunk deep in the Lord's qualities.

notes: Tradition's etymology from āḻ- 'to be immersed'; some modern scholars derive it from āḷvār 'rulers' — recorded as a scholarly alternative only.

definitions.definition: The first tissue (rasa) left uncooked through weakness of the fire, vitiated and lodged in the stomach, is called āma (AHS Sū 13.25); it obstructs the channels and is the ground of many diseases.

notes: AHS Sū 13.25 checked in the DCS e-text; no teaching entry written for it.

definitions.definition: Tamil name for Jain monks (from śramaṇa), common in Tamil literature and in the hymns of the Nāyaṉmārs who opposed them.
The mindless state, a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the name and goal of the Amanaska's rājayoga, attained effortlessly by the guru's grace (Amanaska 2).
The later (uttara) tāraka, in which the mind is like an udder after milking.
The superhuman being who, at the lightning, leads the soul to Brahman.
The state of no-mind: when, through knowing the truth of the self, the mind ceases to imagine, grasping nothing (GK 3.32).
The reckoning of the lunar month as ending at new moon (usual in the south and west).
Immortality, a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.3), and the conquest of death sought through retaining bindu and nectar.
Deathlessness: a synonym of the highest state (HYP 4.3); in the Kaula texts attained by devotion to guru and yoginīs and by the nectar meditations (KJN 5.33).
The essence flowing from the moon when the tongue enters the palate, called 'liquor' in HYP 3.47–49.
(As reported) Evasion by refusing every alternative; the fourth ground (dullness) is Sañjaya's formula.
A wrong view arising from fear of false speech, of grasping or of cross-examination, or from dullness.

equivalents.note: the Pali eel-wrigglers and the Jain annāṇiyas both refuse to affirm; the Jain class (67 kinds) is wider

definitions.definition: A variant of vajrolī reported by the HYP as practised by the Kāpālikas of the Khaṇḍa school (3.96). RESTRICTED: summary only.
A variant of vajrolī named in the haṭha texts associated with the Nāths; restricted, not described.
An epithet of nibbāna: the doors to the deathless are open (MN 26); heedfulness is the path to the deathless (Dhp 21); mindfulness of death merges in the deathless (AN 6.19).
Epithet of nibbāna: where there is no death.
The Mother: the Goddess addressed as mother of all; Lalitā as Śrīmātā (LSN 1) and Lalitāmbikā (LSN 183).

The three days in the month of Āṣāḍha (June) when the Earth — and at Kāmākhyā the Goddess — is held to menstruate; the Kāmākhyā temple is closed and reopens on the fourth day (the Ambubachi Melā). The Prāṇatoṣiṇī lists 'ambuvācī, three days' in its festival calendar.
Distress or anxiety, from which Rudra and the gods are asked to set one free (RV 2.33.2).
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
A 'transmission' of teaching; Paramaśiva taught five āmnāyas through his five faces (PKS 1.2); the four doors of the Goddess's palace are the four āmnāyas (PKS 3.10).
A Kaula transmission: five from Śiva's five faces — Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern and Upper (Kulārṇava 3.7); the Upper is supreme (3.15-19).
The Paścimāmnāya is the Kubjikā transmission, 'the western of all paths' (Kubjikāmata 2.21).
Its authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).
One of the four cardinal monasteries founded, in the tradition's account, by Śaṅkara, each tied to a Veda, a mahāvākya and a group of Daśanāmī names.
Immortality and the immortal: of the gods, of the fathers' world, of soma; 'may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12).

The nectar of immortality dripping from the moon in the head, lost to the sun's fire unless saved by viparītakaraṇī, jālandhara and khecarī (HYP 3.72, 3.77–79; DYŚ 127–128); drinking it the yogin conquers death.
The nectar of immortality flowing from the moon at the head; retaining it the body does not decay (GŚ 57–66).
The nectar without which there is no immortality; 'the Kaula nature, of the nature of kāmakalā' (KJN 14.94).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The remainder of the sacrifice is called amṛta; those who eat it go to the eternal Brahman (4.31).
Tamil amirtam: the nectar of immortality; for the Siddhars the inner nectar that knowers drink (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 10) and that flows from the moon in the head.
The nectar that rains in the sky-circle of the head in the encounter with the Lord; also the guru as 'mine of nectar'.

cross_language.note: nectar in Vajrayāna usage

equivalents.note: The Saṃhitās' immortality is chiefly full life and the immortal world of light; the Upaniṣads and Vedānta distinguish mokṣa from heavenly immortality. Recorded as contested.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: 'Of the nature of nectar/immortality': the second mark of devotion (NBS 3); gaining it one becomes immortal (NBS 4).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The goal for which the steadfast person, unmoved by the contacts of the senses and the same in pleasure and pain, is fit (2.15).

Immortality: the goal named by the early Upaniṣads — 'there is no hope of immortality through wealth' (BAU 2.4.2); 'so much is immortality' (4.5.15); 'the mortal becomes immortal' (4.4.7; KU 2.3.14); 'lead me from death to immortality' (BAU 1.3.28).

cross_language.note: Buddhist epithet of nibbāna

equivalents.note: the early texts' 'immortality' is what the later texts (ŚU 6.16, MaiU 6.20) call mokṣa; the early texts do not themselves equate the two words

definitions.definition: The rite of turning the offering-water into nectar, done with the dhenu gesture.
The eternal portion of the Lord that becomes the living being (BhG 15.7); the fragment of his splendour from which every glory springs (10.41–42).
The soul as a part of Brahman made distinct by adjuncts.
The soul as a naturally distinct part (power) of the Lord.
The soul as a spark-like part of Brahman in which bliss is concealed.
The soul as a separated part (vibhinnāṃśa), distinct from the Lord's own expansions (svāṃśa).

notes: Read as a real part or as an apparent part according to school (see dsp:souls-one-or-distinct).

definitions.definition: A term of the Tirumantiram's 'amuri tāraṇai' section, read in the Siddha tradition as a bodily 'nectar' used in rejuvenation; recorded as a term only.

notes: Restricted subject (bodily-substance practice): summary only; interpretation low confidence.

definitions.definition: Worship of Viṣṇu through fire offerings, without an image.
The vowelless (and consonantless, ahala) sound meditated while closing ears and lower door (VBT 114); used in cutting the flows of breath (Kṣemarāja on PH 18).
The novelty required of a means of knowledge: it apprehends what was not apprehended before (Śāstradīpikā).
A form of non-knowledge — cognition that fails to determine its object ('what is this?') (Praśastapāda).
Days and circumstances (storms, deaths, festivals, the moon's days) on which Vedic recitation is suspended (MDh 4.101–127).
'Free from beginningless time': Śiva, never bound, distinguished from liberated souls who were once bound.
One who has abandoned the five lower fetters and is reborn spontaneously in the pure abodes, attaining nibbāna there without returning (MN 64; MN 10).
Non-returner: one who has abandoned all nine grades; reaches nirvāṇa in the intermediate state, on arising, with or without effort, or going upward.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Freed from offence 'before Aditi', the state asked of Varuṇa when his fetters are loosened (RV 1.24.15).
The state of the soul in transit for one to three instants, when it takes in no matter to build a body (TS 2.30).
The heart centre, twelve-petalled, of air (YAṂ), where the unstruck sound is heard (ṢCN; GŚ 60).
The unstruck sound heard within; also the heart centre.
The unstruck, unbroken inner sound, the Sound-Brahman (VBT 38).
The unstruck sound (anhad nād, anhad bājā) heard within in the encounter with the Lord; a Nāth-derived image used by Kabīr and Dādū.
The inner sound heard in meditation, distinguished into the sounds of the successive regions.

notes: In haṭha sources anāhata is also the heart-cakra; here the unstruck sound.

definitions.definition: The sound not produced by striking, heard within when the knot of Brahmā is pierced (HYP 4.70); within its resonance is the knowable and within that the mind, which dissolves there (4.100).
Unstruck sound, worshipped by sages by the path taught by the guru — an easy means to liberation, but without charm (rakti) for ordinary people (ŚR 1.2.165–166).
The unstruck inner sound heard in the heart and the sky of the head; the 'bull bound threefold roars' at anāhata (GŚ 60); in Hindi 'anahad nād'.
The tāmasa opposite of power (SK 23), bringing obstruction (SK 45).
The essence of bondage for Kauṇḍinya: the soul's lack of lordship, the obstruction of its powers; also listed by him as the fifth impurity.
The nameless phase beyond emission, persistence and withdrawal in the Krama sequence.
The fifth yoga of the Yogaviṃśikā: meditation on the formless Siddha, leading to omniscience.
The 'nameless', the highest region and the supreme being beyond all names, which Radhasoami calls Radhasoami Dhām.
Joy (hlāda), the third level of samprajñāta samādhi (1.17, YBh 1.17); Vijñānabhikṣu: a joy arising from preponderant sattva; Bhoja: bliss when the inner organ's sattva is cultivated.
Bliss produced by soma (RV 9.113.6) and dwelling in the immortal world (9.113.11).
Bliss: the nature of Brahman, not a quality it has; worldly joys are fragments of it, manifest in deep sleep as unobstructed bliss.

Bliss: brahman is bliss (TU 3.6); the self made of bliss (TU 2.5); brahman is understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); the highest bliss of the brahma-world on a fraction of which others live (BAU 4.3.32); measured in the calculus of bliss (TU 2.8; BAU 4.3.33).
The form of Brahman residing in the body; the bliss of the union of Śakti and Śiva is liberation (Kulārṇava 5.79-80).
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the śaraṇa stage. In the SSM the śaraṇa is one possessed of the bliss of union with Śiva (13.2).
Bliss as the power of the Lord and as the relish of consciousness in pleasure, reunion, taste and song (VBT 65-74); seven grades in the contemplation of the breath (TĀ 5.43-52).
The dance of bliss of Naṭarāja at Chidambaram, enacting the five acts.
The gradation of the bliss enjoyed by the liberated, each class a hundredfold above the one below.
Made of bliss: the innermost of the five selves, whose tail and foundation is brahman (TU 2.5).
The sheath of bliss: ignorance (the causal body) with its joys experienced in deep sleep and in pleasure; for Śaṅkara a sheath, not Brahman (BSBh 1.1.19).
The ending of the initiatory name given to a Śrīvidyā initiate (PKS 1.40), as in Bhāsurānandanātha (Bhāskararāya).
The soul's four infinite qualities manifest on destruction of the obscuring karmas: infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy.
The most intense grade of the passions, which obstructs right view and binds to endless rebirth (TS 8.9).
The five deadly acts ripening immediately (in the next life) in hell: killing mother, father or an arhat, dividing the Saṅgha, wounding a Buddha.
Devotion directed to nothing else, by which the supreme person is won (BhG 8.22), the Lord seen in truth (11.54) and gain and security borne (9.22).
Exclusive devotion: the unwavering understanding 'I am the servant, the Lord is the master in the form of all'.
Seeking nothing from the Lord but the Lord himself and his service.
Having no other refuge or goal than the Lord; with ākiñcanya the qualification for surrender.
The soul's being fit to belong to the Lord alone, not to itself nor to any other being; taught in the praṇava of the tirumantra.
Single-mindedness: giving up all other supports (NBS 9–10).

equivalents.note: the Gītā's undivided devotion (BhG 11.54)

definitions.definition: Mindfulness of in- and out-breathing in sixteen steps, which fulfils the four establishments of mindfulness, the seven factors of awakening, and true knowledge and liberation (MN 118; SN 54.1).
Mindfulness of in- and out-breathing in sixteen bases, worked by counting, following, contact, fixing and the later stages; leads to all four jhānas and, with insight, to arahantship.
The complete practice in four tetrads covering all four foundations of mindfulness (Buddhadāsa).
Awareness of natural respiration at the entrance of the nostrils, the first days of a course.
Mindfulness of breathing, entry to cultivation for those dominated by discursive thought; it is wisdom, with wind as object, in six phases (counting etc.).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: An unwanted thing obstructing devotion; of four kinds by origin (sin, pious acts, offences, devotion itself).
Cessation of unwanted things (anartha) — the fourth stage.
Avoiding harmful acts without purpose — evil counsel, careless acts, giving weapons, harmful thoughts and entertainments (TS 7.21).
Abstaining from food for a fixed period or, at life's end, until death (TS 9.19).
The mind born of meditation, which lays down no karmic residue (4.6, YBh 4.6).
Without outflows: the truth of the path and the three unconditioned dharmas.

What is not a self nor belonging to a self: each aggregate is not-self, since it leads to affliction and cannot be commanded (SN 22.59); 'all phenomena (sabbe dhammā) are not-self' (AN 3.136; Dhp 279); seeing 'this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self' (MN 22).
Not-self: no dhamma, conditioned or unconditioned, is a self; there is suffering but no sufferer.

equivalents.note: same word; the Buddhist Sanskrit form

definitions.definition: The impurity of individuality: loss of freedom by awareness, or awareness without freedom (ĪPK 3.2.4); 'limited knowledge is bondage' (Śiva Sūtra 1.2).
The impurity by whose contact the self, resting in the inner organ, has become atomic (aṇu) (SSM 18.5–7).
The innate (sahaja) impurity of the soul, one in substance with countless powers, beginningless, covering its powers of knowing and acting; it ripens and is removed by Śiva's power in initiation.
Āṇavam, the 'dark mala' (iruḷ mala) which hides even itself; never destroyed, only rendered powerless by grace.

notes: Same name as in the Śaiva Siddhānta, where the impurity is held to be a real substance.

definitions.definition: The mind's not being established in a stage it has gained (YBh 1.30).
The individual means: breath, bodily seals, visualization, letters and places (MVT 2.21; TĀ 5).
Macrocosm and microcosm: the Siddhar principle that what is in the cosmic egg is in the body and what is in the body is in the cosmos.
The eternal state of sorrow without return reached by the souls fit for darkness, especially through hatred of Hari and his devotees.
The fifth error, eighteenfold: the despair of one who dies amid, or falls from, the powers and objects (SK 48; Gauḍapāda; Kramadīpikā).
The doctrine of many jīvas, each with its own ignorance or inner organ, so that one is liberated while others remain bound (Bhāmatī and most Advaitins).
The doctrine that reality has infinite aspects (e.g. permanent as substance, impermanent as modes), so that every statement is true only in some respect (TS 5.30–32; Āptamīmāṃsā).
Imperturbability, said of the fourth jhāna and formless attainments.

The soul or devotee in relation to the liṅga: knowledge is the aṅga and the eternal knowable the liṅga, and the aṅgaliṅgī has the liṅga mounted on the aṅga and the aṅga present in the liṅga (SSM 12.42–44); the jīva is a part of Śiva through beginningless ignorance (5.34–36).
'Limb' or topic: a chapter of a Sant anthology gathering sākhīs on one theme (gurudev kau aṅg, birah kau aṅg …).
A subsidiary element of a principal rite (pradhāna), e.g. the prayājas of the new- and full-moon rites.
One of the twelve 'limbs' of the canon (dvādaśāṅga, the 'basket of the gaṇin') composed by the gaṇadharas; eleven survive for the Śvetāmbaras, the twelfth (Dṛṣṭivāda) is lost.

cross_language.note: the twelve limbs as a whole

notes: Disambiguated from other senses of 'aṅga' (limb of yoga; Vīraśaiva devotee).

definitions.definition: What shakes the limbs, an accompaniment of distraction (YBh 1.31); steady posture prevents it (YBh 2.47).

The Nandī's twofold division of scripture: what 'enters the limbs' (the twelve Aṅgas, composed by the gaṇadharas) and what is 'outside the limbs' (composed by later elders); the latter is further divided into kālika (read at set times) and utkālika (read at any time).
The Aṅgirases, ancient priestly clan; with the Atharvans the Atharvaveda is 'Atharvāṅgirasaḥ'.
The subtle being, the size of a thumb, drawn out of the body at death by Yama's messengers.
The person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the middle of the body or the heart, lord of past and future (KU 2.1.12-13, 2.3.17; ŚU 3.13, 5.8).
Arising and passing away; the first mark of all formations (AN 3.136); from the impermanence of the aggregates follows their being suffering and not fit to be taken as self (SN 22.59).
Impermanence, the first characteristic; in insight, seen as the rise and fall of formations.
Experienced directly as the arising and passing of sensations throughout the body (U Ba Khin: 'anicca' as the key).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: The signless concentration and liberation of mind, empty of the 'makers of signs' lust, hatred and delusion (MN 43; MN 121).
Signless: the gateway of liberation through contemplation of impermanence; an aspect of nibbāna.
The fourth form, from whom Brahmā arises; called the great self and ahaṃkāra (MBh 12.326.69; 12.327.26).
The vyūha manifesting power and splendour; in Śaṅkara's report, identified with ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The fifth of the five forms of Viṣṇu invoked in Vaikhānasa worship.

equivalents.note: the Nārāyaṇīya calls Aniruddha ahaṃkāra

definitions.definition: The Advaita category of what is neither real nor unreal; for Dvaita it is established by no means of knowledge and taught by no scripture.
Indescribable: not determinable as real (since sublated) nor as unreal (since it appears); the status of māyā, avidyā and their products.
The Advaita theory of error: the illusory object (shell-silver) is neither real nor unreal but indescribable, produced for the moment by ignorance.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The contacts of the senses with their objects, giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go and are impermanent; they are to be endured (2.14).
The ninth guṇasthāna, where gross passions are subsided or destroyed.
The third process, after which right view arises (granthi-bheda).
The two 'undetermined' offences, judged by the testimony of a trustworthy laywoman.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The signature name for the Lord that closes a vacanakāra's vacanas — Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva (Basava), Guhēśvara (Allama), Cennamallikārjuna (Akka), Rāmanātha (Dāsimayya) — usually received from the guru.
Śaṅkaradeva's genre of one-act devotional plays in Brajabuli, performed as bhāonā.
The soul (also uyir, 'life'): the player of the body's play; when it leaves, the body withers (Kaṭuveḷi 21).

equivalents.note: Tamil form of ātman

definitions.definition: Final knowledge (arahantship) in this life, one of the two fruits of satipaṭṭhāna (MN 10).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In the cycle of 3.14: beings come from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice.
Food: brahman is food (TU 3.2); the person is made of the essence of food (TU 2.1); vows about food (TU 3.7-10); mind is made of food (ChU 6.5.4, 6.7); 'I am food' sings the knower (TU 3.10.6).
Made of (the essence of) food: the outermost self, the person formed from food (TU 2.1).
The sheath made of food: the gross body.
Lack of moral dread; a universal unwholesome factor.
Love for the Lord — the 'lamp-bowl' of Pūtattāḻvār's lamp (IT 1).
Love, which the Siddhars, after TM 270, identify with Civam itself.
Love for Śiva, which is itself Śiva (Tirumantiram 270).
In the Kuṟaḷ (ch. 8), love that makes one belong to others; without it the body is bone wrapped in skin.

equivalents.note: aṉpu is love in general as well as devotion

definitions.definition: Non-cruelty, named the highest dharma by Yudhiṣṭhira to the Yakṣa (MBh 3.297.55, 3.297.71) and by the meat-seller (3.203.41); the reason Yudhiṣṭhira will not abandon the dog (17.3.7).
Untruth and violation of ṛta; what Varuṇa's fetters punish (AVŚ 4.16.6); even sleep does not keep it away (RV 7.86.6).
Buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, the threefold internal instrument operating in all three times; the door-keeper, of which the ten external instruments are the doors (SK 33, 35).

The inner organ, one in substance and fourfold in function — mind (manas, doubting), intellect (buddhi, deciding), memory-store (citta) and ego (ahaṅkāra); the adjunct through which consciousness becomes the knower.
Tamil antakkaraṇam: the four inner faculties (maṉam, putti, cittam, akaṅkāram) among the ninety-six principles.
Mind and the rest, which one contemplates as absent in oneself (VBT 94).

literal: the time of the end, the hour of death

definitions.definition: The hour of death, when the state remembered determines where one goes (BhG 8.5–6); being in the brāhmī state even then brings brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).
Four grounds for holding the world finite, infinite, both, or neither.
The inner fire-offering of Pratardana: offering breath into speech while speaking and speech into breath while breathing, continually, waking or asleep (KauU 2.5).
An existence between death and rebirth — rejected by the Theravāda (Kathāvatthu 8.2), which holds that rebirth-linking follows death immediately.
Intermediate existence between death and birth, having the form of the coming existence, seen by its own kind and the divine eye, feeding on smells.
Accepted (Kathāvatthu commentary on Kv 8.2).
Denied (Vasumitra).
Denied (Vasumitra).
Concentration, meditation and samādhi, inner relative to the first five limbs (3.7).
The Lord's internal, essential power, of three aspects (sandhinī, saṃvit, hlādinī), which constitutes his form, abode and associates.
The soul that discerns itself as distinct from the body — from right view onward (Samādhitantra 5).
An obstacle on the path of yoga; the ten of LiP 1.9 and ŚiP 7.2.38; the powers themselves are antarāyas (BhP 11.15.33).
The nine obstacles, distractions of the mind (1.30), removed through devotion to Īśvara (1.29) and practice on a single principle (1.32).
Karma obstructing giving, gain, enjoyment and energy (TS 8.13, 6.27).

notes: Distinct from trm:antaraya (the Yoga Sūtra's 'obstacles').

definitions.definition: The atmosphere between earth and heaven, the middle of the three worlds.
Any interval less than 48 minutes — the maximum span of one meditation (TS 9.27).
Inner worship, in which knower, knowing and known are offerer, fire and oblation (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad; PKS 1.26); the Yoginīhṛdaya's inner worship is held sufficient for those firm in it (Setubandha).
Mental worship of the deity in the heart and body before external worship.
Mental worship (mānasayāga) preceding external worship.

literal: the one who controls from within

definitions.definition: The inner controller: 'he who dwells in the earth yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who controls it from within' — the self, the immortal (BAU 3.7).
The Lord dwelling within every soul and thing as its self and controller, and, in a special form, in the heart of the meditator.
The Lord dwelling within beings, one of his five modes.
The inner controller: Īśvara as the consciousness governing each being from within (BĀU 3.7), the 'starched canvas' of the Citradīpa.

A verse-chain in which the last word or syllable of each verse begins the next, closing the circle at the end; the form of the first three Tiruvantātis, Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti, Periya Tiruvantāti and Tiruvāymoḻi itself.
Remembering the Lord at the moment of death; required of the bhakti-yogin but not of the surrendered, whom the Lord remembers.
The funeral rite — cremation (or burial of infants), bone-collection, water-offerings and the rites of the first year.
Minute, 'smaller than the small': the self in the heart smaller than a grain yet greater than the worlds (ChU 3.14.3; KU 1.2.20; ŚU 3.20).
The soul is atomic in size, dwelling in the heart and pervading the body by its quality of knowledge.
The soul is atomic, a spark of Brahman.
The soul is an infinitesimal particle of consciousness (cit-kaṇa).
(Tamil report) Four kinds of beginningless, indestructible atoms — earth, water, fire, air — which with life (uyir) make the five principles.
The four preliminaries of a teaching text: qualified student, subject, relation and purpose.
The strength of the karma's fruition, depending on the intensity of passion (TS 8.21–22).
Cognition other than memory; valid or invalid (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The outward expressions of emotion: dancing, rolling, singing, crying out, and the like.
Direct experience of the Lord, set against book-learning ('I speak of what I have seen with my eyes'); aṇbhai vāṇī is speech from such experience.

In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prāṇaliṅgi stage. More widely, lived experience of Śiva — the authority the śaraṇas appeal to, which gave the Anubhava Maṇṭapa its name.
Consequent: the outward signs by which an emotion is known — glances, gestures, movements (NŚ 6–7).

notes: Disambiguated from trm:anubhava ('experience'); U16's aesthetic use of trm:anubhava belongs here.

definitions.definition: The assembly at Kalyāṇa where, in the tradition's account, the śaraṇas of every birth and both sexes discussed their experience of Śiva under Allama's presidency.
Cognition other than memory; every experience is a means of knowledge (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Experience/awareness itself, the self as pure self-established consciousness (Iṣṭasiddhi).
One learned in the Veda, who is 'great among us' regardless of age or wealth (MDh 2.154).
The low accent.
The Lord's fifth power/act — grace — called compassion (kṛpā) and śaktipāta; one of Lakṣmī's five acts.
The Lord's favouring of the effect; also the teacher's right favour to qualified disciples, which preserves the tradition and itself leads to the end of suffering.
Grace, the fifth cosmic act, bestowed as Sadāśiva (LSN 64).
The Lord's grace, identical with puṣṭi.
A topic of the Tattvasamāsa (17); in the Kramadīpikā, Brahmā's creation, from the subtle elements, of provision for the beings he had produced.

The substitute prescribed in place of a Kaula substance for those not eligible or in the Kali age — e.g. the 'sweet triad' of milk, sugar and honey for wine (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171), one's own wife only for the last tattva (6.14).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa pumpkin, sugarcane and spirits are 'equal to' an animal victim, and coconut water or honey replace wine for the twice-born (67.23; 67.114-115).
A substitute used in place of a prescribed substance, notably for the five 'M's in the right-hand mode.
Compassion, one of the marks of right faith; the elephant's compassion for the hare won Megha human birth.
Distinguished into worldly (laukika) compassion that preserves bodily life and spiritual (lokottara) compassion that leads beings to restraint; only the second is dharma.
An index of seers, deities, metres and hymns of a Veda (e.g. the Sarvānukramaṇī).
Favourableness: devotion is cultivation of Kṛṣṇa in a way pleasing to him (not as enemies 'think' of him).
The resolve to do only what pleases the Lord; first limb of prapatti.
The last mundane insight, conforming to the eight preceding knowledges and to the requisites of awakening.
Faultless reasoning (upapatti) based on invariable concomitance; includes presumption and comparison.
Threefold inference preceded by knowledge of the mark and the marked (SK 5); by inference from general correlation supersensible things (prakṛti, puruṣa) are known (SK 6).
Inference: an activity that chiefly ascertains the general through a relation present in like and absent from unlike cases (YBh 1.7); it reaches only the general (1.49, YBh 1.25).
Knowledge preceded by perception, of three kinds (NS 1.1.5); resting on perception and scripture it is anvīkṣā (NBh 1.1.1).
Knowledge from a mark (laiṅgika): effect, cause, connected, co-inherent, opposed (VS 9.18); includes verbal knowledge.
The instrument of inferential cognition, i.e. consideration (parāmarśa); for oneself or for others.
Cognition of an unperceived part from seeing another part whose relation is known; of two kinds, by a relation seen directly or by one seen in general (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
(As reported) Not a means of knowledge, since pervasion cannot be established; or (Purandara) valid only as known in worldly life.
In Bāul usage: inference, hearsay and scripture — everything not verifiable in the living body — set aside in favour of bartamān.
The cognition produced by consideration (parāmarśa).
Rejoicing in the merit of all buddhas, bodhisattvas and beings, itself productive of great merit.
The nibbāna-element in which all that is felt, not delighted in, becomes cool (Iti 44).
Another name for the sixth means of knowledge, by which absence is known.
Proposed (as 'abhāva') as a separate means of knowledge; not different from inference (NS 2.2.2); later, absence is perceived through the qualifier-relation contact.
Non-cognition: the means by which absence is known (a jar's absence on the ground), accepted as a separate means following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā.
Not finding or grasping any dharma as an object — the way the bodhisattva courses in the perfection of wisdom; rejoicing and dedication are done 'without apprehension'.
The vehicle (honey, ghee, juice, decoction) with which a medicine is taken.
The 'means-less': realization by the teacher's word alone for the most intensely graced (TĀ 2).
The means that produce valid knowledge: perception, inference and authoritative word (presumption and comparison fall under inference).
