Repeated contemplation of twelve themes — impermanence, no refuge, the round of births, aloneness, otherness, impurity, inflow, stopping, shedding, the universe, rarity of enlightenment, and the well-taught dharma (TS 9.7); also a kind of study (9.25).
Lunar mansion anurādhā: presiding deity Mitra (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Saturn (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class soft (mṛdu) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
Ever-new passion in which the beloved is experienced as ever fresh.

Generating desire and effort to maintain and increase arisen wholesome states (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four right efforts.
Latent tendencies — to sensual lust, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, lust for becoming and ignorance (MN 18); lust underlies pleasant feeling, aversion painful, ignorance neutral (MN 44; MN 148).
Seven latent tendencies lying dormant in the continuum until conditions arouse them.
Latent defilement, the root of existence: six (seven, ten), ninety-eight by realm and mode of abandonment; subtle, adhering, growing and binding; for the Vaibhāṣika identical with the defilement.
The defilement asleep, i.e. a seed-capacity in the series; awake it is an envelopment.
A further ash-bath after impurities such as eating, sneezing, spitting or evacuation, for purity and to show the sign; a secondary rule.

literal: known from what is heard (the Veda)

definitions.definition: The Vedic ritual means, which are like the seen means because impure, perishable and graded (SK 2).
The ten recollections among the forty subjects.
The metre of four eight-syllable lines (the Puruṣa Sūkta's metre), later the śloka.
A Vedic metre of 32 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
That dharmas do not truly arise or cease; what is born from conditions is unborn by own-nature; non-arising, like suchness, neither comes nor goes and is the Tathāgata.
Knowledge of non-arising, possessed by the unshakeable arhat: 'what was to be known is known; it will not be known again'.

The bodhisattva's settled acceptance that dharmas are unborn and selfless, marking irreversibility; in the Daśabhūmika it is attained on the eighth ground; its merit surpasses gifts of jewel-filled worlds.

literal: acceptance (patience) of the non-arising of dharmas

cross_language.form: mi skye ba'i chos la bzod pa

definitions.definition: The Unsurpassed: the supreme reality of the Trika, identified with the letter A and with the Heart; Parātrīśikā's question concerns how the anuttara grants immediate Kaula perfection.

literal: unsurpassed; that beyond which there is nothing

definitions.definition: The full awakening of a buddha, the bodhisattva's goal; 'not even the least dharma is found in it — therefore it is called unsurpassed perfect awakening' (Vajracchedikā 22); all buddhas of the three times attain it by relying on the perfection of wisdom (Heart).

cross_language.form: bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub
anouduoluo sanmiao sanputi 阿耨多羅三藐三菩提

definitions.definition: The five highest heavens (Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, Aparājita, Sarvārthasiddhi), whose gods are near liberation (TS 4.19, 4.26).
The soul's atomic size: it dwells in the heart and pervades the body by its attributive consciousness.
An arthavāda stating what is already known by another means of knowledge (e.g. that fire is a remedy for cold).
Repetition of what has been enjoined, distinct from mere repetition (NS 2.1.66–68 DCS).
A lesson or section, the recitation unit of the Ṛgveda (within maṇḍalas) and of the Taittirīya texts.
The five vows kept partially by the householder (TS 7.2, 7.20).
A mental perception, following a cognition, of the form 'I know this'; the means by which a cognition is known, since a cognition does not reveal itself.
The reflective cognition 'I know this' that follows a cognition; for Murāri Miśra it grasps the first cognition's validity (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).
The four classes of Digambara literature: narratives (prathama), cosmology and karma (karaṇa), conduct (caraṇa), and substances (dravya) (Ratnakaraṇḍa 43–46).
The locus in which a relation or absence is (the ground, for 'absence of pot on the ground').
Subsequent knowledge: pure knowledge of the truths regarding the upper realms.
A probans with both positive and negative concomitance, e.g. smoke for fire.
The science of reasoning, the fourth of the four sciences, 'the lamp of all sciences' (NBh 1.1.1).
Words express their meanings only as already connected with other meanings, ultimately with what is to be done (kārya), as learned from elders' usage.
Free from desires other than for Kṛṣṇa's service — the first mark of pure devotion.
Wrong knowledge — for Madhva the real sense of 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya: the soul's misapprehension (of its relation to the body and to God), which ceases by God's will when he is known.
The Nyāya theory of error: a thing is cognized as qualified by a property it lacks — the silver seen elsewhere is presented in the mother-of-pearl.
An invariable antecedent that is nevertheless not a cause (e.g. the colour of the potter's staff).
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by identity ('a pot is not cloth').
Substance with cold touch, fluid and viscid; bodies of water in Varuṇa's world.
Conduct permitted when normal dharma cannot be kept, illustrated by Viśvāmitra in famine (MBh 12.139).
The relaxed rules of livelihood and conduct permitted in emergencies (MDh 10.81ff.).
The downward breath at the anus (SS 3.7); turned upward by mūlabandha it meets fire and prāṇa and awakens kuṇḍalinī (HYP 3.61–69).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the navel.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu in the lower region (pelvis, bladder, genitals, thighs), governing the release of semen, menses, faeces, urine and the foetus (AHS Sū 12.9).
The complementary breath to prāṇa in the Gītā's breath-sacrifice (BhG 4.29) and equalization (5.27).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of the two paired breaths: some offer prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa (4.29); prāṇa and apāna moving within the nostrils are to be made even (5.27). The chapters do not define the direction of each.
The downward (or out-) breath; in PrU 3.5 it is in the organs of excretion and generation; the navel's function whose deity is death (AU 1.1.4).
Out-breath, named with prāṇa in the Saṃhitā lists of breaths (TS 4.7; AVŚ 8.1, 15.16).
The downward breath, seated at the anus.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The 'safe bet' teaching: affirming another world and the fruit of deeds is the wiser course whether or not they exist.
The Lord's eightfold divided nature: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego (BhG 7.4).
The lower knowledge: the four Vedas and the six ancillary sciences (MuU 1.1.5).
Not appropriating objects, seeing the faults of acquiring, keeping, losing, attachment and harm (YBh 2.30); when steady, knowledge of the how of births (2.39).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the meditating yogin is to be without possessions (aparigraha) (6.10); cf. the one who has given up all possessions (tyakta-sarva-parigraha) and incurs no fault (4.21).
In Jainism abstention from possessiveness, defined as infatuation (mūrcchā) (TS 7.17).

cross_language.note: fifth Jain vow

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of God — in the form of one's own original (bimba), to the extent one's fitness allows — produced by meditation built on hearing and reflection.
Immediate knowledge: knowledge of the self as oneself ('you are the tenth'); for the Vivaraṇa produced by the mahāvākya directly.

equivalents.note: Dvaita uses aparokṣa-jñāna and sākṣātkāra (direct realization) of God interchangeably.

definitions.definition: A corrupt or incorrect word-form (e.g. vernacular variants of 'gauḥ'); its use is forbidden in ritual contexts and the Asuras were defeated for mispronunciation (Mahābhāṣya Paspaśā).
The Veda's character of having no author, not even God; its words and order are eternal.
The Veda as not composed by any person; the named seers saw or first transmitted it.
Mīmāṃsā's claim that the Veda has no author, rejected by Nyāya: the Veda is composed with understanding and its validity comes from its reliable author.

notes: The term is Mīmāṃsā's (U12); the Saṃhitā lineage's self-understanding is recorded here with the counter-evidence of 'fashioned' hymns (dsp:seen-or-made-hymns).

definitions.definition: The Veda's having no author, human or divine; names like Kāṭhaka come from expounding, not authorship (MS 1.1.30); the unbroken chain of teachers' study has no first term (ŚV vākya 366); since defects of testimony depend on speakers, an authorless Veda is free of them (ŚV codanā 62).
Retraction: showing that what was superimposed is nothing but its substratum, as the snake is only the rope.
Absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), reached when false knowledge and the rest are removed (NS 1.1.2); on the mainstream view without pleasure or cognition (NBh 1.1.22).
Liberation, which comes through knowledge (SK 44); defined in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra as the indifference of one of the two (SS 3.66).
Liberation as the second purpose of the seen: determining the enjoyer's own nature (2.18, YBh 2.18).

equivalents.note: Within Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, apavarga, mokṣa, mukti and niḥśreyasa (in its final sense) name the same state.
Sāṃkhya-Yoga's isolation of puruṣa is also a state without pain and without objects; but Nyāya's self is a substance whose consciousness is adventitious, while puruṣa is consciousness itself.

definitions.definition: The four woeful planes: hell, animal realm, ghosts, asuras.
Contemplating the misery of beings caught in wrong views and how they may be freed (TS 9.36).
The cognition 'this is one, this is one' that produces duality and higher numbers in things; its role at creation (for the magnitude of dyads) is one of Udayana's proofs of the Lord.
Abstraction: the division of the sentence into words and of words into stems and affixes, a device of grammatical analysis with no ultimate reality, since the sentence is partless (VP 1.73; kāṇḍa 2).
One of the Lord's three powers with cognition and memory (ĪPK 1.3.7); every determinate awareness arises by exclusion of an opposite (1.6.5) - a reworking of the Buddhist apoha.
The cadent houses (3, 6, 9, 12) following the succedents (BJ 1.18).

notes: Scholarly account: from Greek apoklima.

definitions.definition: The path to the deathless (Dhp 21); the Buddha's last words urge accomplishing the goal through heedfulness (DN 16).
The four immeasurables (brahmavihāras) and the immeasurable liberation of mind (MN 43).
Full absorption (jhāna), following access.
Desireless: the gateway through contemplation of suffering.
Non-material 'matter': the substance of the Lord's form and abode, beyond prakṛti.
Transcendental, not of māyā: the Lord's body, name and abode and the devotee's perfected body.
Heedfulness, declared by Sanatsujāta to be immortality (MBh 5.42.4); one of the three 'horses of Brahman' with self-restraint and renunciation (11.7.19; 5.43.14).
Attentiveness to what is to come, like guarding a sprout; a niyama, the fifth strength, and the state in which the end of suffering is reached.
Vigilance, never being careless for a moment ('samayaṃ goyama mā pamāyae'); the seventh guṇasthāna is named 'apramatta-saṃyata'.

cross_language.note: cognate; the Dhammapada's 'appamādo amatapadaṃ' is recorded by the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: Immeasurable; four — loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity — antidotes to malice etc., with beings of the desire realm as object.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The seventh guṇasthāna: restraint free of carelessness, alternating with the sixth.

literal: immeasurable; not an object of the means of knowledge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the eternal, indestructible embodied one whose bodies have an end (2.18).
Non-possession, the contrary force; the state of an ordinary person is non-possession of the noble path.
The unmanifest (prakṛti), which does not awaken, and the self while it has not awakened (MBh 12.292–296).
Cessation not through discernment: the absolute obstruction of the arising of a dharma through the lack of its conditions.
Mind (or giving) not resting on any object — form, sound, dharma — as the Tathāgata's mind stands nowhere; Kumārajīva: 'produce a mind that abides nowhere'.

cross_language.form: wuzhu 無住 / ying wu suo zhu er sheng qi xin 應無所住而生其心

definitions.definition: The buddhas' nirvāṇa that abides neither in saṃsāra (because of wisdom) nor in quiescence (because of compassion); prefigured in the sūtras' bodhisattva who neither destroys the conditioned nor dwells in the unconditioned.

cross_language.form: mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa

notes: The technical term is systematized in Yogācāra treatises (Mahāyānasaṃgraha); the idea is in the sūtras.

definitions.definition: The grade of passions that prevents taking even the lay vows (TS 8.9).

The relation of inseparable existence between a substance and its mode (as between Brahman and souls/matter, or a substance and its attribute): the mode can neither exist nor be known apart from the substrate, yet is distinct from it.

One who has directly experienced the thing and speaks from the wish to communicate it as seen — the same definition for seers, āryas and mlecchas (NBh 1.1.7); the Veda is valid because its seers and teachers are reliable (NS 2.1.69).
One who speaks of things as they are (yathārthavaktā) (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The reliable authority: the Jina, free of the eighteen faults (including hunger and thirst), omniscient, and teacher of the good; right faith is faith in the āpta, the scripture and the teacher.

Reliable testimony (reliable revelation, SK 5), establishing what neither perception nor inference establishes (SK 6); the reliable person is devoted to his work, free of passion and aversion, knowing and virtuous (Kramadīpikā).
The word of those freed from rajas and tamas, whose knowledge of the three times is pure — the Veda and teachings not contrary to it (Ca Sū 11.18-19, 11.27; Vi 4.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The state of not coming back (to birth), reached by those whose intellect and self are set on That, who are established in That and have That as their goal and whose impurities are shaken off by knowledge (5.17).
Non-return to rebirth, reached by those who come to the Lord (BhG 8.15–16), by knowers who depart on the bright path (8.24), and by the knowers of the self (5.17).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

literal: one who will not again bind [the maximum]

definitions.definition: A soul that will never again bind karma of the maximum duration — the first qualification for yoga (Yogabindu).
The unseen potency brought about by a perishable ritual act, postulated because the fruit (e.g. heaven) comes later: 'there is an apūrva, since the undertaking is enjoined' (Śabara on MS 2.1.5).
A capacity produced in the self (or the act) by the rite; later Bhāṭṭas distinguish the final apūrva of the fruit from those of the parts and subsidiaries.
The apūrva is the 'what is to be done' (kārya/niyoga) made known by the injunction itself, knowable only from the Veda.

equivalents.note: Both name the unseen result of acts that ripens later; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika places adṛṣṭa in the self and makes Īśvara its overseer, which Mīmāṃsā rejects

notes: The Bhāṭṭa subdivision of apūrvas (e.g. phala-, samudāya-, utpatti-, aṅga-apūrva) is from memory (low); not attached to a teaching.

definitions.definition: An injunction of what is not obtained by any other means at all (e.g. sprinkling the rice).
The eighth guṇasthāna (nivṛtti-bādara), where the ascetic mounts the ladder of subsidence or destruction; also the second of the three karaṇas before right view.
One of the six periods of each half-cycle: very happy, happy, happy-unhappy, unhappy-happy, unhappy, very unhappy (suṣama-suṣamā … duṣama-duṣamā).

The six 'spokes' (ara) of each half of the time-wheel, from 'very happy' (suṣamā-suṣamā) to 'very unhappy' (duḥṣamā-duḥṣamā); Tīrthaṅkaras appear only in the third and fourth; the present is the fifth (duḥṣamā), in which liberation from this region is no longer possible.
The element of initiative (with persistence, exertion etc.) whose evident existence refutes the view that no one acts of his own doing.
'Accomplishment': the perfecting of right faith, knowledge, conduct and austerity, especially as brought to completion at the end of life under a guide.
One who has reconciled with all at Paryuṣaṇa is an 'ārādhaka' (fulfiller) of the discipline.
A subsidiary enjoined by itself, not with reference to a material (e.g. the prayājas), helping only toward the final apūrva.
One whose effluents are destroyed, who has lived the holy life and done what was to be done (DN 2); has ten factors (MN 117).
One who has destroyed the taints; the Kathāvatthu denies that an arahant can fall away, have ignorance or doubt, be defiled by deities, or remain a householder.

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: The hereditary temple performance of the Prabandham in song, gesture and dance by the araiyars, traced to Nāthamuni.
Virtue, righteousness; first of the Kuṟaḷ's three books; 'being spotless in mind is the whole of aṟam' (Kuṟaḷ 34).
Virtue, dharma: in the Jain didactic works (Nālaṭiyār) the right conduct to be done now, before wealth, youth and the body pass away.

equivalents.note: aṟam centres on inner purity and non-harm; dharma includes ritual duty

definitions.definition: The first of the four stages: brahmagranthi pierced, tinkling sounds, a radiant, fragrant, healthy body (HYP 4.70–71; SS 3.29–31).
First of the four stages of yoga.
The effect is a new beginning, not pre-existing in its material cause (the whole produced by the parts is a new substance).
The object of consciousness; six kinds; object condition in the Paṭṭhāna.
The samādhi of non-contention for which Subhūti is foremost; he does not think of himself as having attained it.

literal: to be sung in the forest

definitions.definition: The melodies sung in the forest, regarded as more potent and secret.
A 'forest book' of a Vedic school, containing the dangerous or secret rites and meditations (Mahāvrata, Pravargya, saṃhitā-upaniṣads) studied away from the village, and often an Upaniṣad.
The Lord's descent into consecrated images in temples and homes, the most accessible of his forms, where he depends even on his worshippers.
The Lord present in a consecrated image, the most accessible of his five modes.
The image of Viṣṇu in which he is worshipped; image worship is the best means.
Hereditary Vaikhānasa priest serving a Viṣṇu temple.
Temple priest (in Tamil Śaiva usage the Ādiśaiva/Śivācārya).
Ritual worship of the Lord, the fifth form of devotion; the chief means in the Dvāpara age.
Worship: Vyāsa's definition of devotion is attachment to worship (pūjā) and the like (NBS 16); worship is one of love's eleven forms (NBS 82).
A verse-book of the Sāmaveda (Pūrvārcika, Uttarārcika), the texts on which the melodies are sung.
The path of the gods by which the freed soul travels from the body to Vaikuṇṭha, escorted by the deities of light, day, the bright fortnight, the northern course, the year and the rest.
The path 'beginning with light': the stations of the path of the gods (BS 4.3.1–6).
The path by which the knowers go to Brahmā's world, from which they reach the Supreme with Brahmā at the great dissolution.
The fourth of the ten bodhisattva grounds in the Daśabhūmika.

The 'half-Māgadhī' Prakrit of the Śvetāmbara canon, held to be the language in which Mahāvīra taught; the Jina's speech in it is understood by gods, humans and animals each in their own tongue (an atiśaya).
The fourth, half measure of Oṃ, beyond the guṇas and beyond speech, touched at the crown (MkP 42.5-6, 42.14).
The subtle fourth element of Oṃ beyond a, u and m; the 'head' of the Oṃ-bird.
Lunar mansion ārdrā: presiding deity Rudra (Śiva) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Rāhu (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class sharp (tīkṣṇa) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
'Bolt' or intervention: planets in the 2nd, 4th and 11th from a house or planet that influence it, obstructed by those in the 12th, 10th and 3rd (BPHS 31; Jaimini).
The seed-syllable of the Arhat, central in word-based meditation (YŚ 8) and in the fire concentration (YŚ 7).
Arhat: the non-learner after the knowledge of destruction; six kinds, five of which can fall back (Sarvāstivāda).
The arhat does not fall back from arhatship.

Per the Sarvāstivāda reports, the Mahāsāṃghika side accepted Mahādeva's five points: an arhat may be tempted by others, has non-knowing and doubt, is instructed by others; yet arhats do not fall back (Vasumitra).

In the Lotus and Śrīmālā the arhat's nirvāṇa is not final — he still has the ground of ignorance and is destined for buddhahood; the Vajracchedikā: an arhat who thought 'I am an arhat' would seize a self.
The embodied omniscient who has destroyed the four destructive karmas; the first of the five supreme beings (arihanta 'destroyer of enemies' in popular etymology).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).
Shared word; the Jain arhat is omniscient and will attain siddhahood, the Buddhist arahant has destroyed the āsavas — neither tradition equates the two.

definitions.definition: Signs of approaching death, personal, from other beings, or from the gods (YBh 3.22).
Signs appearing without cause that show the measure of life and approaching death, taught in the Indriyasthāna (Ca In 1.7; Sū 30.25).
A sign foretelling death, by which yogins know their time (e.g. no longer seeing Arundhatī or the pole-star).
A combination threatening early death or calamity, especially to infants (BJ 6), and its cancellation (ariṣṭa-bhaṅga) by benefic influences (BPHS 9–10).
Omen foretelling death.

Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration (SN 45.8), the middle way that avoids sensual indulgence and self-mortification (SN 56.11); grouped into the trainings of virtue, concentration and wisdom (MN 44).

The four noble truths (suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path), to be respectively fully understood, abandoned, realised and developed (SN 56.11); what the Buddha declared because it is beneficial (SN 56.31).

literal: noble truth; truth for the noble ones

definitions.definition: The noble one, the master-guru whom the seeker must find and bow to (Pattirakiriyār 26).

equivalents.note: āriyaṉ here names the guru

definitions.definition: The third virtue: freedom from deceit (TS 9.6).
Superimposition: attributing the svarūpa (Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā) to the rūpa of the practitioner and partner, the key contemplative act of Sahajiyā practice.

literal: offering; that by which one offers

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.24 the offering (or the means of offering) is itself Brahman.
Offering to the liṅga everything meant for one's own enjoyment before enjoying it, so that all is received as prasāda (SSM 11.6–11).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Knowledge of seers arising from particular merits (VS 9.28 C); intuitive knowledge of past, future and supersensible things in the seers (Praśastapāda).
The 'city of mirrors' near the house (the body), where the unseen neighbour (the Man) lives.
Brooding on getting rid of the disagreeable, keeping the agreeable, removing pain, and future rewards (TS 9.30–33).
One who, unable to bear saṃsāra, asks for release at once, at the end of this body.
Wealth and power, the livelihood of the world, the aim served by the Arthaśāstra.

notes: Its sense 'meaning' (of a word) is used in the Vedāṅgas (Nirukta 2.1: 'attend always to the meaning').

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the self, the Lord, the means, the goal and the obstacle — the content a seeker must learn from the teacher.

literal: the five things to be known

definitions.definition: The five things to be known: the worshipped (upāsya), the worshipper (upāsaka), the fruit of grace, the rasa of devotion, and the obstacles.

notes: The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition has its own arthapañcaka (Piḷḷai Lokācārya); definitions differ.

definitions.definition: Supposing an unseen fact without which a seen or heard fact would not be possible (Devadatta, alive and not at home, is outside) — the Vṛttikāra in Śabara; accepted by both Bhāṭṭas and Prābhākaras.
Proposed as a means of knowledge; included in inference (NS 2.2.2).
Included in inference (Praśastapāda).
Presumption: knowing what must be so to account for something otherwise inexplicable (fat Devadatta who does not eat by day eats at night).

Vedic passages that do not themselves enjoin; they are meaningful as praise of what is enjoined, forming one sentence with the injunctions (MS 1.2.7). A fruit stated for a subsidiary is arthavāda (MS 4.3.1).

A sentence whose purport is praise or blame; supplementing an injunction or a prohibition; classified as praise, blame, another's deed and ancient narrative, or as figurative (guṇavāda), restating (anuvāda) and fact-stating (bhūtārthavāda).
The explanatory portion of a Brāhmaṇa (blame, praise, the deeds of others, ancient precedent) as distinct from injunction (ĀpŚS 24.1.33).
Vedic statements of praise, blame, another's practice and ancient precedent (NS 2.1.65 DCS).
The activity toward an act produced by the desire for a purpose, expressed by the verbal ending as such: 'one should bring about heaven by the sacrifice in this way'.
The six tastes — iṉippu (sweet), puḷippu (sour), uppu (salt), kārppu (pungent), kaippu (bitter), tuvarppu (astringent) — each formed of two elements and acting on the humours.

The 'mounted' image of a house: the sign as far from the house-lord as the lord is from the house; it shows how a matter appears in the world (BPHS 29; Jaimini); in Kerala praśna, the sign indicated by the querist.
One who has taken the higher way of Śiva-worship and resorts again to lower practice (SSM 9.39–40).
Tamil form of Arhat, the Jina, invoked in the opening verses of Tamil Jain works.
The Lord's grace: he 'graciously gave' (aruḷiṉaṉ) knowledge-and-love free of delusion (TVM 1.1.1); his grace (aruḷ) is received by all who recite the Tiruppāvai (TP 30).
Grace: Śiva's own power (aruḷ-catti) acting toward the soul; ever present, it removes the power of mala and comes as the guru.
The Lord's grace that saves the devotee from every danger and cuts births.
In the Kuṟaḷ, aruḷ is compassion for all living beings (chapter 25, Aruḷuṭaimai).
Grace: for the Siddha poets the guru's descent and self-showing (Aḻukaṇṇi 33–34) and the Lord's flood of compassion (Pattirakiriyār 62).

equivalents.note: the same Tamil word names Śiva's grace in Śaiva Siddhānta (U18); here Tirumāl's
aruḷ is also Śiva's power itself

definitions.definition: The Āḻvārs' hymns (Divya Prabandham) as graciously given; the Tamil Veda.
A name of kuṇḍalinī (HYP 3.104; 'the sleeping Arundhatī', 3.119).
The four formless attainments beyond the fine-material jhānas.
Lust for existence in the formless realm; the seventh fetter.
Consciousness of the four formless attainments (twelve types).
The formless realm: no place, four by mode of birth; the mind-series rests on homogeneity and life faculty.
The sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, for whom action is the means (BhG 6.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, for whom action (karma) is said to be the means (6.3); contrasted with the one who has ascended (yogārūḍha).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Eager longing; the 'ghee' of Pūtattāḻvār's lamp of love.
Āryabhaṭa's system writing large numbers with consonants and vowels (ka = 1 … with vowels marking decimal places), used for the constants in the Gītikāpāda.
The four noble lineages: contentment with robes, alms-food and lodging, and delight in abandonment and cultivation — antidotes to craving.

A Digambara nun: she wears a single white garment, lives with other nuns, eats seated (not in the hand like the monk), and in Digambara teaching cannot in this body pass beyond the fifth stage in the full sense because she keeps a garment.
The path of the non-learner, the arhat, after the knowledge of destruction.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The manner of action taught in chapter 3: the karma-yogin acts unattached (3.7); one should always perform the action to be done unattached, thereby reaching the highest (3.19); the wise act unattached for the holding together of the world (3.25).

The twenty-eight incapacities: injuries of the eleven organs (deafness, blindness, numbness, etc.) and seventeen injuries of buddhi, the reversals of the nine contentments and eight accomplishments (SK 49).
Attachment to the Lord that makes household life distasteful (Bhaktivardhinī).
The seventh stage: attachment to the Lord's name, qualities and abode.
Attachment — in the Nārada Sūtra the form love takes toward each aspect of the Lord (NBS 82).
A cause inhering in the same thing as the effect or its cause (conjunction of threads for cloth; colour of threads for cloth's colour).
The non-perceptual state of the non-perceiving gods: a cessation of mind and mental factors, a result of ripening.
Attainment of non-perception: entered in the fourth dhyāna by ordinary beings who mistake it for escape.
Incalculable aeon; the bodhisattva's career spans three, ended respectively under Ratnaśikhin, Dīpaṅkara and Vipaśyin.
The 'other' samādhi, preceded by practice of the cognition of cessation, with only impressions remaining (1.18); nothing is cognized in it (YBh 1.2); means: higher dispassion (YBh 1.18).
Fifth stage: from practice of the four, non-association with objects becomes firm and the wonder of sattva is established.
Fifth stage: non-attachment; the excellent knower.
Unconditioned: space, cessation through discernment and cessation not through discernment — real, eternal, without activity.
Not real entities: space is mere absence of resistance; the cessations are mere non-arising.
Nine unconditioned dharmas are counted, including the four formless spheres and the natures of dependent origination and of the path (Vasumitra; low confidence).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Abstaining from worldly transactions; the fourth Pāśupata yama.
Posture; the Vāyavīya names eight (svastika, padma, ardhendu, vīra, yoga, prasādhita, paryaṅka, as one likes); the MkP names padma, half and svastika.
Posture is what is steady and pleasant (SS 3.34); there is no fixed rule (SS 6.24).
Posture, steady and comfortable (2.46), achieved by relaxing effort and coalescence with the endless (2.47); Vyāsa lists seated postures such as padmāsana, bhadrāsana and svastika (YBh 2.46).
Posture, the first limb of haṭha, giving steadiness, health and lightness (HYP 1.17); Śiva taught 84 (HYP 1.33) or 8,400,000 (GS 2.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The firm seat set up in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, spread with kuśa grass, deer-skin and cloth, on which the meditating yogin sits (6.11–12), holding body, head and neck in line (6.13). In these chapters āsana is the seat, not a series of postures.
Posture — four, eight, nine, eleven or seventeen named; inwardly, indifference or the seat where Brahman-thought flows.
In Haribhadra's correlation the limb of the balā view; Hemacandra lists the postures for meditation (paryaṅka, vīra, vajra, lotus, bhadra, daṇḍa, utkaṭikā, godohikā, kāyotsarga) (YŚ 4.124–134).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Religious activity that flows spontaneously without attachment, in the prabhā view; Haribhadra says others call it praśāntavāhitā, visabhāga-parikṣaya, śivavartman and dhruvādhvan (YDS).

equivalents.note: Equivalence asserted by Haribhadra himself; Pātañjala commentators do not make it.

definitions.definition: What is not made by conditions: no arising, no passing, no alteration while standing is discerned (AN 3.47); the destruction of lust, hatred and delusion (SN 43.12).
Not produced by conditions: in the Theravāda only nibbāna is unconditioned; the Kathāvatthu rejects the views that space, dependent origination or the truths are unconditioned.
Dishonour, declared the highest of all restraints; Kauṇḍinya: it removes pride of birth and of householder status.
Gods without perception who fall when perception arises; one who recalls only that arising holds that self and world arose by chance.
Eight grounds for holding the self non-percipient after death.
Non-being or the non-existent, in which the seers found the bond of being (RV 10.129.4); from it being was born (10.72.2–3).
Non-being: some said this was non-being in the beginning (rejected in ChU 6.2.1-2); TU 2.7 and ChU 3.19.1 say non-being was first and being came from it.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.16: what is not (the non-existent or unreal), of which there is no being (bhāva); what exactly is meant is disputed among commentators.

equivalents.note: Śaṅkara reads the asat of creation texts as the unmanifest (unmanifested name and form), not absolute nothing; the Saṃhitā does not say so.

literal: doctrine that the effect is non-existent (before production)

definitions.definition: The rival (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika) view that the effect is new, rejected by Sāṃkhya: the non-existent cannot be produced, like a man's horn (SK 9; SS 1.114).
Before production the effect is non-existent (a prior absence of it is real) (NS 4.1.48–50; effect as counterpositive of prior absence, Tarkasaṅgraha).

equivalents.note: Opposed doctrines: Sāṃkhya's pre-existent effect.

literal: unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects

definitions.definition: Excessive, deficient or wrong contact of the senses with their objects, one of the three causes of disease (Ca Sū 11.37-38, 11.43; Śā 1.118-128).
Uttering the words without delay.
The ritual impurity of relatives after a birth or death, lasting ten days for sapiṇḍas (MDh 5.59) or by class (5.83).
The effluents of sensuality, becoming and ignorance (MN 9; DN 2), with views as a fourth in some lists; their destruction is arahantship.
Taints: of sensual desire, existence, views and ignorance (four in the Abhidhamma).

equivalents.note: same word; in Jainism āsrava is the influx of karmic matter

definitions.definition: The third true knowledge and sixth direct knowledge: knowing the four truths and the effluents, the mind is freed and knows 'birth is ended' (DN 2; MN 4).
The arahant.
The five-syllable mantra formed from the initials of arhat, siddha (or aśarīra), ācārya, upādhyāya, sādhu (Dravyasaṃgraha 49 commentary).
Three kinds: as to the locus (the sky-lotus), as to itself, as to pervasion (with an adjunct).
The self-wish 'may I not cease, may I be', eternal, which makes the latent tendencies beginningless (4.10, YBh 2.9, 4.10).

Lunar mansion āśleṣā: presiding deity the Serpents (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Mercury (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class sharp (tīkṣṇa) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Its junction with Maghā is a gaṇḍānta.

The residual conceit and desire 'I am' in one who no longer takes any aggregate as self, like the smell of soap in a washed cloth (SN 22.89); abandoned by the perception of impermanence (MN 62; Ud 4.1).

(1) The affliction: the seeming identity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing (2.6). (2) The fourth level of samprajñāta samādhi, awareness of a single self (YBh 1.17). (3) 'Asmitā-mātra', the sixth unparticularized principle (YBh 2.19) and the source of created minds (4.4).

equivalents.note: YBh 2.19 names the sixth unparticularized principle asmitā-mātra where Sāṃkhya names ahaṃkāra; Bhoja (RM 1.17) insists asmitā and ahaṃkāra are not the same.

definitions.definition: 'Contactless yoga': Gauḍapāda's discipline of the mind that realizes the unborn, free from contact with objects, feared by yogins who see fear where there is none.

One of the four orders: student, householder, forest-hermit, renouncer (MDh 6.87); whether they are chosen freely, followed in sequence, or whether only the householder's is Vedic is disputed (GDh 3.1–3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27; VDh 7.3; ĀpDh 2.9.21.1).

Stage of life: 'proceeding through one's own āśramas' is part of the remedy (MaiU 4.3); ŚU 6.21 names those beyond the āśramas (atyāśramin); ChU 2.23.1 has three 'branches of dharma' without the word.

literal: stage of exertion; order of life

definitions.definition: Outflow: in the Kośa's list three — of desire, of existence and of ignorance; so called because they make beings stay in saṃsāra and flow out through the six wounds of the senses.
The influx of karmic matter into the soul through the activity (yoga) of body, speech and mind (TS 6.1–2).

cross_language.note: Pali has āsava 'canker, outflow' — same word, different doctrine

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Awakening as the revelation of the stainless element when the stains are removed.
In the Saṃdhinirmocana the dharmakāya is the transformation of the basis.
The pleasure in sensual pleasures, forms and feelings (MN 13).

A planet 'set' in the sun's rays; such a planet loses strength, and renunciation-planets set in the sun give devotion without initiation (BJ 15.2; BPHS 79.4); Jupiter or Venus set bars marriages and other rites.
The eightfold daily play of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa from the end of night to night, the object of meditative remembrance (Govindalīlāmṛta, Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta).
Viṣṇu's agency in the creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release of the world (Tattvasaṅkhyāna adds happiness, sorrow, covering and light).
The eight maṭhas of Uḍupi founded by Madhva's eight ascetic disciples.
The eight fetters — disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct, caste; one bound by them is a paśu, one freed is Maheśvara (Kulārṇava 13.90–91).
The eight-ingredient binding compound that fixes the image to its pedestal, periodically renewed with rites.
Used likewise in Tamil temple practice (aṣṭabandhana).
The 'eight seals': the eight poet-singers of the Puṣṭimārga appointed by Viṭṭhalanātha — Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās, Kṛṣṇadās, Nanddās, Caturbhujdās, Govindsvāmī, Chītsvāmī.
The 'eightfold division': benefic points (bindu) contributed to each sign by the seven planets and the ascendant, used to judge transits and longevity (BJ 9; BPHS 66–72).
Earth and the other elements, sun, moon and the self as Śiva's eight forms — in the SSM his body and effect, over which he presides, neither non-different from him nor separate (10.48–52).

The eight branches: kāyacikitsā, śālākya, śalya, viṣa/agada, bhūtavidyā, kaumārabhṛtya, rasāyana, vājīkaraṇa (Ca Sū 30.28; Su Sū 1.7; AHS Sū 1.5: body, child, seizers, above the clavicle, surgery, fangs, old age, virility).
The eight limbs: restraints, observances, posture, breath-regulation, sense-withdrawal, concentration, meditation, samādhi (2.29), whose practice destroys impurity (2.28).
Tamil aṭṭāṅka yōkam: iyamam, niyamam, ātaṉam, pirāṇāyāmam, pirattiyākāram, tāraṇai, tiyāṉam, camāti (TM 552), commended by Kaṭuveḷi (31).
A song of eight stanzas with refrain, set to a named rāga and tāla — the twenty-four songs of the Gīta Govinda; in Kerala the name of the Gīta Govinda singing tradition itself.
The eight protections of the Liṅgāyata: guru, liṅga, jaṅgama, pādōdaka, prasāda, vibhūti, rudrākṣa and mantra; several appear as sub-sthalas of the bhakta-sthala in the SSM (5.27–30).
Freedom from desire for what is not one's own (YBh 2.30); when established, all jewels present themselves (2.37).
One of the common duties of all (MDh 10.63).
In Jainism abstention from taking what is not given (TS 7.15).
The fifth tissue: supports the body and nourishes marrow (Su Sū 15.5).
The five substances that exist with extension in space-points — soul, matter, medium of motion, medium of rest, space (time excluded) (TS 5.1; Kundakunda's Pañcāstikāya).
The life-breath that leaves at death (the fathers 'have gone to asu', RV 10.15.1); the one life of the gods arose from the waters (10.121.7).
The ten kinds of corpse as meditation subjects, and the perception of the body's foulness, counteracting lust.
Contemplation of the unlovely (skeleton contemplation), entry to cultivation for those dominated by passion; it is non-greed.
Viewing the body as hair, flesh, blood, bone, bile, excrement and so on, cultivated to abandon lustful passion (NBh 4.2.3).

cross_language.note: same term; the Buddhist practice has its own contexts and lists

definitions.definition: The karma of the yogin (4.7): not white, since he renounces the fruit; not black, since he does not take it up (YBh 4.7); others' karma is black, white-and-black, or white.
In the Ṛgveda a lord of mysterious power, applied to Varuṇa and other gods ('great is the one asura-ship of the gods', RV 3.55); later the gods' opponents.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan ahura.

definitions.definition: Hypocrisy, arrogance, pride, anger, harshness and ignorance, leading to bondage (BhG 16.4–5); its bearers deny truth, foundation and a Lord (16.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping (anasūyantaḥ) are freed from actions (3.31); those who carp at it and do not follow it are lost (3.32).
The imperishable tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns, to be cut with the axe of non-attachment (BhG 15.1–4); 'among trees I am the aśvattha' (10.26).
The eternal fig tree with roots above and branches below, which is brahman, the immortal, in which all worlds rest (KU 2.3.1).
The twin horsemen, divine physicians and rescuers, praised by Ghoṣā (RV 10.39–40).
Repeated contraction and expansion of the anus.

Lunar mansion aśvinī: presiding deity the Aśvins (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Ketu (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class swift (kṣipra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Aśvayujau; first in the later lists, 26th in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa's list from Kṛttikā.

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: Quality of the truths the Tathāgata knows beyond all sixty-two views.
Not being 'made of that', by which even equanimity based on unity is abandoned (MN 137).
The renunciant's continual wandering, not staying long in one place.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna calls the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra ātatāyinaḥ, and says sin would come upon them for killing even these aggressors (1.36).
The six supports (āṟu ātāram) of the body: mūlātāram, cuvātiṭṭāṉam, maṇipūrakam, anākatam, vicutti, ākkiñai; the Siddha counterpart of the cakras, burnt away by the guru's grace in Aḻukaṇṇi's song.

equivalents.note: the six ātāras correspond to the six cakras

definitions.definition: The primordial fire-priest who churned out Agni (RV 6.16.13); with the Aṅgirases, the seers of the Atharvaveda.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan āθravan (priest).

definitions.definition: The old name of the Atharvaveda, pairing its auspicious (ātharvaṇa) and fierce (āṅgirasa) portions.
A partial lapse in a vow or in right view, five for each (TS 7.23–37).
The gift of oneself to the Lord, whose fruit is final non-return, as against ordinary gifts of cows, land and gold.
The extension of the procedure of an archetype to an ectype ('the ectype is to be performed like the archetype'), in general (adhyāya 7) and in particular (adhyāya 8).

literal: one who has passed beyond what is to be cultivated

definitions.definition: One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One whose sole aim is the dissolution of the mind, with the sevenfold final insight.
Servitude — the soul's being the Lord's servant, and the service it owes 'at all times without break' (TVM 3.3.1); the Āḻvārs call themselves aṭiyēṉ, 'your servant'.

equivalents.note: aṭimai is the servant-state; kaiṅkarya the service done from it
the Bhāgavata's dāsya is one of nine forms; for the Āḻvārs servitude is the soul's very nature

definitions.definition: Name given by the Śaiva scriptures to the Pāśupata and Lākula (and skull-observing) division of Śaivism: knowledge 'beyond the states of the intellect', 'beyond the world'.
In the Mantramārga's own scriptures, the ascetic Śaiva path (Pāśupata and Lākula) ranked above Vedic and 'spiritual' religion but below the Mantramārga.

notes: U17 owns lin:atimarga and its own account; this is the Mantramārga's classification.

definitions.definition: A Tamil Śaiva monastic house (maṭha) headed by a paṇṭāra-caṉṉiti, e.g. Tiruvāvaṭuturai and Dharmapuram, custodians of the Meykaṇṭa tradition and of temples.
One of the thirty-four 'excellences' (supernatural features) of a Tīrthaṅkara — some from birth, some arising with omniscience, some produced by the gods.
Enduring the three sufferings without remedy while keeping one's rule; the supreme austerity.
The guest, whose honouring is the sacrifice to men (MDh 3.70).
Giving pure food and requisites to ascetics who come unannounced (TS 7.21).
The deities who conduct the departed soul along the path of light.
The airy (vāyavīya) body that the dead takes immediately upon leaving the gross body.
The knower beyond castes and stages of life.
Performing the prescribed acts as the Lord's command; the supreme worship.
The Lord's servants, his devotees; the Āḻvārs hold the servants of his servants, of any birth, to be their masters.
'Those at the feet': Śiva's devotees, to be served and revered as Śiva himself.
The freed soul should join the true devotees (meyyaṭiyār) and revere their garb as Śiva.
The Śrīvaiṣṇava's customary way of saying 'I', expressing servitude.
Giving oneself over to the Lord's protection — the principal (aṅgin) of prapatti in Deśika's account, the sixth of the six in the Ahirbudhnya verse.
The renouncer's own funerary offering, among the eight śrāddhas.
Inquiry into the self: 'Who am I? How did this world arise? Who is its maker? What is its material?' (Aparokṣānubhūti 12); inquiry, not action, attains the Real (VC 11).
The highest dharma, attained by yoga (YS 1.8).
The eight virtues — compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed — without which the forty sacraments do not lead to Brahman (GDh 8.22–25).
The highest of the means to the supreme good, foremost of all sciences, by which immortality is gained (MDh 12.85).
The significator of the self: the planet with the highest degrees in its sign among seven (or eight) (Jaimini 1.1.11; BPHS 32.3); called the king among the kārakas.

The self: in the Upaniṣads the innermost reality of a person — the seer of seeing that cannot be seen (BAU 3.4.2), the inner controller (BAU 3.7), the light of a person (BAU 4.3.6) — which is declared to be brahman (BAU 1.4.10, 2.5.19; ChU 6.8.7; MāU 2). The word also means body or oneself in narrative passages (ChU 8.8.4).

Breath and self: Sūrya is the self of what moves and stands (RV 1.115.1); the dead man's breath (ātman) goes to the wind (10.16.3); Vāta is the self of the gods (10.168.4); knowing the wise, ageless, young self one does not fear death (AVŚ 10.8.44).

The embodied self, unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.20); to be raised by the self, being its own friend or enemy (6.5–6); the Lord as the self in the heart of all beings (10.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self in which the one of steady wisdom is content — in the self alone, by the self (2.55) — and in which one who has nothing to do delights and is satisfied (3.17); knowing what is beyond the understanding (which 3.42 calls only 'he', saḥ; the commentators take it as the self), one steadies the self by the self (ātmānam ātmanā, 3.43). Also used reflexively and for one's person, nature or mind (vidheyātmā 2.64; vimūḍhātmā 3.6, 3.27; ātmavān 2.45; kāmātmānaḥ 2.43). The embodied one of 2.12–30 is called dehin or śarīrin, not ātman.

An eternal substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition, known by the marks desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition (NS 1.1.10); the knower, the one who remembers (NS 3.2.40).
An all-pervading substance marked by breath, eye-movements, life, mind's movement, desire, effort etc. (VS 3.2.4 C); many (VS 3.2.16 C); perceived by yogins (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition; two kinds: the supreme self (the one omniscient Lord) and the individual self, distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The inner self (pratyag-ātman): pure, self-luminous consciousness, the witness of the three states, not the body, senses, mind or ego; identical with Brahman.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the supreme self is changeless, eternal, the cause of consciousness with mind, elements and senses, the seer (Sū 1.56); beginningless, the knower of the field, all-pervading, witness, known by the marks of life (breath, blinking, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, memory, ego-sense) (Śā 1.59-85); knows only through its instruments (Śā 1.54-55).
Suśruta: the knowers of the field in Āyurveda are eternal but not all-pervading (Su Śā 1.16).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Used both reflexively (oneself, one's own mind: 'one should raise the self by the self', the self as its own friend or enemy, 6.5–6) and for the self in which all beings are seen (4.35, 6.29), in which the restrained citta rests (6.18) and the manas is made to abide (6.25) and which is seen by the self (6.20); the yoked yogin's self has become the self of all beings (5.7). In 4.35 and 6.29 the locative ātmani can also be read reflexively ('in oneself').

In ritual contexts the body or trunk (of the altar, of the sacrificer) that the rite constructs; in the teachings of Śāṇḍilya and Aśvapati the inner self 'made of mind, with breath for body' (ŚB 10.6.3).
The self to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), its own witness (MDh 8.84), one in all beings though appearing many like space in pots (YS 3.144).
The one self of the deity of which the many gods are limbs (Nirukta 7.4).
The self, distinct from body and cognition, known to itself, shown by desire, memory and recognition; taught by negation ('not this, not this') (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; manifested as the subject in cognitions of objects (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Eternal, the agent and enjoyer who reaps the fruits of rites in another world; known through reasoning and made firm by the Upaniṣads (ŚV ātmavāda 148).

The eternal self, distinct from body, senses and intellect, known through the I-cognition and memory (SSM 5.55–60); dwelling in the heart like the hundredth part of a hair-tip, shining like a lamp (18.5–7).
The sūtras deny the self of persons and dharmas (Vajracchedikā 25); the Mahāparinirvāṇa calls the tathāgatagarbha 'self'; the Laṅkāvatāra says this is not the self of the tīrthikas.
The self is consciousness (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the bound self is the mind (3.1); the self is a dancer (3.9).

In Jainism the soul (jīva) as knower; each is distinct and eternal, of three conditions (outer, inner, supreme) (Samādhitantra 4); 'the self conquered by passions is saṃsāra, the self that conquers them is liberation' (YŚ 4.5).
U04 usage: the Self in the body-temple, identical with Brahman; threefold as outer, inner and supreme self in the Ātma Upaniṣad.

cross_language.note: the Buddhist texts deny a permanent attā; same word, opposed doctrine

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; corrections logged in interpretation_log.jsonl.

definitions.definition: Complete self-surrender to the Lord, the ninth form of devotion.
Giving one's life over to the Lord who owns release (TVM 1.2.1).
Having offered self, world and Veda to the Lord, the devotee has no anxiety at worldly loss (NBS 61); self-offering is one of love's eleven forms (NBS 82).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The condition of the person who delights in, is satisfied in and content in the self alone, for whom nothing remains to be done and who depends on no being for any purpose (3.17–18).
Private worship by an initiate in the liṅga given by the guru or on a ground-altar, for one's own fruit.
Worship of Śiva for oneself, obligatory daily for the initiate.
One whose aim is the self alone, fit for the true teacher's instruction (Ātmasiddhi).
(Jain report) Five elements and the self as sixth, all eternal.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Seeing the same everywhere, pleasure or pain, by the measure of oneself; the yogin who does this is held to be the highest (6.32).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The direct experience of one's own self as distinct from matter, the fruit of karma- and jñāna-yoga and prerequisite for bhakti-yoga.
One who sacrifices knowing that each rite builds a limb of his own (new) self, and who so sheds the mortal body like a snake its skin (ŚB 11.2.6.13).
One who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and so attains self-rule (MDh 12.91).

In ordinary usage the reflexive 'oneself' (Dhp 160); as a doctrine, a self that would be permanent, controllable and 'mine' — the suttas examine every candidate (the aggregates, feeling, consciousness, the world) and find none (MN 22; DN 15; MN 148).

equivalents.note: the same word; what the Upaniṣadic traditions affirm as ātman the suttas examine and do not find; Theravāda rejects the identification

definitions.definition: What would belong to a self; since neither self nor what belongs to self is found as true and established, views of self are foolish (MN 22; SN 35.85).
A doctrine or theory of self; clinging to it (attavādupādāna) is the fourth kind of clinging (MN 11; SN 12.2).
Renunciation in mortal danger, by mind and speech.
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by a relation for all three times ('no pot on the ground').
Final, without recurrence — of the cessation of suffering in kaivalya (SK 1, 68).
Liberation understood as a dissolution: knowledge cuts the ego-knot and the self abides in itself; dissolution into the eternal Brahman (VP 6.8.1).
Beyond the stages of life: the Pāśupata observance so described by revelation.
The Pāśupata state: the initiate leaves the rules of his former āśrama and follows the restraints and observances of the state beyond the āśramas.
Name used by Śaiva scripture for the Pāśupata branch of the Atimārga.
One beyond the stages of life, to whom Śvetāśvatara declared brahman (ŚU 6.21).
Propriety, appropriateness of every element to rasa and context; for Kṣemendra the life of poetry.
The physical body of humans and animals (TS 2.36).
Letting the mind alone without forcing it — Hemacandra's key to stillness (YŚ 12).
States produced by the fruition of karma: destinies, passions, sexes, wrong view, ignorance, non-restraint, non-perfection, leśyās (TS 2.6).
A Nāth initiate who has received the first initiation (mantra, top-knot cut, black thread) but not yet the ear-splitting.
A name for Aghora ascetics; in Aghora usage the one who has passed beyond all distinctions.
Bhāskara's form: difference of soul from Brahman is due to real limiting adjuncts (upādhi); non-difference is natural.
A state arising from the temporary subsidence of (deluding) karma — right view and conduct (TS 2.3).
The relation of word and meaning, not created by any person (MS 1.1.5); known from the beginningless usage of elders (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Delimitation: consciousness delimited by the intellect, like the space enclosed by a pond; its identity with the whole is taught by the great sayings.
The Goddess appears divided by adjuncts like the space in pots.
Delimitation: the jīva as consciousness delimited by the inner organ, as space by a pot.
The property (or relation) by which a property or relation is specified — e.g. potness delimits the counterpositiveness of 'absence of pot'.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prasādi stage.
Direct knowledge by the soul of material things within a range, innate in gods and hell-beings and acquired by others (TS 1.21–22, 1.27).
One who has 'shaken off' all worldly ties, a liberated wanderer who behaves like a child, madman or dullard; the teacher of King Yadu.

Defined syllable by syllable: a — free of the noose of hope, ever in bliss; va — free of vāsanās, living in the present; dhū — dust-grey limbs, cleansed mind, free of concentration and meditation; ta — held to truth, free of anxiety, darkness and ego.
The renouncer who has shaken off saṃsāra, beyond castes and stages, without marks or rules; etymologized syllable by syllable.
The yogī who has 'shaken off' all conventions and bonds and abides in the supreme state; the ideal described in the sixth upadeśa of the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati; addressed in Hindi as 'avadhū'.
In the Mahānirvāṇa, the saṃnyāsa of the Kali age (8.221); four kinds, complete (paramahaṃsa) and incomplete (14.142-149).
The vīra renunciant who holds 'I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava' (Nirvāṇa Tantra 14.6).
The 'avadhū' whom Kabīr addresses in many songs — the Nāth yogī, challenged to find the Lord within rather than in yogic garb and feats.
The first stage of sensory knowledge: the bare grasping of an object after contact (TS 1.15).
The protective 'veiling' of the deity or offering, made with the right fist and extended index finger turned around.
Inviting the deity into an image for worship; not done for the iṣṭaliṅga, in which Śiva already abides from initiation (SSM 10.44–47).
The bodhisattva who can no longer turn back from full awakening, known by signs (Aṣṭa ch. 17); in the Pure Land sūtras those born in Sukhāvatī attain it.

cross_language.form: butuizhuan 不退轉 / abiba zhi 阿鞞跋致

definitions.definition: Inexpressible: the status of the person, which cannot be stated as other than or the same as the aggregates; a fifth category of knowables.
The fourth predication: a thing as simultaneously existent and non-existent cannot be expressed in one word.
The kapha in the chest that supports the trika and heart and the other seats of kapha (AHS Sū 12.15-16; Su Sū 21.14 describes the function without the name).
Being held in contempt by all beings, sought by the second-stage ascetic.
Eating less than one's fill (Śvetāmbara ūnodarī) (TS 9.19).

An 'enclosure' of the Śrīcakra: each of its nine concentric parts, from the square to the point, with its presiding goddess (cakreśvarī), class of yoginīs, attendant deities and mudrā, worshipped in turn (navāvaraṇa-pūjā).
Obstruction; three — of karma (the deadly acts), of defilement (intense defilement), of ripening (bad destinies, Kuru, non-perceiving gods).
The veiling power of māyā that covers knowledge.
The veiling power of ignorance, which hides the self as a small cloud hides the sun from the viewer.
The half of the time-wheel in which happiness, lifespan and virtue decline through six periods; the present age is its fifth period (TS 3.27).
The practitioner's fixed stations until the gain: manifest, unmanifest, conquest, cutting, completion.
Tamil avattai: the five states among the ninety-six principles — cākkiram, coppaṉam, cuḻutti, turiyam, turiyātītam.
State of the soul: waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond the fourth.
Avattai: the soul's states; also the three great conditions kēvalam (isolation with āṇava), cakalam (embodied) and cuttam (purified).
Change in the strength or condition of a present property (e.g. impressions of stilling growing strong; a pot's newness turning to age) (3.13, YBh 3.13, 3.15).
'Pertaining to states': the Vaibhāṣika interpretation of dependent origination, one of four kinds (momentary, prolonged, connected, of states).

The six obligatory daily practices: equanimity, praise of the twenty-four, salutation, repentance, body-abandonment and renunciation (for householders the Digambaras also teach six daily duties: worship, service of the teacher, study, restraint, austerity, giving).
Viṣṇu's manifestation of his own eternal body of consciousness and bliss, not a birth of flesh; the avatāras are wholly identical with him and flawless.
The Lord's coming into being age after age by his own māyā to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (BhG 4.6–8); the noun itself is not used in the Gītā.
The Lord's successive manifestations (prādurbhāva), foretold by Nārāyaṇa to Nārada (MBh 12.326.72–94).

A descent of the Lord in a form for the protection of the world; innumerable, the principal ones listed as twenty-two (BhP 1.3), ten (Agni, Garuḍa) and in other lists; all are portions and parts, but Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3.28).
The incarnations come from the regions of Kāl to maintain order in the creation; the Saints come from the highest region to take souls home and are above them.
Kabīr's descents in the four ages are not avatāras of Viṣṇu but comings of the Sat Puruṣ's messenger; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś are Kāl's sons.
The Lord's real descent in a body of pure sattva by his own will, not from karma.
The uprooting of desire (Kuṟaḷ ch. 37), desire being the seed of all births.
The third stage: the definite ascertainment of the particular (TS 1.15).
(1) A member of the demonstrative statement — proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion (NS 1.1.32); (2) a part of a whole.
A part, in which the whole (avayavin) inheres.
A new substance over and above its parts, inhering in them and perceived (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17).
The notion of the whole form (e.g. 'woman', 'man') with its embellishments that causes the faults (NS 4.2.3; NBh).
Unshakeable confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha, with the virtues dear to the noble ones — the mirror of the Dhamma of the stream-enterer (DN 16).
The eighteen qualities exclusive to a Buddha: ten powers, four confidences, three applications of mindfulness, great compassion.
'Hatred is appeased by non-hatred: this is an eternal law' (Dhp 5; Vin Mv 10.2).
A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: possession [of the soul by the Lord's qualities].
Among the siddha's powers: he 'enters all' and none can enter him (sarvāṃś cāviśati ... anāveśyaḥ).
Viṣṇu's special presence in a soul (as distinct from an avatāra); one must know which beings are his avatāras and which are only his āveśas.
Faith by understanding in the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha and morality, obtained on the path of seeing.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Vijñānabhikṣu: non-separation — souls and prakṛti are not separate from Brahman, their substrate, though distinct; his preferred name for the relation.
The released soul's non-separation from Brahman (BS 4.4.4).
Jayarāśi's description of everyday practices, which go on though no principle is established.

Taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self (2.5); the field of the other afflictions (2.4) and the cause of the conjunction (2.24); not the absence of knowledge but a contrary cognition (YBh 2.5).

Ignorance: in Śaṅkara, superimposition itself (the non-discrimination of self and not-self); in later Advaita, a beginningless, positive, indescribable power that veils Brahman and projects the world, removed by knowledge alone.
One positive ignorance having pure consciousness as its locus and object.
Ignorance residing in the individual selves (many, one per jīva), with Brahman as its object.

In the Tattvasamāsa, the five-jointed avidyā = the five errors (Tattvasamāsa 12; Kramadīpikā). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra denies that bondage is caused by an avidyā that is unreal (SS 1.20–26) or that avidyā is the world's material cause (SS 5.65).

Ignorance: those living in it think themselves wise and go round like the blind led by the blind (KU 1.2.5; MuU 1.2.8); Īśa 9-11 pairs it with vidyā (read by some as rites); the perishable is avidyā (ŚU 5.1); the teacher takes one across to the far shore of avidyā (PrU 6.8).
VP 6.7.11: taking non-self for self and what is not one's own as 'mine'; VP 1.5.5: fivefold avidyā arising first in creation; VP 6.7.61: the third, 'avidyā-karma' śakti.
A real, beginningless covering in each soul, twofold: one covering the soul's own nature and qualities, one covering (the soul's knowledge of) the Supreme; removed only by the Lord.
Defective cognition arising from defects of the senses and from impressions (VS 9.25–26 C); doubt, error, indefinite cognition and dream (Praśastapāda).

Not an indescribable cosmic ignorance but karma (the third power 'avidyā-karma' of Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.61) and the ignorance it causes in the soul — the contraction of its knowledge and the mistaking of body for self.
The beginningless ignorance covering the jīvas (Kulārṇava 1.9).
Ignorance: a distinct dharma opposed to knowledge, not mere absence of knowledge; as the first limb, the past defilements; as the root, a separate outflow.
Ignorance, which Jñāneśvar's Amṛtānubhava argues cannot exist in the self-luminous reality at all.

equivalents.note: Used interchangeably in Advaita texts (Vedāntasāra prefers ajñāna).
Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

notes: Not the cosmic ignorance of Advaita.

definitions.definition: The subtle, beginningless ignorance that arhats and pratyekabuddhas have not removed; only buddhas remove it.
Not knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation and the way (SN 12.2); the first link of dependent origination, the last fetter and one of the effluents; it has the effluents as its origin (MN 9).
Not knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation and the way; the first link.

equivalents.note: same word; in the suttas not knowing the four truths, not a cosmic power or the locus of an illusory world as in Advaita

definitions.definition: Unmanifest matter: a good or bad continuum derived from the elements, produced by manifest action or concentration, which persists even when the mind is distracted or absent; the substance of vows and non-vows.
Not a real entity; what is called avijñapti is the specific transformation of the series produced by volition.

cross_language.form: rnam par rig byed ma yin pa

definitions.definition: Unmodified transformation: Brahman becomes the world without any change in itself, as gold in ornaments.
Kāśī, where Rudra gives the tāraka to the dying; located in the body between brows and nose.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: That by which all this is pervaded is indestructible (2.17); the knower knows the embodied one as indestructible (2.21).
Freedom from remorse, the purpose of wholesome virtue and the basis of gladness (AN 11.1).
The fourth guṇasthāna: right view attained but no vows yet taken.
Non-abstention: the mind's greed for contact with objects (YBh 1.30).
In Jain usage the lack of renunciation of violence and the other sins — the second cause of bondage (TS 8.1).

equivalents.note: Yoga Sūtra 1.30 avirati is craving for sense objects; the Jain term is non-renunciation of the five sins.

definitions.definition: Manifestation and concealment: Brahman's being, consciousness and bliss are manifest or concealed in its forms; creation and dissolution are manifestation and concealment, not origination and destruction.
The five subtle elements, which lack the calm, turbulent and dull differentiation (SK 38).
The second level: the five tanmātras and I-am-ness alone (2.19, YBh 2.19).
Inference proceeding by difference, negating (the alternatives) — the śeṣavat kind (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Uttering meaningless, repetitive or self-contradictory words.

notes: From the sūtra 'api tad bhāṣeta'.

definitions.definition: Acting as one who cannot tell pure from impure, fit from unfit (e.g. handling sticks and clods), without breaking the restraints.

notes: From the sūtra 'api tat kuryāt'; Ratnaṭīkā: apitatkaraṇa.

definitions.definition: The failure to discriminate puruṣa from prakṛti, the cause of their conjunction and so of bondage (SS 1.55); beginningless, removed by discrimination like darkness by light; bondage is non-discrimination alone (SS 6.12–16). The manifest and unmanifest are 'non-discriminating' (SK 11).
The questions the Buddha set aside (world eternal or not, finite or not, soul same as body or not, Tathāgata after death in four ways) because not beneficial (MN 63; MN 72; SN 44.10).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The embodied one is called unmanifest (2.25); beings have an unmanifest beginning and end and are manifest only in the middle (2.28).

Prakṛti in its unmanifest state: uncaused, eternal, pervasive, inactive, one, unsupported, non-merging, partless and independent — the opposite of the manifest (SK 10) — and known through its effects (SK 8, 14–16).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka the self as knower of the field, and one of the eightfold prakṛti (Śā 1.61-63); in Suśruta the uncaused cause of all beings, threefold in guṇas, support of many knowers of the field (Su Śā 1.3).
The unmanifest: higher than the great self, below the person (KU 1.3.11, 2.3.8).

The unmanifest: from which beings emerge at Brahmā's day (BhG 8.18); another eternal unmanifest beyond it is the Imperishable (8.20); worshipped by some (12.1–5); in the Mokṣadharma the field, prakṛti (12.294.38).
'The unmanifest' (Kaṭha 1.3.11), which the sūtras deny to be Sāṃkhya's pradhāna (BS 1.4.1); Brahman is also called unmanifest (3.2.23).
A name of māyā, the unmanifest power of the Lord (VC 108).

notes: Whether this is the Sāṃkhya pradhāna is debated (Brahma Sūtra 1.4.1).

definitions.definition: The second-stage ascetic who hides his Pāśupata sign while his conduct is manifest.
The second stage, in which birth and sign are hidden and the ascetic courts dishonour among people.
A property that occurs in a locus only in part (e.g. monkey-contact in a tree), coexisting with its own absence — a test case for definitions of pervasion.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of that by which all this is pervaded, which no one can destroy (2.17), and of the self known as indestructible and unborn (2.21).
'This self is Brahman' (Māṇḍūkya 2): the practice sentence (abhyāsa-vākya), mahāvākya of the Atharvaveda and of Jyotirmaṭh.
A fast day with one meal of plain boiled grain without salt, oil, spices or milk, central to the Navapada Olī.

The arc between the moving equinox and the fixed starting point of the sidereal zodiac; the siddhāntas treat the solstitial points as oscillating (the Sūrya Siddhānta's libration of 27°), and schools differ on its value.
The six internal (eye … mind) and six external (forms … mental objects) bases, 'the all' (SN 35.23); also the formless 'spheres' and 'that sphere' of Ud 8.1.
The temple (built by another) where the first-stage practitioner lives; the Ratnaṭīkā says it stands for the teacher.
The twelve bases (six internal, six external); also the formless 'spheres'.
Sense-base, 'gate of arising' of mind and mental factors: twelve (six faculties, six objects).

notes: Homonym of the Buddhist technical term āyatana (sense-base).

definitions.definition: The fourteenth guṇasthāna: all activity stopped, lasting the time to utter five short syllables before liberation.
Beings (bodies) not born from wombs exist, also on the evidence of the Veda (VS 4.2.9 C).
Rests on the purity of mind and supports karma and defilements, as wind rests on space (RGV 1.55-57).
Vitality, on which the five faculties depend and which depends on heat (MN 43).
Karma fixing the lifespan in one of four destinies; bound once in a life (TS 8.10).

The 'gift of life': methods of computing the length of life from the planets' positions — the rival methods of Maya, the Yavanas, Maṇittha, Parāśara, Jīvaśarman and Satya, of which Varāhamihira prefers Satya's (BJ 7).

The science in which the wholesome and unwholesome, happy and unhappy life, what is good and bad for life, and its measure are taught (Ca Sū 1.41); so called because in it life is found or by it one attains life (Su Sū 1.15); it makes life known by its own marks (Ca Sū 30.23). It is beginningless and eternal (Ca Sū 30.27), an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6). Synonyms: śākhā, vidyā, sūtra, jñāna, śāstra, lakṣaṇa, tantra (Ca Sū 30.31).

cross_language.note: Tibetan rendering of āyurveda (recalled)

definitions.definition: The union of body, senses, mind and self; its synonyms are dhāri, jīvita, nityaga and anubandha (Ca Sū 1.42); the continuance of consciousness (Sū 30.22); fourfold as happy or unhappy, wholesome or unwholesome (Sū 1.41, 30.24); in Śārṅgadhara the union of body and breath (Pūrva 5.52).
Rites and hymns for long life (AVŚ 8.1–2; VS 3.62).
Souls bound in saṃsāra by beginningless karma, their knowledge contracted.
In the Dāsbodh: The bound person sunk in the world, first of the four conditions.

The three states of processed mercury in the doctrine: swooned it removes disease, 'dead' it revives, bound it gives sky-going (Rasārṇava 1.19; Rasahṛdaya 1.3); the same said of breath. RESTRICTED: the tests and processes are not recorded.
A pseudo-reason whose probandum's absence is known by another means of knowledge ('fire is not hot').
Sublation: the cancellation of a cognition by a later one that shows its object never was as it appeared (the snake by the rope-cognition); the criterion of the three levels of reality.
The lapse of transferred details that serve no purpose in the ectype, e.g. husking for gold pieces (MS 10.1.1–2).
A later cognition that the object is otherwise, which (with knowledge of a causal defect) alone sets aside a cognition's validity.
The eighth Mahāvidyā; the one-faced Mahārudra, destroyer of the world, is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.14); matched with Kūrma (10.9); goddess of paralysing (stambhana).
The first five limbs; even the inner three are outer relative to seedless samādhi (3.8).
The external power, māyā, which produces the material world and covers the souls turned away from the Lord.
The soul that takes the body and external things for itself (Samādhitantra 5).
Outer worship, e.g. of the Śrīcakra on a physical support; the Yoginīhṛdaya's 'aparā' worship, performed even by Śiva (YH 3.3).
External worship of the deity in liṅga, image, maṇḍala or fire.
Second kind: triple staff, ochre, eight mouthfuls from many houses.
An alternative verse to the Raudrī Gāyatrī for expiation and recitation (usually taken as the Aghora mantra).
The six outwardly visible austerities (TS 9.19).
The ten capacities, operating in the present and presenting objects to the three internal ones (SK 33).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): innate, seasonal/age-born and acquired (Ca Sū 11.36); identified with ojas (Su Sū 15.19).
Bālā Tripurasundarī, the Goddess as a young girl, whose three-syllable vidyā is imparted first at initiation (PKS 1.39).
The five powers — faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom — the faculties become unshakeable; one of the seven groups of the thirty-seven qualities.
Devotion to the teacher, clarity of mind, conquest of opposites, merit and vigilance.
Third view: like wood fire; posture; no distraction; desire to hear (YDS).
The death of one without vows (or without right view), with attachment and fear.
Austerity without right knowledge, 'not worth a sixteenth part' of well-taught dharma.
Kuṇḍalinī as the young ascetic widow seated between the Gaṅgā (iḍā) and Yamunā (piṅgalā), to be seized by force (HYP 3.109–110).
The offering of a victim to the Goddess, taught in the Kālikā Purāṇa's offering chapter with its substitutes and restrictions (67). Restricted: summary only.
Food set out daily for beings (bhūtayajña) (ŚB 11.5.6.2); offerings 'not into fire' (ĀśGS 1.1.2).

A lock that contains the breath: mūla (root), uḍḍiyāna (abdominal) and jālandhara (throat), together the 'three locks' practised by the great Siddhas (HYP 3.74–76); applied at the end of inhalation and of retention (2.45–46).

Bondage comes from error (SK 44) and belongs to prakṛti, which binds herself by seven forms (SK 62–63); it is threefold — to prakṛti, to the modifications, and through gifts (Tattvasamāsa and Kramadīpikā).
The self's threefold connection with the world: the body (seat of experience), the senses (its instruments) and the objects (what is experienced) (Śāstradīpikā).
A lock: uḍḍiyāna, jālandhara and mūla are among the five seals whose knower is fit for success (GŚ 32–37).
The binding of karmic matter with the soul because of the passions, in four aspects: nature, duration, intensity and quantity (TS 8.2–3).
The three locks — root, abdominal, throat.

The hidden correspondence the Brāhmaṇas establish between an element of the rite, the cosmos and the person (e.g. the bricks of the altar = the days and nights of the year = the joints of Prajāpati); knowing the bandhu is what makes the rite effective.
The twelve sub-orders of the Nāth yogīs, said to have been set in order by Gorakhnāth (six from Śiva's and six from Gorakh's panths in one telling).
A disciple of the Kartābhajā, who pays dues through a Mahāśay to the Kartā.
The devotional rāga songs of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva in Brajabuli.
Name for the Lokāyatas as followers of Bṛhaspati; Kamalaśīla calls the deniers of inference 'Bārhaspatyas and others'.
A school of statecraft holding that only economics and government are sciences, the Veda being a cover.

notes: Whether the two uses name the same school is not settled by the texts.

definitions.definition: The strewn grass on which the gods are invited to sit.
'The present': what is here and now, verifiable in the living body; the Bāuls call themselves bartamān-panthī, followers of the present.

equivalents.note: Like perception, bartamān is direct knowledge, but it is specifically the body's own experience and is set against scripture as such.

definitions.definition: The second cleansing act: washing the colon by drawing in water while squatting in navel-deep water (jala-basti); the GS adds a 'dry' basti on the ground.
Medicated enema (decoction or oil), the chief remedy for vāta (AHS Sū 1.25; Ca Sū 25.40 'best of vāta-removers').
A 'madman' (of God): a practitioner who has abandoned convention to seek the Man of the Heart; the word appears in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Antya 19) for the God-mad.
Allama's Kannada word for the void — open space without enclosure — in which the devotee, the liṅga and the world disappear.

equivalents.note: Kannada and Sanskrit words used side by side for the void in Allama's vacanas
