The tenth door of the body: in the Amaraughaśāsana the opening of the śaṅkhinī between the royal teeth through which nectar flows, twofold as the path of nectar and the path of death (AmŚ 32, 70); in Hindi Nāth and Sant usage the opening at the crown.
The 'tenth door' at the crown of the head beyond the nine bodily openings, through which the soul goes out to the Lord; Nāth-derived image in Kabīr and Dādū.
Daswān Dwār: the third region above Trikuṭī (also called Sunn), where the soul, free of mind and matter, sees itself as pure spirit.

equivalents.note: Hindi usage places the tenth door at the crown; the Amaraughaśāsana locates it at the śaṅkhinī-mouth in the palate
Both name an opening at the crown; the Sant Mat Daswān Dwār is a region, not only an aperture.

definitions.definition: The ten descents hymned at the opening of the Gīta Govinda — fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Balarāma, the Buddha, Kalki — all borne by Kṛṣṇa.

(1) The devotee's self-understanding as servant of Śiva and his devotees, which Basava asks for in place of 'I am He'; (2) the giving of the fruits of one's work (kāyaka) to the jaṅgamas and the community, and in later usage free communal feeding.

equivalents.note: dāsōha includes service but also names the servant-stance and the sharing of earned wealth

definitions.definition: The attitude and practice of being the Lord's servant, the seventh form of devotion.
Love 'as an eternal servant' (nitya-dāsya, NBS 66); service is one of love's eleven forms (NBS 82).
Servanthood: 'I am the servant, the Lord is the master in the form of all beings' (Hanumān's model).
The servant's devotion that alone is cultivated; the erotic mood and Rādhā are not.
The rasa of servitude: love for Kṛṣṇa as master, with a sense of his superiority.
Agitation of mind from thwarted desire (YBh 1.31).
Compassion: the asuras' 'da' — be compassionate (dayadhvam) (BAU 5.2.3).
Compassion for living beings, which must be guided by knowledge ('first knowledge, then compassion').
The Lord's compassion, personified by Deśika as a goddess in the Dayāśataka; the schools define it differently.
The 'merciful' — the supreme spiritual power of the pure regions, opposed to Kāl, the negative power; Dayāl Deś is the pure spiritual region above Kāl's domain.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The bodies of the eternal embodied one have an end (2.18); in this body come childhood, youth, old age, and so another body (2.13).
The liṅga abiding in the body, worshipped mentally with eight inner flowers, in place of liṅgas of stone, wood or clay (KJN 3.24–31).
Bodily perfection claimed as a fruit of vajrolī (HYP 3.103) and of the haṭha practices generally.
The 'truth of the body': Bāul body-theology, in which the body contains the cosmos, the gods and the Man, and is the only field of practice.
The Sahajiyā doctrine of the inner body with its lakes and lotuses as the eternal Vṛndāvana.

literal: doctrine that the body is the self

definitions.definition: (As reported) The person is the body qualified by consciousness ('I am fat, I am thin').

notes: Sadānanda's Vedāntasāra (tea:vedantasara:refutation) distinguishes Cārvākas who take the gross body, the senses, the breath or the mind as self.

definitions.definition: The transformation of the body by mercury, the supreme purpose of rasa-śāstra, leading to the sky-going state (SDS Raseśvara 23-24).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The one who dwells in the body: passes through the ages of life and into another body (2.13); casts off worn-out bodies as one casts off clothes (2.22); is eternally unslayable in everyone's body (2.30); objects turn away from it when it does not feed on them (2.59); desire deludes it by covering knowledge (3.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The embodied one who, having renounced all actions by the mind, dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action (5.13).
The self as dweller in the body, which passes through bodily stages and into new bodies as one changes clothes (BhG 2.13, 2.22, 2.30); bound in the body by the guṇas (14.5).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

equivalents.note: Used interchangeably for the embodied one in BhG 2.13–30.
The dehin of 2.12–30 is what the commentators call the ātman; the chunk itself uses ātman for the self in 2.55, 3.17, 3.43.

definitions.definition: The final ending of embodiment that is release (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
The supports by whose power the practitioner grows: teacher, people, cave, cremation ground, Rudra.
Temporary further restriction of the area of one's activity (TS 7.21).
The fifth guṇasthāna: the layman with the small vows.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The gods, nourished by sacrifice, nourish human beings in turn and give the enjoyments they desire (3.11–12).
A god; thirty-three in heaven, earth and waters (RV 1.139.11) or 3,339 (3.9.9).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan daēva (demon).

definitions.definition: In Jain cosmology a class of embodied beings of the four orders, born by spontaneous arising, enjoying the fruits of merit, and not liberated; gods cannot take vows or attain liberation directly.
Minor breath causing yawning (SS 3.8).
The divine cloth placed by Śakra on Mahāvīra's shoulder at his renunciation, which he kept for about thirteen months before going naked.
The third gain, sought in the stage of conquest.

That to which an offering is directed as named in the injunction or mantra; subordinate to the sacrificial act, which alone produces the fruit (MS 9.1.9); not established as embodied or eating the offering (Śabara).
The deity addressed by a verse, recorded with its seer and metre in the Anukramaṇīs; in the person 'all deities dwell as cows in a stall' (AVŚ 11.8.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Deities to whom people sacrifice desiring quick success of their actions in the human world (4.12).
The gods of the Vedas and Purāṇas, one of the four realities: powerful beings who can give worldly fruit but are themselves bound and cannot liberate; not to be worshipped.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The bright path of fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the northern course, by which knowers of Brahman go to Brahman and do not return (BhG 8.24).
The path of the gods, distinct from death's own path (RV 10.18.1) and from the fathers' (10.88.15).

The path of the gods: through flame, day, the waxing fortnight, the northern course, the year (or the gods' world), the sun, the moon and lightning, where a non-human person leads to brahman; those who go by it do not return (ChU 4.15.5, 5.10.1-2; BAU 6.2.15; PrU 1.10; KauU 1.3).
The path of the gods, beginning with light (arcis), by which meditators go to Brahman/the Brahma-world without return (BS 4.3.1).

notes: U05's contribution (the Gītā's form of the Upaniṣadic doctrine).

definitions.definition: The Goddess; for Śāktas the supreme deity, called Mahādevī, Parā Śakti, Ambikā, of whom all goddesses are forms (Devī Māhātmya 11).

The Buddha's teaching, well proclaimed, visible here and now (AN 6.10); what is seen by seeing dependent origination (MN 28); also any phenomenon ('all dhammas are not-self'), a mental object (the fourth satipaṭṭhāna) and a quality.

equivalents.note: same word; the Brahmanical dharma is primarily duty and cosmic order

definitions.definition: In the Abhidhamma, an elementary constituent of experience that bears its own nature; the matrices classify all dhammas, conditioned and unconditioned.
The dust-free eye of Dhamma: 'whatever is subject to arising is subject to cessation' — stream-entry (SN 56.11; Vin Mv 1.23).
In the canon, an epithet of the Buddha as embodying the Dhamma; in the Dhammakāya tradition, the luminous Buddha-form found within the body at the seventh base.
The inner Buddha-body reached through successive refined bodies at the centre of the body.

Contemplating the hindrances, aggregates, sense bases, awakening factors and the four truths (MN 10; DN 22). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four establishments of mindfulness.
One on the path to stream-entry who accepts the teachings after pondering them with wisdom (MN 70).
The natural course of things; 'it is the norm' for a bodhisatta (DN 14) and for the stages of the path to follow one another without volition (AN 10.2).
The fixed course of things — dependent origination and the three marks — which stands whether Tathāgatas arise or not; a Tathāgata discovers and reveals it (SN 12.20; AN 3.136).
The second factor of awakening, investigating states with wisdom; to be aroused when the mind is sluggish (SN 46.53).

Investigating states with wisdom; nourished by attending to wholesome and unwholesome states (SN 46.51). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.
The teaching and the monastic discipline together, the Teacher after the Buddha's passing (DN 16); like the ocean with eight wonders (Ud 5.5).
Minor breath associated with hiccup in SS 3.8; other texts say it pervades the body and remains after death (recalled).

Lunar mansion dhaniṣṭhā: presiding deity the Vasus (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Mars (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class movable (cara) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Śraviṣṭhā, at whose beginning the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa places the northward turning (VJ r.6); with Jupiter's rising here the sixty-year cycle begins (BS 8.27).

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: The five asterisms from the second half of Dhaniṣṭhā to Revatī, during which certain acts — building roofs, gathering wood, southward journeys and cremation without special rites — are avoided.

notes: Rules from the muhūrta digests; exact sources not checked.

definitions.definition: The ninth sign (Sagittarius), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the thighs of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by Jupiter; dual; of the fire triplicity (later texts); odd, male and cruel (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: taukṣika (BJ 1.8); dignities: — (BJ 1.13).
Fixing the mind on a support - the Lord's form (VP, BhP) or bodily places and the subtle elements (MkP).
Concentration: binding the mind to a place (3.1) — navel, heart-lotus, light in the head, tip of the nose or tongue, or an external object (YBh 3.1).
Concentration, especially the five element-concentrations holding breath and mind in the regions of earth, water, fire, air and space (DYŚ 100–110; GŚ 68–75).
Fixation of the mind, which burns away sin (MDh 6.72).
Holding the mind in concentration: 'established in yogic concentration' at death (BhG 8.12); the concentrations of the Mokṣadharma's yoga (12.289).
Holding the mind in the heart.
Holding, concentration: yoga is the firm holding (dhāraṇā) of the senses (KU 2.3.11); fourth limb in MaiU 6.18.

(1) In Jain epistemology the fourth stage of sensory knowledge: retention enabling memory (TS 1.15). (2) In Jain yoga, concentration — Haribhadra's kāntā view; Hemacandra's five visualised concentrations of embodied meditation (YŚ 7).
Concentration; the five element-concentrations; holding mind in the Self.
Each of the 112 'teachings of the waveless state' of the Vijñāna Bhairava (v. 139); in the Mālinīvijayottara, concentrations on elements, subtle elements and senses (chs. 12-17).
The nāga king and attendant yakṣa of Pārśvanātha, who sheltered him with his hoods during Kamaṭha's assault.
A power of retaining the teaching, and the formula that embodies it; dhāraṇīs protect preachers of the Lotus and are recited for merit and protection.

cross_language.form: tuoluoni 陀羅尼 / zongchi 總持

literal: that which upholds; right order, duty

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The field of the battle is the 'field of dharma' (1.1). In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas and the dharmas of the birth-group perish when a family is destroyed, and adharma prevails (1.40–43); he is bewildered about dharma (2.7). Kṛṣṇa speaks of svadharma: for a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma (dharmya, 2.31, 2.33); one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's (3.35); even a little of 'this dharma' (the yoga of understanding) protects from great fear (2.40).

The whole of right conduct — ritual, moral, social and legal — rooted in the Veda, smṛti, the practice of the good and self-approval (MDh 2.6); it protects when protected and alone follows one after death (MDh 8.15–17; 4.238–242); its tenfold mark is steadfastness, patience, self-control, not stealing, purity, sense-restraint, wisdom, learning, truth and absence of anger (MDh 6.92).
The merit that correct usage of words brings, for which grammar restricts usage (first vārttika).

The upholding order and right conduct: its decline occasions the Lord's descent (BhG 4.7); one's own dharma is better than another's (3.35); it is subtle (MBh 8.49) and its truth hidden (vulgate Yakṣapraśna); from it come artha and kāma (18.5.49); non-cruelty is its highest form (3.297.55).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) leading to upward movement (SK 44), not to liberation; Gauḍapāda defines it by compassion, giving and the yamas and niyamas of the Pātañjala. With knowledge, virtue and the rest cease to act as causes (SK 67).

That from which prosperity and the highest good result (VS 1.1.2); a quality of the self produced by enjoined acts (Tarkasaṅgraha); the knowledge of the categories arises from dharma manifested by the Lord's command (Praśastapāda).

The beneficial object (artha) whose defining mark is Vedic injunction (codanā) — concretely the sacrifice and other enjoined acts, which join a person with the highest good; what is enjoined but harmful (e.g. the Śyena, whose aim is violence) is not dharma.
An object with a purpose, made known by the Veda (Arthasaṅgraha): the sacrifice and the like.
Bhagavad Gītā 4.7–8: dharma, whose decline together with the rise of adharma is the occasion of the Lord's coming into being, and whose firm establishment is one of its purposes, age after age.

Dharma: created by brahman as the power of the ruling power, higher than all; dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); 'practise dharma' (TU 1.11); three branches of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); Naciketas asks for what is other than dharma and adharma (KU 1.2.14); one's own dharma rescues the elemental self (MaiU 4.3).
An ultimate constituent that 'holds its own characteristic' (svalakṣaṇa-dhāraṇa); seventy-five kinds in five groups, existing as real entities (dravya) in all three times.
A momentary event in a series; only present dharmas exist, and many Vaibhāṣika dharmas are mere designations.

In Jainism (1) the medium of motion (dharmāstikāya); (2) the tenfold virtue beginning with forbearance (TS 9.6); (3) the three jewels; (4) the nature of a thing and the protection of beings (Kārttikeyānuprekṣā 478).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

cross_language.note: cognate; the Buddhist senses are defined by the Buddhist units

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Meditation examining the Jina's command, the harm of wrong ways, the fruition of karma and the structure of the universe (TS 9.36); leads to heaven and toward liberation.
The inquiry into dharma through the investigation of Vedic sentences, undertaken after Vedic study and before returning from the teacher's house (MS 1.1.1 with Śabara).
The change of a property-bearer's manifest property (e.g. emergence giving way to stilling; lump to pot) (3.13).
The capacity-yoga in which the qualities arising from destruction-cum-subsidence are given up (at the second apūrvakaraṇa) (YDS).
One who keeps, recites, explains and copies a sūtra; in the Lotus the Tathāgata's messenger.

Attributive consciousness: the soul's (and the Lord's) consciousness as a quality distinct from the self-luminous substrate; eternal, it contracts in bondage through karma and expands fully in liberation; it goes out to objects as a lamp's light.
The Buddha's teaching as a turning wheel; the Saṃdhinirmocana distinguishes three turnings of differing definitiveness.
The totality and true nature of dharmas; in the Avataṃsaka the boundless realm filled by Vairocana in which all worlds interpenetrate; synonym of suchness.
Dharma-knowledge: pure knowledge of the truths regarding the desire realm.
The Buddha as the dharma / suchness, not his physical form: 'the guides have the dharma for body'; not sick, not fed by food; later the first of the three bodies.
The dharmakāya is the tathāgatagarbha freed from defilements; it is permanent, blissful, self and pure and pervades all beings.

equivalents.note: Pali DN 27 'Tathāgata has the dhamma as body' is an epithet; the Mahāyāna makes it a body of the Buddha

definitions.definition: The samādhi of one who, detached even from the highest reflection, has complete discriminative discernment and no other cognitions (4.29, YBh 4.29); from it afflictions and karma cease (4.30).
The tenth bodhisattva ground, at which the bodhisattva is consecrated by the buddhas and rains the dharma like a cloud.

notes: The same compound names the tenth bodhisattva ground (dharmameghā bhūmi) in Mahāyāna; see brw:mahayana-yoga-dharmamegha.

definitions.definition: What upholds; an ordinance or foundation; the first sacrifices were 'the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16 = 1.164.50); the dead go to heaven and earth 'according to dharman' (10.16.3).
Follower through dharma: one of sharp faculties on the path of seeing.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: A single, formless, world-pervading substance that assists (without causing) the motion of souls and matter, as water assists fish (TS 5.17); its absence beyond the world stops the liberated soul at the summit (TS 10.8).
The true nature of things, which cannot be cognized by ordinary consciousness; the Buddha is to be seen from it; it abides whether or not buddhas appear.
The substrate that conforms to properties past, present and not yet determinable (3.14).

The seven bodily tissues — rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and semen — called 'the vitiable' (dūṣya) (AHS Sū 1.13); each is formed from the preceding by its own fire, with essence and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16); in Caraka's wider usage every body-constituent whose balance is health (Sū 1.53; 9.4); in Śā 1.16 the six 'dhātus' of the person are the five elements and consciousness.

The four (or six: with space and consciousness) elements of which a person consists (MN 140; MN 62); the eighteen elements of sense, object and consciousness; also 'element' as in nibbāna-element and 'that element stands' (SN 12.20).
A verbal root, listed in the Dhātupāṭha (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.1: 'bhū and the rest are roots').
The eighteen elements (six faculties, six objects, six consciousnesses); the four great elements; nibbāna as the unconditioned element.
Element, 'lineage' (gotra): eighteen — six faculties, six objects, six consciousnesses; mind (manas) is the consciousness just past, posited to give the sixth consciousness a support.
In Siddha medicine the seven body-constituents (uṭal tātukkaḷ): cāram, ceṉnīr, ūṉ, koḻuppu, eṉpu, mūḷai, cukkilam/curōṇitam; in pharmacy tātu also names the mineral-metal class of drugs.

notes: Other senses (bodily tissue, element) belong to other units.

definitions.definition: The effect sought and the purpose of the tantra (Ca Sū 1.53); health (Sū 9.4).
Metallurgical alchemy; rasa-śāstra is not merely for this (SDS Raseśvara 23); the 'vāda-khaṇḍa' of the Rasaratnākara is for alchemists (vādin) (Rasakhaṇḍa 1.5).
The seven fires by which each tissue is cooked, yielding essence (the next tissue) and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16).

The first of the six cleansing acts: in the HYP the swallowing and withdrawing of a moistened cloth; in the GS a class of four kinds (inner, of the teeth, of the heart, of the root) with their variants.
The visionary thought or insight of the seer, which is 'yoked' (RV 5.81.1) and which Savitṛ is asked to impel (3.62.10).
The discerning intellect whose lapse — seeing the eternal and non-eternal, wholesome and unwholesome wrongly — is a cause of suffering (Ca Śā 1.99).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The steadfast one is not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); the steadfast one, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality (2.15).
The wise, steadfast one: chooses the good over the pleasant (KU 1.2.2); turns his sight inward (KU 2.1.1).
The restraining resolve whose lapse leaves the mind unable to turn from the harmful (Ca Śā 1.100); with smṛti and dhī the means of stopping the stream of body and mind (Śā 2.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The firmness in which the intellect is held while the mind is gradually brought to rest (6.25).
Steadfastness, threefold by the guṇas; the sāttvic holds mind, breath and senses by unswerving yoga (BhG 18.33–35).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The immovable principal image standing for Viṣṇu's partless form.

equivalents.note: common temple usage 'mūlabera'

definitions.definition: Unbroken remembrance of the Lord flowing like a stream of oil, the form that liberating meditation takes (from Chāndogya 7.26.2, 'dhruvā smṛtiḥ').
The seventh Mahāvidyā, 'bearing the form of a widow' and so without a Bhairava (Toḍala 1.13); matched with Varāha (10.9).
The sound or melody of the Word heard within; 'Shabd dhun' is the sound current.
The sacred fire kept burning at a Nāth seat or by a wandering yogī; at Gorakhpur an 'unbroken' dhūnī is ascribed to Gorakhnāth; its ash is given as blessing.
The fire of the Aghora ascetic, often kept in or near the cremation ground.

Ascetic practices (twelve or thirteen in the lists): wearing rag-robes, three robes only, alms-round, one meal, living in the forest, at the root of a tree, in the open, in a charnel ground, sitting without lying down, and others.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The thirteen ascetic practices allowed by the Buddha for effacement and contentment.
The austerities central to forest practice: alms-food only, one meal, forest and charnel-ground dwelling, refuse-rag robes, wandering (tudong).
The audible noise (nāda) produced by effort, which manifests the eternal letters; its loudness increases, not the word (MS 1.1.17).

The audible sound that manifests the sphoṭa; Patañjali calls it a quality of the word (on P 1.1.70); the grammarians distinguish the primary sound that reveals the sphoṭa from the secondary sound responsible for differences of speed and length.

Suggestion: the implied meaning (pratīyamāna) conveyed beyond denotation, and poetry in which it predominates; named after the grammarians' dhvani that manifests the sphoṭa; threefold — suggested fact, figure and rasa (DhĀ 1.1, 1.4, 1.13).

equivalents.note: vyañjanā is the power, dhvani the suggested sense or the poetry

definitions.definition: Sustained meditation on Viṣṇu with his qualities, according to one's fitness, which produces direct knowledge; not a mere subsidiary of hearing.
Meditation: the continuous flow of a single cognition on the place of concentration (3.2); the means of abandoning the afflictions' activities (2.11).
Meditation, which burns away the 'ungodly qualities' and lets one see the course of the inner self (MDh 6.72–73).
VP 6.7.91: one continuous flow of the form's awareness, desiring nothing else; ŚiP 7.2.39: with object and then without.
Meditation is the removal of passion, accomplished through the cessation of mental modifications (SS 3.30–31); meditation is mind without object (SS 6.25).
Meditation: with and without qualities (GŚ 76–77; DYŚ 111–114); gross, of light and subtle (GS 6.1).

Meditation: a rung of the ladder (ChU 7.6); the 'yoga of meditation' by which the sages saw God's power (ŚU 1.3); the friction of meditation (ŚU 1.14); a limb in MaiU 6.18; one sees him 'meditating' (MuU 3.1.8).

In Jainism the stopping of the mind's wandering by fixing it on one object, for up to a muhūrta (TS 9.27); fourfold — sorrowful, cruel, virtuous, pure (9.28), only the last two leading to liberation; 'a steady mind is dhyāna' (Dhyānaśataka).
Meditation with or without qualities; 'so'ham'; one-pointedness on consciousness.
Meditative absorption, four, both as births (heavens) and as attainments; the attainment is good one-pointedness with its accompaniment; each has its factors.

cross_language.note: Buddhist absorption levels — broader and differently structured

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Meditation as taught in BhG 6.10–32 (a firm seat, erect posture, gaze on the nose-tip, mind fixed on the self or the Lord) and 18.52; in the Mokṣadharma a fourfold dhyāna-yoga (12.188).
The qualified meditator described in the Jñānārṇava and Yogaśāstra (detached, steady in vows, free of passion).
Seeing beings passing away and reappearing according to their deeds (DN 2; MN 4); the second true knowledge.
Knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their kamma; a mundane direct knowledge.
Lifelong limitation of the distance one will travel in each direction (TS 7.21).
'Sky-clad': the naked monk, and the tradition that holds complete nudity necessary for the fully renounced and for liberation.
Called Boṭika (Boḍiya) in Śvetāmbara sources, which trace it to Śivabhūti's schism.

cross_language.note: self-designation
low confidence on form

definitions.definition: One, all-pervading, eternal substance, cause of the notion 'this (is) from here' and of directions (VS 2.2.12 C).

That by which supreme knowledge is given (dī) and the bondage of fetters destroyed (kṣī) (SSM 15.7); in Vīraśaiva practice the liṅga-initiation, with bathing, the whispered five-syllable mantra and the giving of the liṅga into the disciple's hand (6.19–25); by it the duality of guru and disciple is removed (19.6–7).

The consecration that makes the sacrificer fit for the soma rite, with restraint, vigil and tapas; with tapas it is among the powers that uphold the earth (AVŚ 12.1.1) and was first undertaken by the seers (AVŚ 19.41.1).
The consecration of the sacrificer before a Soma rite, by which the priests 'make him an embryo again' (AB 1.3); he keeps vows and is reborn at the final bath.
The consecration for sacrifice counted as the twice-born's third birth (MDh 2.169).
Initiation, threefold: śāktī by the entry of power, śāmbhavī by the placing of the foot, māntrī by mantra (PKS 1.32); Bālā is given first, with a name ending in '-ānandanātha' (PKS 1.39-41).
Consecration of a tested brahmin with mantra-sanctified ash before the southern image, with the hearing of the mantra.
Initiation by touch, sight or piercing (sparśa, dṛk, vedha), given only after mutual testing (Kulārṇava 14); there is no initiation higher than the Śākta (12.12).
Initiation in which a qualified guru gives the mantra to a qualified, tested disciple (ŚT 2.141–153).
Initiation into Hari's worship and mantra by the ācārya (with the sipping of the Lord's foot-water and vows); those without it are called 'beasts among men'.

The rite performed on the soul — not on caste or body — by which the guru, empowered by Śiva's mantras, joins the soul to Śiva and destroys its bonds; it is the cause of the other means (ritual, knowledge, conduct).
Initiation into Bhagavān's mantras and worship, in Śrīvaiṣṇava usage centred on the five sacraments (pañcasaṃskāra).

Initiation, in many forms (TĀ 14-22); for one who knows the Heart, initiation needs no sesame and ghee (Parātrīśikā 25); Spanda calls identification with the meditated 'the initiation of nirvāṇa' (SK 2.7).
Initiation, so called because it gives divine knowledge and destroys sin; the guru gives the mantras (gopāla-mantra, kāma-gāyatrī), which are not published.
Two initiations: the refuge mantra (nāma-nivedana) and the brahmasambandha.

notes: The vacana and manual tradition speak of three modes (by touch, by mantra, by rite: vedhā, mantra, kriyā) — moderate confidence.

definitions.definition: Material (the threefold effect: disciple's and teacher's knowledge, the kalās such as darbha, ash, sandal, thread, flowers, incense, mantras, and the brahmin to be consecrated), time (forenoon), rite, image and teacher.
The daily regimen of the healthy: rising at the brāhma muhūrta, cleansing, collyrium, nasal oil, gargling, oil massage, exercise, bathing, conduct and timely sleep (AHS Sū 2; Ca Sū 5; Su Ci 24).
A company of Vārkarī pilgrims walking and singing together behind a flag, with cymbals (ṭāḷ) and drum, as a unit of the vārī.
'Live as islands to yourselves, with the Dhamma as island' (DN 16; SN 47.13); nibbāna is 'the island' (SN 43.44).
Fourth view: like a lamp; breath-control (inner sense); no agitation; hearing (YDS).
(Jain report) Six wandering teachers who drew the Mahānimitta from the Pūrvas and taught Gosāla.
Five grounds for holding supreme nibbāna here and now: sense pleasure, or one of the four absorptions.
A view or theory, especially the speculative views (the sixty-two of DN 1, the ten undeclared of MN 72) that are 'a thicket, a fetter of views'; right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is the first path factor.
A speculative view; the sixty-two grounds are views of those who do not know or see, conditioned by contact and craving.
View; as an unwholesome factor, wrong view, especially of self and of the world.
The sixty-two grounds as a fine-meshed net in which every theorist is caught.
A trainee who has understood and reviewed the teaching with wisdom (MN 70).
The divine eye given by Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna to see the universal form (BhG 11.8) and by Vyāsa to Sañjaya to see the war (MBh 6.2).

The body 'born of the creation of Hara and Gaurī' (mercury and mica), permanent though the six-sheathed body is not; to be produced first by the yogin seeking jīvanmukti (SDS Raseśvara 7-9; Rasahṛdaya 1.7).
The divine body of the perfected yogī (a Nāth synonym of siddha-deha).
The 108 temples sung by the Āḻvārs (106 on earth, with the Milky Ocean and Vaikuṇṭha), where the Lord abides in his image form.
A temple site of the Lord sung by the Āḻvārs; 108 in the reckoning (106 on earth with the Milk Ocean and Paramapadam).
A year of the gods, equal to 360 human years (a human year is a day and night of the gods).
The highest disposition, in which the worshipper sees all as divine; by the Kālīvilāsa's account proper to the Satya–Tretā ages.

The 'divine sound' of the omniscient Jina: a single, undifferentiated sound issuing from his whole body at set times, without movement of lips, which the gaṇadharas render into scripture and all beings understand.
Śvetāmbaras speak rather of the Jina's speech in Ardhamāgadhī, understood by all beings in their own languages.
The Tīrthaṅkara's teaching-sound, understood by every being in its own language (Digambara: a sound without syllables emanating from his body).
'Divine sage': the Śrīvaiṣṇava honorific for the Āḻvārs, whose lives and works are told in the Divyasūricaritam.
Divine madness: the highest state of mahābhāva in separation, with speech such as citra-jalpa, seen in Rādhā and in Caitanya's last years.

In Āyurveda the three bodily factors vāta, pitta and kapha, which balanced sustain the body and disturbed destroy it (AHS Sū 1.6-7; Ca Sū 1.57), and the two mental doṣas rajas and tamas (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21). Suśruta counts blood with them in origin, maintenance and dissolution (Su Sū 21.3-4).
Characterized by impelling to activity (NS 1.1.18); three groups: attachment, aversion, delusion (NS 4.1.3).
The second unwholesome root (MN 9), one of the three fires (SN 35.28).
Hatred, the unwholesome root; characteristic ferocity.
In Siddha medicine the three humours (Tamil tōṣam, kuṟṟam) — vātam, pittam, kapam — which with the seven tissues make up the ninety-six principles' 'tōṣam 3'.

cross_language.note: the three nyes pa of Tibetan medicine
Pali dosa usually 'hatred'; the humours are named individually (pitta, semha, vāta)

notes: Homonym: in Nyāya and Buddhism 'fault' (attachment, aversion, delusion).
alt_notes: Homonym: in Āyurveda doṣa means the three humours.

definitions.definition: The Lord as relishing, out of motherly love, the very faults of those who take refuge in him.

literal: one for whom faults are enjoyable

definitions.definition: 'The Tamil Upaniṣad': the Śrīvaiṣṇava name for Nammāḻvār's Tiruvāymoḻi.
The seer, the puruṣa: seeing alone, pure, seeing by conforming to cognitions (2.20); the witness of the buddhi (YBh 2.17); its conjunction with the seen is the cause of suffering (2.17).
Puruṣa as seer (SK 19), who sees prakṛti like a spectator once knowledge arises (SK 65).
Cause of the first flowing; natural in water, occasioned (by fire) in earth (ghee) and fire (gold).
What possesses motion and qualities and is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C); nine (VS 1.1.4 C).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the nine substances — five elements, self, mind, time, directions; with senses conscious, without them unconscious (Ca Sū 1.48); the inherent cause in which qualities and action reside (Sū 1.51); every substance is made of the five elements, and nothing in the world is not a medicine when rightly used (Sū 26.10-12).

Six substances make up the universe — soul, matter, the media of motion and rest, space and time; a substance is the existent, endowed with origination, cessation and persistence, and possesses qualities and modes (TS 5.2, 5.29–30, 5.38). Also, in nikṣepa, 'potentiality'.

Substance: synonymous with self, thing, own nature, body and reality; ultimately the Real that all words denote, as gold is denoted by all ornament-words (VP 3.2); Vyāḍi held that words denote the individual substance.

Material worship with substances (water, sandal, flowers, incense, lamp, rice, sweets, fruit — the eightfold pūjā), proper to householders, and inner worship by praise and meditation, proper to all; the first is a means to the second.

Physical sex (the bodily marks) as against psychological sex (the rise of the sexual-desire karma); Digambaras say liberation occurs from any bhāva-veda but only from the male dravya-veda, and read canonical 'female siddhas' as referring to bhāva-veda.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Sacrifice made with material things (4.28), declared inferior to the sacrifice of knowledge (4.33).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The root standpoint that looks to the enduring substance (Sanmati 1.3).
Existing as a real entity (dravya), with its own nature; for the Vaibhāṣika, all dharmas, including those of past and future.
The Vātsīputrīyas deny that the person is dravyasat, while also denying that it is a mere designation.
Firm conception or imagining, the second seed of the mind, identified with vāsanā.
The third-part (decan) of a sign; its figures and the 22nd decan (reckoned for death) are described in BJ 27 and 25.11.

notes: Scholarly account: from Greek dekanos.

definitions.definition: The guru, absorbed in the highest reality, looks fully at the disciple (Kulārṇava 14.55).
The liberated's power of knowing: seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing (all treatises) and omniscience.

equivalents.note: Kauṇḍinya calls the same power jñānaśakti (PABh 5.46)

definitions.definition: One who surrenders and waits until his begun karma is exhausted.
Perception, defined as determination concerning each object (SK 5); in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, the cognition that, in contact, reflects its object's form (SS 1.89).

literal: to be experienced in the seen (present) birth

definitions.definition: Karma ripening in this life, e.g. from intense practice or grave harm (2.12, YBh 2.12).
A thing about which ordinary people and critical examiners agree (NS 1.1.25).
A parable by which Cakradhar illustrated a teaching, collected in the Dṛṣṭāntapāṭh.
The fixed gaze of the yogin — at the nose-tip, between the brows, or outward while attending to the inner target (śāmbhavī); in trāṭaka it is unblinking.
View; as a latent defilement, five: satkāya-view, view of extremes, wrong view, attachment to views, attachment to rules and observances.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: A planet's 'glance' at other houses: all aspect the 7th fully, and the 3rd/10th, 5th/9th and 4th/8th partially; Saturn, Jupiter and Mars aspect these respectively in full (BJ 2.13).

notes: Homonym of dṛṣṭi 'view' (Jain/Buddhist); id disambiguated.

definitions.definition: The doctrine that perception is creation: objects exist only while perceived, as in dream (Prakāśānanda).
The seen, the whole world of objects; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha's teaching turns on the realization that the seen does not exist apart from consciousness.
The seen: of the nature of illumination, activity and inertia, consisting of elements and senses, for experience and liberation (2.18), existing for the seer's sake (2.21).
Wiping away of the seen: the mind's erasure of the world through the knowledge 'the seen does not exist', from which the bliss of nirvāṇa arises.
Deceit and injurious intent; wrongs against the gods (RV 7.86.5 'drugdhāni').

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan druj (the Lie).

definitions.definition: Pain, the first accompaniment of distraction, threefold — from oneself, other beings, the gods (1.31, YBh 1.31); for the discerning everything is suffering (2.15); future suffering is what is to be avoided (2.16).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Pleasure and pain come from sense-contacts (2.14) and are to be made the same (2.38); the steady-minded is not agitated in sorrows (2.56); in serenity all sorrows cease (2.65).
Characterized by affliction (NS 1.1.21); twenty-one kinds (Vācaspati); its absolute cessation is liberation.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Contact-born enjoyments are wombs of sorrow (5.22); yoga destroys sorrow for one measured in food, rest and effort (6.17); in the state of yoga one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow (6.22); yoga is defined as the unyoking from union with sorrow (duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyoga) (6.23).
Of the self (bodily and mental), from beings and from the gods; also fivefold as womb, birth, ignorance, old age and death.
Suffering: everything with outflows is suffering by the three kinds of suffering (of pain, of change, of conditioned existence).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Liberation: twofold - the absolute cessation of all suffering, and the attainment of lordship consisting in the powers of knowing and acting; reached through the Lord's grace.
Yāmuna reports it as the absolute cessation of pain understood as the destruction of the soul's special qualities (opponent's report).

equivalents.note: the Pāśupata name for liberation; it adds the Lord's powers to cessation
Nyāya's apavarga is cessation only; the Pāśupatas insist theirs is more (SDS 6/3)

definitions.definition: The three kinds of suffering that prompt the inquiry (SK 1): internal, from other beings, and from the divine (named by the commentaries); their complete cessation is the supreme goal (SS 1.1).
Bad company, to be shunned in every way, as the source of desire, anger, delusion and ruin (NBS 43–45).

The first noble truth: birth, ageing, illness, death, union with the disliked, separation from the liked, not getting what one wants — in brief the five aggregates of clinging (SN 56.11); also one of the three marks, applying to all formations (AN 3.136).
The second characteristic and first truth; 'there is suffering but no one who suffers'.

equivalents.note: same word; Sāṃkhya and Yoga also begin from duḥkha, with a different account of its cause and end

definitions.definition: (Ājīvika, as reported) The end that fool and wise alike reach after the fixed round of 8,400,000 great aeons.
(Early Buddhist) The end reached by cutting off craving, not by transmigration.
A holy sound like a bull's bellow made by touching tongue-tip to palate; part of the offering.

notes: Also written huḍukkāra (SDS, Ratnaṭīkā) and dunduṃkāra (Sagar text).

definitions.definition: Texts other than and contrary to the true scriptures; Janārdana is not known through them; some are said to have been produced to delude.
The seventh of the ten bodhisattva grounds in the Daśabhūmika.
'Hard to approach': the Goddess as the warrior who destroys demons and protects devotees; her nine forms are worshipped in Navarātri.
The 6th, 8th and 12th houses — enemies and disease, death, loss — whose lords and occupants afflict.
'The end of the twelve' above the head, where the haṃsa dissolves and a throbbing garland of jewels is seen (KJN 13.6; 17.18).
The point twelve finger-breadths beyond (above or outside) the body where the breath ends and the mind is to be cast (VBT 28, 50-51).
Duality: 'where there is duality, as it were, one sees another' (BAU 2.4.14, 4.5.15).

The usual outside name for Madhva's Vedānta, stressing real difference; Madhva himself reads 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya as what is 'known otherwise' (wrongly) and 'advaita' as the Lord who has no equal.
'Dual-non-dual': name of Nimbārka's Vedānta, synonymous with svābhāvika-bhedābheda.

equivalents.note: the school uses both names

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The pairs such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (6.7); one who has gone beyond them (dvandvātīta) is not bound though acting (4.22); one free of them (nirdvandva) is easily released from bondage (5.3).
Pairs such as cold and heat, which no longer assail one who has mastered posture (2.48); bearing them is austerity (YBh 2.32).
The pairs such as heat and cold, pleasure and pain, from which one should be free (BhG 2.45, 5.3); the delusion of opposites born of desire and aversion (7.27).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The third strength; endurance of heat and cold and the like, as cows and deer endure them.
The third age, in which worship/service (paricaryā, arcana) is the principal means; in each Dvāpara a Vyāsa divides the Veda and condenses the Purāṇa.
The six feigned behaviours (snoring, trembling, limping, amorous gestures, senseless acts, senseless speech) that are 'doors' to the increase of merit and loss of demerit by producing dishonour.
The two-sentence mantra of surrender: in the first the soul takes refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa with Śrī; in the second it prays for service to the divine couple.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: With rāga, set in each sense towards its object — a waylayer not to be yielded to (3.34); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); the one of steady wisdom neither rejoices nor hates (2.57).
Aversion, which follows on pain (2.8).
A mark and special quality of the self; as a fault, one of the three groups (NS 4.1.3); 'aversion is anger' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A member of the first three classes, born a second time by initiation (MDh 2.169–171; 10.4).
One of the seven concentric island-continents of Bhū-maṇḍala (Jambu, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, Puṣkara), each ringed by an ocean.
The product of two atoms, still imperceptible; through dyads and so on the gross elements arise (Praśastapāda).
Heaven, paired with Earth.
The doctrine that there is only one jīva, other beings being appearances within its ignorance, as figures in a dream.
The aikya sub-stage in which, contemplating the universe as made of Śiva, one's self is the single vessel of Śiva (SSM 14.28–33).
Four grounds for holding some beings eternal and others not: Brahmā as creator, gods corrupted by play, gods corrupted by mind, and the reasoner's eternal mind.
Renouncer with a single staff; truly, 'one who bears the staff of knowledge'.

The eleven forms in which the one love appears: attachment to the Lord's qualities and glory, form, worship, remembrance, service, friendship, parental love, conjugal love, self-offering, absorption, and supreme separation (NBS 82).

equivalents.note: overlapping lists: remembrance, worship, service, friendship and self-offering are common; NBS adds form, parental and conjugal love, absorption and separation, and lacks hearing, singing, feet-service and obeisance as separate items

definitions.definition: The eleventh lunar day of both fortnights, kept by fasting, with detailed rules for days overlapped by the tenth.
The eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, kept with fasting for Viṣṇu; so powerful by the Nārada's praise that Yama's realm was emptied.
Unification of mind, which is concentration (MN 44); a factor of the jhānas (MN 111).
Unification of mind on its object; a universal factor, developed as concentration and the jhāna factor.

equivalents.note: same word
Yoga uses ekāgratā for a level of mind; the Abhidhamma makes it a factor present in every consciousness

definitions.definition: The one-pointed mind, in which samprajñāta yoga occurs (YBh 1.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 6.12: seated on the seat, making the mind one-pointed, one should practise yoga for purification of the self.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The definition of meditation in TS 9.27.
One-pointedness of mind, a mental property that rises as all-objectness dwindles (3.11–12); a fruit of purity (2.41).

cross_language.note: a jhāna factor

definitions.definition: The state in which the subsiding and arising cognitions are alike (3.12).
A form or companion of Tārā in the Tārā cycle.
'The One Being the inspired call by many names' (RV 1.164.46).

equivalents.note: Both name the One of the speculative hymns; 1.164.46 speaks of the One named by the gods' names, 10.129 of That One before creation.

definitions.definition: An absolutist view that takes one aspect for the whole; the root of all rival doctrines in the Jain analysis.

The dharma of the ekāntins, the best and dear to Nārāyaṇa, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga, by which one goes to the imperishable Hari (MBh 12.336.4, 12.336.69); sung by the Lord to Arjuna before the battle (12.336.8).
One devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, dwelling in the White Island or entering Vāsudeva directly without the intermediate goals (MBh 12.323.26; 12.336.3–4; 12.332.18).
The one-pointed devotee, 'chief' among devotees (NBS 67), who purifies families, holy places and scriptures.
Taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone, to the exclusion of every other deity and of Vedic rites; the defining principle of Śaṅkaradeva's dharma.
Resting the mind on a single principle to counter the obstacles (1.32, YBh 1.32).
(Jain report) That the one knower appears manifold throughout the world, as one earth-mound appears manifold.
Oneness with the Lord (merging), the fifth kind of liberation, which pure devotees do not accept.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Established in oneness, the yogin worships the Lord as abiding in all beings and abides in him however he lives (6.31).

equivalents.note: later Vaiṣṇava lists name the fifth liberation sāyujya; the Bhāgavata verse says ekatva

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

literal: with unity and reasoning, without shifting

definitions.definition: The second pure meditation: fixed on one aspect without shifting; it destroys the remaining destructive karmas and yields omniscience (TS 9.39, 9.42).
Being one sentence with another, by which arthavādas and subsidiary statements share the purport of an injunction (MS 1.2.7, 2.1.46).
The Vrātya become sole lord (AVŚ 15.1.6).
The single buddha-vehicle: the three vehicles are its skillful presentation (Lotus 2-3); the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles enter the great vehicle (Śrīmālā 5).
Name of the Veda-branch claimed as the root of the Pāñcarātra; Vedānta Deśika's Pāñcarātrarakṣā gives primary eligibility to the Ekāyanins.

notes: The Chāndogya (7.1.2) lists an 'ekāyana' among Nārada's studies; the identification is the tradition's.

definitions.definition: The SSM's elaboration of the path into 101 sthalas — 44 on the side of the soul (aṅga) and 57 on the side of the liṅga — from piṇḍa to jñānaśūnya (1.28–31; 15.1–3).
The one-stringed drone instrument of the Bāul singer, a sign of the one Truth.
Sin as a burden or stain, one's own or inherited from the fathers, from which Varuṇa is asked to release (RV 7.86.5, 7.89.5).

The eight qualities of the Lord (Kuṟaḷ 9's 'eṇkuṇattāṉ'), glossed by Parimēlaḻakar from the Śaiva Āgamas: self-dependence, pure body, natural understanding, omniscience, natural freedom from bonds, boundless grace, infinite power, boundless bliss.
Read by Jain interpreters of the Kuṟaḷ as the eight qualities of a liberated Siddha (reported here from the dispute; U34 may refine).
The eight examinations of Siddha diagnosis: pulse (nāṭi), touch (paricam), tongue (nā), colour (niṟam), voice (moḻi), eyes (viḻi), stool (malam) and urine (mūttiram).

equivalents.note: Āyurveda's later eightfold examination (aṣṭavidha-parīkṣā) overlaps

definitions.definition: The three desires to be pursued: for life, for wealth and for the other world (Ca Sū 11.3).
Desire, pursuit: the three desires — for sons, for wealth and for worlds — which knowers of the self rise above to live as mendicants (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22).
The three desires — for wife/sons, wealth and worlds — risen above in renunciation.
Desire, pursuit; the 'three desires' (ēṭaṇai mūṉṟu) of the ninety-six principles, called evil by Kaṭuveḷi.

equivalents.note: Tamil form of eṣaṇā

definitions.definition: The standpoint that applies a word only when the thing is actually performing the action the word names — Indra only while ruling (TS 1.33).
A mendicant; the self-designation of Muslim Bāuls and of Lalon's line ('Lalon Fakir').

A monastic lineage or order among the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjakas (Tapā, Kharatara, Añcala and others), with its own succession of ācāryas, ritual details and calendar; earlier sources use gaṇa, kula and śākhā.
The 'circle of the sky' in the head, where the upside-down well of nectar is (Gorakh Bānī).
The 'sky-circle' in the head where nectar drips, light shines and the unstruck sound is heard; Nāth-derived image in Kabīr and Dādū.

equivalents.note: Both name the highest centre in the head; the Sant image is not systematized as a lotus.

definitions.definition: Vomiting the contents of the stomach by raising apāna to the throat (HYP 2.38); one of the Haṭharatnāvalī's eight acts.
'Elephant-lion' yoga: Jupiter in an angle from the Moon, giving fame and prosperity (later horā texts, e.g. Phaladīpikā 6).
Ornamental oscillation or inflection of a note, essential to the rendering of a rāga.
A Sāmaveda song-book giving the verses transformed into melodies.
Śiva's attendants — the pramathas such as Reṇuka and Dāruka (SSM 2.25–27; 3.67–77) — and by extension the community of devotees whose defence is gaṇācāra.
A group of three syllables classified by its pattern of heavy and light, used to define metres (Piṅgala, ch. 1).

Defence of the faith and the devotees against insult and harm; the SSM bids the devotee protect liṅgas and devotees even at the cost of life and, on meeting a reviler of Śiva, to have him killed, curse him or leave (9.33–36).
Epithet of the six teachers: 'having an order, a following, teacher of a following' (saṅghī gaṇī gaṇācariyo).

A 'holder of the group': one of the chief disciples of a Tīrthaṅkara, who hears his teaching and composes it as scripture and leads a section of the community; Mahāvīra had eleven, headed by Indrabhūti Gautama.
The calculator-astronomer who computes positions and calendars; the lives of such are told in the Gaṇakataraṅgiṇī.

The junctions of water and fire signs (Revatī–Aśvinī, Āśleṣā–Maghā, Jyeṣṭhā–Mūla) and of corresponding tithis and ascendants; birth there endangers the child or parents and requires pacification (BPHS 94).
Quality grasped by the nose; fragrant or not; in earth only.
The third factor (with the parents' union and the mother's season) needed for conception (MN 38); the commentaries read it as the being about to enter the womb.
Sulphur, used with mercury in rasa medicine; impure sulphur is said to cause severe skin disease, burning and giddiness (Rasaratnākara, Rasakhaṇḍa 5.4).

notes: Restricted subject.

definitions.definition: A name of the intermediate being ('eater of smells'); the sūtra's gandharva present at conception is cited as scriptural proof of the intermediate existence.
The sacred music of the gods (dear to the gods, NŚ 28), of notes, rhythm and words; the upaveda of the Sāmaveda.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Four bodily ties: covetousness, ill will, clinging to rules, dogmatic insistence 'this alone is true'.
The Vaikhānasa self-description: made Vaiṣṇavas before birth by the prenatal viṣṇubali rite, they need no further Vaiṣṇava initiation such as branding.
The removal of Mahāvīra's embryo by Hariṇaigameṣin, at Śakra's command, from the brāhmaṇī Devānandā to the kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā; counted among the ten 'wonders' of this era.
Rejected: Mahāvīra was conceived by Triśalā alone.
The western, household fire of the three śrauta fires.
Scriptures of the eastern stream for neutralising poison with Garuḍa mantras.
The eight principles of respect accepted by Mahāpajāpatī as her ordination (Cv 10.1.4; AN 8.51).
Kamma that ripens with priority: the five heinous crimes, fixed wrong view, or the jhānas.
The five destinations: hell, animal realm, ghost realm, humans, gods (MN 12).
One of the four states of embodied existence — hellish, animal, human, divine — determined by karma (TS 2.6, 8.11); also motion.
Destiny: five — hell-beings, ghosts, animals, humans, gods; the intermediate existence is not a destiny.
A sign of the coming destination (hell-fire, a womb, celestial mansions) presenting itself to the dying.
The seven secondary rasas: humour, wonder, heroism, compassion, anger, fear and disgust, appearing within devotion.

Secondary devotion: threefold by the guṇas or by the seeker's motive (the distressed etc.), each earlier better than the later (NBS 56–57); in the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra the practices that lead to supreme devotion.

equivalents.note: Gauḍīya devotion-in-practice likewise leads to bhāva and prema, within a different scheme

definitions.definition: The metre of three eight-syllable lines, and the Sāvitrī verse in it (RV 3.62.10), repeated with the vyāhṛtis (VS 36.3).
The Vedic Gāyatrī read as Śrīvidyā (Tripurātāpinī Upaniṣad); the Pañcadaśī is called the 'full Gāyatrī' and its first meaning is the Gāyatrī meaning (VR 57); the Goddess is the Gāyatrī (LSN 90).

The Sāvitrī mantra (RV 3.62.10) with Oṃ and the vyāhṛtis, repeated at the twilights, and the Goddess Gāyatrī who is its deity; the mantra manuals give its seer (Viśvāmitra), metre (gāyatrī) and deity (Savitṛ), its nyāsa and puraścaraṇa.
A Vedic metre of 24 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
The most complex common recitation (ab ba abc cba abc, …), guarding the order of every word.
The body as 'pot' or vessel in which the Lord dwells ('ghaṭ ghaṭ rām'); the site of the search.
(1) The body as a pot (GS 1.6–8; HYP 2.23). (2) The second stage, when the breath 'made one' enters the middle and prāṇa–apāna, mind–breath, individual and supreme self unite (HYP 4.72; DYŚ 81–83).
Second stage, in which breaths, mind and selves unite.
Scriptural texts (such as the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa and Subāla Upaniṣad) that teach the body–self relation and so reconcile the texts of difference and of non-difference.
Pot-space: space delimited by a pot, stock illustration of the jīva as the one self delimited by bodies (GK 3.3).
The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā's name for its yoga: the body (ghaṭa, 'pot') is baked in the fire of yoga through seven means (GS 1.1–11).
A unit of 24 minutes, a sixtieth of a day; six prāṇas make a vināḍī and sixty vināḍīs a nāḍī (SS 1.11).
The four karmas that obscure the soul's own qualities — knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding and obstructive; their destruction yields omniscience (TS 10.1).
Disgust — first of the eight fetters, overcome in Aghora practice.
'Holder of the mountain': Kṛṣṇa who lifted Govardhana; Mīrā's Giridhar Gopāl or Giridhar Nāgar, her husband and the signature of her songs.
Singing of the Lord's qualities, according to the rules of music; a vocal act of the offering.
The current movement of the planets counted from the natal Moon, 'generally used in practice': each planet is good in certain houses from the Moon and bad in others (BS 103.2–4).

notes: Homonym of gocara 'sense-field'; id disambiguated.

definitions.definition: The mendicant's alms-round, 'grazing like a cow' or taking 'like a bee' a little from many houses, accepting only food not prepared for him and free of the faults of alms.
Kṛṣṇa's highest abode, where he plays eternally with his associates; the manifest Vraja on earth is non-different from it.
In HYP 3.47–48, 'eating cow's flesh' means the entry of the tongue (go) into the palate in khecarī — a transgressive expression given a yogic sense.
Guarding: the non-disclosure of the mantra being repeated, itself the tenth purification (ŚT 2.122).
The women of Vraja whose love for Kṛṣṇa, in union and separation, is the Bhāgavata's model of devotion.
White clay from Dvārakā for Vaiṣṇava marks.
Asking the Lord to be one's protector; fourth limb of prapatti.
The status of haṭha teachings: 'kept secret it is potent, revealed it is impotent' (HYP 1.11); mudrās to be guarded like a jewel box (3.9).
'Gorakh's puzzle': a ring-and-wire puzzle associated with Nāth yogīs and, by extension, any intractable entanglement — an image of the world's tangle that only the yogī's knowledge unties.

notes: Popular usage; meaning in the tradition recalled in outline.

definitions.definition: The spiritual lineage determining a being's vehicle: the Laṅkāvatāra lists five (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, Tathāgata, indeterminate, none); Vimalakīrti calls the passions the Tathāgata's family.
The buddha-lineage present in all beings is one of the three reasons they are tathāgatagarbhas.
Karma determining high or low status (TS 8.12, 6.25–26).
The moment that takes nibbāna as object and passes from the worldling's lineage to the noble lineage (also, before a jhāna, from the sense sphere to the exalted).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): a seizing being — of eight classes: gods, their enemies, gandharvas, yakṣas, ancestors, serpents, rākṣasas, piśācas — whose seizure shows as superhuman knowledge and action (Su Utt 60.4-7); the subject of bhūtavidyā. Summary only.
A 'seizer': the nine planets — Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu — which 'moving, grasp the asterisms' (BPHS 3.4); forms of Janārdana giving the fruits of karma (BPHS 2.3).

notes: Homonym: in Jyotiṣa, a planet.

definitions.definition: The grasping instruments, the senses (1.41); the first of the five forms of the senses mastered by saṃyama (3.47).
The sacrifice to the nine planets for prosperity, peace, rain, long life or nourishment, with their images, mantras, fuel-sticks and gifts (YājñSm 1.295–308; BPHS 84).
The grasper, the puruṣa (as it appears to the mind), one of the three objects of coalescence (1.41, YBh 1.41).
Objects to be grasped — gross and subtle elements, the world (1.41, YBh 1.41).
The correlated objects and subjects that make the universe manifold (PH 3).
The yogin's distinction is attentiveness to their relation (VBT 106).
The nine heavens at the 'neck' of the cosmic person (TS 4.19).
A 'village' or system of seven notes with fixed śruti-intervals — ṣaḍja-grāma and madhyama-grāma (and a lost gāndhāra-grāma) — the basis of the mūrchanās and jātis.

literal: to be sung in the village

definitions.definition: The melodies sung in the village (public ritual).
The three knots — of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra — pierced in succession by the awakened power; in the HYP their piercing marks the first, second and fourth stages of nāda (4.70–77).
The three knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra that the Goddess pierces in her ascent (LSN 38-39).
One of three knots (of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra) pierced by kuṇḍalinī.
The breaking of the dense knot of attachment and aversion, at which right view first arises; Haribhadra places it at the sthirā view.
The householder, 'eldest' of the orders, supporting the others as air supports beings (MDh 3.77–78; 6.89–90).
Keeping the vow, knowledge and pure words (mantras) concealed.
The cave: the hidden place (in the heart) where the self or brahman is set (TU 2.1.1; KU 1.2.12, 1.2.20, 1.3.1; MuU 2.1.10).
The secret teaching: the ancient yoga (BhG 4.3), the royal secret (9.2), the most secret (15.20, 18.63–64), not to be told to the undisciplined or undevoted (18.67).
The many-faced Kālī of the Nepalese Uttarāmnāya, treated in the Mahākāla Saṃhitā.
The upagraha 'son of Saturn' computed from the portion of the day or night ruled by Saturn; much used in Kerala horā; Rudra's Kerala commentary finds it encoded in BJ 1.3.

The three constituents of prakṛti — sattva, rajas, tamas — of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion, serving illumination, activity and restraint, and functioning by mutual domination, support, production and pairing (SK 12).
What resides in a substance, has no qualities and is not an independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (VS 1.1.15 C); twenty-four (Praśastapāda).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act helplessly (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas, and the deluded think 'I am the doer' (3.27); the knower thinks 'the guṇas move among the guṇas' (3.28); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain, and Arjuna is to be free of them (2.45); desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
Strand: the nine-gated lotus is 'covered with three strands' (AVŚ 10.8.43).

The three strands born of prakṛti — sattva, rajas and tamas — which bind the embodied one (BhG 14.5), act upon one another as the true agents (3.27–28), and classify faith, food, austerity, giving, knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness (chs. 17–18).

The three constituents of the seen — sattva (illumination), rajas (activity), tamas (inertia) (2.18); their conflicting activity makes all suffering for the discerning (2.15); everything is a particular arrangement of them (4.13); at kaivalya they return to their source (4.34).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the twenty qualities in ten opposed pairs — heavy/light, cold/hot, unctuous/dry, slow/sharp, stable/mobile, soft/hard, clear/slimy, smooth/rough, subtle/gross, dense/liquid (Ca Sū 25.36; AHS Sū 1.18); the qualities as a category (Ca Sū 1.49); and the three guṇas of the mind (Śā 4.36).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The division of guṇas and actions according to which the Lord made the fourfold class-order (4.13); the guṇas are not further explained in chs. 4–6 (rajas is named in 6.27).
The three qualities of the self — sattva, rajas, tamas — determining destinies (MDh 12.24–51).

The three qualities belong to the intellect, not to the self; everything is classed by them with a fourth, attributeless class belonging to the Lord; one conquers rajas and tamas by sattva and sattva by desirelessness.
The three qualities of Prakṛti (sattva, rajas, tamas) by which devotion (BhP 3.29), Purāṇas (Matsya 53.68-69) and the measures of Oṃ (MkP 42.4) are classified.

Quality, strand: God's power hidden by its own guṇas (ŚU 1.3); the jīva is bound to the guṇas and has three guṇas (ŚU 5.7); tamas, rajas and sattva as successive states and as Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (MaiU 5.2).

In horā, the planets carry the three qualities: Moon, Sun and Jupiter sattva; Mercury and Venus rajas; Mars and Saturn tamas (BJ 2.7); a sāttvika, rājasa or tāmasa person is recognized by his conduct (BS 68.8–9).
In Jain usage an inherent quality of a substance, present in all its modes and itself without qualities (TS 5.38, 5.41).

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: Distinct from the Sāṃkhya sense (the three constituents of prakṛti).
alt_notes: The Sāṃkhya sense (three qualities) is contributed by other units; identifying the two is a later reading (see interpretation_log).

definitions.definition: The dharmakāya's perfections of permanence, bliss, self and purity, reversing the four inversions as applied to the Tathāgata.

cross_language.form: chang le wo jing 常樂我淨
gtsang bdag bde rtag gi pha rol tu phyin pa

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu's possession of infinite auspicious qualities, each unlimited; the reason he is called 'great' (Brahman).
Three lay vows strengthening the small vows — commonly limiting direction, purposeless harm, and consumables (lists differ by author).

One of fourteen stages of the soul's purification from wrong view to the omniscient without activity, defined by the rise, subsidence and destruction of deluding and other karmas (Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama; Sarvārthasiddhi 1.8; Gommaṭasāra).

One who neither hates nor longs for the guṇas' effects, sits as if indifferent knowing that the guṇas act, is the same in pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour, and has renounced all undertakings (BhG 14.22–25); reached by unswerving devotion (14.26).

An arthavāda that conflicts with another means of knowledge and is taken figuratively (e.g. 'the sacrificial post is the sun'; 'the sacrificer is the grass-bundle') (MS 1.2.10; grounds listed at MS 1.4.23–28).
'Secret': the hidden core of the Kartābhajā teaching and the hidden presence of the Master, kept behind outward conformity.
Proper restraint of the activity of mind, speech and body (TS 9.4) — three controls.

Teacher: the self is its own chief teacher; yet ignorance-bound persons need a knower of the principles to give knowledge; the avadhūta takes twenty-four teachers from nature; the guru is the helmsman of the human boat.
In the Guru Gītā: 'gu' is darkness, 'ru' its remover; the guru is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara and the supreme Brahman; the root of liberation is his grace.

Īśvara is the teacher (guru) even of the ancients, unlimited by time (1.26); devotion offers all actions to the supreme teacher (paramaguru, YBh 2.1); Vyāsa: in the stages of saṃyama 'yoga itself is the teacher' (YBh 3.6).

'Gu' is what is beyond the qualities and 'ru' what is beyond form; the guru gives that (SSM 15.8–9); Śiva stands present as the guru and the two are not to be distinguished (11.19–21); without devotion to the guru no devotion to Śiva arises (11.22–24).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's venerable elders (Bhīṣma, Droṇa), whom he would rather not kill even if it meant living on alms (2.5).
'The teacher is the means' (Śiva Sūtra 2.6); from the teacher comes awakening to the wheel of letters (2.7).
The teacher who is learned in scripture and established in Brahman, through whom alone the knowledge is to be sought (MU 1.2.12); approached with humility, service and questioning.
The one who knows the nine groups and consecrates the disciple; a mere knower of texts without faith is a semblance of a teacher.
'Gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover (Kulārṇava 17.7); the guru is father, mother and Maheśvara (12.49); rare is the guru who removes the disciple's suffering (13.108).
Teacher: 'he should go to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in brahman' (MuU 1.2.12); devotion to the teacher as to God (ŚU 6.23).

The teacher from whose grace the qualified disciple gains the supreme knowledge; the lineage runs from Nārāyaṇa and Vyāsa through Madhva and the maṭha pontiffs; devotion to the teacher as to God is enjoined.
Tamil kuru, ācāṉ, āriyaṉ: for the Siddhars the guru comes of his own accord, shows his own form and burns the bonds; guru and Lord are one (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).
The living guru (also murśid, sāṃi) through whom alone the Man of the Heart is found; Bāuls distinguish the initiating guru (dīkṣā-guru) and the instructing guru (śikṣā-guru).
The Mahāśay, in whom the Kartā is present; 'the guru is truth'.
The tiered wooden throne, often borne by carved figures, on which the sacred book (Bhāgavata or Kīrtana-ghoṣā) is enthroned and worshipped in place of an image.
The circle of gurus; the Goddess 'is of the form of the gurumaṇḍala' (LSN 138).
The guru-principle, without knowing which sacrifice, vows and pilgrimage are fruitless; the guru as not other than the Self.
The first strength.
The eight weighty rules accepted by nuns, subordinating the bhikṣuṇī order to the bhikṣu order in formal matters.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the māheśvara stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The lineage from the Lord and Śrī through Viṣvaksena, Nammāḻvār, Nāthamuni, Yāmuna and Rāmānuja, recited before study.
Approaching and surrendering to the guru as the means, for one unable to follow the other means.
Non-inherent cause of the first falling; in earth and water.

The material base of the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, identified by the commentaries as the heart; the Paṭṭhāna speaks only of 'the matter in dependence on which' they occur, and the Dhammasaṅgaṇī does not list it.

The form of the Śrīvidyā beginning with 'ha', called after Lopāmudrā; the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad says it teaches according to both Kādi and Hādi doctrines; the Bahvṛca Upaniṣad names Kādi, Hādi and Sādi vidyās.
The swan seated in the bright, in men, in ṛta, in the sky (RV 4.40.5); in the Atharvaveda the swan rising from the waters that never lifts one foot is Prāṇa (AVŚ 11.4.21).
The jīva as the breath-syllable 'haṃsa', the 'person' of Śakti, moving up and down and dissolving at the dvādaśānta (KJN 6.5; 13.2; 17.18).
The word dwelling in the bodies of breathing beings, repeated naturally 21,600 times a day and called 'so 'ham' (Yogaviṣaya 28–29).

Goose, swan: the self or God as the goose seated in the bright (KU 2.2.2); the goose that wanders in the wheel (ŚU 1.6); flutters outward in the city of nine gates (ŚU 3.18); the one goose in the midst of the world (6.15).
The self moving with the breath (ha out, sa in), meditated as a bird and repeated naturally 21,600 times a day; also the third kind of renouncer.
The mantra the living being repeats with each breath, going out with sa and in with ha (VBT 155b).
The breath, which goes out thirty-six finger-breadths (GŚ 40); the haṃsa in the thousand-petalled lotus (GS 6.10; Pādukāpañcaka).
The haṃsa upon which the self rests, itself within the breath (Kubjikāmata 11.14).
One of the names of the final abode in the crown (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 50).
The freed soul, a swan that returns to Satlok when it receives the true Name; Kāl's prey is the crow, the Name makes it a swan.
The soul as a swan that feeds on pearls (the Name) at the Mānasarovar within.

equivalents.note: Yogaviṣaya 29: the haṃsa 'is called so 'ham'
Haṃsa reversed is so'ham ('I am He'): the same breath-mantra read as identity.

definitions.definition: Third kind: one night in a village, five in a town; lunar fasts.
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): The absence of the conjunction, the seer's kaivalya (2.25).
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): Unwavering discriminative discernment (2.26); right seeing (YBh 2.15).
Name of Viṣṇu in the formula 'Hari is supreme over all' (Hari-sarvottama); controller of all, under whom all dependent reality stands.
The central tenet that Viṣṇu is supreme over all beings; the 'great purport' (mahātātparya) of all scripture.
A week of continuous singing of the name and reading of the Jñāneśvarī or Gāthā in a village, ending in kīrtan and a common meal.
Loud laughter ('a-ha-ha', aṭṭahāsa) offered to the Lord; a vocal act.
Lunar mansion hasta: presiding deity Savitṛ (the Sun) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord the Moon (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class swift (kṣipra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).

The yoga of force: the physical methods — postures, retentions, mudrās and bandhas, cleansing acts — that force the breath into the central channel and awaken kuṇḍalinī; taught 'solely for the sake of rājayoga' (HYP 1.2) and inseparable from it (HYP 2.76). The Yogabīja and the Jyotsnā gloss ha as the sun and ṭha as the moon, haṭha being their union, i.e. of prāṇa and apāna. The Śārṅgadhara Paddhati distinguishes Gorakṣa's haṭha from that of Mṛkaṇḍu's son.
'Force': the yoga of the body and breath taught by Ādinātha as a stairway to rājayoga (HYP 1.1); later texts gloss ha and ṭha as sun and moon.
Haṭha-yoga: eight limbs with mudrās; in the Yogaśikhā, the union of ha (sun) and ṭha (moon).
The mansion-temple in which the Lord's form is served as a householder's child and lord, with its own music (havelī saṅgīt).
That which is offered into the fire.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.24 the oblation is Brahman.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The member that proves what is to be proved by similarity or dissimilarity to the example (NS 1.1.34–35).
'Of things that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has told the cause and their cessation' (Vin Mv 1.23).
The six roots — greed, hatred, delusion and their opposites — that give stability to consciousness; also the root condition of the Paṭṭhāna.
Cause; six kinds: efficient, co-existent, homogeneous, associated, pervasive, ripening.
A reason that only appears to be one; five in the sūtra: inconclusive, contradictory, prakaraṇasama, sādhyasama, kālātīta (NS 1.2.4).
Five in the Navya list: inconclusive, contradictory, counterbalanced, unestablished, sublated (Tarkasaṅgraha); defined generally in the Tattvacintāmaṇi's hetvābhāsa-sāmānya-nirukti.
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): Suffering yet to come (2.16); saṃsāra full of suffering (YBh 2.15).

literal: cause of what is to be avoided

definitions.definition: One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): The conjunction of seer and seen (2.17).
Brahman's freedom from, and opposition to, every defect: ignorance, karma, change, suffering.

literal: opposed to all that is to be shunned

definitions.definition: Injury to living beings; meat cannot be had without it (MDh 5.48).
The severing of life-forces through careless activity (TS 7.13); twofold — material (dravya) and psychic (bhāva, the passion itself) (Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya).
A polemical Mahāyāna term for the vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas when their goal is taken as final; not a self-designation of any school.

notes: Recorded as the Mahāyāna sūtras' own polemical usage; Theravāda does not use it of itself.

definitions.definition: The Goddess of the Hiṅglāj seat in Balochistan, venerated in Aghora as the lineage goddess; Kīnārām is said to have gone there.
The humming sound 'hiṃ' preceding a sāman.
The Golden Germ that arose in the beginning as the one lord of what exists (RV 10.121.1).
In the Purāṇas the cosmic creator Brahmā as the first embodied being; in VP 6.7.51 the being whose contemplation is of both Brahman and action.
The cosmic subtle being: consciousness identified with the aggregate of subtle bodies (sūtrātman), collective counterpart of taijasa.
The golden germ, whom Rudra saw being born (ŚU 3.4, 4.12).

equivalents.note: The last verse of RV 10.121 answers the refrain with 'Prajāpati'; the Anukramaṇī names the deity Ka (Prajāpati).

definitions.definition: The inner sense of shame that, with ottappa, protects the world; the first quality of a true ascetic (MN 39).
Shame at wrongdoing, arising from self-respect; a beautiful universal.
The channels called hitā, extending from the heart, fine as a hair split a thousandfold, into which the self slips in deep sleep (BAU 2.1.19, 4.3.20; KauU 4.19).
Love, the supreme principle: the divine pair are two forms of hita, and hita is also the path and the goal; Harivaṃśa is its embodiment.

equivalents.note: hita is prema taken as the ultimate principle itself, not only as the devotee's highest state

notes: Distinct from trm:hita (the Upaniṣadic hitā channels).

definitions.definition: The pleasure-giving aspect of the internal power; its essence is prema and its fullest embodiment is Rādhā.
A regional custom discussed as an example of practices of some that are dharma for all (MS 1.3.15–23, per commentaries).

(1) Horoscopy, the branch revealing the ripening of karma of former births; the word is said to come from aho-rātra by dropping first and last syllables (BJ 1.3). (2) Half of a sign, ruled by the Sun or Moon (BJ 1.11). (3) A planetary hour.

notes: Scholarly account: from Greek hōra.

definitions.definition: The priest who recites the Ṛgveda verses; Agni is the divine hotṛ (RV 1.1.1).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan zaotar.

definitions.definition: The heart as the place of inner seeing: the seers searched in the heart (RV 10.129.4); the light is set in the heart (6.9.6); the wise see with heart and mind (10.177.1); the mind is heart-seated (VS 34.6).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): called 'mahat' and 'artha'; the seat of consciousness, the self with its qualities, mind and its objects, of the supreme ojas and root of the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.3-7); the seat of consciousness and abode of ojas (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 5.49); root of the channels of prāṇa and rasa (Ca Vi 5.6).
The Heart of the Supreme: consciousness as vibrancy and great being (ĪPK 1.5.14).
The Heart of Bhairava, the seed in which the universe lies like a tree in a banyan seed (Parātrīśikā 24); also the heart-centre of meditation (VBT 49).
