The heart: seat of the self and of the space within it (ChU 3.14.3, 8.1.1-3); analysed as 'hṛdi ayam', 'this is in the heart' (ChU 8.3.3) and as hṛ-da-yam (BAU 5.3.1); where the knots and desires dwell (KU 2.3.14-15).
The Heart-mantra of Bhairava taught in the Parātrīśikā (identified by the commentators as SAUḤ), in which the universe lies in seed form.

The knot(s) of the heart: when they are cut the mortal becomes immortal (KU 2.3.15); when he is seen the knot is cut (MuU 2.2.8); the knot of ignorance (MuU 2.1.10); knots loosened by firm memory (ChU 7.26.2).
The knot of the heart: the ego-knot binding consciousness and the insentient, cut by knowledge (MU 2.2.8).
The Goddess's seed-syllable hrīṃ ('heart-letter'), placed in the body in daily worship.

'Heart-letter': the name for the seed-syllable that closes each of the three sections of the vidyā (SL 32); the Varivasyārahasya analyses the subtle phases of its pronunciation. (Syllable not recorded.)
A mark and special quality of the self (NS 1.1.10); 'desire is wanting' (Tarkasaṅgraha); eternal in the Lord.
The power of will, first of the three powers; in the Trika the goddess Parā; the Śiva Sūtra calls it Umā, the virgin (1.13).

In the Laṅkāvatāra, one who has abandoned all roots of merit by rejecting the Mahāyāna — though the Tathāgata's power may revive his roots — or the bodhisattva who never enters nirvāṇa for beings' sake.
In the Mahāparinirvāṇa, first said to lack buddha-nature (in the sense of good qualities), then declared to have it and to be able to attain buddhahood; a fixed icchantika is denied.
The power of will; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad it is Mahātripurasundarī herself, with the power of knowledge as her house and the power of action as her seat.
Practice by one who wishes to practise but is careless (YDS).
The left channel, of the moon, identified with the Gaṅgā (HYP 3.110); inhalation 'through the moon' begins alternate-nostril purification (HYP 2.7).
The channel on the left, of the moon (GŚ 20, 23).
The left channel, carrying the moon.
Tamil iṭakalai: the left channel (lunar), first of the ten nāṭis of the Siddha ninety-six.

The principle 'when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be' (SN 12.21), which stands whether or not Tathāgatas arise (SN 12.20).
The many kinds of power — becoming many, passing through walls, walking on water, flying, touching sun and moon (DN 2); the first direct knowledge; its display is disparaged as a 'wonder' (DN 11).
Supernormal power, tenfold (by resolve, transformation, mind-made, etc.); the worldling's power is fragile and an impediment to insight.

equivalents.note: the Yoga and haṭha texts' siddhis overlap with the iddhis; the suttas treat display of them as unfit

definitions.definition: Concentration due to desire, energy, mind or investigation, with formations of striving (SN 51.20); for a monk, 'long life' (DN 26).
The second stage: the inquiring wish to know the particular (TS 1.15).
The third daily period: worship of Bhagavān.
The warrior king of the gods, soma-drinker, slayer of Vṛtra who released the waters (RV 1.32); some doubted him, and he answered 'here I am' (8.100.3–4).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): an Indra appears among the demons of the Avesta.

definitions.definition: 'Indra's birthplace': the passage between the palates, where the hair parts, by which the person made of mind goes out (TU 1.6.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The senses are to be withdrawn from their objects like a tortoise's limbs (2.58); they are turbulent and carry off the mind even of the wise (2.60, 2.67); they are to be restrained (2.61, 2.68) and controlled first when fighting desire (3.41); rāga and dveṣa are set in each sense towards its object (3.34); they are one of the seats of desire (3.40); the senses are high, the mind higher (3.42).
The eleven capacities produced from ahaṃkāra: five sense capacities, five action capacities and manas (SK 24–27); not made of the elements (SS 2.20, 5.84).
Smell, taste, sight, touch, hearing, made from the elements (NS 1.1.12).
Each located in a bodily seat — nose-tip, tongue-tip, the black of the eye, the whole skin, the ear's ākāśa; manas is the inner sense.

The senses, which carry off the mind (BhG 2.60, 2.67), are withdrawn like a tortoise's limbs (2.58), and are high but lower than mind (3.42); in the Anugītā they are among the seven priests of the inner sacrifice (14.20).
The senses (ten, with manas eleven, YBh 2.19), part of the seen (2.18); withdrawn in pratyāhāra (2.54) and mastered by saṃyama on their five forms (3.47).
The five spiritual faculties — faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom (SN 48.10); also the six sense faculties, to be developed not by blindness but by equanimity (MN 152).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The senses are offered into the fires of restraint and their actions into the fire of self-restraint (4.26–27); they are to be restrained to gain knowledge (4.39) and in meditation (6.12, 6.24); the knower holds that 'the senses move among the sense-objects' (5.9).
The twenty-two faculties, including the sense faculties, life, the feelings, the five spiritual faculties and the three supramundane faculties.
Faculty, 'dominant': twenty-two — six sense faculties, female, male, life, five feelings, five spiritual faculties and three pure faculties.
In Jain analysis five senses, each twofold: physical (formation and instrument) and psychic (attainment and use) (TS 2.15–19).
The eleven faculties — five of knowledge, five of action and mind — to be restrained like horses (MDh 2.88–92).
The doors of pleasure and pain, to be abandoned for abiding in the self (VBT 136); in the Śiva Sūtra, the spectators of the self's dance (3.11).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Supreme mastery of the senses from sense-withdrawal (2.55); also from saṃyama on their five forms (3.47); Vyāsa records several views of what it is (YBh 2.55).
Guarding the doors of the senses: seeing a form one does not grasp at its signs and features through which covetousness and grief might invade (DN 2; MN 27).
Guarding the sense doors so that covetousness and grief do not invade; the second purity of virtue.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The objects from which the senses are to be withdrawn (2.58, 2.68), on which the hypocrite dwells in mind (3.6), and in which attraction and aversion are set (3.34).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the yoked knower holds that the senses move among the objects of the senses (indriyārtheṣu) (5.9); one attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions has ascended to yoga (6.4).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Love and its joy; the Kuṟaḷ's third book (25 chapters), in the akam tradition of love poetry.
(Tamil report) The Ājīvaka's lord: 'the boundless knower' present in all things everywhere and always.
The two deeds, good (puṇṇiyam) and bad (pāvam), both binding the soul to birth — 'golden and iron fetters'.
In the Kuṟaḷ (v. 5) the two deeds 'born of darkness' do not cling to those who praise the Lord.
The two deeds, good and bad, both binding: the Lord drives us 'by the rope of the two deeds' (Paṭṭiṉattār, Tiruttillai 11); the knower no longer seeks either (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 13).

The 'equality of the two deeds': the state in which the soul's good and bad karma balance, so that it turns with equal indifference from both, a precondition, with the ripening of mala, of the descent of grace.

cross_language.note: the Sanskrit Āgamic term, with a debated sense

equivalents.note: Tamil usage stresses the soul's equanimity toward both deeds; the Sanskrit term the timing of śaktipāta

definitions.definition: Inflow of one without passions (stages 11–13), which does not stay bound beyond an instant (TS 6.4).
Lord; the Vrātya 'became Īśāna' (AVŚ 15.1.5); a name of Rudra.
The Lord as 'Īśāna of all knowledges, lord of all beings', invoked in the fifth brahma-mantra that closes the Sūtra.
The sectarian tenet that whatever one experiences is due to God's creation, rejected as leading to inaction (AN 3.61).
One of the three sectarian tenets: that all experience is due to God's creation.
The deity with whom self-study brings contact (2.44); Vyāsa: gods, sages and perfected beings appear to the one devoted to self-study (YBh 2.44).

The gross liṅga given by the guru at initiation and worn outwardly on the body for life (SSM 6.49–50), worshipped on the palm (6.54–55) without invocation or dismissal because Śiva abides in it from the moment of initiation (10.44–47).

equivalents.note: both name the devotee's own chosen form of the divine; the iṣṭaliṅga is a physical sacrament worn on the body, which the iṣṭa-devatā need not be

literal: what is sacrificed and what is given

definitions.definition: The accumulated merit of sacrifices and gifts, with which the dead are reunited in the highest heaven (RV 10.14.8).
Sacrifices and works of merit (such as digging wells): those who venerate them win the moon and return (ChU 5.10.3; PrU 1.9); fools who think them best go to lower worlds (MuU 1.2.10).

literal: being a means to the desired

definitions.definition: Maṇḍana Miśra's account of what the injunctive form conveys: that the act is a means to what the agent desires.

notes: Assigned to lin:bhatta-mimamsa because Maṇḍana is placed there by tradition; the view differs from Kumārila's.

definitions.definition: The Lord dwelling in the heart of all beings, moving them by his māyā (BhG 18.61); the great Lord of beings who comes into being by his own māyā (4.6); in the Mokṣadharma, the Yoga thinkers' argument that without a Lord no one is freed (12.289.3).

Classical Sāṃkhya recognizes no established Īśvara as creator: Gauḍapāda argues the attributeless could not produce what has guṇas (on SK 61); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds 'Īśvara is not established' (1.92–99; 5.2–12; 6.64), yet admits emergent lords — the one absorbed in prakṛti who becomes all-knowing and all-doing (3.55–57). Theistic Sāṃkhya (Vijñānabhikṣu) salutes the Lord.

A special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by the praṇava (1.27); his lordship has no equal or superior (YBh 1.24).

A distinct self free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness, possessing merit, knowledge and concentration, who assists human effort and sets karma and the elements in motion; like a father to beings (NBh 4.1.21); the all-knowing maker of the world proved by inference (NK 5.1).
Maheśvara, by whose will the world is dissolved and created through the selves' adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The one omniscient supreme self with eternal cognition, desire and effort; author of the Veda; whose convention fixes word-meanings (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The Lord: Brahman associated with māyā (or reflected in it), omniscient ruler, creator, sustainer and dissolver, giver of the fruits of action; his lordship depends on adjuncts of name and form.
The prototype (bimba) consciousness, of which the jīva is the reflection.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Kṛṣṇa is lord of beings though unborn (4.6), and great lord of all the worlds (sarva-loka-maheśvara), enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities and friend of all beings, knowing whom one attains peace (5.29).
Rejected as director of dharma and adharma and as creator: the fruit comes from dharma and adharma with place, time and circumstance (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116); later Bhāṭṭas (Āpadeva, Laugākṣi Bhāskara) teach offering dharma to Īśvara/Govinda.
Nārāyaṇa, the third reality: the self of all, cause of the world, opposed to all evil and abode of infinite auspicious qualities, present in five forms.

The Lord: all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord (Īśa 1); the two birds, the Lord and the one who grieves (MuU 3.1.2); the great Lord of lords (ŚU 6.7); the māyin (ŚU 4.10); lord of all (BAU 4.4.22; MāU 6).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Devotion to Īśvara: a special bhakti by which Īśvara, won over, favours the yogin (YBh 1.23); offering all actions to the supreme teacher or renouncing their fruit (YBh 2.1, RM 2.1); a means to samādhi (1.23, 2.45), part of kriyā-yoga (2.1) and a niyama (2.32).
Fourth tattva: knowledge predominant; the outward 'unmeṣa' (ĪPK 3.1.3), 'this am I' with the 'this' prominent.
Performing dharma with the thought of offering it to Īśvara (Laugākṣi Bhāskara) or Śrī Govinda (Āpadeva), which makes it a cause of the highest good.
Traditional narrative (above all the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa), named with purāṇa as the fifth Veda.
The genre of the Mahābhārata, which calls itself a Veda of Kṛṣṇa (MBh 1.1.205).
The procedure — the subsidiaries (e.g. the prayājas) — that answers the question 'how?' of the bhāvanā; in an ectype it is taken from the archetype (MS 7.4.1).
The Tājika yoga of applying aspect, when a faster planet approaches exact aspect with a slower; the first and chief of the sixteen Tājika yogas.

notes: Scholarly account: from Arabic ittiṣāl.

definitions.definition: The 'natural verse' portion of the Prabandham (the third thousand), recited rather than sung to fixed melodies.
The freed share all the Lord's powers except creating, sustaining and ruling the world (BS 4.4.17).
The world as Brahman's real, divine form, to be honoured, as opposed to saṃsāra.
The metre of four twelve-syllable lines.
A Vedic metre of 48 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
Waking: the field of the first quarter, vaiśvānara, outward-knowing, enjoying the gross (MāU 3).
Waking: the state in which the self, as viśva, experiences gross objects through the senses; empirically real.
Waking is [external] cognition (Śiva Sūtra 1.8).
Waking-dream: the waking mind's fancies and misperceptions (two moons, silver in shell, mirage).

literal: implication that leaves and does not leave

definitions.definition: Exclusive-non-exclusive implication: dropping the incompatible part of each word's meaning and retaining the compatible part, as in 'this is that Devadatta'; applied to 'tat tvam asi'.
Exclusive implication, which abandons the direct meaning entirely (the village 'on the Gaṅgā' = on its bank); rejected for 'tat tvam asi'.
The throat lock that binds the network of channels and stops the nectar falling into the fire (HYP 3.70–73; DYŚ 126–128).
The 'word' (pada) level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where Satī's breasts fell; the goddess there is Caṇḍī (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.43, 18.49).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: The throat lock, by which the nectar does not fall into the fire (GŚ 36).
Rudra's healing remedy (RV 1.43.4, 2.33.7).
Debate with the features of vāda in which quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat are also used (NS 1.2.2); permitted to protect the ascertainment of truth (NS 4.2.50).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): each party establishing its own thesis and attacking the other's, e.g. 'rebirth exists' against 'it does not' (Ca Vi 8.28).
Debate aimed at victory, one of the three kinds of debate among the learned.
The central island-continent with Meru at its centre, divided into nine varṣas, Bhārata being the southern one.
The central, round continent of the middle world, 100,000 yojanas across, with Meru at its centre (TS 3.9).
Simultaneous disease of many through vitiated air, water, land and season, whose root is adharma arising from prajñāparādha (Ca Vi 3.6-23).

(1) The living, moving devotee or body as Śiva's true temple, against the fixed (Basava's vacana); (2) the wandering Śivayogin teacher whose greatness is taught in the prasādi-sthala — to see him gives accomplishment, to worship him is a means of liberation (SSM 11.37–43); (3) the order of Liṅgāyata priests and monks.
A holy person who, carrying the Lord within, makes even the tīrthas holy.
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the prāṇaliṅgi stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The bondage from which the wise, yoked with understanding and abandoning the fruit of action, are freed (2.51).
Repetition of the praṇava together with contemplation of Īśvara, making the mind one-pointed (1.28, YBh 1.28); self-study includes repetition of purifying formulas (YBh 2.1).
Repetition of a mantra; audible, whispered and mental japa are ten, a hundred and a thousand times better than ritual sacrifice (MDh 2.85–87).
Muttering of the five brahma-mantras (the 'five purifiers') and the Raudrī Gāyatrī; the last limb of the offering; mental for the Ratnaṭīkā.
Repetition of a mantra: loud (vācika), whispered (upāṃśu) or mental (mānasa), each superior to the previous (Vāyavīya Saṃhitā quoted in the Padārthādarśa).
Repeated contemplation of the supreme state; the self-arising sound is what is repeated (VBT 144-145); the liberated's conversation is japa (Śiva Sūtra 3.27).
Silent recitation, the best of sacrifices ('among sacrifices I am japa', BhG 10.25).
Decay, brokenness, greying and wrinkling, and the passing away, death and laying down of the body (SN 12.2); the last link, conditioned by birth.
A nativity or birth-horoscope, and the genre of horā texts on it (Bṛhajjātaka, Laghujātaka, Jātakapārijāta); distinct from the Buddhist Jātaka birth-stories.
Recitation in which each pair is said forward, backward and forward (ab ba ab, bc cb bc …).
The chief digestive fire in the abdomen, fanned by samāna, which cooks the food and on which the other fires depend (Ca Ci 15.6-8; AHS Sū 12.8, 12.11-12 as pācaka).

(1) In debate: a futile rejoinder based merely on similarity or dissimilarity (NS 1.2.18), of twenty-four kinds (NS 5.1.1). (2) The universal, 'that whose nature is to produce sameness' (NS 2.2.71), part of a word's meaning (NS 2.2.68).
The universal (synonym of sāmānya), e.g. substance-hood; genuine universals are limited by six impediments (Udayana).

The SSM tells the māheśvara to give up the dharmas of his jāti and family that oppose steadfastness in the liṅga (10.30–31), yet prescribes commensality with twice-born of one's own jāti on the path (9.29), and makes brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike for those in the contemplation of Śiva (14.19–20).
The vacanas reject caste among devotees: Basava calls himself the son in the house of the cobbler Mādāra Cennayya and asks to say of every devotee 'he is ours'.
The birth of beings, their coming to be, the manifestation of the aggregates, the obtaining of the sense bases (SN 12.2); 'birth is ended' marks liberation.
Birth-group; the mixed classes arising from unions across the varṇas (anuloma, pratiloma) described in MDh 10.
The real universal; in MS 6.1.8 the class (human) as the eligible agent.
Birth-group or caste, which the Sants declare has no standing before God ('do not ask a sādhu's caste').
Jāt: caste and creed; Lalon has 'never seen its form' and asks where it is at birth and death.
The universal, which words denote; the true part of things; ultimately Being (sattā) itself (VP 3.1).

notes: Homonym: other units define jāti as birth or social class.

definitions.definition: One of the eighteen ancient melodic types of gāndharva music, precursors of the rāgas.

notes: Disambiguated from trm:jati (universal; birth-group).

definitions.definition: Six conditions that disqualify a property from being a genuine universal (Udayana).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The dharmas of the birth-group which, with the family dharmas, Arjuna says are uprooted by the faults of family-destroyers (1.43).
Recollection of former births, a form of sensory-mental knowledge that often awakens renunciation — as when Mahāvīra reminded Megha of his elephant birth.
The active phase of a cognitive process, normally seven moments, where wholesome or unwholesome kamma is made (functional in arahants).
Kṛṣṇa's birthday when the dark eighth coincides with Rohiṇī at midnight; kept by fasting.
The third stage, aimed at conquering the senses (and constant union with the god), in a cave or empty house.

The four meditative absorptions: the first with applied and sustained thought, rapture and bliss born of seclusion; the second with rapture and bliss born of concentration; the third with bliss and equanimity; the fourth with purity of mindfulness through equanimity (DN 2; SN 45.8); remembered by the bodhisatta as 'the path to awakening' (MN 36); a basis for destroying the effluents (AN 9.36).
Meditative absorption with specific factors; fourfold in the suttas and fivefold in the Abhidhamma method; mundane or supramundane.
Full absorption on a counterpart sign in which the mind is unbroken for long periods; required (or access) before seeing ultimate realities.

equivalents.note: same word; the Pali jhāna is a specific fourfold absorption, Yoga's dhyāna the seventh limb

definitions.definition: In the Śūraṅgama the seeing-nature which does not move, age or perish, shown as the true mind.

notes: Distinct from Chan 'seeing the nature' (kenshō), though the same characters.

definitions.definition: The inquiry into the means of destroying the three sufferings, prompted by being struck by them (SK 1).
One who has conquered attachment and aversion — the Tīrthaṅkara or any omniscient.
A consecrated image of a Jina (always in meditation, seated or standing), a support for recalling his qualities; worshipped with material (dravya) and inner (bhāva) worship.
Not to be worshipped: the canon gives no such injunction and worship harms beings.

The 'mode of the Jinas': the solitary, naked (or nearly equipment-less), hand-eating ascetic life of highest rigour, open in the Śvetāmbara view only to those with special capacities and discontinued after Jambū.
Rites for renovating a temple or replacing a damaged image.
Renovation followed by re-consecration (punaḥpratiṣṭhā) under the tantri.

The fifth and last ground of monastic judgment: the practice established by accepted teachers, used when no higher authority (supernormal knowledge, scripture, instruction, tradition) is available; the Jītakalpa fixes atonements by it.

The living self: the 'living self' (jīva ātman) with which being enters the elements (ChU 6.3.2); life which does not die when the body dies (ChU 6.11.3); in ŚU 5.9 the jīva is a hundredth part of a hundredth of a hair's tip yet fit for infinity.

The individual self: Brahman appearing as limited, reflected or semblanced through the adjunct of the inner organ (and ignorance); agent, enjoyer and transmigrant only through adjuncts; in truth Brahman.
The reflection of Brahman in avidyā/the inner organ, real and identical with the prototype.
Brahman delimited by the inner organ; the locus of ignorance.

A part of the formless Śiva through connection with beginningless ignorance, in whom Śiva abides as fire in the sunstone (SSM 5.34–36); at the prāṇaliṅgi stage the breath is the jīva and the great liṅga brahman (12.21–24).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the inner self of the embryo, eternal, unaging, deathless, that enters the womb through its connection with mind and 'produces itself' as the embryo (Ca Śā 3.3, 3.8).

The living being: the Lord's higher nature has become the life-element (BhG 7.5), and an eternal portion of him becomes the jīva (15.7); the living self in the body whose existence Bhṛgu defends (MBh 12.175–185).
The jīva is Saṃkarṣaṇa, arising from Vāsudeva (Nārāyaṇīya 12.326.38).
The individual self: eternal, atomic, a knower by nature and possessing attributive consciousness, agent and enjoyer dependent on the Lord, essentially his servant (śeṣa); countless in number.
Śiva clothed in body and coverings (PKS 1.5).
(As reported) The soul is the seventh of Pakudha's unmade bodies; the Ājīvika texts (as reported) speak of 'all souls' (sabbe jīvā) as powerless.
(As reported) For the materialist the soul is the body itself, bounded by the skin (tajjīva-taccharīra).
A part of Śiva like a spark of fire, covered by ignorance (Kulārṇava 1.8-9); bound it is jīva, freed it is Sadāśiva (9.42-43).

The soul: an eternal, formless, conscious substance whose mark is cognitive activity (upayoga), agent and enjoyer of its karma, co-extensive with its body, innumerable in number, each distinct; worldly or liberated (TS 2.8, 2.10, 5.3, 5.16).
An eternal, sentient, dependent self, atomic, distinct from God and from every other soul, a reflection (pratibimba) of God, with an innate fitness that fixes its destiny.
The inner self born with the body that experiences pleasure and pain (MDh 12.13).
The embodied soul, a part of the Lord who dwells in the same body unrecognized, like musk in the deer.
The soul, one of the four eternal realities: countless, bound by ignorance, liberated only by Parameśvara's grace.
Living samādhi: the tradition's belief that a Siddhar enters samādhi and is interred alive, remaining present at the shrine; the samādhi places of the eighteen are pilgrimage sites.

notes: Recorded as the tradition's belief; no practice details.

definitions.definition: The world of the living to which the widow is bidden to rise (RV 10.18.8).
The individual-soul portion present in every being alongside the supreme-Self portion; where it predominates the being is a jīva (BPHS 1.22; 2.8).
'Dead while living': the devotee who has let the self, hope and pride die while still alive; death has nothing left to take.
Dying while living: daily withdrawal of the attention from the body to the eye centre as at death.
jyānte marā: the lover who has died to lust and self while alive.

equivalents.note: Both describe freedom in the living body; the Sant term stresses the death of the self rather than the dawning of knowledge.

definitions.definition: Liberation while living: in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha the seventh stage, in which one acts as custom requires, unimmersed in pleasure and pain, the mind 'dead' (manonāśa).
The liberated one, though in the body, is not in it; his functions are free of intention; the body lives on while its karma lasts.
The destruction of ignorance, the fruit of human birth and the state of liberation while living.

The state of one who, after perfect knowledge, remains embodied through the momentum of impressions like a potter's wheel (SK 67); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra names the 'one liberated while living' and grounds it in the need for liberated teachers (SS 3.78–84).

Liberation while living, promised by knowledge of the cakra-code (YH 1.86) and of worship (YH 3.1), by three muhūrtas of the Bhāvanā contemplation, and to the steadfast practitioner who may die anywhere (PKS 10.82); the Dīpikā defines it as release from the eight bonds.
A synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the yogin in samādhi is 'liberated' though living (4.107–112); from nirguṇa meditation and samādhi one becomes jīvanmukta (DYŚ 114).

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): knowledge of identity with Śiva in an ageless, deathless body (Rasārṇava 1.8); attained through the stable body made by mercury, not after the body falls (Rasārṇava 1.9-13; SDS Raseśvara 1-5).
Firm realization of oneness with consciousness even while body and the rest are experienced (PH 16).
One who sees the whole world as play is liberated in life (SK 2.5).
Though living he is liberated, though acting not stained (VBT 142); liberated though joined to a body (Paramārthasāra 61).
One whose mind is settled that the liṅga is liberation itself is liberated even while embodied (SSM 12.46); the liṅga-sthalas are directed to it (15.1–3).
Liberation while living: the knower remains embodied till prārabdha is exhausted, free of bondage, agency and sorrow.
Liberation while living: the state in which the mind is the seed and the spotless (AmŚ 57–59); a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4).
Liberation while the body continues: the cessation of the mind's properties through destruction of vāsanā, dissolution of mind and knowledge of truth.
Rejected: while the body lasts karma remains; liberation comes only when the body falls.
Denied by Bhāskara: while the body lasts, real adjuncts remain.
Redefined: one engaged in Hari's service in all conditions is jīvanmukta.
The state of the soul freed by grace while the body, sustained by prārabdha, continues; such a one lives among devotees and acts as Śiva's servant.

notes: The SK itself does not use the word.

definitions.definition: Distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Selves are many because of the distinctness of their states (VS 3.2.16 C).
The life faculty, i.e. lifespan (āyus), the support of heat and consciousness.
The faculty that sustains its co-arising dhammas; mental (a universal factor) and material (in kamma-born matter).
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), highest of souls, equal in rank with Brahmā, surpassed only by Lakṣmī and Viṣṇu; paired in the formula 'Hari-sarvottama, Vāyu-jīvottama'.
The title of Śrīvaiṣṇava renouncers who head maṭhas (Vānamāmalai, Ahobilam, Parakāla and others).
Puruṣa as knower, the third member of 'the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower' whose discriminating knowledge is the better means (SK 2).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Knowledge is covered by desire, the constant enemy of the knower (3.38–40); desire is the destroyer of knowledge and realization (jñāna-vijñāna, 3.41); those who carp at Kṛṣṇa's teaching are deluded about all knowledge (3.32).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23); through knowledge comes liberation (SK 44); in its highest form the complete, pure, single knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64). Gauḍapāda distinguishes external (scriptural) from internal knowledge (of prakṛti and puruṣa), only the latter liberating.
Synonym of buddhi (NS 1.1.15); a mark and quality of the self (NS 1.1.10), not of the mind (NS 3.2.19).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.33–42 and 5.15–17: knowledge — learned from knowers who have seen the truth through prostration, questioning and service (4.34); by it one is not deluded again and sees all beings in the self and in the Lord (4.35); a raft across all wrong (4.36); a fire that burns all actions (4.37); the supreme purifier, found within oneself in time by one perfected in yoga (4.38); obtained by the faithful, intent and sense-restrained, and followed by supreme peace (4.39); it cuts doubt like a sword (4.42). It is covered by ignorance, which deludes creatures; where ignorance is destroyed, knowledge illumines the highest like the sun (5.15–16). 6.8 pairs it with realized knowledge (vijñāna).
Knowledge of Viṣṇu's supremacy, the five differences and gradation, culminating in direct knowledge (aparokṣa); it wins the abundant grace that alone liberates.
Knowledge: as the Lord's power, one of the three; as limited knowing, bondage (Śiva Sūtra 1.2); as right knowledge, the sole cause of liberation (TĀ 1.22).
Knowledge, of five kinds (mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, kevala), the soul's own nature; to be gained before compassion can be rightly exercised.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A stage (ground) of knowledge; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha counts seven, with liberation beyond them, and says others count the stages of yoga differently.
The combination of knowledge (meditation on Brahman) with the Vedic and social duties of one's station, maintained until death, as the means to liberation.
Bhagavad Gītā 4.28, 4.33: the sacrifice of knowledge, offered by ascetics of strict vows; better than sacrifice made of material things, since all action without exception culminates in knowledge.

The sacrifice of knowledge, better than the sacrifice of material things (BhG 4.33); some worship the Lord with it (9.15); the study of the Gītā itself is worship by the sacrifice of knowledge (18.70).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The commitment (niṣṭhā) of the sāṃkhyas, one of the two taught by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3).
The path of knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas, one of the two ancient paths named at BhG 3.3; its culmination is steadfastness in knowledge of the self.
The yoga of knowledge, fitting those disgusted with action who have renounced it.
Contemplation of the self as distinct from matter, leading to the vision of the self (ātmāvalokana), which prepares for bhakti.
The Tathāgata's knowledge and vision, which the buddhas appear in order to open, show, awaken and lead beings into.
Bhagavad Gītā 4.19, 4.37: the fire of knowledge, which burns up actions — the learned one's actions are burnt in it, and as a kindled fire turns firewood to ash, it turns all actions to ash.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Extraordinary contact in which a prior cognition presents its object (e.g. fragrance in 'fragrant sandal' seen); used to explain some errors.
The liṅga-sthala in which the knowledge that makes feeling known itself dissolves; brahman beyond the three forms and the three qualities (SSM 15.45–49, not separately recorded as a teaching here).
The power of knowledge; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad it is kuṇḍalinī, the Goddess's house.

notes: The Bhāvanā passage reads 'kuṇḍalinī jñānaśaktir gṛham'; the assignment of powers is as in the eBhāratī text.

definitions.definition: Karma veiling the five kinds of knowledge (TS 8.4, 8.6).
The knower, the fourth and highest of the devotees, whom the Lord regards as his very self (BhG 7.16–18).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The knowers who see the truth and teach knowledge (4.34); in 6.46 the yogin is held greater than the jñānins.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A property produced in the object by cognition (its being manifest, prākaṭya), from which the cognition — itself not perceived — is inferred (Śāstradīpikā).

equivalents.note: two Bhāṭṭa names for the same property

definitions.definition: The soul as pure knower, neither careless nor careful, beyond all states it knows (Samayasāra 6).
A Nāth ascetic; in north India also the name of householder communities of Nāth descent who sing the Nāth sagas.
Attendant goddess of Candraprabha, subject of Indranandi's mantra manual.
The highest Brahman to which homage is paid as presiding over past, future and all (AVŚ 10.8.1; 10.7.32–34).

equivalents.note: The Atharvaveda's 'highest Brahman' is the nearest Saṃhitā use to the Upaniṣadic Brahman.

definitions.definition: Lunar mansion jyeṣṭhā: presiding deity Indra (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Mercury (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class sharp (tīkṣṇa) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Its junction with Mūla is a gaṇḍānta (BPHS 94).
The inner light seen without sun or moon in the encounter with the Lord; Kabīr's first ramainī places light and sound at the origin.
The light of the inner regions (the flame at Sahasdal Kanwal, 'Jot Nirañjan'); the soul follows the sound and sees the light.

In the SSM, the liṅga of light that always shines in the base, the heart and between the brows of all beings, called brahman in the Āgamas, contemplated as the inner wearing of the liṅga (6.35; 6.39–41).
The twelve self-manifest liṅgas of Śiva's radiance in sacred sites, told in the Śiva Purāṇa's Koṭirudra Saṃhitā.

notes: Distinct from, though related to, the Purāṇic usage for the twelve self-manifest liṅga shrines.

definitions.definition: Light — the highest light reached by the worshipper (RV 1.50.10), the light set in the heart (6.9.5–6), the light reached by soma-drinkers (8.48.3), the light of lights that is mind (VS 34.1).
Light: the light beyond heaven which is the light within a person (ChU 3.13.7); the highest light which the serene one reaches (ChU 8.3.4, 8.12.3); the light of lights (MuU 2.2.9).

The science of the lights in three branches — computation (gaṇita/siddhānta), horoscopy (horā) and mundane omens (saṃhitā) — of which the horā is called best; the 'eye of the Veda' (BS 1.9; BPHS 1.1–6).
In its Vedāṅga form, time-reckoning by sun, moon and lunar mansions to fix the times of sacrifice; 'at the head of the Vedāṅgas' (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa Ṛk 3, 35).

cross_language.note: loan form of jyotiṣa
'star-calculation', the Indian-derived astral science (translation, not a loan)
astrology as listed among the 'low arts' in DN 1; narrower than jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: The third order of gods: sun, moon, planets, lunar mansions and stars, whose motion around Meru measures time (TS 4.12–15).

The sorrowless, luminous activity (1.36): awareness of the buddhi in the heart-lotus, shining like sun, moon and gems, and I-am-ness alone like a waveless ocean (YBh 1.36); its light is directed in 3.25.
The 'banana-grove' kingdom of women in which Matsyendra forgot himself until awakened by Gorakṣa; a Nāth image of forgetfulness through sense-life.
The form of the Śrīvidyā beginning with 'ka', called after Manmatha (Kāmarāja); the doctrine of the Tantrarāja ('Kādimata') and the form encoded in SL 32.
Service to the Lord (and his devotees) that expresses the soul's nature as his śeṣa; the goal both here and in Vaikuṇṭha.
Service to the Lord 'at all times without break' (TVM 3.3.1) — the true meaning of the drum the girls ask for (TP 29).

The aloneness of the seer: the absence of the conjunction (2.25); arising when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity (3.55) or from dispassion even toward the highest power (3.50); defined as the guṇas' return to their source, or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34).

(1) Puruṣa's intrinsic isolation (SK 19). (2) The goal: isolation that is certain and final, attained when the body falls and pradhāna, its purpose fulfilled, ceases (SK 68); prakṛti's activity is for its sake (SK 17, 21).
What remains when the mind is dissolved by abandoning the knowable (HYP 4.62).
The Bhāgavata names kaivalya as its sole purpose (BhP 12.13.12).
The state of oneness granted by the Goddess ('giver of the state of kaivalya', LSN 125, 171).
The only true liberation, gained by knowledge alone (Muktikā); also the fruit of yoga in six months (Amṛtanāda).
The enjoyment of one's own pure self apart from the Lord, sought by some seekers; a lesser goal than the Lord's service.
Not permanent: those who attain it eventually go on to the Lord.
A permanent state, in a region at the edge of the eternal realm, from which there is no return.
In the Jaimini system, the liberation indicated by the kārakāṃśa exalted, or by Ketu in the twelfth from it (Jaimini 1.2.13, 1.2.69).

cross_language.note: Jain kevala-jñāna, omniscient knowledge of the liberated soul — a different doctrine

equivalents.note: Kaivalya is Yoga's name for liberation; YBh 2.15 calls the goal 'mokṣa' and 2.26 calls discernment 'the path of mokṣa'. Yoga's liberation is isolation of one puruṣa, not union.

notes: The Śākta sense (liberation as oneness with the Goddess) is only analogous to Pātañjala kaivalya (isolation of puruṣa); the two definitions should not be merged as one sense.

definitions.definition: The 'crow and palm-fruit' coincidence: used for the uncaused, chance-like arising of the world-appearance and of the turn toward inquiry.

literal: like the crow and the palm fruit

definitions.definition: Drinking air slowly through the mouth shaped like a crow's beak (kākacañcu).

The son of the Sat Puruṣ who by austerity won the three worlds, begot Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś, and as Kāl (time/death) devours souls and keeps them from Satlok; the adversary from whom Kabīr frees souls.

Kāl, the 'negative power' (also Brahm, Jot Nirañjan at the lower levels), ruler of the three worlds up to Trikuṭī, the universal mind, who administers karma; contrasted with Dayāl, the merciful supreme.
Kāl as death, who stands over every head and grinds the world.
An eternal-and-non-eternal insentient reality, directly perceived by the witness even in deep sleep.
Time as the first god and lord of all, father of Prajāpati, from whom the waters, brahman, tapas and the Vedas arose (AVŚ 19.53–54).
Time, counted by Kapila as the twenty-fifth principle and identified with the Lord, from whom prakṛti's movement arises.
From the unmanifest arose time, pradhāna and the supreme person (Īśvara Gītā).
One, all-pervading, eternal substance, cause of the notions 'earlier', 'later', 'simultaneous', 'quick' (VS 2.2.6 C).
The insentient part of the effect, dependent on the sentient: ten 'effects' (five elements, five qualities) and thirteen 'instruments' (ten senses, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas); they are the bonds.

Time: 'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds' (BhG 11.32); 'Time takes all and gives all' (Bali, MBh 12.217.25); time is the sixth with the five eternal elements (12.267); in the Gautamī story, Time points to karma (13.1).
Time: a candidate cause (ŚU 1.2) rejected as the cause (6.1); God is the maker of time (6.2, 6.16); two forms of brahman, time and the timeless (MaiU 6.15-16).

In jyotiṣa, time is twofold: the time that ends the worlds, and reckonable time, gross (from the prāṇa) and subtle (from the truṭi) (SS 1.10–11); without beginning or end, it is inferred from the planets and stars (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11).

The substance that makes possible continuity, change, activity and priority (TS 5.22); for the Digambaras a real substance consisting of innumerable time-atoms, one in each space-point; for some Śvetāmbaras only a mode of other substances ('according to some', Śv 5.38). Conventional time is measured by the luminaries.
A subtle stage of the praṇava after nāda and bindu; a light seen in the west.
Time, a form of Viṣṇu that joins and separates pradhāna and puruṣa (VP 1.2); the Lord's form that carries off all beings (BhP 12.4.36-38).
An eternal insentient substance without the guṇas, the Lord's body and instrument; in the eternal realm time exists but does not govern.
Kañcuka: limited agency ('only a little I do').
The time-power of the Word-Brahman, its independent power (svātantrya) by which sequence and the six modifications of being appear (VP 1.3; 3.9).
Kañcuka: time, limiting to sequence ('only now').

literal: doctrine that time is the cause

definitions.definition: Time as sole cause, one of the five one-sided causal views (with own-nature, destiny, former deeds, effort) that are wrong alone and right together.
'Cheating time (death)': the yoga that overcomes death (GŚ 2; HYP 3.3).
Taught by Bhairava as the most secret practice; placing the mind in the heart until unmanī destroys death (KJN 6.16–28).
The fire of the end of time, visualized rising and burning body and world (VBT 52-53).
Foreknowing the time of death by signs in breath, body and dreams (YŚ 5).

notes: Restricted/summary only.

definitions.definition: Traditional study of the Śrībhāṣya, Gītābhāṣya, the Tiruvāymoḻi commentaries and the rahasyas at the feet of a teacher.
The first embryonic stage; the stages beginning with kalala rest on the body, as the dispositions rest on buddhi (SK 43).
Name of the Śaiva order known from Karnataka inscriptions; Yāmuna attributes skull and corpse-ash practices to it; Guṇaratna counts the Kālamukhas as the fourth kind of Śaiva ascetic.
The activity of consciousness named by the root kal: projecting (kṣepa), knowing, counting, moving, sounding (TĀ 4.173).
The act of devouring (grasana) that gives Mahākāla and Kālī their names (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32 with Hariharānanda's gloss).
The smallest units of matter: groups of inseparable elements (at least eight) arising and ceasing together.
Tiny particles seen with the light of access or jhāna concentration and analysed into their elements as the basis of insight.
The subtle units whose rapid arising and passing is experienced as vibration in the body (U Ba Khin).

The 'Person of Time': the zodiac as a body whose limbs are the twelve signs from the head (Aries) to the feet (Pisces) (BJ 1.4), whose self is the Sun and mind the Moon (BJ 2.1); an ocean no non-seer can cross (BS 2.4).

equivalents.note: the cosmic Person whose limbs are the world (RV 10.90) — an analogy of form, not an identity the jyotiṣa texts assert

definitions.definition: A consecrated water-pot in which the deity is invoked for bathing and installation rites.
Kalaśa rites (e.g. sahasrakalaśa) by which the tantri renews an installed deity's power.
The supreme Kālī of the Krama, the last of the goddesses of cognition.
In Abhinavagupta's Trika the fourth goddess above Parā, Parāparā and Aparā.
A pseudo-reason adduced when its time has passed (NS 1.2.9 DCS).

The conquest or postponement of death through yoga: the Siddhas break the staff of time (HYP 1.9); mudrās give 'cheating of time' (3.130); one established in rājayoga cheats time (4.103); a chapter of the Haṭhatattvakaumudī is devoted to it.

She who devours (kalana) Time: because she devours Mahākāla she is the primordial Kālikā (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32); black because all beings enter her as colours enter black (13.5-6); standing on Śiva as a corpse (Toḍala 1.20-25).
The Mother of the Śyāmā-saṅgīt; Dakṣiṇakālī of the Tantrasāra.
The goddess as the power of kalana - projecting, knowing, counting, moving, sounding - in twelve phases of cognition (TĀ 4.148-173).

literal: the Black One; she of Time

definitions.definition: The fourth and present age, an ocean of faults with one great virtue: that singing the Lord's name gives what meditation, sacrifice and worship gave in the earlier ages; reckoned by tradition from 3102 BCE.

The age in which only the path of the Āgama avails and Vedic mantras are powerless (Mahānirvāṇa 2.7-15); in which only householder and mendicant stages remain (8.8); in which, for the Kālīvilāsa, only the paśu disposition is allowed (4.2-3).

The present, fourth age, whose beginning (3102 BCE by the siddhāntic epoch) is the zero of calendrical computation; Āryabhaṭa was 23 when 3600 of its years had passed (Āryabhaṭīya 3.10); in it the Viṃśottarī is the chief period-system (BPHS 46.14).
The degenerate age in which neither ritual, devotion nor discernment stands on its own and the name is the one support — yet the best of ages for one with faith.
Crossing the Kali age by the sixteen names.

Practices once permitted by the smṛtis but declared forbidden in the Kali age by later authorities (e.g. levirate, the great departure, cow-sacrifice), justified by the principle that dharma differs by age.

literal: to be avoided in the Kali age

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Impurity destroyed by sacrifice (4.30), shaken off by knowledge (5.17), destroyed in the seers who attain brahma-nirvāṇa (5.25); the yogin who has become Brahman is stainless (akalmaṣa, vigata-kalmaṣa) (6.27–28).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The cosmic period at whose end beings enter the Lord's prakṛti and at whose beginning he sends them forth (BhG 9.7).
A day of Brahmā of a thousand cycles of four yugas with fourteen Manus; his night of equal length is the occasional dissolution; each kalpa bears a name (e.g. the present Śveta-Vārāha).
In the siddhāntas, a day of Brahmā of 1,000 caturyugas with fourteen Manus and their junctions (SS 1.19–20); Āryabhaṭa counts 14 × 72 yugas (Āryabhaṭīya 1.5).
Aeon: of destruction, formation, intermediate (from immeasurable lifespan to ten years and back), and great (eighty intermediate aeons).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The science of ritual procedure, set out in the Śrauta-, Gṛhya-, Dharma- and Śulba-sūtras of each Vedic school.

notes: Id disambiguated from kalpa as a world-eon.

definitions.definition: Vaimānika gods above the kalpas — the Graiveyakas and Anuttaras — without ranks, all equal ('ahamindra') (TS 4.17).
Vaimānika gods of the kalpa heavens, with ranks such as Indra (16 heavens for Digambaras, 12 for Śvetāmbaras) (TS 4.17, 4.19).
Mental impurity whose absence (akaluṣamati) is the condition for yoga to arise; its removal is the first stage's purification.

The Lord's infinite, unsurpassed auspicious qualities — knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour and countless others such as compassion, accessibility and motherly love — not born of prakṛti.

One of the five 'auspicious events' in every Tīrthaṅkara's life — descent into the womb (cyavana/garbha), birth (janma), renunciation (dīkṣā), omniscience (kevala-jñāna) and final liberation (nirvāṇa) — celebrated by the gods and re-enacted in temple consecrations and festivals.

The teacher or companion who leads to awakening; the Aṣṭa says the buddhas and the perfections are the bodhisattva's good friends; Sudhana's pilgrimage and Sadāprarudita's search model devotion to them.
The teacher who gives the meditation subject, endowed with the seven qualities; the Buddha is the best good friend.
Spiritual friendship, 'the whole of the holy life' (SN 45.2); the first condition for maturing the liberation of mind (Ud 4.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire: the ritual-minded are 'desire-souled' (2.43); the one of steady wisdom gives up all desires that enter the mind (2.55, 2.71) and is entered by desires like the ocean without being moved (2.70); desire is born of attachment and gives rise to anger (2.62); named with anger as the enemy born of rajas that covers knowledge, seated in the senses, mind and understanding, to be slain (3.37–43).
Desire, which arose in the beginning as the first seed of mind (RV 10.129.4; AVŚ 19.52.1).

Desire, born of rajas, the all-devouring enemy that veils knowledge, seated in senses, mind and intellect (BhG 3.37–41); one of the three gates of hell (16.21); yet 'in beings I am desire not opposed to dharma' (7.11); born of intention (saṃkalpa), as Maṅki says (MBh 12.171.25).
The five cords of sensual pleasure (MN 26); like the sores of a leper (MN 75); gratification, danger and escape (MN 13).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: undertakings free of desire mark the learned (4.19); the unyoked is bound through the drive of desire (5.12); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood before leaving the body (5.23); brahma-nirvāṇa is near those free of desire and anger (5.26); desires born of intention are to be abandoned in meditation (6.24); the yoked one is free of craving for all desires (6.18).
Desire: not praiseworthy in itself, yet no action is without it (MDh 2.2–4); never quenched by enjoyment (MDh 2.94).
The aim of love and pleasure, proper to youth, to be pursued without harming dharma and artha (Kāmasūtra 1.2).

Desire: 'a person is made of desire' (BAU 4.4.5); the desiring one returns for action, the one without desire goes to brahman (BAU 4.4.6); when all desires in the heart are released the mortal becomes immortal (BAU 4.4.7; KU 2.3.14). The self's 'real desires' (ChU 8.1.5) are distinguished from ordinary ones.
Desire for one's own pleasure, which is not destroyed but refined into prema by the Sahajiyā discipline, as gold from ore; the washerwoman's love had no trace of it.
Lust, the downward current that must be mastered before the Man can be held.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

cross_language.note: same word

definitions.definition: (As reported) Pleasure is the only human aim; the pain mixed with it is to be avoided as the fish's bones are.

notes: The Prabodhacandrodaya gives artha and kāma as the two aims.

definitions.definition: The first hindrance, fed by unwise attention to the sign of the beautiful and starved by attention to the sign of foulness (SN 46.51).
The desire realm: hells, ghosts, animals, humans and six classes of gods, in twenty places.
Forms, sounds, odours, tastes and tangibles that are desirable, enticing (MN 26).

The 'digit of desire': the white and red points, Śiva and Śakti, and the point of their union (the 'I'); kāma because it is lovely, kalā the two points of fire and moon; knowing this vidyā one becomes Mahātripurasundarī (KKV 6-8); the Goddess 'whose form is the kāmakalā' (LSN 73).
The Goddess of Kāmarūpa, worshipped at the yoni-pīṭha on Nīlācala; she is dharma, artha, kāma and liberation (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.9).
'She whose eyes are desire' (LSN 23); the Goddess of Kāñcī, praised in the Mūka Pañcaśatī; by tradition Śaṅkara installed a Śrīcakra before her.
The tenth Mahāvidyā (Kamalātmikā), a tantric Lakṣmī; Sadāśiva in Viṣṇu's form is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.16).
The renouncer's water-pot, among the permitted articles.
The fourth fetter, abandoned by the non-returner (MN 64).
The middle section of the mantra; the Goddess's body from neck to waist (LSN 35).

literal: section of the king of desire

definitions.definition: The yoni-place between the root and svādhiṣṭhāna centres, called Kāmarūpa/Kāmākhyā (GŚ 10–11).
The land (Assam) where the Kaula scripture is 'in every house of the yoginīs' and the seat Kāmākhyā (KJN 8.20; 22.10–12).
Assam; the seat where Satī's yoni fell at Kāmagiri and Kāmākhyā dwells (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42, 18.49).
Kāmākhya is the 'beyond form' level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where the Kaula scripture is found in every yoginī's house (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 22.10).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: The power to govern at will endless forms and instruments, independent of karma.
In the Mattavilāsa the Kāpālika claims that austerity gives the power to take any form (satire).
Consciousness that mostly occurs in the sense-sphere planes: fifty-four types.
'Lord of desire': Śiva as Lalitā's consort, seated in the bindu of the Śrīcakra with the Goddess on his lap (LSN 21; PKS 4.5).
The Goddess as Kāmeśvara's consort; also the first of the fifteen Nityās and one of the three goddesses of the inner triangle (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad: the unmanifest).
The Lord's quality of willing: because he wills, he produces the effects at once or in sequence as he wishes and does not depend on karma.

Intention (cetanā): 'having intended, one acts by body, speech and mind' (AN 6.63); beings are owners and heirs of their deeds (MN 135); kamma ripens in this life, the next or later (AN 3.34; AN 6.63) and is one of the four unthinkables in its details (AN 4.77); four kinds, dark, bright, mixed and neither, the last leading to kamma's end (AN 4.232).
Volition (cetanā) and the wholesome or unwholesome action it motivates; kamma condition for results and kamma-born matter; classified by function, weight, time and place.

equivalents.note: same word; the suttas define kamma as intention and reject its identification with ritual action or with fate

definitions.definition: An object connected with a past deed (e.g. a weapon, an offering) presenting itself to the mind of the dying.
The ending of kamma through the volition to abandon dark, bright and mixed kamma (AN 4.232–233).
The ten unwholesome courses (three bodily, four verbal, three mental) and their opposites (MN 41; AN 10.176).
'Beings are owners of their deeds, heirs of their deeds; deeds are their womb, kin and refuge' (MN 135); one of the five reflections (AN 5.57).
A meditation subject (forty in the Visuddhimagga), given by a teacher; also meditation practice generally.
In Thai usage 'kammathan' names meditation practice and the forest monks devoted to it (phra kammathan).
The old meditation system itself (kammaṭṭhāna borān).
Acts enjoined for one who desires a particular fruit (e.g. heaven, cattle); the seeker of release abstains from them because they produce further bodies.
Desire-prompted rites for particular results (heaven etc.), to be avoided by the seeker.
Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): the seven adventitious 'coverings' (impurities) of mercury, from earth, rock and water, causing skin disease, dullness and wind disorders (RRS 11.22-25).
The 'jackets' covering Śiva and making him a jīva; without them he is Paraśiva (PKS 1.5).
The five (with māyā, six) sheaths that limit the individual: kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati (Paramārthasāra 16-17).
The 'sheaths' from māyā — kalā (limited agency), vidyā (limited knowledge), rāga (attachment), kāla (time) and niyati (restriction) — which partly awaken and limit the soul for experience.

notes: Homonym: in Kashmir Śaivism the (five/six) 'coverings' limiting consciousness.

definitions.definition: The egg-shaped bulb between the genitals and navel from which the channels arise (GŚ 16); kuṇḍalinī sleeps above it (HYP 3.107).
The bulb near the navel from which the channels spread.
Kṛṣṇa in Tamil — the cowherd child and lover of the Āḻvārs' hymns.
A couplet stanza with a recurring refrain, the favourite form of the Siddhar songs (Kuṭampai, Pattirakiriyār, Paraparakkaṇṇi).
'Split-ear': a Nāth yogī whose ear cartilages have been split at initiation to wear the large earrings; such an initiate is also called darśanī.
Love as of a beloved wife — 'eternal love as a beloved' (nitya-kāntā-bhajana, NBS 66), one of the eleven attachments (NBS 82).
The Āḻvārs' bridal love: Āṇṭāḷ's longing to wed the Lord and Nammāḻvār's and Tirumaṅkai's voice as the love-sick girl.

equivalents.note: Gauḍīya madhura-rasa is the same love systematised as an aesthetic rasa

definitions.definition: Sixth view: like a star; concentration; no delight in other; reflection (YDS).
The patched cloak of the wandering yogī, a mark of the Nāth guise in poetry (e.g. Padmāvat).
The pit of the throat below the tongue and throat; saṃyama there stops hunger and thirst (3.30, YBh 3.30).
The bead necklace (of tulsī wood) given at initiation into the Kabīr Panth (and Dādū Panth).

The sixth sign (Virgo), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the waist of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by Mercury; dual; of the earth triplicity (later texts); even, female and gentle (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: pāthona (BJ 1.8); dignities: Mercury exalted (15°); Venus in fall (BJ 1.13).
The human skull carried as begging-bowl; with the khaṭvāṅga a sub-insignia (upamudrā) of the Kāpālas (Yāmuna); eating from a skull is ascribed to the Kālāmukhas.
The skull, 'best of all vessels' for the Kaula rite (KJN 12.13).
The skull bowl carried by the Aghora ascetic.
In the HYP rapid exhalation and inhalation like bellows, drying up phlegm; in the GS a threefold act (vāmakrama with the breath, vyutkrama and śītkrama with water).
The cavity above the palate into which the reversed tongue enters in khecarī.
The tīrtha (at Vārāṇasī in the Purāṇic story) where the skull fell from the Lord's hand and he was freed from brahmin-murder.
The observance of those called kapālavratins, whom the Svacchanda places with the Pāśupatas beyond re-creation.
A Śaiva ascetic keeping the skull vow; named with Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas and Śaivas as one of four Māheśvara groups (Yāmuna; Vācaspati).
Śiva/Bhairava as bearer of Brahmā's skull; his 'excellent skull-bearer's guise' destroys the sin of those who remember it.
Epithet of Rudra (RV 1.114; VS 16).

literal: phlegm; also śleṣman 'that which embraces' (√śliṣ, Su Sū 21.5)

definitions.definition: The doṣa of cohesion and stability: heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, sweet, stable and slimy (Ca Sū 1.61); it upholds the body by the action of water — binding joints, lubrication, healing, strength and firmness (Su Sū 15.4); fivefold as avalambaka, kledaka, bodhaka, tarpaka and śleṣaka (AHS Sū 12.15-18).
Tamil aiyam or kapam: the water-earth humour, third of the three.

cross_language.note: = Skt śleṣman

definitions.definition: A cosmic period of contraction and expansion of the world (DN 27); the seven Buddhas arose within ninety-one aeons (DN 14).
A world-age with four incalculable phases (contraction, contracted, expansion, expanded).
The small casket in which the iṣṭaliṅga is worn on a cord at the chest or neck.
A participant in an action as analysed by Pāṇini — agent, object, instrument, recipient, source, locus; 'the independent one is the agent' (1.4.54).

A planet signifying a person or matter: fixed natural significators (the Sun of the father and self, the Moon of the mother and mind…) and, in Jaimini and Parāśara, the variable significators (cara-kāraka) by degrees (BPHS 32).

notes: Homonym of the grammatical kāraka; id disambiguated.

definitions.definition: The navāṃśa sign occupied by the ātmakāraka, from which Jaimini judges dharma, the next world and liberation: Ketu in the twelfth from it gives kaivalya (Jaimini 1.2.13, 1.2.68–69; BPHS 33).
The thirteenfold instrument — buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and the ten capacities — which seizes, holds and illuminates (SK 32); it acts only for puruṣa's purpose (SK 31).
Cause (kāraṇa): what invariably precedes an effect (and is not otherwise established); instrument (karaṇa): the special cause (Tarkasaṅgraha).
From the absence of the cause, absence of the effect, not vice versa (VS 1.2.1–2 C).
The Lord, who alone is independent and produces the effect at will, without depending on karma.
Śaṅkara: the Māheśvaras wrongly make Paśupati only the efficient cause; Brahman is both material and efficient cause.
A (divine) technique — used of the mudrās (HYP 1.56, 1.67) and especially of viparītakaraṇī, which cheats the sun of the nectar (3.78).
A defect in the conditions producing a cognition (e.g. in the sense organ, or in a human speaker), knowledge of which sets aside its validity.
Half a lunar day; eleven karaṇas — seven movable (Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vaṇij, Viṣṭi) and four fixed (Śakuni, Catuṣpada, Nāga, Kiṃstughna); Viṣṭi (Bhadrā) is shunned (BS 99).

notes: Homonym of karaṇa 'instrument'; id disambiguated.

definitions.definition: The means (e.g. the sacrifice) answering the question 'by what?' of the bhāvanā.
The causal body: beginningless, indescribable ignorance, the seed of the other two, experienced in deep sleep; the bliss-sheath.
The palm of the hand as the seat on which the iṣṭaliṅga is worshipped, better than an outer pedestal (SSM 6.54–55).
Activity: the capacity of a present dharma to project its result; the Vaibhāṣikas distinguish the three times by it (Vasumitra's theory of state).

The fourth sign (Cancer), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the heart of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by the Moon; movable; of the water triplicity (later texts); even, female and gentle (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: kulīra (BJ 1.8); dignities: Jupiter exalted (5°); Mars in fall (BJ 1.13).

literal: action; ritual act; the deed and its result

definitions.definition: Action, which no embodied being can abandon (BhG 3.5, 18.11) and which binds only through attachment to its fruit (2.47); also the ritual act (3.14) and the deed that follows its doer 'as a calf finds its mother' (MBh 12.174.16).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action: one's entitlement is to it, never to its fruits (2.47); mere action is far inferior to buddhiyoga (2.49); no one remains without acting even for a moment (3.5); action is better than inaction (3.8); it binds except when done for sacrifice (3.9); sacrifice arises from action and action from brahman (3.14–15); done unattached it leads to the highest (3.19); Janaka and others reached perfection by it (3.20); all actions are done by the guṇas (3.27) and are to be renounced in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).
Ritual action, whose fruit is secured by correct performance and knowledge.
Action of mind, speech and body, bearing good or bad fruit in high, middle or low births (MDh 12.3–9); its residue shapes the next birth (ĀpDh 2.1.2.3).
Motion: residing in one substance, without qualities, the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (VS 1.1.16 C); five kinds (VS 1.1.6).
Action whose results bind; the body arises from the fruits of past actions (NS 3.2.60); 'activity' (pravṛtti) of speech, mind and body (NS 1.1.17).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) action as a category — movement, the cause of conjunction and disjunction (Ca Sū 1.49, 1.52); (2) the deed of a former body, called daiva, whose fruit is this life (Sū 11.31; Vi 3.30); karma-born diseases subside only with its exhaustion (Śā 1.116-117); (3) the five purificatory acts.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Action is the central theme of chs. 4–6: its course is deep and must be understood together with vikarma and inaction (4.16–18); actions do not stain the Lord (4.14); the ancients seeking liberation acted (4.15); all sacrifices are born of action (4.32); all action culminates in knowledge (4.33) and is burned by the fire of knowledge (4.37); for one wishing to ascend to yoga action is the means (6.3); one should do the action that ought to be done without depending on its fruit (6.1).

Action and its result: 'one becomes good by good action, bad by bad action' (BAU 3.2.13); 'as one acts, so one becomes' (BAU 4.4.5); rebirth 'according to action and learning' (KU 2.2.7; KauU 1.2); action does not cling to one who knows (ChU 4.14.3; Īśa 2).
Action: volition and what is produced by volition (bodily and vocal action, manifest and unmanifest); the variety of the world is born of it.
Its result comes not from past karma existing now but from the specific transformation of the series it initiated.

Action and its residue; it cannot be exhausted by experience because new karma is always made, so liberation comes by grace through knowledge, while ritual action at best wins the lowest grace (heaven).

Subtle matter drawn into the soul by its activity and bound by its passions, veiling its qualities and producing its states until shed (TS 8.2); 'material karma' (dravya-karma) as distinct from the soul's passional states (bhāva-karma).
Of three kinds: pralabdh (destiny, lived out in this body), sinchit (stored, burnt by the Master and by practice) and kriyaman (new, avoided by the disciple's vows).

cross_language.note: same word; the Buddhist sense (intention as action) is defined by the Buddhist units

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Cast off by one joined with the understanding according to yoga (2.39); the world is bound by action (karmabandhana) except for action done for sacrifice (3.9); the wise joined with understanding are freed from the bondage of birth (janmabandha, 2.51).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The bondage from which one free of the pairs of opposites is easily released (5.3); the unyoked one, attached to fruit through desire, is bound (5.12); actions do not bind one who knows the Lord's freedom from them (4.14), the one beyond the pairs (4.22), or the one who has renounced actions by yoga and cut doubt by knowledge (4.41).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The words in chs. 4–6 are bandha ('bondage', 5.3) and forms of the verb bandh- (badhyate 4.14; nibadhyate 4.22, 5.12; nibadhnanti 4.41); the compound karmabandha itself is 2.39's.

definitions.definition: The impurity of action in an unconscious agent (ĪPK 3.2.5).
The soul's beginningless stream of good and bad deeds (dharma and adharma) that determines birth, lifespan and experience; distributed by the Lord.
Kaṉmam / iruviṉai: the two deeds, good and bad, both binding.

notes: Same name as in the Śaiva Siddhānta, where the impurity is held to be a real substance.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The commitment of the yogins, one of the two declared by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3); undertaken with the organs of action by one who controls the senses with the mind and is unattached (3.7).
Performing one's prescribed action without attachment to its fruit, as a discipline that frees from the bondage of action (BhG 2.47–48, 3.3–9); judged better than mere renunciation of action (5.2).
The yoga of action, fitting those not yet disgusted who still have desires; performed without desire, it purifies and leads to knowledge or devotion.

Bhagavad Gītā 5.2: the yoga of action, which together with renunciation brings the highest good and is superior to the renunciation of action; in 5.10–12 it is acting with actions placed in Brahman, abandoning attachment and the fruit, for purification of the self.
Action according to one's duty, without sense of agency, ownership or desire for fruit, as the Lord's worship; it purifies the mind and itself can lead to the vision of the self.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Bhārata, where deeds are done and bear fruit and liberation can be won; the other regions are lands of enjoyment.
Regions where people live by work, where religious practice and liberation are possible and Tīrthaṅkaras arise (TS 3.37).
The subtlest body, made of the soul's bound karma, beginninglessly connected with every worldly soul and carrying it between births (TS 2.25, 2.36, 2.40–42).
The ten courses of action, good and bad, the grossest actions of body, speech and mind.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fruit of action, to which one has no right and which should not be one's motive (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are wretched (2.49); the wise abandon the fruit born of action (2.51); the ritual-minded's speech offers birth as the fruit of action (2.43).
Giving up the fruit of all actions — what the discerning call relinquishment (tyāga) (BhG 18.2, 18.11); the fourth and most accessible step of 12.11, praised above meditation in 12.12.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: expressed as abandoning attachment to the fruit of action (karmaphalāsaṅgaṃ tyaktvā, 4.20), giving up the fruit (karmaphalaṃ tyaktvā, 5.12, which brings lasting peace) and not depending on the fruit (anāśritaḥ karmaphalam, 6.1).

equivalents.note: BhG 18.2 defines tyāga as relinquishing the fruit of all actions

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The state in which opposed karmas are equal, neither exceeding the other, marking the time of śaktipāta.
The equality of karmas that the soul attains when looked upon by Viṣṇu with grace; the two karmas fall silent.

The residue of meritorious and demeritorious action, rooted in the afflictions, to be experienced in this or a future birth (2.12); ripening as birth, life-span and experience (2.13); normally 'of one life' (YBh 2.13).
Five agents: vaikārika (good acts), taijasa (bad), bhūtādi (deluded), sānumāna (good-deluded), niranumāna (bad-deluded) (Kramadīpikā on Tattvasamāsa 11).
The formula of a legal act of the Saṅgha (motion and proclamations).

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The ripening of karma; a genre relating specific afflictions and inauspicious births to specific sins of former lives and prescribing expiations (Karmavipākasaṃhitā; BPHS 83).
Five sources of action — steadfastness, faith, seeking happiness, the wish not to know, the wish to know — of which only the wish to know leads to liberation (Kramadīpikā on Tattvasamāsa 9).
Speech, hands, feet, anus and genitals (SK 26), whose functions are speaking, grasping, walking, excreting and delight (SK 28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Restraining the organs of action while recalling objects in the mind is hypocrisy (3.6); karmayoga is undertaken with the organs of action, the senses controlled by the mind (3.7).
Rejuvenating preparations and regimens (kāya kaṟpam) — herbal, mineral-metal, breath and yogic — meant to make the body firm and long-lived; dismissed as needless for the true knower by Kuṭampai (2).

equivalents.note: both name rejuvenation; kaṟpam also covers breath and yogic means

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fault (kārpaṇya-doṣa) by which Arjuna says his very nature is struck when he asks for instruction (2.7).
The humble awareness of one's inability to adopt any other means; fifth limb of prapatti.
The fault of pity or faint-heartedness that strikes Arjuna's nature (BhG 2.7).
The first of the temple-building rites (ploughing the site), opening the series that ends in installation.
The 'Master' or 'Doer': God as the one Lord, present in Āulcānd and in the hereditary head (Kartā) of the sect; the Kartābhajā are 'worshippers of the Kartā'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27); Kṛṣṇa says that by not acting he would be the doer (cause) of confusion (3.24).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the Lord is the maker (kartṛ) of the fourfold class order, yet is to be known as the non-doer (akartṛ), imperishable (4.13).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the linking of action with its fruit; svabhāva is at work (5.14); the yoked knower thinks 'I do nothing at all', the senses moving among their objects (5.8–9).
Agency, imperishable, as opposed to effect-hood, which perishes (SK 1.14).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Compassion cultivated toward the suffering, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Saṃyama on it yields its strength (3.23).
The second brahmavihāra, abandoning cruelty (MN 62; DN 13).
Compassion is the nurse of the buddha's children (RGV 1.34); love for beings seen as reflections and echoes (Vimalakīrti 6).
In Jainism compassion toward the afflicted (TS 7.11: kāruṇya).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

notes: Shared slug with the Sanskrit term.

definitions.definition: All that is dependent: vidyā, kalā and paśu - eternal, yet wholly subject to the Lord's will.
The meaning of Vedic sentences and of the injunction: the act as what is to be done, known only from the Veda; all words mean in connection with it (kāryānvitābhidhāna).

equivalents.note: Prābhākaras use kārya (the to-be-done) and niyoga (the command) for the injunction's content from two sides

definitions.definition: One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
Latent attachment: the mind's stiffening under impressions of attachment even without distraction.
The four passions — anger, pride, deceit, greed — which make karma stick to the soul (TS 6.4, 8.2); each in four grades of intensity.
The discoloured or ochre cloth of the renouncer.
Ten kasiṇas — earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, space, consciousness — perceived above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable (AN 10.25).
A device (disk of earth, water, fire, colour, light, space) used to produce the learning and counterpart signs and the jhānas; ten are listed.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The dejection that has come upon Arjuna at the critical moment, not practised by the noble, not leading to heaven, bringing disgrace (2.2).
Passionate love, the love of the heroine for the Lord in the akam hymns.
The letter-numeral code (k, ṭ, p, y = 1 …) used to encode numbers in words — in the Jaimini Sūtras (signs, periods), in Kerala astronomy (candravākyas) and in many mnemonic verses.
Debate as a genre, of three kinds: vāda, jalpa and vitaṇḍā.
The robe-making ceremony after the rains with its privileges.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: 'Binding': a fixed (solidified) mercury or mineral preparation; also a bandage.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
Kula is Śakti and akula Śiva; their relation is kaula; worship of the cakra drawn in outer space is conventionally called Kaula (Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
Outer worship on a physical support, and the Kaula doctrines of the pūrva and uttara schools, which the Samaya way rejects (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8, 23, 34-35).
The Kaula Upaniṣad's teaching: knowledge is the sole cause of liberation, which is being the self of all; inwardly Śākta, outwardly Śaiva, among people Vaiṣṇava.
The Kula path and its initiate; the highest of the seven modes of conduct (Kulārṇava 2.7-8), of the nature of both enjoyment and yoga (2.23).
The seventh and highest mode, beyond which there is nothing (Kulārṇava 2.8)
The initiate of the Kula, skilled in joining Kula and Akula (Kulārṇava 17.27); knower of the seven ullāsas (8.95).
The Goddess as Kaula, 'possessing kaula' — the fusion of Śiva and Śakti (Bhāskararāya); also the eighth goddess of speech.
Children's medicine: rearing of children, purification of the wet-nurse's milk, and diseases arising from bad milk and seizing spirits (Su Sū 1.8); the subject of the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā.
The loincloth kept by most kinds of renouncer, or abandoned by the highest.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.50 yoga is defined as 'skill in actions' (karmasu kauśalam).
The smaller movable image, linked to the fixed image, standing for Viṣṇu's partite form and receiving the full daily worship.
An inspired poet-sage, one who sees and speaks what is hidden (RV 10.129.4, 1.164.6).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Even kavis are bewildered about what action and inaction are (4.16).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Poetry: word and meaning together (Bhāmaha 1.16); faultless word and meaning with qualities (KP 1.4); a sentence whose soul is rasa (SD 1.3); a word conveying a charming meaning (Jagannātha).
Faults of word, sense and rasa that diminish poetry (SD 1.3); treated at length in KP 7.
The qualities of poetry — sweetness (mādhurya), vigour (ojas) and clarity (prasāda) in the later scheme, ten in Daṇḍin and Vāmana — which for Mammaṭa belong to rasa as heroism belongs to the self.
Perfection of the body — the Siddhar goal of an undecaying, powerful body as the vessel of liberation; 'after kāyacitti removed my karma' (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 14).
