Beauty, grace, strength and adamantine firmness (3.46).
Perfection of the body: the deathless, adamantine body of the siddha, gained by retaining bindu and nectar.
Internal medicine: diseases affecting the whole body such as fever, bleeding disorders, consumption, insanity, epilepsy, skin disease, urinary disorders and diarrhoea (Su Sū 1.8).
In the Visuddhimagga, the contemplation of the thirty-two parts as repulsive, leading to the first jhāna.

Honest work in one's occupation undertaken as worship; 'work is Kailāsa' (Āydakki Mārayya's vacana), not to be interrupted even for the guru, the liṅga or a jaṅgama, and not to gather more than the day's need.

equivalents.note: both make work an offering; kāyaka is specifically one's livelihood, with its fruit shared (dāsōha)

definitions.definition: Enduring bodily hardship — difficult postures, exposure — in the list of external austerities (TS 9.19).

Contemplating the body in the body — breathing, postures, clear comprehension, the parts, the elements, the charnel-ground stages (MN 10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four establishments of mindfulness.
A trainee who contacts the formless liberations and has some effluents destroyed (MN 70).
In-and-out breathing (MN 44), calmed in the fourth step of mindfulness of breathing (MN 118).
Standing (or sitting) motionless, indifferent to the body, for a set period measured in recitations; an essential duty and a form of internal austerity (vyutsarga).
The angles: the 1st, 4th, 7th and 10th houses (kaṇṭaka, catuṣṭaya), where planets are strong (BJ 1.17).

notes: Scholarly account: from Greek kentron.

definitions.definition: Plucking out the hair of head and face by hand, at initiation and periodically thereafter, as a practice of endurance and non-attachment to the body.
The ascetic's periodic plucking out of the hair of head and face by hand, at initiation and thereafter.
The long-haired one who bears fire, poison-drink, heaven and earth and is called light (RV 10.136.1); the Anukramaṇī names the keśins Agni, Sūrya and Vāyu.

(1) The descending node, the headless trunk of the asura, counted as the ninth graha (BJ 2.3 'Śikhin'); the Fish avatāra is born from him (BPHS 2.6); period 7 years; in the twelfth from the kārakāṃśa he gives kaivalya (Jaimini 1.2.69). (2) A comet (the Ketus of BS 11).
Alone, isolated: the knower of God is 'alone, with desires fulfilled' (ŚU 1.11); God is 'alone and without qualities' (6.11); aloneness (kevalatva) through the suṣumṇā (MaiU 6.21).
Kēvalam: the soul's condition before embodiment, alone with āṇava, knowing nothing.
The omniscient's perception of all things in their general aspect; whether it occurs in sequence with, simultaneously with, or identical to omniscient knowledge is debated.
Perfect knowledge of all substances in all their modes, past, present and future, arising when the knowledge-obscuring and other destructive karmas are destroyed (TS 1.29, 10.1).
Spontaneous retention free of inhalation and exhalation; when mastered nothing is unattainable and rājayoga is reached (HYP 2.73–75); no retention equals it (1.43).
Spontaneous suspension of breath; its signs and the awakening of kuṇḍalinī. Summary only.
Knowledge that accords with its object, of four grades: the Lord's, Lakṣmī's, the yogins' and others'.
A probans or probandum with only positive concomitance, as 'knowable' or 'nameable', which has no absence anywhere; a test case for definitions of pervasion.
A probans with only negative concomitance, e.g. 'earth differs from the rest because it has smell'.
The omniscient takes morsel-food (kavalāhāra) while his body lasts; hunger, thirst and the other feeling-karma hardships occur in him.
Affirmed and argued by Śākaṭāyana.
Denied: the omniscient is free of hunger and thirst (two of the eighteen faults) and his body is sustained without morsel-food.

cross_language.note: morsel-eating

definitions.definition: One who has attained omniscience; the Tīrthaṅkaras are kevalins who found a teaching-ford, others are ordinary kevalins.
A celibate devotee who lives in the sattra, devoted wholly to worship; the ideal set by Mādhavadeva.
The five aggregates — form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness — whatever of each is past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle (SN 22.48).
The five aggregates: matter, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness.

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Concentration lasting only for the moment, named in the Visuddhimagga among the three kinds; in the sub-commentary, the unification of mind of the pure-insight practitioner.
Concentration arising from uninterrupted moment-to-moment noting, strong enough to suppress the hindrances and support insight without prior jhāna.
Patient endurance of abuse and injury (MN 21; MN 145); the sixth perfection (Bv 2).
The begging bowl of the yogī.
The skull or skull-shaped bowl from which the Aghora ascetic eats and drinks.
Staff crowned with a skull, a sub-insignia of the Kāpālas; its bell rings as Kapālakuṇḍalā flies.
Carried with the skull in the lokātīta observance.
The power of sky-going given by 'bound' mercury and bound breath (Rasārṇava 1.19), and the aim of dehavedha (SDS Raseśvara 24).

notes: Not the haṭha khecarī mudrā.

definitions.definition: (1) The mudrā in which the tongue, reversed, enters the cavity above the palate and the gaze is between the brows — best of mudrās (HYP 1.43, 3.32); RESTRICTED. (2) In HYP 4.43–47, the state in which the breath moves in the middle between sun and moon; the name is explained as 'the mind moves in space (kha) and the tongue moves in space' (3.41).
The seal of the tongue turned back into the cavity of the skull with the gaze between the brows (GŚ 34); a restricted practice.
Also a name of Śakti, 'moving in the sky' (KJN 20.10), and of the class of sky-going yoginīs.
A secret seal learned from a guru with its mantra; bodily procedures recorded summary-only; inwardly the gaze or the renouncer's seal.
The state of Śiva when innate knowledge arises (Śiva Sūtra 2.5).
A seal named among five (VBT 77) and a power-group in the pañcavāha.
Tamil kēcari: the Tirumantiram's kēcari yōkam section (third tantra), revered by the Siddhars; restricted, summary only.

notes: Not the haṭha tongue-practice of the same name.

definitions.definition: Gods who fall from their state through excessive play; one of the grounds of partial eternalism.
A supplementary hymn transmitted with a Saṃhitā but not counted in it.
Among Muslim Bāul-Fakirs: the initiation into renunciant fakirhood (the fakiri counterpart of bhek).
'Mad one': a name of affection for the God-mad Bāul.
Theory of what appears in erroneous cognition; the Mīmāṃsā schools hold akhyāti (Prābhākara) and viparītakhyāti (Bhāṭṭa).
The 'pin' or 'bolt' of a mantra, named with its seed (bīja) and power (śakti) in the preliminary formula before recitation.
White spots of the skin, treated with the dark plant (AVŚ 1.23–24).
The ten bases of defilement: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing.
Greed, hatred, delusion and the states born of them (a mostly commentarial collective term).

equivalents.note: Yoga's five kleśas and the Abhidhamma's ten overlap partly

definitions.definition: Consciousness that performs a function without being kamma or result — e.g. adverting, and all the impulsions of an arahant.

literal: doctrine of action / of the efficacy of deeds

definitions.definition: The doctrine that deeds are effective, taught by all Buddhas (kammavāda, kiriyavāda, viriyavāda); the one Ājīvaka who went to heaven held it.
The first 'assembly': 180 kinds; the true kiriyavāda is taught by one who knows self and world, influx, stopping and wearing away of karma; a rival 'kiriyāvāda' of intention alone is rejected.
Singing or reciting the Lord's names and deeds, the chief means of the Kali age.
Singing the Lord's names and deeds: the girls of the Tiruppāvai 'sing with the mouth'; the devotees roam the earth singing and dancing (TVM 5.2.1).
Hearing and singing the Lord's qualities is a means to devotion even in worldly life (NBS 37); being sung of, he quickly manifests (NBS 80).
Kīrtan: a sung and spoken discourse on an abhaṅga, with the chorus singing the name, led by a kīrtankār; with bhajan the heart of Vārkarī practice.
Singing the Lord's names and deeds, with hearing (śravaṇa) the foremost of the nine devotions; the Kīrtana-ghoṣā is its text.
Devotional song, especially singing the Lord's names and deeds, alone or in a group; in Karṇāṭaka music also the name of a composed song form (kṛti).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The unmanliness to which Arjuna is told not to yield, with 'petty weakness of heart' (hṛdaya-daurbalya) (2.3).
The kapha in the stomach that moistens and breaks down the mass of food (AHS Sū 12.16-17; Su Sū 21.12-14).

The five afflictions — ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion, clinging to life (2.3) — the five errors (YBh 2.3), rooted in ignorance (2.4), root of the karmic residue (2.12); thinned by kriyā-yoga, abandoned by meditation and involution (2.2, 2.10–11), ceasing through the cloud of dharma (4.30).
Defilement; what calms them is the discernment of dharmas; a defilement arises complete from an unabandoned anuśaya, a present object and improper attention.
The afflictions, whose destruction comes by yoga alone (VP 6.7.25).

cross_language.note: Buddhist defilements; lists differ

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Class of mental factors (six): delusion, heedlessness, laziness, lack of faith, torpor, restlessness.
Said of activities caused by the afflictions that become the field for accumulating karmic residue (YBh 1.5).
Non-killing: 'sharing food and protecting all life is the foremost precept' (Kuṟaḷ ch. 33).
Taught among the virtues of the first tantra of the Tirumantiram.
Non-killing, which Pattirakiriyār longs for: regarding living beings as one's own life (14).
The dharma as a raft to be left behind once the crossing is made — even dharmas must be abandoned, still more non-dharmas.
Sheath, case: the golden sheath in which brahman is (MuU 2.2.9); the cosmic chest (ChU 3.15). The later Vedānta name 'pañca-kośa' for the five selves of TU 2 is not used in the TU itself.
Tamil kōcam: the five sheaths among the ninety-six principles.
Sequence: the unbroken flow of moments, apprehended at the end of a transformation (3.15, 3.52, 4.33).
The order of performance, fixed by direct statement, purpose, textual order, position, the order of principals and the order once begun (MS 5.1.1; Arthasaṅgraha).
Gradual liberation: meditators on the qualified Brahman reach the Brahma-world by the path of light and are liberated with its ruler at the end of the cycle (BS 4.3.10).
Liberation by stages: the yogin ascends to Satyaloka and is liberated with Brahmā at the dissolution (BhP 2.2.22-31).
Renunciation after passing through the stages.
Recitation of overlapping word pairs (ab, bc, cd …).
Recitation in overlapping pairs of words (ab, bc, cd…), the first of the modified recitations that guard the text.
Feigning sleep while awake, with a snoring sound in the throat.
Effective will and resolve; 'may auspicious intentions come from all sides' (RV 1.89.1); the gods go toward one kratu (6.9.5).
The purpose or resolve that constitutes a person: as his resolve at departure, so he becomes in the next world (ŚB 10.6.3.1).
Resolve, will: 'a person is made of resolve; as his resolve here, so he becomes on departing' (ChU 3.14.1; cf. BAU 4.4.5); 'O resolve (mind), remember' (Īśa 17).

literal: for the sake of the rite

definitions.definition: What is done for the rite rather than for the person, as opposed to puruṣārtha (MS 4.1.1).
The flesh-eating cremation fire sent away to Yama's realm after the cremation (RV 10.16.9).
A class of expiatory penances regulating food over a set number of days (MDh 11.211–215) — restricted content.
The Lord's nature and motive: in play he produces, favours and conceals the threefold effect; 'deva' is derived from div 'to play'.

equivalents.note: both name divine activity as play, without need

definitions.definition: The tank at Kīnārām Sthal, Śivālā, Varanasi — the chief seat of the Aghora lineage, whose water is held to heal.
Worms in body and animals, destroyed by charms (AVŚ 2.32).
The Lord's power of action, his creatorhood, making things appear by his will (ĪPK 2.4.1).
Kiriyai: ritual worship of Śiva in the liṅga and image, the son's path (satputra-mārga), leading to sāmīpya.
In the Uddhava Gītā: ritual worship of the Lord — Vedic, tantric or mixed — in an image, ground, fire, sun, water or the heart.
Austerity, self-study and devotion to Īśvara (2.1), for cultivating samādhi and thinning the afflictions (2.2); taught for the unconcentrated mind (YBh 2.1).

notes: Distinct from the Yoga Sūtra's kriyā-yoga (austerity, study, devotion to Īśvara).

definitions.definition: The six stages of a disease at each of which treatment may intervene — accumulation, provocation, spreading, lodging, manifestation, differentiation (Su Sū 21.18-36).
The liṅga-sthala where action dissolves through the guru's knowledge; all rites are a fraction of liṅga-worship (SSM 15.30–36).
The liberated's power of acting: swiftness of mind, taking forms at will, and acting without organs.
The power of action; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad it is the Goddess's seat (pīṭha).
Minor breath causing hunger (SS 3.8; attributions vary between texts).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Anger: arises from desire and gives rise to delusion (2.62–63); the sage of steady thought is free from it (2.56); named with desire as the enemy born of rajas (3.37).
Anger, born of desire (BhG 2.62), twin of desire from rajas (3.37), a gate of hell (16.21).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: those free of passion, fear and anger came to the Lord's being (4.10); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood (5.23); the ascetics free of desire and anger have brahma-nirvāṇa near (5.26); the sage from whom desire, fear and anger are gone is ever liberated (5.28).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The supreme compassion that overcame Arjuna on seeing his kinsmen (1.28, 2.1).
Grace, compassion: 'a drop of the Lord's grace' (bhagavat-kṛpā-leśa) and the grace of great souls are the chief means to devotion (NBS 38).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit of action (2.49).
The Yajurveda Saṃhitās in which mantra and explanatory prose are mixed (Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka, Kapiṣṭhala).
The first and best age (also Satya-yuga), when dharma stands on four feet and meditation (dhyāna) on Viṣṇu is the means.
'Made' — the Kaula path of effort in which kuṇḍalī is impelled by seals and mantras, contrasted with the innate (sahaja) (Akulavīra B.43–45).
The insulted wise ascetic, whose austerity is thereby complete.
Totality; ten — eight (earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white) in the fourth dhyāna, two (space, consciousness) formless.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Lunar mansion kṛttikā: presiding deity Agni (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord the Sun (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class mixed (miśra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). First in the Vedic lists (VJ r.25; ŚB 2.1.2.3 on laying the fires under the Kṛttikās).

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: A harmful spell or effigy sent by an enemy, turned back by counter-rites.
Forgiveness, 'the highest peace' (MBh 5.33.48) and 'the highest strength' (3.203.41); a mark of the dear devotee (BhG 12.13).
Forbearance, the first of the ten dharmas ('supreme forbearance', uttama-kṣamā), the virtue by which anger is conquered.

Asking and granting forgiveness — to all beings in daily and annual confession, and person to person at Paryuṣaṇa; the Kalpa Sūtra makes it the condition of being a true 'fulfiller' of the discipline.
Mutual asking and granting of forgiveness, above all at the end of Paryuṣaṇa ('micchāmi dukkaḍaṃ').

equivalents.note: the Buddhist end-of-rains 'invitation' to be admonished is a comparable communal reconciliation; the contents differ

definitions.definition: The smallest unit of time, the time in which a moving atom passes from one point to the next; only the moment is real (YBh 3.52).

cross_language.note: Buddhist momentariness doctrine differs

definitions.definition: Momentariness: the conditioned is momentary, perishing as soon as it arises (the reason bodily manifestation is shape, not movement).
Destruction has no cause: what arises perishes of itself.
Some formations are momentary, others endure for a time (Vasumitra).
Acceptance: the third root of penetration (one who obtains it never goes to bad destinies); also the pure acceptances of the path of seeing, uninterrupted paths.
The third perfection, shown when the king of Kaliṅga cut the Buddha's limbs and he had no notion of self; also the 'acceptance' of dharmas' non-arising.
The ascent (stages 8–10, 12) by destroying the deluding karma, leading without fall to omniscience.
All souls whose bodies perish — Brahmā, Śiva, the gods and the rest.
All beings, the perishable puruṣa (BhG 15.16); perishable existence is the adhibhūta (8.4).
The perishable, paired with the imperishable: primal matter (pradhāna) is the perishable, Hara the imperishable (ŚU 1.10); the perishable is ignorance (ŚU 5.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: For a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma (2.31); happy the kṣatriyas who meet such a battle, an open door to heaven (2.32).
The warrior's duty, for whom nothing is better than a righteous war (BhG 2.31); heroism and not fleeing in battle are born of his nature (18.43).
A rare 'lost' lunar month containing two solar ingresses.
Knowledge of destruction (of the outflows), arising when the vajra-like concentration has done its work; with the knowledge of non-arising, it is awakening.
A state arising from the destruction of karma — knowledge, perception, giving, gain, enjoyment, energy, right view and conduct (TS 2.4).
A state arising from partial destruction and partial subsidence of karma — most ordinary knowledge and perception (TS 2.5).

The body and the whole of prakṛti with its modifications — elements, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, the organs, the objects, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness and steadfastness (BhG 13.1, 13.5–6).
A sacred territory such as Kāśī or Puruṣottama; seven cities are liberating (GP 2.38.5).

The one who knows the field (body); the Lord declares himself the knower in all fields (BhG 13.1–2); it illumines the field as the sun the world (13.33). In the Mokṣadharma, the knower is the twenty-fifth, distinct from yet joined to sattva like fish and water (12.294, 12.187.39).
Vāsudeva, the knower of the field whose self is without guṇas (Nārāyaṇīya 12.326.38).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the unmanifest self, knower of the field of the twenty-three (Ca Śā 1.61-65); for Suśruta many, eternal, not all-pervading (Su Śā 1.3, 1.16).
In the VP the lower (aparā) śakti of Viṣṇu, the embodied knower veiled by avidyā-karma; in MkP 38.15 the self other than the aggregate of guṇas.
The self that makes the embodied self act, distinguished from the elemental self (bhūtātman) that acts (MDh 12.12).
Knower of the field: God is lord of pradhāna and of the kṣetrajña (ŚU 6.16); the part that is pure consciousness in each person (MaiU 5.2).

equivalents.note: the knower of the field of ch. 13 and the puruṣa of 13.19–23 are the same principle described from the side of knowing and of experiencing

definitions.definition: An inherited or chronic disease (AVŚ 3.7).
The twelfth guṇasthāna: delusion destroyed; the other destructive karmas follow, yielding omniscience.
The scattered mind, the first level (YBh 1.1).
Agitation whose subsidence reveals the supreme state (SK 1.9).

The advanced Digambara lay renunciants of the eleventh pratimā: the kṣullaka keeps two cloths and a bowl, the ailaka a single loincloth and eats from the hand; the next step is muni-initiation into nudity. Women may become kṣullikās.
The goddess of the Paścimāmnāya, who emerged from the liṅga and became bent out of shame (Kubjikāmata 2.3-5; 2.14); praised as the coiled power (2.2).

equivalents.note: the hymn of KMT 2.2 describes her as 'coiled like a sleeping serpent'; she is also a cult goddess with her own consort and maṇḍala

definitions.definition: The 'fault of Mars': Mars in certain houses (commonly the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th or 12th) of a marriage chart, held to endanger the spouse unless matched or cancelled.

notes: Widely applied in marriage matching; the classical verse usually quoted is of uncertain source.

definitions.definition: Śakti; also the body, family, country and the lower thousand-petalled lotus (Bhāskararāya on LSN 36-37); the Goddess delights in kula-nectar and guards the kula conventions.
Śakti — the totality of powers, the 'family' of the Goddess, her yoginīs and mothers, and the manifest world; paired with akula, Śiva (Kulārṇava 17.27).
The Goddess's family of powers ordered in the six centres; the Kubjikāmata calls itself the Kula lineage of the Kulālikāmnāya.
The 'family' — the domain of Śakti in the body and cosmos; the Kula aim, foundation and scripture (KJN 2.10; 3.1).
In the Trika's Kaula dimension, the totality of the powers (Śakti) as opposed to akula (Śiva); the Kaula rule dwelling in Bhairava's heart (Parātrīśikā 4).

equivalents.note: Kulārṇava 17.27 identifies Kula with Śakti

definitions.definition: The ancient dharmas of a family, whose destruction in war Arjuna fears (BhG 1.40).
The Kaula way itself, in which enjoyment becomes yoga, sin merit, and saṃsāra liberation (Kulārṇava 2.24); those established in it do not return to rebirth (2.30).

The consecrated substances of Kaula worship (the five tattvas); held to manifest the bliss of Brahman in the body when used within the rite, and condemned outside it (Kulārṇava 5.72-80; 5.96-105). Summary only.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The destruction of a family, whose fault Arjuna says the greedy Kauravas do not see but he does (1.38–39); it destroys the family dharmas (1.40).
Trees in which the Kula yoginīs always dwell; one should not eat from their leaves but worship them (Kulārṇava 11.66).
A person born with the dharma of yogins, fit for instruction (YDS).
The rules of conduct of the Kaula, taught in Kulārṇava 11 — honouring women and Kula yogins, keeping the samayas, secrecy.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas perish when a family is destroyed (1.40), are uprooted by the family-destroyers (1.43), and those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell (1.44).
One of the patriarchs who, at the end of the age of wish-fulfilling trees, guided people and instituted the first laws; the last was Nābhi, father of Ṛṣabha (lists of seven or fourteen).

cross_language.note: Digambara usage

definitions.definition: The 'pit of kula' at the base of the spine where the Goddess sleeps coiled (SL 10); she 'dwells in the kula-pit' (LSN 93).
The Goddess as head of the Kula, addressed throughout the Kulārṇava; worshipped with Kuleśvara/Bhairava.
A pill; in the Siddhar legends also the magic pill that gives flight or invisibility.
A young girl worshipped as the Goddess, especially in Navarātri (Devī Bhāgavata 3.26).
Worship of a young girl as the Goddess, prescribed in the eastern tantras (Rudrayāmala and others) and part of Durgā-pūjā in Bengal and of Kāmākhyā worship.

The eleventh sign (Aquarius), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the shanks of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by Saturn; fixed; of the air triplicity (later texts); odd, male and cruel (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: hṛdroga (BJ 1.8); dignities: — (BJ 1.13).

Breath-retention: of two kinds, sahita (with inhalation and exhalation) and kevala (alone) (HYP 2.71); eight named varieties in HYP 2.44 and a different eight in GS 5.47. Extreme retention is restricted in this ontology (summary only).
Retention of breath; sahita (with inhalation and exhalation) or kevala (spontaneous). Methods recorded summary-only.
Retention, at whose end, as at the end of exhalation or inhalation, the Peaceful shines (VBT 27).
The prescribed fire-pit, of various shapes, for homa; described in the Kāmika's kuṇḍa chapter.

The power (śakti) coiled at the base of the central channel, blocking its mouth; the support of all yoga (HYP 3.1); awakened by the guru's grace (3.2) and by breath, locks and mudrās (3.5, 3.66–69), she pierces the lotuses and knots and makes the mind supportless. Synonyms: kuṭilāṅgī, bhujaṅgī, śakti, īśvarī, kuṇḍalī, arundhatī (3.104); coiled eightfold (GŚ 30) or three and a half times (ṢCN). For yogins she is for liberation, for fools for bondage (HYP 3.107).

The Goddess herself as the coiled power: dwelling in the mūlādhāra she pierces the three knots, mounts the thousand-petalled lotus, showers nectar, and returns to sleep in three and a half coils (LSN 38-40; SL 9-10).
The coiled power lying eightfold above the bulb, closing the door of Brahman, awakened by the fire of yoga or by the guru's grace to rise through suṣumṇā (GŚ 30–31; HYP 3.2).
One of the names of Śiva's Will-power (KJN 20.11); in the Akulavīra the kuṇḍalī is the 'made' (kṛtaka) path, the innate abiding in samarasa (B.43).
The world-mother, pedestal of the liṅga of the void (Jñāneśvarī 6.272–273), coiled three and a half times (6.223).
The Goddess coiled three and a half times around the Svayambhū liṅga at the base, led up through the centres to unite with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 51-53, Pūrṇānanda).
Kubjikā praised as 'coiled like a sleeping serpent' (Kubjikāmata 2.2).
Śabda-brahman in the body: consciousness dwelling coiled in the middle of the body, from which the letters arise (ŚT 1.14).
The power of Brahman in the root centre which, straightened up to the brahmarandhra, bestows nectar (ŚR 1.2.121–122).
The coiled power at the base that blocks the door of Brahman and, awakened, rises to Śiva.
The coiled power in the root centre, meditated upon at dawn as moving up and down the inner path and led through the six centres to union with the supreme.
The power rising from the root through the wheels to the dvādaśānta (VBT 28-29), 'curved in form' as the breath (VBT 154); the Trika distinguishes its forms as power of breath and of consciousness.
Tamil kuṇṭali: the coiled power at the root, roused by the guru's grace to pass the six supports (Vināyakar akaval; Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam invocation).
The coiled power whose waking and ascent Jñāneśvar describes in Jñāneśvarī 6 as the Nāths' royal road (summary only).

equivalents.note: the Vajrayāna inner fire (caṇḍālī, gtum mo) that rises in the central channel; functional analogy only — the traditions do not identify them
kuṇḍalinī is the Goddess in the body

notes: The word kuṇḍalinī itself is not in VBT 28-29 (the text says 'śakti'); the identification is the commentators'.

definitions.definition: Worship offering vermilion with each name of the Sahasranāma or Triśatī.
The coiled power at the root, in whose seat Guha is invoked (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam kāppu); Tamil form of kuṇḍalinī.

equivalents.note: Tamil form

definitions.definition: A tortoise-shaped channel in the chest below the throat-well; saṃyama there gives steadiness (3.31, YBh 3.31).
Minor breath causing the opening (and closing) of the eyes (SS 3.8).
The division of the land into nine regions like a tortoise, each ruled by three asterisms from Kṛttikā, by which omens are assigned to countries (BS 14.1).
A goddess of the Śrīkula; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad 'the mother', deity of the offering; named in LSN 93.
Wholesome: consciousness and factors rooted in non-greed, non-hatred and (often) non-delusion, blameless and producing pleasant results.
Class of mental factors (ten): faith, heedfulness, tranquillity, equanimity, shame, dread of blame, non-greed, non-hatred, non-harming, vigour.
A 'peak' or section of the Śrīvidyā mantra; the three kūṭas (vāgbhava, kāmarāja/madhya, śakti) form the Goddess's subtle body from face to feet (LSN 35-36).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Epithet of the yoked yogin who is satisfied with knowledge and realised knowledge and whose senses are conquered (6.8).
The unchanging: epithet of the imperishable puruṣa (BhG 15.16) and of the unmanifest worshipped by some (12.3).
The immutable, 'anvil-like' consciousness underlying the body and mind, distinct from the reflected consciousness (cidābhāsa); another name for the witness.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The unchanging permanence of the puruṣa (YBh 4.33).
(As reported) Epithet of Pakudha's seven bodies and of the eternalist's self and world: barren, peak-steady, pillar-firm.
The akiriyavādins' world is 'barren and fixed' (vañjho niyao).
First kind of renouncer: keeps topknot, thread, staff and water-pot; eats in one place.
A decoction.

The principal and most difficult mode of rasāyana, taken in a specially built three-chambered hut after purification (Ca Ci 1.1.16-24, 1.4.27-28; AHS Utt 39.5-8); contrasted with vātātapika, taken amid ordinary life exposed to wind and sun.
A hall where ascetics, brahmins and wanderers of various sects met to debate; the six teachers' claims about their dead disciples were discussed there.

(1) A power arising from the destruction-cum-subsidence of karma through austerity — e.g. the transformable or fiery body, healing powers, sky-travel (TS 2.47–48); (2) one of the nine destructional attainments of the omniscient (TS 2.4).
The fruits of the means: knowledge, austerity, permanence (constant union with the god), steadiness and perfection.
The principle preferring the simpler definition or explanation.
The ascendant: the sign (and degree) rising in the east at the moment of birth or of the query — 'the rising of the signs is the lagna; by it the results for the born are to be judged' (BPHS 3.6).
The shame by which the Goddess became bent (kubjikā) when asked for the transmission (Kubjikāmata 2.14).

(1) The three characteristics impermanence, suffering and not-self; (2) in the commentaries' defining method, the characteristic of a dhamma, given together with its function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).
Implication (secondary signification), used when the direct meaning of words is incompatible; in 'tat tvam asi' the words indicate pure consciousness by implication.
Also: a definition or defining mark (as svarūpa- and taṭastha-lakṣaṇa).
Lakṣaṇa: the distinguishing property by which what has been named is set apart from others — the second of the three activities of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
Lakṣaṇā: secondary signification, when the primary meaning does not fit (e.g. 'the village on the Ganges').
Indication of a related meaning; for the Bhāṭṭas the sentence-meaning is always 'indicated' by the word-meanings (as the Prakaraṇapañcikā reports their saying), and arthavādas indicate praise.
Indication, the secondary power by which a word conveys a meaning connected with its primary sense when the primary sense does not fit ('a village on the Ganges').
The passage of a property from future to present to past time-path (3.13, YBh 3.13).
Viṣṇu's consort, eternally free and dependent, the 'akṣara' whose body never perishes, higher than all souls in every quality; as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā she is the higher prakṛti (śakti).
The Lord's eternal consort, inseparable from him, mother of the world and mediator; her rank is disputed between the northern and southern schools.
All-pervading like Viṣṇu and of the Lord's rank; with him the means and the goal; the divine couple is the object of surrender.
The mediator (puruṣakāra) who reconciles soul and Lord; not herself the means; commonly reported as atomic in essence and of the rank of souls, though ever inseparable from the Lord.
Nārāyaṇa's eternal, independent power, whose body is the six qualities and who performs his five acts.
An object of fixed attention; the Nāth body-map counts three (inner, outer, middle); śāmbhavī mudrā is attention on an inner target with the gaze outward (HYP 4.36).
Object of attention in tāraka-yoga: inner, outer or intermediate.
The club held by Lakulīśa ('Lord with the club'), in the left hand in the Kāravaṇa-māhātmya's image.
Carrying a club is among the practices Yāmuna ascribes to the Kālāmukhas.
The supreme Goddess of Śrīvidyā, 'she who plays': Mahātripurasundarī, seated on Kāmeśvara's lap in the Śrīcakra, whose form is the oneness of Śiva and Śakti (LSN 183).
The Goddess Tripurasundarī of the Lalitopākhyāna, who arises from the gods' sacrificial fire to slay Bhaṇḍāsura.

equivalents.note: Lalitā is Brahman, nirguṇa and saguṇa

definitions.definition: The uvula or the region of the palate above which the tongue is inserted in khecarī; also used of the tongue itself when lengthened (GS 1.29-32).

literal: the hanging one (the uvula / soft palate)

definitions.definition: The emblem by which each Tīrthaṅkara's otherwise identical image is recognized, carved on the pedestal: the bull of Ṛṣabha, the conch of Nemi, the serpent of Pārśva, the lion of Mahāvīra, and so on.
Lightening therapy — fasting, digestives, exercise and the like — against heaviness and excess; opposed to bṛṃhaṇa (Ca Sū 22).

notes: Ca Sū 22 not in the DCS portion checked; from memory. Prolonged fasting is not taught as a practice here.

definitions.definition: Gods of the Brahmaloka who, being near liberation, come to urge each Tīrthaṅkara to renounce (TS 4.24–25).
The fourth root of penetration, lasting one moment, immediately followed by the path of seeing.
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
The first ocean ringing Jambūdvīpa (TS 3.7).

Dissolution of mind (with breath): 'the forgetting of objects because latent impressions do not arise again' (HYP 4.34); the lord of the breath, resting on nāda (4.29); Ādinātha taught a crore and a quarter kinds, of which nāda is chief (4.66).

In the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā, 'dissolution' of the world into the Self by four recognitions (space and pot, ocean and waves, shell and silver, all in me), after which there is nothing to renounce, accept or dissolve.
Torpor in meditation, from which one must turn away, 'say the teachers' (SS 6.30).
Dissolution of mind and breath into the supreme; one of the four yogas and a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.3).
Dullness: the mind's lapse into sleep for want of support, first obstacle to nirvikalpa samādhi.
Dissolution of mind; laya-yoga meditates on the Lord in all activity; 'laya is lord of the breath'; also an obstacle in samādhi (torpor).
Tempo: the rest between the actions of tāla, slow, middle and fast.

notes: Distinct from laya-yoga of the haṭha texts.
alt_notes: Musical sense; the term also means 'absorption' in yoga (other units' definitions).

definitions.definition: The yoga in which the mind is dissolved (cittalaya) through 'indications' (saṅketa) — fixing attention on the void, the nose-tip, the brow-centre, the back of the head, the big toes, lying like a corpse — of which Ādinātha taught eight crore (DYŚ 14–24); the third of the four yogas, given to the middling aspirant (SS 5.12). The HYP holds nādānusandhāna the chief laya.
An electuary (confection) of herbs in sugar, honey or ghee.

The coloration of the soul by passion-tinged activity, in six grades — black, blue, grey (inauspicious), yellow-red, lotus-pink, white (auspicious); physical (dravya) and psychic (bhāva) (TS 2.6; Uttarādhyayana 34).

The Lord's free, purposeless-yet-gracious activity in creation and in the avatāras, above all Kṛṣṇa's play in Vraja; VP 6.7.71-72 says his activity is not caused by karma but is for the good of the worlds.
Sport: creation is the Lord's play, without need (BS 2.1.33).
Creation undertaken as spontaneous play, like breathing; the account belongs to the empirical realm.
The realm of prakṛti and time, where creation, maintenance and dissolution are the Lord's play and bound souls transmigrate.

Śiva himself as the unlimited, eternal brahman in which the world dissolves (laya) and from which it arises again, delimited by his own māyā for the sake of worship (SSM 6.36–38); the liṅga is Paraśiva and its pedestal Śakti, their union the universe (11.32); worn on the body as the iṣṭaliṅga.
(1) The manifest, as that which 'merges' into its cause (SK 10). (2) The subtle body that transmigrates (SK 20, 40–42). (3) The inferential mark (SK 5).
Śiva's sign: the manifest (unmanifest Prakṛti) whose root is the unmarked Śiva; the formless (niṣkala) liṅga of worship; the column of fire.
A mark from which something is known; desire and the rest are marks of the self (NS 1.1.10).
Mark; synonymous with hetu, apadeśa, nimitta, pramāṇa, kāraṇa (VS 9.20 Candrānanda).
Three kinds: with positive and negative concomitance, positive only, negative only.
The aniconic form of Śiva used in worship; the Kāmika distinguishes self-manifest, divine, bāṇa, sages' and man-installed liṅgas, and the liṅga given by the guru at initiation.
Bearing the liṅga, outwardly on the body and inwardly in the mind; the given liṅga is never to be separated from the body (SSM 6.26; 6.30–33; 6.48).
The third level: the great principle (mahat), pure being, from which the unparticularized evolve (YBh 2.19).
The second means of determining subsidiarity: the capacity of a word or mantra to express something, which applies the mantra to it (MS 3.3.14).

The subtle body produced first, unattached, constant, made of the principles from mahat down to the subtle elements, which transmigrates, perfumed by the dispositions, and plays its parts like an actor (SK 40–42); it cannot stand without a support (SK 41).
The subtle body that persists from birth to birth until liberation (Kulārṇava 1.11).

equivalents.note: Within Sāṃkhya the 'subtle' (sūkṣma) bodies of SK 39 are the liṅga of SK 40; Vedānta's sūkṣma-śarīra is composed differently.

definitions.definition: Exclusive worship of Śiva in the liṅga; the SSM forbids worshipping, remembering or praising other gods (9.30–32).
One who bears the Pāśupata sign (ash-bath, lying in ash etc.) that marks his stage, as other āśramas have their marks.
Union with the liṅga — the aikya stage, and in common usage the death of a devotee, who is buried rather than cremated.

literal: equal flavour of liṅga and aṅga

definitions.definition: The goal of the path: the soul (aṅga) and Śiva (liṅga) in a union of equal flavour, 'like water poured into water' in common exposition; in the SSM, contemplation of the self dissolved in the sky of consciousness by the nature of sāmarasya (14.42–44).
The union in equal essence of the liṅga (Śiva) and the aṅga (soul), the goal of Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita (Śrīkarabhāṣya).
A member of the community that wears the personal liṅga; the preferred name of the Basava-centred strand, some of whose writers distinguish it from 'Vīraśaiva' while others treat the two as synonyms.

notes: Alternative Kannada form: liṅgavanta.

definitions.definition: Designation used in an early-twentieth-century printed series of Sanskrit Vīraśaiva texts (the 'Vīraśaiva-liṅgi-brāhmaṇa-dharma-granthamālā') presenting Vīraśaiva dharma in brāhmaṇical terms.

notes: Evidence: series titles on the Muktabodha e-texts M00602, M00612, M00620; relevant to dsp:lingayata-hindu-identity.

definitions.definition: The first unwholesome root (MN 9); a source for the origination of kamma (AN 3.34).
Greed, the third gate of hell (BhG 16.21); a sign of increased rajas (14.12).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The Kauravas' minds are overcome by greed (1.38); Arjuna laments being ready to kill his own people out of greed for the pleasures of kingship (1.45).
Greed, the unwholesome root of attachment to objects; characteristic grasping.
Eager longing to attain the emotions of the Vraja residents — the sole qualification for rāgānugā practice.
The transmutation of metals by mercury, to be tested first before application to the body (SDS Raseśvara 24-25).
A world or realm: the world of the living, of the fathers, of the well-doers, the immortal world (RV 9.113.7).
A world or plane of beings; the Purāṇas count fourteen within the egg - seven above from Bhūr to Satya and seven below.
The world of the six senses: 'in this fathom-long body with its perception and mind I declare the world, its origin, cessation and the way' (SN 2.26); 'empty of self' (SN 35.85).
The finite universe of the six substances within infinite empty space, shaped like a standing man (loka-puruṣa), uncreated and beginningless.
A sphere of existence or post-mortem state; the sacrificer constructs his future world through rites — 'a man is born into the world he has made' (ŚB 6.2.2.27).
Public shame and family honour (kul-kī-maryādā), which Mīrā casts off for Kṛṣṇa.

literal: inference as known in the world

definitions.definition: (Purandara) The worldly inference the Cārvākas accept, as against inference that transgresses the worldly path to reach the unseen.
The universe pictured as a man standing with arms akimbo: the lower world as legs, the middle world at the waist, the heavens as chest and head, the abode of the liberated at the crown.
The finite portion of space occupied by the other substances — the universe (TS 5.12).
The mountain range beyond the seventh ocean dividing the lit world from the dark regions beyond.
Conformity to the world: the Buddhas wash, eat, drink, take medicine and show age while free of dirt, hunger, thirst, illness and ageing.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The holding together of the world, with a view to which one should act (3.20) and the wise act unattached (3.25), since people follow the standard the best person sets (3.21).
The welfare and cohesion of the world, for whose sake the wise act unattached, as Janaka did (BhG 3.20, 3.25).
The skull observance of the Lākulas (and Kāpālikas), 'beyond the world'; the Svacchanda calls the Atimārga knowledge lokātīta.

literal: extended in / directed to the world (of the people)

definitions.definition: The school's name: the view that only this world, as far as the senses reach, exists; the doxographies call it the teaching most people follow.
In the Arthaśāstra, one of the three branches of investigation (ānvīkṣikī), with Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

cross_language.note: Tibetan name of the Lokāyata/Cārvāka school
in the Pali canon a branch of brahmanical learning (disputation/nature-lore), not clearly the school

definitions.definition: Kumārila's description of the state of Mīmāṃsā before him: 'mostly made into Lokāyata' (ŚV pratijñā 10); the Nyāyaratnākara names Bhartṛmitra and others.
(As reported) For the Bārhaspatyas the Veda is a mere cover for one who knows the course of the world.
Supramundane: the Buddha's conduct, roots of merit, postures, body, robes and food are beyond the world.
All Tathāgatas are supramundane and without outflows (Vasumitra).
In the Kośa, 'supramundane' qualifies the pure path (e.g. detachment by the supramundane path), not the Buddha's body.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: 'Supramundane' dharma — acts that stop karmic inflow and foster self-restraint — as against laukika (worldly, social) duty, which may be good conduct but is not spiritual dharma.
The noble, taintless path factors, as distinct from the mundane ones affected by the effluents (MN 117).
Transcending the world of the five aggregates: the four paths, four fruits and nibbāna.
The Goddess addressed as Mother in Bengali devotion; the songs of Rāmprasād and Kamalākānta speak to her as her child.
Eight kinds of pride obstructing right view — in knowledge, honour, family, caste, power, wealth, austerity and body (Ratnakaraṇḍa).
The exhilaration of soma (RV 9.1.1 'most exhilarating'; 10.119).
(As reported) The simile for emergent consciousness: as the power to intoxicate arises from kiṇva and other ingredients, none of which has it alone.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The state of the Lord, reached by many who were free of passion, fear and anger and purified by the austerity of knowledge (4.10).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One at the honey stage, whose insight is truth-bearing; the celestials invite him (YBh 3.51).
The bee's way of begging: taking a little food from many houses without troubling any.
Alms gathered a little from many houses, after the cooking fires are out.
The bee's way of alms: taking a little from each house as the bee from flowers, harming none (Daśavaikālika 1).
The stage at which the celestials invite the yogin (YBh 3.51); 'the lamp of yoga' from this stage on is part of knowledge born of discrimination (YBh 3.54).
Name of the three powers of 3.48 — swiftness like mind, action without instruments, mastery of pradhāna (YBh 3.48).
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
The amorous or 'brilliant' rasa, love for Kṛṣṇa as beloved, as of the gopīs; the highest of the five, treated in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi.
Milk, sugar and honey, offered as if wine by householders in the Kali age (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171).
The central consciousness whose unfolding yields the bliss of consciousness (PH 17).
The middle between two breaths, cognitions or states, where reality shines (VBT 26, 61-62, 103).

equivalents.note: the central channel is one sense of madhya (VBT 35; Śiva Sūtra 3.44)

definitions.definition: The disc of concentric continents and oceans around Jambūdvīpa, where humans and animals live (TS 3.7–9).

The middle level of speech: its material is the intellect alone; it follows sequence and goes beyond the working of breath (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); for Nāgeśa, speech in the heart, the level at which the sphoṭa conveys meaning.
The third level of speech, in the heart, where it buds.
Puruṣa's neutrality (SK 19).
(1) Equanimity toward the unruly and incorrigible (TS 7.11); (2) impartiality of mind between doctrines, following reason (Jñānasāra 16; Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 8).
Identified by the commentaries with the Pali of the texts and called the root language of all beings, the language of intrinsic nature.
The fourth noble truth, the way leading to the cessation of suffering: the noble eightfold path (SN 56.11; SN 45.8); in the commentaries also the supramundane path-moment of each of the four stages.
The supramundane path consciousness, occurring once for each of the four stages, which abandons the corresponding fetters.

equivalents.note: same word; in Buddhist usage specifically the noble eightfold path

definitions.definition: Lunar mansion maghā: presiding deity the Fathers (pitṛ) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Ketu (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
Great waking: the notion 'this is I, this is mine' grown firm through past births.
The second mudrā, which stops the upward movement of all channels except the central and brings about the triple confluence (HYP 3.19–24).
Great emotion, the summit of love, found only in the gopīs and fully in Rādhā; divided into rūḍha and adhirūḍha (with modana and mādana, the latter in Rādhā alone).
The supreme love of Rādhā, which the Sahajiyā sees embodied in Caitanya and attainable in the sahaja state of the couple.
The 'great enjoyer' who hates nothing, praises nothing and enjoys all that comes.
Class of mental factors (ten): feeling, volition, perception, desire-to-act, contact, understanding, mindfulness, attention, resolve, concentration.
Space, air, fire, water and earth, produced from the five subtle elements (SK 22; Gauḍapāda on SK 22); specific (viśeṣa), and calm, turbulent or dull (SK 38).
Earth (solidity), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion), internal and external, each seen 'this is not mine' (MN 28; MN 62).
The four primary elements — earth (hardness), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion/support) — on which all derived matter depends.

The four great elements — earth, water, fire, wind — with the natures of solidity, moisture, heat and motion and the functions of supporting, cohering, maturing and expanding; derived matter depends on them.
The 'great point' formed when the rays of Paraśiva are reflected in the mirror of vimarśa; it is the 'I' (Kāmakalāvilāsa 4-5).
The 'Buddhist land' beyond the Himalaya to which Vasiṣṭha was sent to learn the Goddess's Kula worship (Rudrayāmala 17.122-125).
The sixteen great gifts described in the Matsya and other Purāṇas.
The perfected yogin endowed with the powers, chief among Mahādeva's troops (Nandin, Mahākāla and the rest).

notes: Distinct from the Gāṇapatya deity Mahāgaṇapati.

definitions.definition: The twelve who know the Lord's dharma: Brahmā, Nārada, Śambhu, Kumāra, Kapila, Manu, Prahlāda, Janaka, Bhīṣma, Bali, Śuka and Yama.
Śiva who devours all beings; Kālī devours him (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31); Dakṣiṇakālī's Bhairava (Toḍala 1.3).
Kālī as primordial Śakti, whose abode is in the thousand-petalled lotus and from whom Brahmā and the gods arise and into whom they dissolve (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.38-43).

equivalents.note: name of the same goddess

definitions.definition: (As reported) The Ājīvika measure of the fixed round: 8,400,000 great aeons through which every being passes.
The 'great doer' who does whatever comes, without regard to attraction, aversion, merit and demerit, free of ego, like a witness.
The compassion that embraces all beings as an only child and from which the bodhisattva's illness arises; eating meat cuts off its seed.
Great compassion, one of the Buddha's exclusive qualities: a conventional knowledge differing from ordinary compassion in eight ways.
The supreme liṅga identical with supreme brahman (SSM 12.21–24; 12.38–41); in the ṣaṭsthala correspondences the liṅga of the aikya stage.
Human flesh as offering, in hostile literary portraits of Kāpālika and cremation-ground rites.
The 'great mantra' of sixteen names (hare kṛṣṇa … hare rāma …) from the Kalisantaraṇa Upaniṣad, chanted and sung without rules of time or place.
The 'great head-anointing' of the colossal image of Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, held about every twelve years, pouring water, milk, sugarcane juice, saffron and other substances.

The Goddess as the great power of māyā, who makes the universe whirl yet is the queen of the supreme Brahman (SL 98), who drags even the wise into delusion and when pleased grants liberation (Devī Māhātmya 1).
The Goddess as the power that deludes even the wise and creates the world, and when pleased grants liberation.
The deluding aspect of the root Nature, by which creation proceeds (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.102); in Bengal and Assam a common name of the Goddess.
Another name of bindu, the pure material cause.
The third error, tenfold: attachment to the five objects, divine and human (SK 48; Gauḍapāda).
The first of the ten mudrās; kuṇḍalinī becomes straight like a snake struck with a stick (HYP 3.10–14); first taught in the Amṛtasiddhi. (Not the Buddhist Mahāmudrā realization.)
In the haṭha sense, the 'great seal', a posture-and-breath practice destroying sins (GŚ 32–33).

notes: Homonym of the Buddhist Mahāmudrā (U46); only the haṭha sense is defined here.

definitions.definition: (Jain report) The eightfold prognostication Gosāla learned from the six disācaras, drawn from the Pūrvas.
The eightfold lore (year-lore, dreams, marks, portents, bodily signs, omens and the rest) by which some claim to know the future; the Jain text says it sometimes fails and gives no release.
Head of a Nāth monastery (maṭh), e.g. the mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh at Gorakhpur.
The active spiritual leader Rāmdās describes: learned, tireless, organising people, teaching and protecting dharma.
The four great references by which a claimed teaching is checked against the discourses and the discipline (DN 16).
The five great sins: killing a brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, theft (of gold), violating the teacher's bed, and associating with such sinners (MDh 11.54).
One of the eighteen principal Purāṇas; the lists differ in naming the Śiva or the Vāyu and in their order (VP 3.6.21-23; BhP 12.7.23-24; KūP 1.1.13-15).
Title of Śaṅkaradeva (and Mādhavadeva) in the tradition, which is therefore also called Mahāpuruṣīyā.
The fourth upper world, where the wise dwell for a kalpa; passed by the yogin's gradual ascent.
The bodhisattva's resolve to liberate all beings, 'put on' as armor, while knowing that there are no beings to be liberated.
Epithet of the bodhisattva: one armed with the great armor who has set out in the great vehicle to lead countless beings to nirvāṇa.
'Great-souled': a Kartābhajā guru who initiates and collects dues from the disciples (barātī).

The first evolute of prakṛti (SK 22), identical with buddhi; Gauḍapāda lists its synonyms buddhi, āsurī, mati, khyāti, jñāna, prajñā. Vijñānabhikṣu salutes mahat as the self-born Lord, sprout of the world.
The great self: higher than the intellect, below the unmanifest (KU 1.3.10-11); speech is restrained step by step into it (KU 1.3.13).
'Great Brahman', the Lord's womb (BhG 14.3); in the Nārāyaṇīya Aniruddha is called the great self (12.327.26).
The grace of the great souls — the chief means to devotion, together with a drop of the Lord's grace (NBS 38).
Company of the great: hard to gain, unfathomable, unfailing, itself gained by the Lord's grace (NBS 39–40).
In the Mahāparinirvāṇa and Aṅgulimālīya, the Tathāgata's true self, identified with the tathāgatagarbha, in contrast to the imagined self of the aggregates.
The rare one who knows 'Vāsudeva is all' (BhG 7.19); great souls resort to the divine nature and worship with undistracted minds (9.13).
A text or section glorifying a deity, place, time, vow or scripture and its fruits (e.g. Devī Māhātmya, Kāśī-māhātmya, Bhāgavata-māhātmya).
Understanding of Viṣṇu's supremacy and perfection, which must precede and ground bhakti.
Knowledge of the Lord's greatness, which the gopīs never lacked; love without it is a paramour's love (NBS 22–23).
The 'great renouncer' who has given up all notions of dharma and adharma, desire and thought.
The great saying ('that thou art' and the like) that teaches the identity of the delimited consciousness with the whole; understood by partial implication.

'Great saying': a later (Advaita) name for four Upaniṣadic statements of identity, one from each Veda — prajñānaṃ brahma (AU 3.1.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (BAU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (ChU 6.8.7), ayam ātmā brahma (MāU 2; BAU 2.5.19). The word does not occur in these texts.

A 'great saying' of the Upaniṣads teaching the identity of self and Brahman: prajñānaṃ brahma (ṚV/Aitareya), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (Yajur/BĀU), tat tvam asi (Sāma/ChU), ayam ātmā brahma (Atharva/Māṇḍūkya); each is assigned to one of the four āmnāya maṭhas.
U04 usage: the four sayings given as secret teaching (Śukarahasya) and at renunciation; read as the Goddess in the Bahvṛca.
The third mudrā, without which mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless (HYP 3.25–29).
An unimagined activity of mind outside the body, which destroys the covering of the light (3.43).
The ten goddesses — Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā — as forms of the one Goddess (Muṇḍamālā in the Tantrasāra; Toḍala 1 and 10).
Satī's ten forms shown to Śiva before Dakṣa's sacrifice (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.125-134).
The consort Śiva worshipped at each Mahāvidyā's right side (Toḍala 1.3-19).
Firm faith that the Lord will certainly protect ('rakṣiṣyati'); third limb of prapatti and, for Deśika, the most essential.
The restraints when unlimited by class, place, time or occasion (2.31, YBh 2.31).

The skull-bearer's great vow: living with a skull-bowl and skull-staff in imitation of Bhairava's penance; its keepers are 'mahāvratins'. Yāmuna reports 'by taking the Kāpāla vow a man becomes an ascetic'.
The observance of the Lākula division (lokātīta), with skull and khaṭvāṅga.
In Jainism the five vows taken in full by ascetics, to be kept in thought, word and deed, doing, causing and approving (TS 7.2).

cross_language.note: the Jain five great vows of the ascetic — a related but distinct list

notes: Homonym of the Vedic śrauta Mahāvrata rite, which is unrelated.

definitions.definition: Name for skull-observing Śaiva ascetics; Guṇaratna counts the Mahāvratadharas as the third of four kinds of Śaiva ascetics, the Śiva Purāṇa honours them among Śaivas.
The 'great sacrifice': the Goddess is 'worshipped by the sequence of the great sacrifice' (LSN 56).
The five great sacrifices to beings, men, ancestors, gods and Brahman (ŚB 11.5.6.1; TA 2.10).
The householder's daily five sacrifices, expiating the 'five slaughter-places' (MDh 3.68–70).
The vehicle that carries all beings to full awakening; by its own account the Buddha's highest teaching, contrasted with the 'lesser' vehicle (hīnayāna) of those seeking personal nirvāṇa.
Yoga as one, though called fourfold (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja) — a doctrine of the Yogabīja and the Haṭharatnāvalī (recalled).
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā the highest of five yogas: contemplation of Śiva's own nature alone, without adjuncts.
Twelve thousand divine years = 4,320,000 solar years, the unit in which revolutions are counted (SS 1.15; BSS 1.7).
A cycle of the four yugas (catur-yuga) of 12,000 divine years (4,320,000 human years).

notes: Also: caturyuga

definitions.definition: A married woman's mother's home; the saints call Paṇḍharpūr their māher, with Viṭṭhala and Rakhumāī as parents and the saints as kin.
The second sthala: the bhakta in whom devotion rises through dispassion to steady discernment, steadfast in the liṅga even at the loss of life (SSM 10.2–3; 10.21–22).
The Lord whose southern image is worshipped and whose troops the perfected yogin leads; source of the scriptural tradition.
The Lord to be recognized as one's own self: the knower and agent, established from the beginning, full of the undivided awareness 'I am this' (ĪPK 1.1.2, 4.1).
The name under which Praśastapāda's account of dissolution and creation speaks of the Lord.
Friendliness cultivated toward the happy, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Saṃyama on it yields its strength (3.23).
In Jainism friendliness toward all beings — 'may no one do evil, may no one suffer, may the world be freed' (TS 7.11; YŚ 4.118).
Loving-kindness, the first immeasurable, in substance non-hatred, with the aspect 'may beings be happy'.

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The sixth tissue: gives affection, unctuousness and strength, nourishes semen and fills the bones (Su Sū 15.5).

The practice that avoids the two extremes of devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification (SN 56.11); also the teaching 'by the middle' that avoids 'all exists' and 'all does not exist' through dependent origination (SN 12.15).

The tenth sign (Capricorn), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the knees of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by Saturn; movable; of the earth triplicity (later texts); even, female and gentle (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: ākokera (BJ 1.8); dignities: Mars exalted (28°); Jupiter in fall (BJ 1.13).
Impurity binding the soul; Śiva is so called because he is free of the three impurities (SSM 8.8–11); in union the bond of impurity is shaken off (14.5–7).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the body's wastes — urine, faeces, sweat and the rest (AHS Sū 1.13); each tissue has its waste (Ca Ci 15.18-19); the doṣas when vitiating are also called malas.
Impurity, which is ignorance - the cause of the sprouting of saṃsāra (MVT 1.23; TĀ 1.23); not a substance.
What the practitioner strives to destroy: false knowledge, demerit, the cause of attachment, falling away and the root of the paśu-state.
In the narrow sense āṇava mala; in the wide sense any of the bonds. A real substance (dravya), not ignorance.
Malam: impurity; 'the three malas' (mummalam) are āṇavam, kaṉmam and māyai.
The ripening of āṇava mala, whose powers turn away until it is ready to be removed.
Malaparipākam, the ripening that accompanies the balance of deeds and precedes grace.
The alphabet in a scrambled order (beginning NA and ending PHA), with vowels and consonants mixed, uniting Śiva and Śakti; the name of the Mālinīvijayottara's goddess.

notes: Order 'NA ... PHA' from memory.

definitions.definition: The sense of 'mine', root of suffering (MkP 38.6), one of the two forms of ignorance (VP 6.7.11).
The third tissue: gives bulk to the body and nourishes fat (Su Sū 15.5).
Conceit — 'I am better, equal, worse' (Snp 4.9); the eighth fetter, abandoned only at arahantship.
Conceit: measuring oneself as better, equal or worse; a fetter abandoned only by arahantship.
Love-pique: love so intense it takes the form of feigned anger or sulking, a stage above sneha.
Rādhā's jealous pride that makes her withdraw from Kṛṣṇa; the friend counsels her to give it up, and Kṛṣṇa pleads with her (GG 2, 9, 10).

literal: knowledge of the modes of minds

definitions.definition: Direct knowledge of the thoughts of others, only in restrained ascetics; straight or extensive (TS 1.23–25, 1.28).
Reasoned reflection on what was heard, removing doubts (e.g. with companions); a principal means to knowledge.
In the Śiva Purāṇa the third and greatest of the three means (hearing, singing, reflecting on Śiva).
Reflection: continual consideration of the teaching by reasoning in accord with it, removing doubts about the object.

Mind: the swiftest of flying things (RV 6.9.5); the divine mind that goes far in waking and returns in sleep, the one light of lights, heart-seated charioteer (VS 34.1–6); it can wander to Yama and be called back (RV 10.58); desire was its first seed (10.129.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The turbulent senses carry away the mind (2.60), and the mind following the roving senses carries away wisdom (2.67); recalling objects in the mind while restraining the organs of action is hypocrisy (3.6); the senses are controlled by the mind in karmayoga (3.7); higher than the senses, lower than the understanding (3.42); a seat of desire (3.40).
The mind, declared the supreme cause that turns the wheel of saṃsāra (Bhikṣu Gītā); attached to the guṇas it binds, devoted to the Person it frees (Kapila).
The eleventh organ, partaking of both the sense and action capacities, whose function is constructive thought (saṅkalpa) (SK 27); one of the three internal instruments (SK 33).
One in each body and atomic; its mark is the non-simultaneity of cognitions (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56, 3.2.59).
An eternal atomic substance; its mark is the presence or absence of cognition when self, sense and object are in contact (VS 3.2.1, 7.1.30 C).
The inner sense, instrument of apprehending pleasure etc.; endless in number, atomic, eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): beyond the senses, called sattva or cetas; one in number though it seems many; the senses grasp objects only when led by it (Ca Sū 8.4-7); its marks are the presence or absence of knowledge, its qualities atomicity and oneness, its objects what is thought, considered, reasoned, meditated and resolved, its acts directing the senses and restraining itself (Śā 1.18-21); unconscious though active (Śā 1.75); in Bhela located between head and palate (Ci 8).

Mind as the first existent — 'neither non-being nor being; there was only mind' (ŚB 10.5.3.1); the greater of the pair mind and speech (ŚB 1.4.4.7); the brahman priest's track of the sacrifice (ChU 4.16).
The eleventh sense, of the nature of both the organs of knowledge and of action (MDh 2.92), and the instigator of all action (MDh 12.4).

The mind, higher than the senses (BhG 3.42), restless and hard to restrain like the wind (6.34), the sixth with the senses drawn by the jīva (15.7); in the Nārāyaṇīya the liberated 'become mind' in Pradyumna (12.332.15).
The mind, cause of bondage when attached to objects and of liberation when free of them (VP 6.7.28).
Used in YS for the mind made fit for concentrations (2.53) and steadied (1.35); YBh 2.19 counts manas as the eleventh sense.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (6.34), but is held by practice and dispassion (6.35); it is to be made one-pointed (6.12), made to abide in the self (6.25) and brought back wherever it wanders (6.26); all actions are renounced 'by the mind' (5.13).

Mind: made of food (ChU 6.5.4); desire, intention, doubt, faith, shame, fear are all mind (BAU 1.5.3); the reins of the chariot (KU 1.3.3); 'the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation' (MaiU 6.34); 'by the mind alone is it to be seen' (BAU 4.4.19).
Mind: the inner organ as doubting and deliberating; for the Bhāmatī, when purified by contemplation, the instrument of direct realization.
The internal sense (the sixth, after the five outer senses), a non-eternal product of prakṛti (with mahat, ahaṃkāra and buddhi); memory arises from mental perception.

In Jain usage the 'quasi-sense' (anindriya/noindriya): the physical mind (dravya-manas) is fine matter, the psychic mind (bhāva-manas) the soul's capacity; its object is scriptural knowledge (TS 1.14, 2.21, 5.19).
The mind, cause of bondage when attached to objects and of liberation when free of them; bound to prāṇa like a bird on a string.
The mind: restless elephant, thief and bird, the seat of both defeat and victory; it must be tamed by the guru's word and remembrance, for the Name recited while the mind wanders is useless.
The mind is the agent of Kāl, attached to the soul; it is left behind at Trikuṭī/Daswān Dwār.
Man: the mind or heart, addressed in the songs ('o my mind'); also the seat of the Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Mental repetition of the series of letters with remembrance of meaning, without movement of head, tongue or lips; a thousand times better.
The diseases of the mind: delusion the root, lust as wind, greed as phlegm, anger as bile, with jealousy, pride and the rest; cured by Rāma's grace through the guru, faith, restraint and devotion.
Truth, forbearance, sense-control, compassion and the other virtues as tīrthas; purity of mind the highest.
Mental service, the highest form, to which bodily and material service lead.
Attention, a component of name (SN 12.2) and a factor defined in each jhāna (MN 111).
Attention: the turning of the mind to the object; a universal factor.
One of the ten books of the Ṛgveda.
The coloured diagram on which the deity is worshipped, especially at initiation.
Diagram for worship and initiation, richly described in the Pauṣkara.
The 'Man of the Heart': the divine dwelling in the human body, sought, longed for and met through the guru; also called the unknown bird, the uncatchable man, the neighbour in the mirror-city.

equivalents.note: The Bāul maner mānuṣ and the Sahajiyā sahaja mānuṣa name the same indwelling divine person in the two idioms.

definitions.definition: Mars: strength (sattva) of Kālapuruṣa and the general (BJ 2.1); male, kṣatriya, tamas; lord of fire (BJ 2.6–7); rules Aries and Scorpio, exalted in Capricorn 28°; period 7 years; Narasiṃha is born from him (BPHS 2.5); his Greek-derived name is Āra (BJ 2.2).
Praying for the Lord's own welfare out of love — Periyāḻvār's 'many years' (Tiruppallāṇṭu); the Āḻvārs' singing of each temple is called their maṅgaḷāśāsana of it.
Praying for the Lord's well-being out of love, as the Āḻvārs did, instead of asking anything for oneself.
An amulet (of wood, plant or other material) bound on with Atharvaveda hymns for protection and healing.
The jewel island in the ocean of nectar, the Goddess's highest abode (SL 8; Devī Bhāgavata 12.10-12).
The Goddess's supreme abode beyond the worlds, described in the Devī Bhāgavata.
The sanctum of a sattra or nāmghar in which the guru-āsana with the sacred book is kept.
The Tamil–Sanskrit mixed idiom of the Śrīvaiṣṇava commentaries and rahasya works.

The navel centre, where the Goddess rises (LSN 38); the Saundaryalaharī assigns water to it (SL 9) and there worships the dark rain-cloud with its lightning (SL 40); the Samayins see the Goddess manifest there (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 7; Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
The navel centre, ten-petalled, of fire (RAṂ), where the bulb is strung on suṣumnā like a jewel (GŚ 15).
The navel centre, a twelve-spoked wheel where the jīva wanders.
The inspired wisdom with which the seers searched their hearts (RV 10.129.4).
The mood of Rādhā's young maidservants (mañjarī), who serve the divine couple under Rādhā and seek no union with Kṛṣṇa for themselves; cultivated in rāgānugā practice through an inner identity.
Conceiving things as self, in self, from self or as 'mine' (MN 1); 'I am' is a conceiving, a disease, a tumour, a dart (MN 140).
The sixth internal base, cognising mental objects; 'mind is the forerunner of all states' (Dhp 1–2).

equivalents.note: same word; in the suttas the sixth sense, not an evolute of prakṛti

definitions.definition: Destruction of the mind: not the loss of function but the end of the shrinking notions 'this is I, this is not I'; the state of the one liberated while living, in which pure sattva arises.
The power of acting with unsurpassed speed.
Made of mind: the self within the breath-self (TU 2.3); also the person made of mind in the heart (TU 1.6; BAU 5.6; ChU 3.14.2).
The sheath of mind: mind with the five organs of knowledge, the seat of doubt and desire.
A body created from this body, complete in its limbs, drawn out like a reed from its sheath (DN 2).
The sixth kind of samādhi in the GS (7.6, 7.16), and in the HYP the effect of mūrcchā retention (2.69).
Dissolution of mind, 'with form' in the jīvanmukta and 'without form' in the videhamukta.
Dissolution of the mind: the mind's ceasing to take on forms, practised by the knower for stable abidance.
The steadiness of mind when the breath moves in the middle (HYP 2.42); the one state (3.54); saluted as a goddess (4.64).
Synonym of unmanī and samādhi (HYP 4.3); also a name of Śakti (KJN 20.11).
The end of sound and of mind; the goal of nāda-yoga; also a measure of the sixteen-measured praṇava.
'Jewel of the mind' — the supreme goddess as mother and light in the Siddhar worship; in yoga texts also the name of the state beyond mind (manonmanī).
The 'kingdom of the mind': fancy or day-dream, which in the stories (Śukra, Lavaṇa) creates whole lives.
The sixth consciousness, cause and support of the others in the Laṅkāvatāra's account.

cross_language.form: yid kyi rnam par shes pa

definitions.definition: A circle: (1) the three circles of fire, sun and moon among the ninety-six principles; (2) in Siddha medicine a fixed course of treatment (commonly forty or forty-eight days).
Walking as if one's foot were injured.

notes: SDS reads mandana.

definitions.definition: A Vedic verse or formula used in rite and recitation; its meaningfulness was defended by Yāska against Kautsa (Nirukta 1.15–16); in the Saṃhitā 'common be your mantra (counsel)' (RV 10.191.3).
The portion of the Veda recited during the rite as prompting its performance; the rest is Brāhmaṇa (MS 2.1.32–33). Mantras have meaning like ordinary sentences (MS 1.2.40).
Mantras are meaningful by reminding the performer of items connected with the performance; an unseen purpose for their recitation is assumed only where no seen purpose is possible.
The Heart Sūtra calls the perfection of wisdom the great mantra and gives gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.
The Saṃhitā portion of the Veda — verses, formulas and chants — which, with the Brāhmaṇa, makes up the Veda (ĀpŚS 24.1.31); to be recited with exact accent (PŚ 52) and understood (Nirukta 1.15–18).

A sacred formula made of the letters (mātṛkā), each with its seer, metre, deity, seed, power and pin; mantras proper have male deities, vidyās female; they are male, female or neuter by their endings (ŚT 2.57–59) and fiery or lunar (ŚT 2.60–63).
Śiva's powers present as sound-forms through which ritual acts; the perfected mantras paralyse and destroy the soul's bonds in initiation.
The mind is mantra (Śiva Sūtra 2.1); mantras rest on the strength of spanda and dissolve in it with the worshipper's mind (SK 2.1-2).

Tamil mantiram: the Siddhars use seed-syllables (the three letters of Vālai, the five letters) yet ask 'for those who stand in the true tantra, why mantra?' (Kuṭampai 7) and prize the unspoken mantra.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan maθra.
alt_notes: Contribution from U08; U31 owns mantra theory.

definitions.definition: The 'consciousness' or life of a mantra: without it a mantra is only letters; it is awakened by the guru's transmission, purification and the practitioner's absorption.

equivalents.note: the Śaiva 'potency of mantra' (Śiva Sūtra 1.22, 2.3)

definitions.definition: A defect of a mantra (cut, obstructed, powerless, asleep and forty-five more, ŚT 2.64–70) that makes it fail to protect the practitioner.
The knower at the level of śuddhavidyā.
The ten purifications of a mantra — generation, enlivening, striking, awakening, consecration, cleansing, strengthening, satiation, kindling, guarding (ŚT 2.112–113).
Success or perfection in a mantra, when after purification and puraścaraṇa the mantra 'awakens' and gives its fruit — enjoyment and liberation.
The first and lowest of the four yogas: placing the mātṛkā letters on the body and repeating a mantra; fit for the mild (mṛdu) practitioner, who succeeds in twelve years (DYŚ 11–13; SS 5.11).
The first of the four yogas; repetition, or the natural haṃsa reversed.
The knower at the level of Sadāśiva.

The initiatory division of Śaivism whose scriptures (Siddhānta and non-Saiddhāntika tantras) give both powers/enjoyment and liberation through initiation, mantra-worship and yoga; the fifth and highest stream after the worldly, Vedic, spiritual and Atimārga paths.
The other great division of Śaivism, beside the Atimārga, whose scriptures (Siddhānta and Bhairava tantras) describe and outrank the Atimārga.
The division of the Bhairava tantras centred on a male Bhairava, chiefly Svacchandabhairava.
Experienced by attending to the great lake (Śiva Sūtra 1.22); in PH 20 the perfect I-ness is the potency of the great mantra.
The knower at the level of Īśvara.
Progenitor and law-giver presiding over a manvantara; the present is the seventh, Vaivasvata; the eighth will be Sāvarṇi (the Devī Māhātmya's Suratha).
Worship of the human: God is served and found in the human being, above all in the guru.
The Kartābhajā maxim 'worship the human'.
The ring-mountain in Puṣkaradvīpa marking the limit of the human world of two and a half continents (TS 3.35).
The period of one Manu, seventy-one ages of the gods (MDh 1.79).
Seventy-one caturyugas with a closing junction of a Kṛta's length, a flood (SS 1.18).
The period ruled by one Manu, about 71 cycles of the four yugas; fourteen make a day of Brahmā; each has its own Manu, Indra, gods, seven sages and avatāra.

The tempter who obstructs the bodhisattva; four Māras are named in Mahāyāna texts (of the aggregates, the defilements, death and the god-son Māra); in the Śūraṅgama demonic states arise from the aggregates.
A 'killer': the lords of and planets in the 2nd and 7th houses (the houses of death reckoned from the 8th and 3rd), whose periods may bring death when longevity is ending (BPHS 44).
Obstacles Māra raises against the perfection of wisdom — distraction, weariness, doubts, preferring lesser sūtras, false visions of the Buddha.
(As reported) Liberation is nothing but the destruction of the body; not knowledge.
Recollection of death, 'may I live for one breath', of great fruit, merging in the deathless (AN 6.19).
Recollection of death, by simple attention or in eight ways; it leads to access.
The second virtue: freedom from pride (TS 9.6).

The two kinds of music: mārga, the 'sought-out' divine music fixed by Brahmā and Bharata that gives well-being when performed before Śiva, and deśī, regional music that delights people (ŚR 1.1.22–23; Bṛhaddeśī 13).

One of the fourteen 'ways of search' through which souls are investigated in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Gommaṭasāra (destiny, sense, body, activity, sex, passion, knowledge, restraint, perception, leśyā, capacity for liberation, right faith, rationality, nourishment).
A householder with the thirty-five preliminary virtues (honest wealth and the rest) that prepare for the vows (YŚ 1.47–56; Dharmabindu).
Gnosis: the fourth and inmost of the four ways (after śariyat, tarikat, hakikat) by which Bāul-Fakirs place their path beyond the law — recorded as context (Sufi vocabulary).
The image, attached to the Teṅkalai, of the kitten carried by the mother cat: the Lord saves without the soul's effort.

notes: As for trm:markata-nyaya.

definitions.definition: The image, attached to the Vaṭakalai, of the baby monkey that clings to its mother: the soul must make the act of surrender.

literal: the maxim of the young monkey
notes: Label used in the dispute literature and modern accounts; the schools' own texts argue in other terms.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one hundred and seven vital points of five kinds — of flesh (11), vessels (41), ligaments (27), bone (8) and joints (20) (Su Śā 6.3-4); the three great marmas are head, heart and bladder (Ca Sū 29.3). (Marma in depth: U58.)
The eighteen vital points of the body through which the breath is moved in one kind of withdrawal (Yoga Yājñavalkya; Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā).
One of eighteen vital points through which breath and attention are moved in pratyāhāra; 'cut' in the Kṣurikā.
The storm-gods, sons of Rudra (RV 2.33.1).
Visualising a wind that scatters the ashes (YŚ 7).
The written code of the Terāpanth order laid down by Ācārya Bhikṣu (a single ācārya, no personal disciples, collective discipline), celebrated in the annual Maryādā Mahotsava (from Jayācārya's time).
The path of rule: devotion and liberation pursued through scriptural discipline and means.
Rāma as the supreme person who keeps every bound of dharma — as son, brother, husband and king.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Kṛṣṇa's teaching (me matam), which those who follow with faith are released from actions and those who cavil at are lost (3.31–32).
The palmyra-stem 'horse' ridden through the streets by a spurned lover to shame the beloved; Tirumaṅkai's heroine threatens to ride it, though convention reserved it for men.
The ninth Mahāvidyā; Mataṅga (Dakṣiṇāmūrti) is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.15); matched with Rāma (10.10); also worshipped as Ucchiṣṭa-Mātaṅgī.
The gross body, which perishes (SK 39); in the Kramadīpikā made of six sheaths — hair, blood and flesh from the mother, sinew, bone and marrow from the father.
A name of the One named in RV 1.164.46; the messenger who brought fire.
