Kañcuka: restriction of cause and place ('only this, here').

notes: The same word names the Ājīvika doctrine of necessity (U33); the ŚU names no school.

definitions.definition: The appointment of a widow or wife to bear a son by a brother-in-law or sapiṇḍa; permitted and then condemned in Manu (9.59–68).
The command conveyed by the injunctive, which by itself prompts the qualified person, independent of his desire for the fruit.
The nine passion-like emotions: laughter, liking, disliking, grief, fear, disgust and the three sexual drives (TS 8.9).
A vow of observance: fasting from certain foods, bathing before dawn, abstaining from adornment and harsh speech, and giving alms (TP 2).
Dance according to the dramaturgical rules, offered to the Lord; a bodily act.
Pure dance, movement without representational meaning; with song and instrument part of saṅgīta (ŚR 1.1.21).
Expressive dance that conveys bhāva through gesture and glance.

Placing: the installation of letters, mantras and deities on parts of the body by touch and visualization (mātṛkā-nyāsa, ṛṣyādi-nyāsa, the six-limbed nyāsa), making the body divine before worship and japa.
Placing mantras (e.g. the five brahma-mantras and six limbs) on the body and on the image to make them divine.
Placing mantras on the body (and, in another sense, 'depositing' oneself — see trm:nyasa-surrender).
Placing of mātṛkā and deity mantras, as taught in the Prapañcasāra and Śāradātilaka.
Placing mantras and deities on the body; Śrīvidyā uses many sets (karaśuddhi, the vāgdevatā-nyāsa, the sixfold ṣoḍhā-nyāsa and others), taught in the Vāmakeśvara and the Kalpasūtra.

notes: Homonym: see trm:nyasa-surrender.

definitions.definition: Surrender of oneself to the Lord, which alone attains what other means cannot; equated with the six-limbed śaraṇāgati.

equivalents.note: AS 37 treats nyāsa and śaraṇāgati as one

definitions.definition: The examination of things by the means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); also the five-membered demonstration.
An interpretive principle established in an adhikaraṇa and applied elsewhere (e.g. the viśvajit maxim that heaven is the fruit where none is stated).

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense ('maxim'); distinct from Nyāya as a school.

definitions.definition: Light arising from insight; the first imperfection of insight.
The seat named because the Goddess 'flew up' (oḍḍitā) there (Kubjikāmata 2.40); the 'body' (piṇḍa) level of the fourfold yoni (11.7).
Uḍḍīyāna, where Satī's thighs fell (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.41).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: The four floods (sensual pleasure, becoming, views, ignorance) crossed 'without halting and without straining' (SN 1.1; SN 35.238).
A 'stream' of gurus; Śrīvidyā worship honours three: the divine (divyaugha), the perfected (siddhaugha) and the human (mānavaugha) teachers, forming the circle of gurus.
Flood: desire, existence, views, ignorance — the outflows with views separated out.
The ordinary view of beings carried along by the stream of worldly existence, contrasted with the yoga views (YDS).
Nutritive essence, present in every material group; nutriment as an originator of matter.

The supreme essence (tejas) of the tissues from rasa to semen, identical with strength (bala) (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); seated in the heart, pure, slightly reddish-yellow, ghee-coloured, sweet, smelling of parched rice, the first thing produced in the body, whose loss is death (Ca Sū 17.74-75); the 'supreme' (para) ojas in the heart as distinct from the ojas carried by the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.7-9, as the commentators read it).

The one-syllabled Brahman to be uttered at death while remembering the Lord (BhG 8.13); the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8); the first of the threefold designation 'oṃ tat sat' with which the expounders of Brahman begin their rites (17.23–24); 'among words I am the one syllable' (10.25).
The syllable made by Prajāpati from the sounds a, u, m drawn out of the three utterances (AB 5.32); expounded at length in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.
The imperishable syllable, Brahman and Prajāpati, recited with the utterances and the Sāvitrī (MDh 2.76–84; VDh 10.5).

The syllable Om: the udgītha (ChU 1.1.1); brahman and all this (TU 1.8; MāU 1); the word all Vedas proclaim (KU 1.2.15); the bow (MuU 2.2.4); the higher and lower brahman (PrU 5.2); its measures A, U, M and the measureless (MāU 8-12).

The sacred syllable, which in the Saṃhitā layer appears at the close of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā ('Oṃ, kratu, remember'; 'Oṃ, the void is brahman', VS 40.15–17) and as the first of the four quarters of speech in one reading (Nirukta 13.9).
Uttered and prolonged, with the void contemplated at its end (VBT 39).

notes: U05's definition (the Gītā usage); Oṃ in the Upaniṣads and mantra-śāstra is defined by U03 and U31.

definitions.definition: The threefold designation of Brahman by which the brāhmaṇas, Vedas and sacrifices were ordained; Oṃ begins the rites, 'tat' marks acts done without seeking fruit, 'sat' denotes reality, goodness and praiseworthy action (BhG 17.23–27).
The object of meditation, with fixation in the heart, in the third stage.
The syllable Oṃ, explained in the Atharvaśiras as that which raises the breaths; its measures correspond to worlds, Vedas, fires and deities.
Beings reborn without parents (gods, hell-beings); Ajita and Pāyāsi deny them; Sañjaya refuses to declare on them.
Regard for consequences and for others' blame, paired with hiri (MN 39).
Dread of wrongdoing, arising from regard for others and fear of consequences; a beautiful universal.
Temple singers who sing the Tirumuṟai in their paṇs during worship.
The Marathi verse-form of the Jñāneśvarī, Amṛtānubhava and Eknāthī Bhāgavat, also used in women's grinding songs.
The verse form of the classic Mahānubhāva poems.
Leaving the household for the homeless life; its first visible fruit is the honour paid even to a slave who has gone forth.
Leaving the household life for homelessness (DN 2); the going forth of a slave brings the first visible fruit of the contemplative life (DN 2).
'This mind is luminous, but defiled by adventitious defilements' — understood by the noble disciple, for whom there is development of mind (AN 1.51–52).
The mind called luminous in AN 1.49–52, identified by the commentary with the life-continuum.
The radiant citta of the forest teachers' experience; Ajahn Maha Boowa warns that ignorance hides in this radiance.
The pitta between the stomach and the intestine, which digests the four kinds of food and separates essence and waste and supports the other pittas; called 'fire' (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-12).
Reviewing knowledge after path and fruit: nineteen kinds in all.
The sign of reviewing, well grasped, like one standing who looks at one seated — the fifth factor of noble right concentration (AN 5.28).
That which is helpful to the arising or persistence of another dhamma; the Paṭṭhāna enumerates twenty-four modes.
One who awakens by himself but does not found a teaching; the Khaggavisāṇa verses are traditionally ascribed to them (Snp 1.3, commentary).
Step, place, quarter (speech has four padas, RV 1.164.45) and, in recitation, the word (as in padapāṭha).
A word, defined as what ends in a nominal or verbal ending (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.14); also a quarter of a verse.
Sounds ending in a case-ending (NS 2.2.60 DCS); its meaning is individual, form and universal (NS 2.2.68).
What possesses denotative power (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The supreme state ('the state') with which the body is brought to one taste (piṇḍa-pada-samarasa); 'param pad' in Hindi.
Meditation, the second of the four (KJN 3.4).
One of the four sections of an ideal Āgama: knowledge (vidyā/jñāna), ritual (kriyā), yoga, and conduct (caryā); all of Śiva's scriptures are said to have the four pādas.
The Pādma Saṃhitā is arranged in the same four pādas (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā).
Patamutti: the 'liberations in a station' — sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya — reached by caryā, kriyā and yoga; not final.
The recitation of a Saṃhitā word by word, with sandhi undone.
The analysed text in which each word is recited separately without sandhi (for the Ṛgveda, Śākalya's).
The categories: substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence (six), with absence as seventh in later works.
The sixteen topics of NS 1.1.1; also 'word-meaning' (NS 2.2.68).
Seven categories (Tarkasaṅgraha, Bhāṣāpariccheda); Raghunātha re-examines the list.
The meaning of a word; the word-meanings, once conveyed, convey the sentence-meaning (Śabara on MS 1.1.25). Also 'category' in ontology (Bhāṭṭas five, Prābhākaras eight).
In Jain usage the nine categories (nava padārtha): the seven realities plus merit and demerit (Kundakunda, Śvetāmbara canon).
Sixth stage: objects no longer appear.
Sixth stage: delighting in the Self, one no longer conceives inner or outer objects and understands them only when long prompted by others.
Service of the Lord's feet, the fourth form of devotion.
Serving and dwelling at the Lord's feet — to lie as a step before his sanctum (PT 4.9), to have his feet enter one's eyes (Amalaṉātipirāṉ 1).
Meditation on sacred syllables, letters and mantras (YŚ 8).
A ritual manual systematising the procedures of the Āgamas (e.g. Somaśambhu's, Aghoraśiva's).
The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati as a principal authority of Kerala temple ritual.
The attendant goddess (śāsana-devī, yakṣī) of Pārśvanātha, with Dharaṇendra; worshipped for protection and worldly aims, especially by Digambara bhaṭṭārakas and in Karnataka (Hombuja).

Water sanctified by washing the feet of the guru or jaṅgama, received as one of the eight shields; the SSM also reads it as the oneness of guru ('foot') and disciple ('water') through initiation (19.6–7).

The guru's 'sandals' — the mantra of the guru's feet given before the Bālā (PKS 1.41); the feet are contemplated in the crown each morning (PKS 2.2); immersion in the Goddess's sandals is complete meditation (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
The guru's sandals and the mantra of the lineage's feet; 'there is no mantra beyond the pādukā' (Kulārṇava 12.12).
The task regarding the second truth: its origin, craving, is to be abandoned (SN 56.11); also the second right effort.
Abandoning of defilements by substitution of opposites, suppression, cutting off, tranquillization and escape.
Generating desire and effort to abandon arisen unwholesome states (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four right efforts.

A 'gift' or treatise-section: in the Pūrvas, a subdivision of a vastu (the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa is such a prābhṛta); in Kundakunda's usage, a treatise (Samayapāhuḍa, the eight Pāhuḍas). Tradition credits Kundakunda with eighty-four pāhuḍas.
Religious hypocrisy and empty show; Viśvanāth Siṃh's Bījak commentary is 'the destroyer of pākhaṇḍ'.
That in which the probandum is doubted, e.g. the mountain (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A side or thesis in debate (NS 1.1.41, 1.2.1).
The bright (śukla) and dark (kṛṣṇa) halves of the lunar month; the quality of tithis reverses between them (MC 1.4).

notes: Homonym of pakṣa 'thesis' in logic; id disambiguated.

literal: presence of the probans in the subject

definitions.definition: The probans's occurring in the mountain etc.
Absence of certainty (of the probandum in the subject) not accompanied by a desire to infer.
The body ripened by the fire of yoga (opposite apakva).
The body 'ripened' in the fire of yoga (liberated) versus the unripe body subject to karma and rebirth (Yogabīja).
The ten impediments to be cut before meditation: dwelling, family, gain, following, building work, travel, kin, affliction, books, supernormal powers.
The palanquin carrying the silver sandals (pādukā) of a saint — above all Jñāneśvar's from Āḷandī and Tukārām's from Dehu — at the head of the vārī.
'Many years': Periyāḻvār's benediction for the Lord's long life and safety, the model of maṅgaḷāśāsana.
A vast unit of time measured by emptying a pit filled with fine hairs, one per century (TS 3.29, 3.38).
Gladness arising from faith or from non-remorse, leading to rapture (SN 12.23; AN 11.1).
A melodic mode of old Tamil music to which each Tēvāram patikam is set; some two dozen are used in the Tēvāram.
The consecrated betel-leaf 'passport' given in the Dharamdāsī initiation and death rites, which Kāl's messengers honour.
(Jain report) Four kinds of drink permitted and four not permitted, taught by the dying Gosāla.

notes: Items not recalled reliably; not listed.

definitions.definition: The succedent houses (2, 5, 8, 11) following the angles (BJ 1.18).

notes: Scholarly account: from Greek epanaphora.

definitions.definition: The five concentrations in which breath and mind are held in the place of each element with its colour, shape, seed and deity; the GS counts them among its twenty-five mudrās, the GŚ calls them the stabilising, liquefying, burning, whirling and drying concentrations.
The fivefold truth: Caitanya, Nityānanda, Advaita, Gadādhara and Śrīvāsa as forms of Kṛṣṇa as devotee.
The five images of a Vaikhānasa temple: fixed (dhruva), movable worship (kautuka), festival (utsava), bathing (snapana) and offering (bali) images.
The five real and eternal differences: soul–Lord, soul–soul, matter–Lord, matter–matter and matter–soul; they hold in all states, including liberation.
Resolve, self-assertion, desire, the task of awareness, and action — the functions of buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and the two sets of capacities (Tattvasamāsa 8; Kramadīpikā).
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, one closing each adhyāya of the Sūtra; the Ratnaṭīkā calls them the five purifiers (pavitra).
The flesh eye, divine eye, wisdom eye, dharma eye and buddha eye, all possessed by the Tathāgata.
The five codes: liṅgācāra, sadācāra, śivācāra, bhṛtyācāra and gaṇācāra.
The fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā mantra in three sections (kūṭa); called the 'full Gāyatrī' and given fifteen meanings in the Varivasyārahasya. (Syllables not recorded.)

equivalents.note: the Gāyatrī read as Śrīvidyā

definitions.definition: Sign (nimitta), name (nāman), discrimination (vikalpa), right knowledge (samyagjñāna) and suchness (tathatā).

The knowledge of the five fires: yonder world, the rain-god, the earth, man and woman as sacrificial fires, into which faith, Soma, rain, food and semen are offered, so that the waters come to be called person at the fifth offering (ChU 5.3-10; BAU 6.2).
The five periods of the Pāñcarātrin's day: abhigamana, upādāna, ijyā, svādhyāya, yoga.
The five cosmic divisions — nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti, śāntyatīta — into which the principles are grouped and which are purified in initiation.

notes: Not to be confused with trm:pancakala (Pāñcarātra five periods).

definitions.definition: The five purificatory therapies — emesis, purgation, the two kinds of enema (decoction and oil), and nasal evacuation (bloodletting is counted instead by the surgeons) — preceded by oleation and sudation; the best medicines for the bodily doṣas (AHS Sū 1.25; Ca Sū 2, Si). Summary only.
The degeneracies of the aeon, of beings, of defilements, of views and of lifespan, in which buddhas teach the one vehicle as three.
The five sheaths (food, vital air, mind, intellect, bliss) which seem to cover the self; the self is known by discriminating it from each.
The five incarnations of Parameśvara: Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Dattātreya, Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ, Govindaprabhu and Cakradhar.
The five cosmic acts — creation, preservation, withdrawal, concealment and grace — performed by the Goddess through Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva (LSN 63-64; SL 24).
Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment and grace; the individual performs them too, as manifesting, relishing, reflecting, planting the seed and dissolving (PH 10-11).
Śiva's five acts: emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace.
Aintoḻil: paṭaittal, kāttal, aḻittal, maṟaittal, aruḷal — enacted in Naṭarāja's dance.

The mantra 'namaḥ śivāya', designation of Śiva and root of all mantras, at the head of all the śrutis; there is no mantra greater (SSM 8.2–7); whispered into the disciple's right ear at initiation (6.19–21).
The formula 'namaḥ śivāya', which the Śaiva traditions trace to the eighth section of the Śatarudrīya (TS 4.5.8).
Śiva's mantra 'namaḥ śivāya' (six syllables with Oṃ), praised as the essence of the Veda.
Tamil añceḻuttu: the five letters (na-ma-ci-vā-ya); chanting them yields birthless release (Paṭṭiṉattār, Tiruttillai 17).
The five letters na-ma-śi-vā-ya (Tamil namaccivāya): concealment, mala, Śiva, grace, soul; gross form 'namaḥ śivāya', subtle 'śivāya namaḥ'.
Namaccivāya: the devotee's refuge in every danger.

notes: U01 contribution: the Vedic locus only. Śaiva units contribute the mantra's doctrine and practice.

definitions.definition: The five marks of a Purāṇa: sarga, pratisarga, vaṃśa, manvantara and vaṃśānucarita.
The fifth human aim: love of Kṛṣṇa, beyond the four (dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa).
The epic's claim to Vedic status: it calls itself the 'kārṣṇa veda' (MBh 1.1.205).
(Jain report) That five elements — earth, water, fire, air, space — exist and from them a self arises that perishes with them.

The five 'M's — wine, meat, fish, parched grain or gesture, and sexual union — said to manifest the bliss that is Brahman's form; used in secret, and exposure leads to hell (PKS 1.12); daily worship continues without them when they are unavailable (PKS 1.24). Summary only.
The five tattvas named by their initial 'm': madya, māṃsa, matsya, mudrā, maithuna. Restricted: summary only.
A seat built over five skulls used for sādhana in Bengal (Tārāpīṭh; Ramakrishna's seat at Dakshineswar in the tradition's account). Restricted: named only.
The five-limbed almanac: lunar day (tithi), weekday (vāra), asterism (nakṣatra), yoga and karaṇa, by which the quality of any time is judged.
The five seats founded by the five ācāryas — Rambhāpurī, Ujjayinī, Kedāra, Śrīśaila and Kāśī.

The seat of five 'corpses' — Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara as the legs and Sadāśiva as the plank of the Goddess's couch, lifeless without her (LSN 61; PKS 3.10); in SL 94 the four gods become the couch and Śiva its coverlet.

The system of Nārāyaṇa worship called Pañcarātra in the Nārāyaṇīya, 'this great upaniṣad made by Sāṃkhya-yoga' (12.326.100), whose whole knower is the Lord himself (12.337.63); one of the five systems of knowledge (12.337.59).
The scripture and tradition of Bhagavān; the Pādma derives the name from the five other śāstras becoming 'night' before it; other explanations link it to Nārāyaṇa's five-day rite (ŚB 13.6.1).

notes: U05's definition (the early usage); the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās are covered by U08.

definitions.definition: The five categories that sum up the Pāśupata teaching: effect, cause, union, rule and the end of suffering; also the name of the system ('Pāñcārthika').
The Vaiṣṇava initiation in Pāñcarātra-based Śrīvaiṣṇava usage: branding (tāpa) with discus and conch, the sectarian mark (puṇḍra), a new name (nāma), the mantra, and worship (yāga).
Purification of oneself, the place, the substances, the mantras and the liṅga before worship.
The five kinds of pollution the Liṅgāyatas reject: of birth, of death, of menstruation, of leftovers (ucchiṣṭa) and of caste (jāti).

notes: Membership of the list from memory; verify.

definitions.definition: Wine, meat, fish, mudrā (parched grain) and maithuna, the five 'realities' of Śakti worship (Mahānirvāṇa 1.57; 5.22). Restricted: summary only.
In the Kālīvilāsa's view not to be used in the Kali age, when only the paśu disposition is allowed (Kālīvilāsa 4.2-3).

equivalents.note: two names for the same five

definitions.definition: Sadāśiva's five faces, identified with the five brahma-mantras (Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta), whose combinations yield the Śiva-, Rudra- and Bhairava-tantras.
The twenty-fifth principle, the knower beyond the twenty-four; the unawakened self called 'the one awakening', which on knowing itself becomes alone (MBh 12.294.42–43).

equivalents.note: the twenty-fifth of the enumeration is the puruṣa

definitions.definition: Quintuplication: each subtle element is halved, one half divided into four, and each gross element formed of half of itself and an eighth of each of the other four.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The wise, who grieve neither for the dead nor for the living (2.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The wise call paṇḍita one whose undertakings are free of desire and intention and whose actions are burnt by the fire of knowledge (4.19); the paṇḍitas see all beings equally (5.18) and do not call Sāṃkhya and Yoga separate (5.4).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The death of a restrained ascetic by renunciation of food in equanimity (Bhagavatī Ārādhanā).
The simile for the conjunction of puruṣa (who sees but cannot move) and prakṛti (who moves but cannot see) (SK 21).
'Hand as bowl': the Digambara monk eats once a day, standing, from his cupped hands, at a house where he is properly received.
Understanding of the four truths and of rise and fall (SN 48.10); conjoined with consciousness (MN 43); the third training; born of meditation (Dhp 282), inseparable from jhāna (Dhp 372).
Understanding: insight knowledge associated with wholesome consciousness, penetrating dhammas as they are; the third training.

equivalents.note: same word
the same Buddhist term; Hindu usages of prajñā differ

definitions.definition: Wisdom as a power unshaken by ignorance (SN 50). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five powers.

A concept or designation: either the concept as meaning, which is made known (e.g. 'person', 'direction', a kasiṇa sign), or the concept as name, which makes it known; it lacks intrinsic nature and is not an ultimate reality.
One whose effluents are destroyed by wisdom without contacting the formless liberations (MN 70).
One whose taints are destroyed by wisdom without having touched the eight liberations.
Liberation of mind through wisdom, destroying the effluents; paired with liberation of mind (AN 3.33; MN 70).
Noble penetrative wisdom into rise and fall (SN 48.10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five faculties.
'Path': an organized following of a Sant (Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth), with initiation, seats and sādhus — which the Sants' own verses often warn against making sectarian.
A sub-order of the Nāth yogīs; tradition counts twelve (bārah panth).
'The king of paths': Jñāneśvar's name in Jñāneśvarī 6 for the Nāth yoga of kuṇḍalinī's awakening and ascent (summary only).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sin: Arjuna fears it would cling to them for killing kin (1.36, 1.39, 1.45); Kṛṣṇa says refusing the dharmic battle incurs it (2.33) while fighting with equanimity does not (2.38); those who cook only for themselves eat sin (agha, 3.13); Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will (3.36).
(As reported) Pūraṇa denies that the doer incurs it.
Inauspicious karma (TS 8.26); also the five sins — violence, falsehood, theft, unchastity, possessiveness.
Declaring one's evil deeds before the buddhas, with regret and resolve, to purify karma — as in the Golden Light's confession, the Triskandhaka and Samantabhadra's vows.
One who turns a new bodhisattva from the perfection of wisdom and makes him fearful.

The proliferation of concepts that follows feeling, perception and thought, by which 'perceptions and notions tinged with proliferation' beset a person (MN 18); rooted in the thought 'I am' (Snp 4.14); the Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation (AN 8.30).

equivalents.note: same word; in Vedānta prapañca is the manifest world, in the suttas the mind's proliferation

definitions.definition: The supreme form of Bhagavān (Para Vāsudeva) in his highest realm, first of the five modes.
The supreme Goddess; in the Kalpasūtra one of the vidyās worshipped (the eighth section, parākrama); the commentators call Mahātripurasundarī Parābhaṭṭārikā.
Supreme devotion to the Goddess beyond the guṇa-graded forms, seeing her in all beings and ending in non-dual knowledge.
Supreme devotion, to which secondary devotion leads (ŚBS, second adhyāya, as recalled).

equivalents.note: the Śrīvaiṣṇava parabhakti is a named stage before parajñāna and paramabhakti; the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra's parā is simply primary devotion as against gauṇī

definitions.definition: The highest of the Trika's three goddesses; Bhairava's own state proclaimed as the Goddess (VBT 17); the power of will (TĀ 1.271-272).
Eighth view: like the moon; absorption; omniscience and liberation (YDS).
Paramutti: final release, sāyujya, inseparable union with Śiva reached by jñāna.
The supreme body — the first of the bodies emanated from the Supreme before the human body (SSP 1).
The Lord's higher nature that has become the life-element (jīvabhūtā), by which the world is upheld (BhG 7.5).

literal: other doctrine; the self in the other

definitions.definition: (1) A rival doctrine — as many as the standpoints (Sanmati 3.47); (2) in the Samayasāra, the soul dwelling in the non-self (karma, body), opposed to sva-samaya, the soul in its own nature.
Freedom from thirst for the guṇas themselves, from discernment of the puruṣa (1.16); only the clarity of knowledge; the means to asamprajñāta samādhi (YBh 1.16, 1.18).
Consciousness as reflexive awareness is supreme speech, arising of itself (ĪPK 1.5.13); higher than paśyantī.
The first, unmanifest level of speech, where it 'sprouts'.
Accepted by Nāgeśa as the fourth, highest level of speech, motionless and unmanifest in the root centre — a level not named by Bhartṛhari.
The supreme level of speech, identical with the Goddess (Śakti) as consciousness, above paśyantī.
The Lord's highest form in Vaikuṇṭha, seated with Śrī, Bhū and Nīlā, served by the eternal and freed souls.
The higher knowledge: that by which the imperishable is grasped (MuU 1.1.5).
The first of three states Rāmānuja prays for: intense longing that cannot bear separation, arising from knowledge of the Lord.
Śiva, partless, all-knowing, without qualities, being–consciousness–bliss (Kulārṇava 1.7-8).
'Acquaintance': the direct encounter with the Lord (paracā kau aṅg); also the genre of hagiography that makes a saint known (paracaī).

Mercury, so called because it gives the far shore (pāra) of saṃsāra (SDS Raseśvara 1-2), or because adepts proclaim it for others (para-artha) (Rasārṇava 1.35); Śiva's seed (harabīja), also called rasa, sūta, rasendra, rasarāja (Rasārṇava 1.28, 1.34-36).

notes: Restricted subject: no processes recorded.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Another's dharma, even well performed, is worse than one's own deficient dharma and brings danger (3.35).
The dharma of another, which is 'fraught with fear' even when well performed (BhG 3.35, 18.47).
The drum the cowherd girls ask of Kṛṣṇa in the Tiruppāvai — at the end revealed to mean kinship and service to him alone (TP 29).
Defeat: the four gravest offences for a monk (sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, killing a human, falsely claiming superhuman states), entailing loss of monkhood.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The second state: direct vision of the Lord granted to the one filled with parabhakti.
Discernment, assaying (as a jeweller tests a gem): the Bījak's key virtue of testing every doctrine and deity as the mind's creation; the basis of the 'Pārakh' school of Bījak interpretation.

Love for one who is not one's spouse, taken as the model of the practitioner's relation with the partner, because it is free of social motive and full of risk and longing — recorded in summary only (restricted context).
Paramour love: love for Kṛṣṇa by those married to others, held by Rūpa (UN 1.21) to be the supreme form in Vraja; its status is the subject of the svakīyā–parakīyā debate.
Arthavāda recounting a deed done by another great person.
(As reported) There is no other world, because there is no one who goes to it.
One of the four topics on which Sañjaya refuses every alternative.
The Lord's supreme abode, not illumined by sun, moon or fire, from which there is no return (BhG 15.6, 8.21).
Supreme love: the Nārada Sūtra's definition of devotion (NBS 2).

equivalents.note: both define bhakti as the highest love; the Nārada Sūtra calls it prema and nectar, the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra anurakti (attachment) toward Īśvara
Gauḍīya prema is the ripened stage of a graded path; NBS prema is devotion's own nature

definitions.definition: Supreme separation — the last of the eleven attachments (NBS 82); cf. Nārada's own definition, supreme anguish on forgetting the Lord (NBS 19).
Supreme anguish on forgetting the Lord — half of Nārada's definition of devotion (NBS 19).
The highest heaven, where the syllable rests on which the gods sit (RV 1.164.39), where the dead meet the fathers (10.14.8), and where the overseer of creation is (10.129.7).
The third state: love so intense that separation from the vision would be unbearable; it ripens into attainment.
Fourth kind: no topknot or thread; knowledge as staff; beyond dharma and adharma; attains the world of truth or liberation.
The highest class of renunciant, established in knowledge of the self, beyond ritual marks; the model of the vidvat-sannyāsin.
The supreme ether: Śiva's cit-śakti, the ākāśa of the Upaniṣads read as Brahman.
Viṣṇu's highest step, which the wise ever see and where there is a well-spring of honey (RV 1.22.20, 1.154.5).

notes: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad (1.3.9) names it the end of the road (reference only).

definitions.definition: The eternal, partless, imperceptible ultimate constituent of earth, water, fire and air; of spherical size (VS 4.1.1, 4.1.7, 7.1.26 C).
Division ends in atoms, which lie beyond the truṭi (NS 4.2.16–17); atoms are imperceptible (NS 2.1.37).
The partless unit of matter, occupying one space-point, with one taste, colour, smell and two touches; atoms bind by degrees of smoothness and roughness (TS 5.25–37).

equivalents.note: Jain atoms are also partless and eternal but are undifferentiated as to element; the Vaiśeṣika holds four kinds of atoms.

definitions.definition: Cognition of the probans as qualified by pervasion and present in the subject ('this mountain has smoke pervaded by fire'), the instrument of inference.
Kapila, by whom the secret knowledge was expounded (SK 69; Gauḍapāda).
The highest aim — God and liberation — pursued within household life.
The spiritual goal, which the Dāsbodh teaches alongside skilful worldly life.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa's name for buddha-nature: an emptiness that sees both empty and non-empty, which is wisdom and the middle way.
That which exists ultimately: what does not lose its identity when broken or analysed into parts (like matter or feeling), as opposed to a pot or water.

equivalents.note: The Kośa's 'ultimately existent' vs the Pali 'ultimate'.

definitions.definition: Ultimately real: never sublated — Brahman alone.
Wrong view grasping beyond the true nature of things.
The one reality, consciousness that is both light and reflexive awareness, free, performing the five acts, transcending and containing the thirty-six tattvas.

equivalents.note: Both name a non-dual conscious absolute; the Kashmir Śaivas insist theirs is active (vimarśa, svātantrya) and object to an inactive Brahman and to the world as vivarta

definitions.definition: The supreme-Self portion present in all beings; it predominates in the planets, the gods' powers and the full avatāras (BPHS 1.22–24; 2.2–8).

The supreme person in the body — witness, permitter, supporter, experiencer, great Lord (BhG 13.22); the highest puruṣa (15.17); beginningless and without guṇas, it neither acts nor is tainted (13.31).
In the Bhāgavata one of the three names of the non-dual reality (with Brahman and Bhagavān).
The supreme self whose subtlety the renouncer discerns by yoga (MDh 6.65).
The supreme self, i.e. Brahman as the self of all; not different from the inner self.
In Jainism the soul in its perfected state — the embodied omniscient (arhat) and the bodiless Siddha; by the ultimate standpoint every soul's own nature (Paramātmaprakāśa; Yogasāra 22).
The Lord, one and omniscient, as one of the two kinds of self (Tarkasaṅgraha).
'This supreme self is examined here' (NK 1.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: For one who has conquered himself and is at peace, the paramātman is steadily composed amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (6.7); the reading (the supreme self established in him, or his self supremely composed) is disputed.
The supreme Self, whose sovereignty is the reflexive awareness that is supreme speech (ĪPK 1.5.13).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: In Nyāya the supreme self is a distinct self, not the self of all.

definitions.definition: What exists by its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) and is not further reducible: consciousness, mental factors, matter and nibbāna, in contrast to concepts (paññatti).
In the ultimate sense (paramatthato) no person is found (Mil 3.1.1); in the commentaries paramattha-sacca and the four ultimate realities (citta, cetasika, rūpa, nibbāna).
The five supreme beings — Arhat, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, Sādhu — with 12, 8, 36, 25 and 27 qualities (108 in all).
The supreme Lord, splendid with being, consciousness and bliss, with parts (sakala), source of Śakti, nāda and bindu (ŚT 1.7).
The one Supreme, distinct from souls, deities and world, who alone grants liberation and incarnates as the five Kṛṣṇas.
The ten perfections fulfilled by a bodhisatta — giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, equanimity (Bv 2.116–165).
The perfections fulfilled by a Bodhisatta (ten in the Theravāda list), treated systematically in Dhammapāla's commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka.

equivalents.note: Mahāyāna lists six or ten pāramitās with different members

definitions.definition: The act done in worship with the hand-gesture called mahāmudrā (thumbs interlocked, fingers extended).

The bodhisattva's six (giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom) or ten (adding skillful means, vow, power, knowledge) perfections, each perfected only when informed by the perfection of wisdom.
Perfection; the Kośa names the fulfilment of giving, patience, morality, vigour, meditation and wisdom in the bodhisattva career.

cross_language.form: boluomi 波羅蜜 / du 度

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The succession through which the ancient yoga was received and known by the royal sages before being lost over time (4.2): Kṛṣṇa to Vivasvat, Vivasvat to Manu, Manu to Ikṣvāku (4.1).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Supreme attachment to the Lord: the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra's definition of devotion (ŚBS 2), a form of rāga, the opposite of hatred.

equivalents.note: Rāmānuja makes bhakti a steady remembrance that is knowledge (upāsana); the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra denies that bhakti is knowledge

definitions.definition: The Supreme beyond the supreme; Tāyumāṉavar's address to the ultimate in the refrain of the Paraparakkaṇṇi.
Half of Brahmā's lifetime of a hundred years of such days and nights; the whole life (two parārdhas) ends in the elemental dissolution.
Public temple worship on behalf of king and realm, performed by qualified priests in installed liṅgas.
Temple worship for others, performed by Ādiśaiva priests consecrated for it.
The five-membered statement by which one who has inferred makes another infer.
That aggregates exist for another's sake, proving puruṣa (SK 17); prakṛti's undertaking is for another as if for itself (SK 56, 60).
The mind's entering another body after loosening the cause of bondage and knowing its pathways (3.38); the senses follow it like bees their queen (YBh 3.38).
Entry into another's body, described by Hemacandra as a mere wonder of no use for liberation (YŚ 5–6.1).
Śiva as the liṅga itself, with the supreme Śakti as its pedestal (SSM 11.32).
'Souls render service to one another' (TS 5.21) — the function of souls toward each other; now a motto of the Jain community.
All reality other than Viṣṇu — Lakṣmī, souls, matter, time, the Veda, negations — which exists, knows and acts only as dependent on and controlled by him.
In the Saṃdhinirmocana, the dependently arisen nature of dharmas, basis of the imagined.
Complete dependence on the Lord for existence, knowledge and action; the Teṅkalai hold it deeper than śeṣatva, excluding any independent act of one's own toward salvation.
Spatial (far/near) and temporal (older/younger) qualities.
The Lord's supremacy — 'he who has the highest good, beyond which there is none higher', lord of the eternal ones (TVM 1.1.1).
The contempt the ascetic courts; the wise one who is insulted becomes complete in austerity.
The third stage: the breath reaches the great void; drum sound; natural bliss (HYP 4.74–75); the breath enters suṣumnā and pierces the centres (DYŚ 97–99; SS 3.60–61).
Third stage, in which kuṇḍalinī enters the suṣumnā.
Possession or grasping, which brings suffering in proportion to how dear the thing is (the osprey).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One who has given up all possessions (tyakta-sarva-parigraha), doing only bodily action, incurs no fault (4.21); the meditating yogin is without possessions (aparigraha) (6.10).
Infatuation with things (TS 7.17); external (ten kinds of property) and internal (fourteen: wrong view, passions, quasi-passions).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Falling back: from what is obtained, what is not obtained, or enjoyment; possible for five of the six kinds of arhat, not from stream-entry; one fallen does not die before regaining the fruit.
No falling back from arhatship, since defilements abandoned by seeing do not return.
Stream-enterers can fall back, arhats cannot (Vasumitra).

A remedy that averts or lessens the evil shown in the chart: worship, mantra-recitation, fire-offering, gifts, vows, gems and pacification rites prescribed per planet or yoga (BPHS 84–96; Praśna Mārga).
The nature of dharmas as designated by names and conventions — like hairs seen by one with cataract.
Testing by the means of knowledge whether a definition fits — the third activity of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
Cause of measuring; four kinds: minute, large, long, short.
The minimal, eternal magnitude of atoms (VS 7.1.26 C).
Real transformation: prakṛti operates through the guṇas by combination and transformation, like water taking on different tastes in different receptacles (SK 16).
Real change of form in the guṇas and their products (3.9–15, 4.14, 4.32–33).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): time, marked by the seasons, called 'transformation'; excessive, deficient or contrary seasons are the third cause of disease (Ca Sū 11.42-43); in Suśruta one of the candidate 'sources' (Su Śā 1.11).
Transformation of a cause into an effect (BS 1.4.27).
Real transformation (as milk into curd); Advaita accepts it only for māyā/avidyā in relation to the world, never for Brahman, which undergoes only apparent transformation (vivarta).
The becoming of qualities and substances through their modes (TS 5.42); change within persistence.
The real change of Brahman's body from subtle to gross in creation, Brahman as self remaining unchanged; opposed to Advaita's apparent transformation (vivarta).
The doctrine that the world is a real transformation of Brahman (through its śakti).
The world is a real transformation of the Lord's power.
Accepted in the form avikṛta-pariṇāma: transformation without change in Brahman.
Accepted as śakti-pariṇāma: the external power transforms, the Lord remains unchanged.
Turning one's own and others' merit toward full awakening for all beings; supreme when done without apprehending merit, dedicator or goal.
The permanence of the guṇas, whose nature is not destroyed as they transform (YBh 4.33).
States belonging to the soul by its own nature, independent of karma: being a soul, capability and incapability for liberation (TS 2.7).
The final passing of the Buddha or an arahant (DN 16), attained by the Buddha from the fourth jhāna; also used of full extinguishing of defilements in life.
The suchness of dharmas, the object of the pure eye; ultimate naturelessness.
The task regarding the first truth: suffering is to be fully understood (SN 56.11).
Three full understandings: as the known, as investigation, as abandoning.
Code language: the veiled names the Siddhars gave herbs, minerals, processes and yogic states, so that only the guru's disciple could decode them; glossaries (e.g. Akattiyar paripāṣai) explain some.

cross_language.note: Sanskrit: technical convention

definitions.definition: Inquiry put to the wise, the second way to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of three ways (with prostration and service) of approaching the truth-seeing knowers for knowledge (4.34).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The council of learned brāhmaṇas that decides dharma where texts are silent — ten, three, or even one who knows the Veda or the self (MDh 12.108–113; YS 1.9).
One of twenty-two afflictions (hunger, thirst, cold, heat, nakedness, abuse, and the rest) to be endured without swerving from the path (TS 9.8–9).
Enduring the hardships calmly, a means of stopping and shedding karma (TS 9.2, 9.8).

An injunction that, where something is obtained both in the stated case and elsewhere, serves to exclude the others (e.g. 'five five-nailed animals may be eaten'); explicit (śrautī) or implied (lākṣaṇikī).
A contemplative exercise in the Upadeśasāhasrī's prose part: reviewing sound and the other objects as not-self and oneself as pure unrelated awareness.
A text recited for protection: the Āṭānāṭiya verses (DN 32), the Ratana and Mettā suttas; the tradition's chanted protection.
Class of mental factors (ten): anger, enmity, dissimulation, envy, spite, concealment, avarice, deceit, pride, harmfulness.
The wandering ascetic; one night in a village, five in a town, the rains in one place.

equivalents.note: Parivrājaka stresses wandering, saṃnyāsin the act of renunciation; the texts use both for the fourth āśrama.

definitions.definition: The rain-god, 'father' beside mother Earth (AVŚ 12.1.12).
The indirect, hidden name or form preferred by the gods — 'the gods love the cryptic and dislike the obvious' (ŚB 10.5.2.20; 14.6.11.2; AB 3.43).
Knowledge through senses, mind or words — sensory and scriptural knowledge (TS 1.11); later memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and testimony.
Mediate knowledge: knowing that something is, without its being immediately one's own ('there is a tenth').
Indirect or veiled statement: the Vedic seers speak indirectly and the indirect is dear to the Lord.
A calcined (white) preparation of a mineral, metal or shell.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: First of the five concentrations: visualising the middle world as an ocean of milk with a golden lotus and oneself on it (YŚ 7).
The relation by which a number such as 'two' resides in both relata together, not in each singly.
Envelopment: eight (or ten) secondary defilements — shamelessness, lack of dread of blame, envy, avarice, restlessness, remorse, torpor, sleepiness (+ anger, concealment).
The defilement awake (manifest), as opposed to its latent seed.
A changing state of a substance; modes arise and cease while the substance persists (TS 1.26, 1.29, 5.38).
The rotation of the worship of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi among the eight maṭhas; now two years per maṭha (a change credited to Vādirāja Tīrtha).
The root standpoint that looks to the changing modes (Sanmati 1.3).

A negation that does not attach to the injunctive but forms a positive injunction of 'not-doing' (e.g. the snātaka's vow not to look at the rising sun), used where a prohibition proper is impossible or would create an option.
The eight-day festival at the height of the rains (Bhādrapada), of fasting, confession and forgiveness, with the public reading of the Kalpa Sūtra, ending in Saṃvatsarī.
The Digambaras keep the ten days of Das Lakṣaṇa (the ten dharmas) at the same season.
The chief Jain festival at the end of the rains-retreat season — eight days for Śvetāmbaras ending with forgiveness, ten days of the ten virtues (Daśalakṣaṇa) for Digambaras.
The noose of māyā with which the Lord binds the paśus in play.
The bonds are the kalās called effects and instruments, by which the paśus are bound and made subject to sense-objects.

Bond; the eight bonds beginning with disgust whose destruction is liberation while living (Dīpikā on YH 1.86); burned away by the guru at initiation (PKS 1.36); in the Goddess's hand the noose is attachment (LSN 2).
The fetter of Varuṇa (or of death, Nirṛti) that binds the offender (RV 1.24.15, 7.88.7; AVŚ 4.16.6).
The bond of the paśu, loosened by the pāśupata vow.
The bonds: āṇava mala, karma and māyā (with Śiva's concealing power counted as a bond, and bindu for souls in the pure worlds); eternal realities, not appearances.
Pācam: the three (or five) malas that bind the soul; eternal, their power quelled in release.
A 'stone', i.e. a poisonous mineral; the tradition counts 64 (32 natural, 32 prepared).

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: 'The gift of grace': the closing prayer of the Jñāneśvarī for the good of all beings, sung at the end of Vārkarī gatherings.
The Western transmission: the cult of Kubjikā and Navātman (Kubjikāmata 2.21-22).
Calming of body and mind; the fifth factor of awakening; arising from rapture and leading to happiness (SN 12.23; MN 118).
Tranquillity of the mental body and of consciousness; beautiful universals; an awakening factor and an imperfection of insight when grasped.

Tranquillity of body and mind (MN 118); to be developed when the mind is restless (SN 46.53). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.
All selves wandering in saṃsāra, the Lord's 'cattle'.

Every conscious being other than the Lord - with body and organs (sāñjana) or without (nirañjana), including the gods from Brahmā down and those liberated by Sāṃkhya-Yoga - bound by the kalās; so called from 'seeing' (only the body) and 'being bound'.
Used in the same sense in the Śaiva sources that report on the Kāpālikas; no independent Kāpālika definition survives.
The soul dependent on the Lord, its servant at the stage of practice (SSM 10.40); 'who is paśu, who pati?' when māyā dissolves (14.8–9).
The bound 'animal' — one whose tendency is outward, who worships external liṅgas or falls from the pledge (KJN 3.17, 3.31, 11.4).
One bound by the eight fetters (Kulārṇava 13.91).
The jīva bound by ego and the bonds.
The soul: eternal, formless, ignorant, inactive, without qualities or lordship, pervasive, lodged in māyā and bound through kalā, vidyā, rāga, prakṛti and the instruments.
The bound soul; the Goddess's devotee is freed from 'the entanglement of the paśu's bonds' (SL 99).
The bound soul: eternal, countless, by nature a conscious knower and agent (cit), all-pervading, whose powers are covered by beginningless mala; 'tethered animal' of the Lord.
The soul (Tamil uyir, āṉmā, pacu): sadasat, knowing only when made to know, taking on the nature of what it is joined with.
The bound soul, deprived of his glory by the kalās and made the object of the powers of the mass of sounds (SK 3.13).
In Kaula usage the uninitiated or the one in the paśu disposition, from whom Kula knowledge is kept; the guru 'takes up the paśu' as disciple (Kulārṇava 13.79).

equivalents.note: both name the individual embodied soul; for the Pāśupata the paśu is eternal, pervasive and never becomes the Lord

notes: Contribution from U08; U18 owns the Siddhānta definition.

definitions.definition: The first disposition — ritually pure worship without the Kaula substances; 'always pure' (Kālīvilāsa 6.10), the only one allowed in the Kali age by the Kālīvilāsa, and the beginning of the path in the Buddha's teaching to Vasiṣṭha (Rudrayāmala 17.137).
The observance and doctrine taught by Paśupati for the release of the paśus; also a follower of it. The Pāśupata Sūtra opens by announcing 'the Pāśupata rule of yoga'.
In the Purāṇas also the Vedic ash-vow of the Atharvaśiras ('pāśupata vrata'), distinguished by the Kūrma Purāṇa from the non-Vedic Pāśupata scriptures.
Smearing ash with 'fire is ash …' for release from bonds.

The yoga of smearing the body with sacred ash while reciting the 'agnir iti' mantras and meditating on Īśāna as the supreme light, for freeing the bound soul; called the essence of Vedānta and 'beyond the stages of life'.
Epithet of Rudra as lord of beasts, to whom the five kinds of animals are allotted (AVŚ 11.2); also in the Śatarudrīya.
The Lord (Rudra, Maheśvara) as master of all bound souls; he 'reaches' and 'protects' them by infinite knowledge and lordship, and releases them by grace.
The Lord of beings, all-knowing, doer of the five acts; witness who empowers the senses.
A verse-hymn of the Āḻvārs; the unit of the four thousand.

literal: the state of being a paśu

definitions.definition: Bondage: a beginningless lack of lordship (anaiśvarya) and dependence; its complete removal through connection with Maheśvara's lordship is the fifth purification.
The grammarians' highest level of speech; for Somānanda it is only the knowledge-power at the Sadāśiva level, not the ultimate (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1).

The highest of Bhartṛhari's three levels of speech: undivided, all sequence withdrawn, the inner light of its own form, subtle and imperishable (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); identified by the grammarians with the Word-Brahman.
The second of four levels of speech, above madhyamā and below parā; placed by Nāgeśa and the tantric manuals at the navel.
The second level of speech, where it puts forth two leaves.

equivalents.note: the grammarians treat paśyantī as the supreme; Somānanda and Utpaladeva place parā vāk above it

definitions.definition: The seven netherworlds below the earth (bila-svarga), full of palaces, named differently in the Bhāgavata and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa; also the name of the lowest of them.
Offences requiring confession (90 in the Dharmaguptaka and Sarvāstivāda codes, 92 in the Pali and Mahāsāṃghika).

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Whatever is hard and solid, internal (hair, nails, bones …) or external; simply the earth element, not self (MN 28, MN 62, MN 140).
Wholesome diet and conduct: that which keeps the balanced tissues balanced and restores the unbalanced (Ca Sū 25.33).
Śiva as Paśupati, lord of the bound selves, who binds them and alone frees them.
The Lord as possessor of unsurpassed powers of seeing and acting, eternally related to that lordship and not acquiring it (SDS ch. 6); he alone is not a paśu.
Mahādeva as the Lord on whom the bound soul depends (SSM 10.40); at union lordship and boundness are seen as imagined by māyā (14.8–9).
The Lord, Śiva: one, eternally free (anādimukta), omniscient and omnipotent, the efficient cause who by his single power performs the five acts for the souls' release; distinct from souls and bonds.
Pati (Tamil pati, iṟai): the Lord who is one with, other than and together with souls; the Real (cat).

equivalents.note: the Pāśupata Pati is the independent efficient cause, not the Nyāya Īśvara who acts in dependence on karma

definitions.definition: A purified, stable image born of perception, free of the device's faults, appearing with access concentration; for the breath it may appear as a star, gem, cotton, smoke, cloud and so on.

The twelvefold arising of suffering from ignorance through formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming and birth to ageing-and-death, and its cessation (SN 12.1); 'whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma' (MN 28).

The twelve-linked arising of suffering from ignorance; expounded by the commentaries across three lives (three periods, twenty modes, four groups, three links), and by the Abhidhamma method within one moment.
The arising of suffering and of the 'I' in the present, from contact without mindfulness; 'birth' is the birth of the ego (Buddhadāsa).
The chart of dependent origination to be understood before contemplating the arising and passing of mind and feeling.

equivalents.note: same doctrine under its Sanskrit name

definitions.definition: The phenomena that arise dependently (ageing, birth … ignorance), impermanent, conditioned, subject to cessation (SN 12.20).
Ill will as the fifth fetter (MN 64).
The three wonders of psychic power, mind-reading and instruction, of which only instruction is praised (DN 11).
In the Prabandham, a decad of hymns (usually ten verses and a signature verse) — each 'tiruvāymoḻi' of the Tiruvāymoḻi is such a decad.
A hymn of (usually) ten or eleven verses, the unit of the Tēvāram, the last verse often naming the poet and promising fruit.
The code of rules (227 for monks, 311 for nuns) recited on the uposatha; restraint by it is the training in higher virtue (AN 3.89).
Restraint by the Pātimokkha as the first step of the gradual training (DN 2; MN 107).
The monastic code; restraint by it is the first of the four purities of virtue.
The four analytical knowledges: of meaning, Dhamma, language and ready expression.
Rebirth-linking consciousness, the first moment of a new existence, conditioned by the last process of the previous one.
The devoted wife, whose power humbles the angry Kauśika (MBh 3.196–197), whom Sāvitrī exemplifies (3.281), and whose dharma Anasūyā teaches Sītā (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119).
Explanation of conditionality through the twenty-four conditions, as opposed to the dependent-origination method.
Sharing or dedication of merit to others, especially the departed; the Kathāvatthu denies a literal transfer of the gift itself.
The dietary and behavioural restrictions to be kept during a course of Siddha treatment, held strictest for mineral-metal medicines.
A reciter/teacher of the Purāṇas; the six paurāṇikas who learned from Romaharṣaṇa (BhP 12.7.5).

Human effort: mental and bodily activity guided by the instruction of the good and by scripture; by it everything is attained. It is twofold, former (whose fruit is called fate) and present, and the present overcomes the former.

equivalents.note: puruṣakāra, the usual epic/smṛti word for human effort opposed to daiva

definitions.definition: Rites for prosperity (increase of cattle, crops, wealth).
(Jain report) Gosāla's doctrine, drawn from the regrowing sesame plant, that beings may die and re-enter a body; he claimed to be the seventh such re-entry.
The maidens' vow of the month of Mārkaḻi, kept by the cowherd girls of the Tiruppāvai to win Kṛṣṇa.

notes: The Śaiva Tiruvempāvai (Māṇikkavācakar) is a parallel Mārkaḻi vow-song (prc:tiruvempavai-vow, U18).

definitions.definition: Soma as it flows through the filter; the ninth maṇḍala.
Annual offering of a thread-garland (pavitra) to Śiva in Śrāvaṇa or Nabhasya, removing all defects in the year's worship.
Annual pavitra offering to Viṣṇu with the same function.
The unspoken mantra: the identity of guru and Lord, He and She, known without utterance (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).

equivalents.note: both name a mantra not recited aloud; the Tamil verse does not mention the breath

definitions.definition: Tamil names of the Lord (Viṣṇu) in the temples; Rāmānuja is 'Emperumāṉār', 'the one who is (like) our Lord'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One is never entitled to the fruits of action (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are pitiable (2.49).
The result produced by activity and faults (NS 1.1.20).
The result of a rite. A fruit stated for a subsidiary is praise (MS 4.3.1); where none is stated, heaven is the fruit (MS 4.3.15); for a principal rite the stated fruit is real (Ātreya, MS 4.3.18).
The fruition consciousness following the path, and re-entered as fruition attainment.
Result; five kinds: of ripening, outflow, dominance, human effort and disjunction.
Being of the nature of the fruit: why devotion is higher than action, knowledge and yoga (NBS 26) and is its own fruit (NBS 30).
The meeting of sense faculty, object and consciousness, condition for feeling (MN 18; SN 12.2); one of the four nutriments (MN 9).
Contact: the coming together of object, sense faculty and consciousness; the first of the universal factors.
Every one of the sixty-two views is experienced through contact at the six sense-bases.
The whisk of naturally shed peacock feathers carried by Digambara monks and nuns to remove small beings without harm; with the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and a scripture it is all they own.
The Vaiśeṣika view that when a clay pot is baked the pot dissolves into atoms, whose colour changes, and is then re-formed.
The body as the microcosm of the whole cosmos; the SSP's six upadeśas are organised around the piṇḍa (its origin, knowledge, vision, support and samarasa with the pada).
The 'place' among the four (piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, rūpātīta) of the Kula aim (KJN 3.4).
The body as microcosm containing Meru, the continents, stars and gods (SS 2.1–5).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna says that when classes are mixed the ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water (piṇḍodaka-kriyā, 1.42).
The rice-ball offered to the dead and ancestors; the ten daily piṇḍas build the preta's body and the monthly ones feed him on the road.
The rice-ball offered to the father, grandfather and great-grandfather in the ancestral rites.
The body as the place where nāda becomes manifest; hence the Saṅgītaratnākara's section on 'the origin of the body' (piṇḍotpatti) (ŚR 1.2.3).
The first sub-sthala: the embodied soul made fit for the path by the ripening of karma and Śiva's grace (SSM 5.27–30; cf. 5.34–36).

notes: Homonym of piṇḍa, the rice-ball offered to ancestors (other units' definitions).

definitions.definition: Awareness of the body as containing the cosmos (SSP 3).
The firmness of the body, the precondition of jīvanmukti in the rasa doctrine (SDS Raseśvara 1; Rasārṇava 1.11, 1.18).
Grasping a composite (a world, a heap of atoms) as a real unity; the Vajracchedikā says it is inexpressible yet seized by common people.
The body of the preta built up limb by limb by the ten days' piṇḍas, which merges with the airy body.
Discernment of the self as distinct from body, senses and intellect, and of the Lord as distinct from the selves (SSM 5.55–60).
Meditation on the embodied self through the five visualised concentrations (YŚ 7.8–28; Jñānārṇava).
The right channel, of the sun, identified with the Yamunā (HYP 3.110).
The channel on the right, of the sun (GŚ 20, 23).
The right channel, carrying the sun.
Tamil piṅkalai: the right channel (solar), second of the ten nāṭis of the Siddha ninety-six.
Birth, and the round of births the Āḻvārs pray to be freed from — the 'sea of sorrow' (iṭar āḻi).
Seat: the four seats Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍḍiyāna, located in the subtle body (YH 1.41-42; LSN 82); the Goddess is 'of the form of the fifty seats', the letters (LSN 156).
A sacred seat of the Goddess where a part of Satī's body fell and Śiva stays as a liṅga (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.46).
The four seats as levels of the supreme yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7).
A seat, used in the haṭha texts as a synonym of āsana (posture): 'the eighty-four seats', 'Matsyendra's seat', 'the lord of yoga-seats'.
Four seats in the body — Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Uḍyāna.
A sacred seat of the Goddess and yoginīs: Kāmākhyā, Pūrṇagiri, Oḍiyāna, Arbuda with their sub-seats (KJN 8.20–22).
The Naiyāyika view that heat changes the colour of the pot as a whole without its dissolution.
Rapture born of seclusion or concentration, factor of the first two jhānas (DN 2); the fourth factor of awakening; arises from gladness and leads to tranquillity (SN 12.23).
Rapture: delight in the object; fivefold (minor, momentary, showering, uplifting, pervading); a jhāna factor.
Spiritual rapture arising in one who has aroused energy (MN 118). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.
The ancestors, to whose company the dead is joined by sapiṇḍīkaraṇa and who are fed by śrāddha; they dwell in the south below the earth.
The dead ancestors, lower, higher and middle, who have gone to the life-breath and rejoice with Yama in svadhā (RV 10.14–15).
The ancestors, who receive food monthly, svadhā as drink, the moon as their light (ŚB 2.4.2.2).
The primeval deities of several classes (Somasads, Agniṣvāttas, Barhiṣads…) (MDh 3.192–199).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The ancestors, who fall when deprived of the rice-ball and water offerings because of varṇa-mixture (1.42).

cross_language.note: ancestors

definitions.definition: The dark path of smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the southern course, by which one reaches the lunar light and returns (BhG 8.25).

The path of the fathers: through smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the southern course, the fathers' world, space and the moon, and back as rain and food into a womb (ChU 5.10.3-6; BAU 6.2.16; PrU 1.9).
The path of the fathers, one of the two paths 'I have heard of' (RV 10.88.15).
The path of the fathers, taken by performers of rites, leading to the moon and return to earth with residual karma (BS 3.1).

The doṣa of heat and transformation: slightly unctuous, hot, sharp, liquid, sour, flowing and pungent (Ca Sū 1.60); there is no fire in the body apart from pitta (Su Sū 21.9); fivefold as pācaka, rañjaka, sādhaka, ālocaka and bhrājaka (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-14).
Tamil aḻal or pittam: the fire humour, second of the three.
The retention in which the belly is filled with air so that one floats on water.
Wealth, polity, the things of life; the Kuṟaḷ's second book (70 chapters).
The fortnightly observance at which the monastic community of a boundary gathers, confesses and recites the prātimokṣa.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Seventh view: like the sun; meditation; action without attachment (YDS).
The third of the ten bodhisattva grounds in the Daśabhūmika.
The thought of awakening is no-thought, since the nature of thought is luminous (Aṣṭa 1).
The self-nature pure mind that is nonetheless defiled — hard to understand (Śrīmālā); the mind's nature rests on nothing, like space (RGV).

cross_language.form: sems kyi rang bzhin 'od gsal ba
zixing qingjing xin 自性清淨心

equivalents.note: the Pali luminous mind is not identified with a buddha-nature

definitions.definition: The specific action of a substance not explained by its taste, potency or vipāka (Ca Sū 26).
The unit of extension occupied by one atom; souls and the media have innumerable, space infinite (TS 5.8–11).
The mass of karmic particles bound to the soul's space-points, depending on activity (TS 8.24).
Synonym of prakṛti as the principal cause of the world (SK 11, 57); the term under which Vedānta and other critics discuss the Sāṃkhya cause.
The guṇas as the unmanifest source, 'neither being nor non-being' (YBh 2.19); mastery of pradhāna is one of the three 'honey-like' powers (3.48).
Primal matter: the perishable (ŚU 1.10); God is lord of pradhāna and of the field-knower (6.16); like a spider covering himself with threads from pradhāna (6.10).
Primal matter, one of the four forms of Viṣṇu in the VP (with puruṣa, vyakta and kāla).
The principal act, which bears the fruit; its subsidiaries serve it (MS 9.1.1).

cross_language.note: as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Absence after destruction: with a beginning, without end.
The Nārāyaṇīya's word for the Lord's appearances: Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi, the appearance at Mathurā, and earlier the Swan and the Horse-headed one (12.326.72–94).
The third form, born from Saṃkarṣaṇa; the liberated, 'becoming mind', enter Pradyumna (MBh 12.326.68; 12.332.15).
The vyūha manifesting lordship and virility; in Śaṅkara's report, identified with mind (manas).

equivalents.note: Pradyumna corresponds to the mind in the Nārāyaṇīya's ascent

definitions.definition: Absence of a product before it arises: beginningless, with an end; an effect is defined as the counterpositive of a prior absence.
The renunciation declaration ('I have renounced'; 'I have risen above the desires for wife, wealth and worlds').

The lord of creatures, named in the last verse of the Hiraṇyagarbha hymn (RV 10.121.10) and in the White Yajurveda as moving unborn within the womb and born in many ways (VS 31.19); in the Atharvaveda Time is his father (AVŚ 19.53.8).

The creator who, alone in the beginning, desired to multiply, heated himself with austerity and emitted the worlds and beings; exhausted and fallen apart after creating, he is the year and is rebuilt in the fire-altar and the sacrifice.
In Manu, the creator-lord who milked the syllables a-u-m and the Sāvitrī from the Vedas (MDh 2.76–77); one of the names by which the one supreme Person is called (MDh 12.123).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The creator who in the beginning created beings together with sacrifice and told them to prosper by it (3.10).
The form of Viṣṇu that presides over deep sleep, in which the soul, covered by tamas, rests in him.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The wisdom that is 'firmly established' in the one who neither rejoices nor hates, withdraws and restrains the senses (2.57, 2.58, 2.61, 2.68); carried away when the mind follows the senses (2.67). Arjuna is said to speak prajñāvāda, words of (seeming) wisdom (2.11).
Insight: the fifth means (1.20); truth-bearing in nirvicāra lucidity (1.48); sevenfold at the final stage (2.27); its light comes from mastery of saṃyama (3.5).

Wisdom, intelligence: the wise brahmin should cultivate prajñā (BAU 4.4.21); Indra as 'breath, the intelligent self' (prajñātman, KauU 3.2); by intelligence one obtains thoughts and desires (KauU 1.7).

The perfection of wisdom that does not apprehend any dharma; it is the mother of the buddhas and leader of the perfections; wisdom without skillful means is bondage and means without wisdom is bondage (Vimalakīrti 4.16).
Intelligence or cognition, most developed in man, who says and sees what he has known and seeks the immortal (AA 2.3.2).
The self as experiencer of deep sleep, identified with the causal body (counterpart of Īśvara); bound by cause only (GK 1.11).

cross_language.note: Buddhist technical sense differs

cross_language.form: banruo 般若 / zhihui 智慧

definitions.definition: The 'intelligent one', the third quarter of the self, whose field is deep sleep, a mass of cognition, made of bliss (MāU 5); the intelligent self that embraces the sleeper (BAU 4.3.21).

notes: Distinct from prajñā (wisdom); id disambiguated.

definitions.definition: One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One who has mastered the elements and senses and guards what has been cultivated.
Intelligence, cognition: the sixteen faculties of heart and mind are its names; 'the world is guided by intelligence; intelligence is brahman' (AU 3.1.2-3).
A solid mass of cognition: the great being is a mass of understanding like salt dissolved in water (BAU 2.4.12, 4.5.13); the sleeper as prājña is a mass of cognition (MāU 5).
'Consciousness is Brahman' (Aitareya 3.3): the defining sentence (lakṣaṇa-vākya), mahāvākya of the Ṛgveda and of Govardhana (Purī).

literal: offence against (one's own) wisdom; failure of discernment

definitions.definition: The inauspicious act of body, speech or mind done by one whose intellect (dhī), resolve (dhṛti) and memory (smṛti) have lapsed; the provoker of all doṣas (Ca Śā 1.102); wrong knowing and wrong acting of the intellect (Śā 1.109); one of the three causes of disease (Sū 11.43); the source of adharma and so of epidemics (Vi 3.20) and the cause of exogenous insanity (Ni 7.10); all mental disorders are born of it (Sū 7.52).

equivalents.note: both name a root error of understanding behind suffering; prajñāparādha is an act (karma) proceeding from lapsed intellect, not a cosmic ignorance

definitions.definition: The sixth perfection: wisdom that apprehends no dharma, not even itself; the 'mother of the buddhas' and leader of the other five perfections; also the name of the sūtras that teach it and, personified, a goddess.

literal: perfection of wisdom; wisdom gone beyond

cross_language.form: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa
banruo boluomi(duo) 般若波羅蜜(多)

definitions.definition: Existing only as a designation over a collection (like milk over colour, smell etc., or a heap of grain); for Vasubandhu the person is such a designation over the series of aggregates.
A mode: an entity that exists only as the attribute of another (its prakārin) and cannot be known apart from it; souls and matter are modes of Brahman.
What appears in a cognition as qualifying something; its property is prakāratā.

The fourth means of subsidiarity: mutual expectancy between a principal needing a procedure and subsidiaries without a stated fruit; major (of the main rite) and minor (of a subsidiary) (MS 3.3.14; Arthasaṅgraha).
A pseudo-reason in the Nyāya Sūtra's list (NS 1.2.7 DCS).
The light of consciousness by which anything appears; never without vimarśa, else it would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11).
Light: Śiva's nature, 'whose body is pure light' (KKV 1); the Goddess is its fusion with self-awareness (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); Bhāskararāya's 'great light, seeing which nothing else is seen' (VR 3).
The karma that covers discriminative knowledge, dwindling through prāṇāyāma (2.52) and destroyed by the great bodiless concentration (3.43).
The manifestness of an object produced by cognition; another name for jñātatā.

A 'miscellaneous' canonical text, ten in the standard Mūrtipūjaka list (Catuḥśaraṇa, Āturapratyākhyāna and others), many on devotion and the discipline of dying; the Nandī says there were as many prakīrṇakas as disciples of a Tīrthaṅkara. Rejected by Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs.

literal: that which brings forth; nature, source

definitions.definition: The unconscious, productive principle consisting of the three guṇas in equilibrium (SS 1.61), from which mahat and the other principles emerge (SK 22); one and common to all puruṣas (SK 11); inferred from its effects (SK 8, 15–16); it acts for puruṣa's experience and liberation and binds and releases itself (SK 57–63). In SK 3 'prakṛti' also names any principle that produces another (the seven prakṛti-vikṛtis).
Material nature, the seen, of three guṇas; in YS 4.2–3 'prakṛti' (plural) are the material causes whose overflow transforms beings.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) bodily constitution — the doṣa predominating from conception, giving vāta-, pitta-, kapha-, mixed or balanced natures (Ca Sū 7.39-40; Vi 8.95; AHS Sū 1.9-10); (2) the normal state, i.e. balance of the dhātus (Ca Sū 9.4); (3) the eightfold prakṛti of the person's principles (Ca Śā 1.63); (4) for Suśruta 'in medicine' nature, the Lord, time, chance, destiny and transformation are held to be the source (Su Śā 1.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); beings deluded by its guṇas are attached to their workings (3.29); one's own nature, which even the knower follows (3.33).

The Lord's nature: the lower, eightfold prakṛti and the higher life-element (BhG 7.4–5); beginningless, the cause of effect, instrument and agency, from which the guṇas arise (13.19–20); all action is done by its guṇas (3.27); under the Lord's oversight it brings forth the world (9.10).
The unmanifest pradhāna of three guṇas, cause and effect in one; in Kapila's teaching it is powerless before the self that sees with knowledge, dispassion and devotion.
Nature whose properties (suffering, ignorance) belong to it and not to the self (VP 6.7.22-24); the Goddess as the primordial unmanifest Prakṛti (DM 4).
Mixed-sattva matter with the three guṇas, eternal and real, the Lord's body, transforming into the twenty-three evolutes; it is also called māyā because it produces wonderful effects.
Nature, primal matter: 'know prakṛti to be māyā' (ŚU 4.10).
The eternal material cause of the world, insentient and dependent, presided over by Lakṣmī (as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā); God is the efficient cause only.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.6 the Lord comes into being presiding over his own prakṛti (svāṃ prakṛtim adhiṣṭhāya).

cross_language.note: also renders svabhāva; as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
also renders svabhāva; as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

equivalents.note: Gauḍapāda lists māyā among the synonyms of prakṛti (on SK 22) and Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.10 equates them, but Sāṃkhya holds prakṛti real and independent, while Advaita holds māyā indeterminable and not a second reality.
In the Yoga texts pradhāna names the unmanifest prakṛti (YBh 2.18–19, YS 3.48).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The kind of karma bound — which of the eight types (TS 8.3–4).
Mind luminous by nature, defiled by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).
Attributed to the Vibhajyavādins and rejected by the Vibhāṣā.

cross_language.note: AN 1.51–52 'pabhassaram idaṃ cittaṃ'

equivalents.note: The Mahāsāṃghika 'naturally luminous mind' and the Pali 'luminous mind' (AN 1.51–52) — the schools read the luminosity differently.

definitions.definition: A rite whose subsidiaries are all taught in its own context (e.g. the new- and full-moon rites) is an archetype; one that lacks them and takes them by transfer is an ectype.
The dissolution at the end of Brahmā's life when the cosmic egg and all principles return into Prakṛti.

The result of dispassion (without discrimination) (SK 45): a dissolution into prakṛti or its evolutes, taken for liberation, from which one rises again like a diver (SS 3.54); the Kramadīpikā calls it 'bondage to prakṛti'.
Those whose mind, with its task unfinished, is dissolved in prakṛti, experiencing a quasi-kaivalya until it returns (YBh 1.19); Bhoja: those who rest content in I-am-ness samādhi (RM 1.17).
The dissolution of beings or worlds, fourfold: constant, occasional, elemental and final.
A dissolution destroying everything, for which there is no means of knowledge; creation and dissolution are to be understood 'as today' (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 68, 113).
The periodic dissolution of all products into atoms at the end of a Brahmā's lifespan by Maheśvara's desire (Praśastapāda).
Division of wholes does not end in nothingness, because atoms exist (NS 4.2.16).
Dissolution, fourfold: daily (deep sleep), occasional, elemental, and final (liberation).
A soul bound by mala and karma, whose māyic body is dissolved in the cosmic dissolution.
The knower resting in the void, as in deep sleep or cosmic dissolution, with the kārma impurity (ĪPK 3.2.8).
Valid cognition: cognition of an object not already known and not contradicted.
Experience that apprehends, in what has a property, that property as its qualifier (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Correct determination (Udayana, NK 4.5).
Heedlessness, which Sanatsujāta calls death (MBh 5.42.4); a mark of tamas (BhG 14.8, 14.13).
Carelessness: not cultivating the means of samādhi (YBh 1.30); Vyāsa warns that carelessness watches for an opening to revive the afflictions (YBh 3.51).
In Jain usage heedlessness in conduct (fifteen kinds in Digambara analysis: gossip, passions, senses, sleep, affection) — the cause that makes killing 'violence' (TS 7.13, 8.1).

equivalents.note: Yoga Sūtra 1.30 pramāda is neglect of the means of samādhi; the Jain term is broader heedlessness of conduct.

definitions.definition: The first activity of mind: valid cognition, of three kinds — perception, inference and testimony (YS 1.7).
The instrument of valid cognition; four: perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3). That by which the knower knows; purposeful because it makes action succeed (NBh 1.1.1).
Two only: perception and inference, verbal knowledge being explained as inference (VS 9.18–19 in Candrānanda's recension; Praśastapāda).
The special cause (karaṇa) of a valid cognition; the four khaṇḍas of the Tattvacintāmaṇi follow the four means.
What accords with its object (yathārtha); twofold — valid knowledge itself (kevala) and its means (anupramāṇa).
Three are accepted — perception, inference and reliable testimony — since all others are included in them (SK 4); Vācaspati reduces postulation, absence, inclusion and tradition to these.
Three: perception (sensory and of the self), inference (as-before, from-the-remainder, seen-in-general), and scripture.
A cognition that apprehends what was not apprehended before and is free from defects in its causes and from contradicting cognition (Śāstradīpikā); six in number.
Every experience (anubhūti), as distinct from memory; five in number (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Three are accepted — perception, inference and scripture; all of them apprehend qualified objects, none an undifferentiated reality.

Means of valid knowledge: six in Advaita (perception, inference, comparison, testimony, presumption, non-cognition), all valid empirically and all within the sphere of ignorance; scripture alone reveals Brahman.
(Lokāyata, reported variously) One (perception); or not fixable in number (suśikṣita); or none establishable (Jayarāśi).

In Jain epistemology valid knowledge itself — the five knowledges (TS 1.10); knowledge illuminating itself and its object, free from contradiction (Nyāyāvatāra 1); the right ascertainment of an object (Pramāṇamīmāṃsā 1.1.2).
The validity of a cognition, which arises and is known from the cognition itself; invalidity comes from outside.
Validity of a cognition, known extrinsically (parataḥ).
Produced by excellences in the causes and known by inference, not by the cognition that apprehends the cognition (Prāmāṇyavāda).
Beings emitted by Śiva, equal to him in splendour and able to create and dissolve worlds, among them Reṇuka and Dāruka (SSM 2.25–27).
The one who acts, impelled by the wish to obtain or avoid, and who knows through a means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1).
