The sixth guṇasthāna: the ascetic under the great vows with residual carelessness.

The twelve objects whose true knowledge leads to liberation: self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, faults, rebirth, fruit, pain, liberation (NS 1.1.9); other objects (the Vaiśeṣika categories) are acknowledged (NBh 1.1.9).
The knowing that results from a means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); it culminates in perception (NBh 1.1.3).
Delight at the qualities of those more virtuous (TS 7.11); Jain counterpart of muditā.
The first of the ten bodhisattva grounds in the Daśabhūmika.
Breath and life-force; in the Atharvaveda Prāṇa is lord of all, death and fever, awake among sleepers (AVŚ 11.4); wind was born from the Puruṣa's breath (RV 10.90.13).

The breath: life is its staying in the body and death its departure (HYP 2.3); as one of the ten vāyus it abides in the heart (SS 3.7); with apāna it pulls the living soul up and down (GŚ 26–29); their union is the aim of mūlabandha (HYP 3.64).

Breath as the vital power: the seers are the breaths (ŚB 6.1.1.1); the breath is the consecrated (KB 7.1); the one god is the breath, called 'that' (ŚB 11.6.3); the breaths are enumerated as five (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna).
The breath impelled by the body's fire that, striking the places of articulation, produces the phonemes (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 6–9).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at mouth and nose.
The breath expelled and retained in 1.34; the chief of the five vital airs, moving through mouth and nose up to the heart (YBh 3.39).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the first of the five vāyus, seated in the head and moving in chest and throat, upholding intellect, heart, senses and mind and governing breathing, swallowing, spitting, sneezing and belching (AHS Sū 12.4-5); in Śārṅgadhara the breath that rises from the navel, touches the heart-lotus, drinks the nectar of the sky and returns to nourish the body (Pūrva 5.51); the 'prāṇas' also denote the seats of life (Ca Sū 29.3; Śā 7.9).

Breath, life-breath: the eldest and best of the vital powers (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1); the one god (BAU 3.9.9); the gatherer in the body (ChU 4.3.3); born from the self like a shadow (PrU 3.3); brahman (KauU 2.1) and 'the intelligent self' (KauU 3.2); also the collective name of the five breaths (BAU 1.5.3).

The (in-)breath, offered into apāna in breath-sacrifice (BhG 4.29), fixed between the brows (8.10) or in the head (8.12) at death; the Lord as vaiśvānara joined with prāṇa and apāna digests food (15.14).
The air moving within the body; one, named prāṇa, apāna and the rest by differences of adjunct (Tarkasaṅgraha); inhalation and exhalation are marks of the self (VS 3.2.4 C).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.27–30, 5.27: the activities of prāṇa are offered into the fire of self-restraint (4.27); prāṇa is offered into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, and their movements restrained (4.29); those regulating food offer prāṇas into prāṇas (4.30); prāṇa and apāna moving within the nostrils are made equal (5.27).
The vital breath; the self in the Brahma Upaniṣad; chief of the ten vāyus; its vibration is a seed of mind.
The breath-power (marudrūpā śakti) whose arising, turning and suspension are contemplated (VBT 24-27, 64); in the āṇava means its five forms carry the seven blisses (TĀ 5).
Prāṇa and apāna prevail in waking and dream, samāna in deep sleep, udāna in the fourth, vyāna beyond (ĪPK 3.2.19-20).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: In Jain usage the ten vitalities of an embodied soul: the five senses, the three powers (mind, speech, body), breath and lifespan; violence is the severing of these (TS 7.13).

notes: Distinct from the yogic prāṇa (breath/vital wind) — see trm:prana-vayu-jain.

definitions.definition: The vibration of the life-breath, one of the two seeds of the mind: when it moves awareness arises, when it rests the mind does not arise.

equivalents.note: shares the word spanda with Kashmir Śaivism, where spanda is the divine self-vibration of consciousness; in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha passage it is the breath's movement; not asserted as the same

definitions.definition: In Hemacandra's account the five winds (prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna) with their colours and seats, and the breath's four circles — described but not made a means to liberation (YŚ 5).

The offering of the first morsels of a meal to the five breaths (prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna, udāna) with svāhā, so that eating becomes an Agnihotra offered in all worlds and selves (ChU 5.19–24; Mahānārāyaṇa Up. = TA 10.69–70; Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
The meal-rite of the twice-born incorporating the breath-oblations, prescribed in the Dharmasūtras' rules on eating.
Offering food to the five breaths as an inner agnihotra.

The fire-offering into the breaths: in ChU 5.19-24 the first morsels of food are offered to prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna and udāna as an agnihotra into the vaiśvānara self; the name is from later texts (e.g., the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad).

The subtle liṅga, made of inner contemplation (SSM 6.49–50): the light that arises from the navel-bulb when prāṇa and apāna meet, in which breath dissolves like frost in the sun (12.6–8); the initiation formula also calls the given liṅga 'your prāṇaliṅga, to be borne like your breath' (6.26).

equivalents.note: internal equivalence within the SSM: the inner liṅga is described as the liṅga of light (6.35; 12.6–9)

literal: one who has the liṅga in the breath

definitions.definition: The fourth sthala, where the yoga of knowledge begins: one who knows the liṅga as consciousness-brahman whose power is the breath (SSM 12.2–3).
Made of breath: the self within the food-self, with prāṇa as head (TU 2.2).
The sheath of vital air: the five prāṇas with the five organs of action.
The movement of prāṇa, one of the two seeds of the mind-tree.
The designator of Īśvara (1.27), whose relation to him is fixed, not conventional (YBh 1.27); repeated with contemplation of its meaning (1.28).

The designator of Viṣṇu, eightfold (a, u, m and five further subtle components up to 'atiśānta'), naming his forms Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya, Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman and Jñānātman; source of the other mantras.
The single syllable that reveals the partless, second-less Śiva; it arises from 'so'ham' by dropping the 'h' and the 's' (SSM 8.17–22).
Om as the sacred syllable: 'praṇava is the bow' (MuU 2.2.4); the upper fire-stick of meditation (ŚU 1.14).
The syllable Oṃ, whose three measures and half-measure are meditated upon; raised in the heart like a bell's sound.
Oṃ as analysed into measures and taught as the means of meditation, the renouncer's only study, the 'thread' and the tāraka; of three, four, twelve or sixteen measures.
In Jain explanation Oṃ is formed from the initials of the five supreme beings: a (arhat) + a (aśarīra, the Siddha) + ā (ācārya) + u (upādhyāya) + m (muni).
In the tirumantra, a-u-m teach that the soul (m) exists for the Lord (a) alone (u).

Oṃ, the 'tāra', prefixed to mantras; its letters a, u, m are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, and its subtle phases (bindu, ardhacandra, nirodhikā, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā, unmanā) are traversed in meditative utterance.
The one word from which the Veda's knowledge springs, opposed to no doctrine (VP 1.9, low confidence).

equivalents.note: praṇava is the name of the syllable Oṃ
same syllable; duplicate ids to be merged

definitions.definition: Intimacy: love free of reverence, feeling oneness with the beloved.

Breath-control, practised after posture is firm (HYP 2.1); threefold as exhalation, inhalation and retention (2.71); correct practice destroys disease, improper practice causes it (2.16–17); the Jyotsnā identifies haṭha itself with prāṇāyāma, the union of prāṇa and apāna.
Breath-restraint as a form of sacrifice: offering in-breath into out-breath and the reverse, restraining their courses (BhG 4.29); equalizing the breaths in the nostrils (5.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Those intent on breath-regulation offer prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, restraining their courses; this is one of the sacrifices (4.29).
Mastery of the breath, in recaka, pūraka, kumbhaka; with or without support; it burns the faults (BhP 3.28.11) and yields the states of calm and clarity (ŚiP 7.2.39).

The cutting off of the movement of inhalation and exhalation (2.49); external, internal or suspended, regulated by place, time and number (2.50); a fourth transcends both spheres (2.51); it thins the covering of the light (2.52).

Breath-control performed with Oṃ, the utterances and the Gāyatrī with its 'head' — the highest austerity, burning away the faults of the senses as smelting burns the dross of ores (MDh 6.70–72; YS 1.23; VDh 10.5).
Breath-control: first limb of the Maitrī's yoga (MaiU 6.18); ŚU 2.9 describes restraining the breaths and breathing out gently through the nose.
Regulation of breath; inwardly, seeing all as Brahman (exhalation negating the world, inhalation 'I am Brahman', retention steadiness).

Described by Hemacandra and Śubhacandra (inhaling, holding, exhaling; the winds and their circles) but declared not a means to liberation because it torments the mind (YŚ 6.4–5); Haribhadra's dīprā view gives it an inner sense — expelling outer states and taking in inner ones.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The Gītā names no counts or retention durations.

definitions.definition: Ten seats where life resides: the temples, the three vital points (head, heart, bladder), throat, blood, semen, ojas and anus (Ca Sū 29.3); or head, throat, heart, navel, anus, bladder, ojas, semen, blood and flesh (Ca Śā 7.9).
The bodhisattva's vows — Dharmākara's forty-eight, Bhaiṣajyaguru's twelve, Śrīmālā's ten, Samantabhadra's; the perfection of vow predominates on the eighth ground.
The vow to become a Buddha, first made by Śākyamuni before a former Buddha Śākyamuni; the second of the four conducts.
Prostration before the wise, the first of the three ways to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Prostration before the truth-seeing knowers, with questioning and service, as the way to receive knowledge (4.34).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The sevenfold insight of the discerning yogin: four releases regarding what is to be done and three releases of the mind (2.27, YBh 2.27).
Worldly household life; the saints teach that prapañca and paramārtha (the highest aim) can be joined.
Worldly life, to be conducted with vigilance and effort together with the pursuit of the highest.
The world, one of the four eternal realities: made of māyā, distinct from souls, deities and Parameśvara.
The stilling of the world's diversity: an epithet of the fourth (MāU 7, 12).

notes: The same compound appears in the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (src:mulamadhyamakakarika); see brw:mandukya-madhyamaka-prapancopasama.

literal: one who has come for refuge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple who has taken refuge in him and asks to be instructed (2.7).
One who has performed (V) or accepted (T) surrender; he has done what is to be done and lives in service.
Taking refuge in the Lord (prapad-): Arjuna 'has taken refuge' as a disciple (BhG 2.7); those who take refuge in the Lord cross his māyā (7.14); 'I take refuge in that primal person' (15.4).
Surrender to the Lord alone, who frees from all sins (BhG 18.66); in the Rāmāyaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa's refuge (6.18.33).
Surrender to the Lord (with Śrī) as one's sole refuge, the path of those who have no other means.
An independent means (upāya) performed once with its limbs, the occasion (vyāja) for the Lord's grace.
Not a means but the soul's acceptance of the Lord as the already-accomplished means, befitting its dependent nature.
Going for refuge: 'I, desiring liberation, go for refuge (śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye) to that God' (ŚU 6.18); the verb, not the later noun, is used.
Surrender to the Lord, one of the five means; the refuge of Kṛṣṇa's feet (Daśaślokī 8).
Surrender (śaraṇāgati) with six limbs, underlying all devotion.

equivalents.note: the Gītā uses the verb prapad- and 'śaraṇaṃ vraja'; later Śrīvaiṣṇava usage treats prapatti and śaraṇāgati as synonyms
used interchangeably with śaraṇāgati, nyāsa and bharanyāsa

definitions.definition: Possession: a real dissociated force that links a dharma to a particular series (acquisition and endowment); it explains why a defilement 'belongs' to someone even when not manifest.
Not a real entity; 'possession' is the presence of an intact seed in the series.
Karma that has begun to bear fruit; for the knower it moves the body but does not bind; its exhaustion brings bodiless liberation.
Karma that has begun to fruit and keeps the body of the liberated alive until exhausted (BhP 3.28.38: 'the body ... lives on while its karma lasts').
Karma that has begun to bear fruit in the present body and is exhausted by experiencing it; for the surrendered the Lord may end it at once.
The destiny karma that made the present body; not altered by the Master, only borne with detachment.

In jyotiṣa (interpretive gloss): the karma 'earned in a former birth' whose ripening the horā reveals as a lamp reveals objects (BJ 1.3; LJ 1.3). The jyotiṣa texts say 'karma of a former birth'; the Vedāntic word prārabdha is applied by later practitioners.
Karma that has begun to bear fruit and produced the present body; not destroyed by knowledge but exhausted by experience, like the momentum of a potter's wheel.

Viṣṇu's grace, without which there is no liberation; lowest when won by ritual (giving heaven), middling by hearing etc., highest by fullness of knowledge (giving liberation); it reaches lower beings through the higher.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attained by the disciplined one who moves among objects with senses free of passion and aversion (2.64); in it all sorrows cease and understanding quickly becomes steady (2.65).

Purity of mind achieved by Śiva's grace; whatever is offered to Śiva is his prasāda, and eating only what has been offered purifies the mind (SSM 11.2; 11.6–11); devotion and grace arise from each other like seed and sprout (9.11–12).

Two senses: the serenity of mind of one who moves among objects free of attraction and aversion (BhG 2.64–65, 18.37); and the Lord's grace, by which one attains the eternal abode (18.56, 18.62), sees the universal form (11.47) and regains memory (18.73).
The Lord's grace (īśaprasāda), by which alone the end of suffering is reached; also listed as the fifth means. As 'clarity of mind' (mateḥ prasāda) it is one of the strengths.

Serenity; grace: 'through the serenity of the constituents' (dhātuprasāda, KU 1.2.20) or 'through the grace of the creator' (dhātuḥ prasāda, ŚU 3.20); by the serenity of knowledge one sees the partless (MuU 3.1.8); by God's grace Śvetāśvatara knew brahman (ŚU 6.21); by serenity of mind one destroys karma (MaiU 6.20, 6.34).
Grace received from the guru met in the unseen.
Parshād: food or grace blessed by the Master.

equivalents.note: Both name divine grace; in Dvaita prasāda is won by knowledge and devotion and graded, so the overlap is partial.

definitions.definition: One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the śaraṇa stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The third sthala: one whose bonds of sin are destroyed through steadfastness in the liṅga and who attains serenity of mind through receiving Śiva's grace (SSM 11.2).
A subsidiary performed for one principal also incidentally benefiting another, e.g. the animal's prayājas benefiting the animal-cake (adhyāya 12).
The meditation called the cloud of dharma (YBh 1.2); its fire burns the seeds of affliction (YBh 2.2); one who takes no interest even in it attains the cloud of dharma (4.29).
Repeated contemplation of objects (and then of the body) that removes false construction and the I-notion (NBh 4.2.2, 4.2.46).

Repeated meditative contemplation of the Upaniṣadic knowledge to make it direct and to destroy the impressions of difference — required by Maṇḍana, rejected as necessary by Śaṅkara (US 18) and Sureśvara.
The mind's peaceful flow from the impressions of stilling (3.10, YBh 3.10).
Answering a question from the chart of the moment it is asked, together with the omens then present (Ṣaṭpañcāśikā; Praśna Mārga).
In Kerala the query is an elaborate rite (aṣṭamaṅgala-praśna, devaprāśna) diagnosing afflictions from curses and spirits and prescribing remedies (Praśna Mārga).
The opening portion of a sāman, sung by the prastotṛ.
The three foundations of Vedānta: the Upaniṣads (śruti), the Bhagavad Gītā (smṛti) and the Brahma Sūtras (nyāya).
The Upaniṣads, the Brahma Sūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā, the three canonical sources of Vedānta; the Gītā counts as the smṛti source. BhG 13.4 refers to 'the words of the Brahma-sūtra'.

notes: A later Vedāntic term; the Gītā does not use it.

definitions.definition: A state of the afflictions (2.4): Existing in the mind as mere potency, like seeds (YBh 2.4).
One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): The beginner, in whom the light has only begun to shine.
What prevents an effect when present (e.g. a gem or mantra stopping fire's burning); its absence is a cause.
Intuition, forerunner of knowledge born of discrimination, like dawn before sunrise (3.33, YBh 3.33); with divine hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell arising from knowledge of the puruṣa (3.36).

The flash of intuition in which a sentence's unitary meaning is grasped, indescribable even by its possessor; also the instinct by which animals act (the cuckoo's song, nest-building); sixfold by source (VP 2.143–152).
Poetic genius: the cause of poetry (śakti, KP 1.3); for Rājaśekhara twofold, creative (kārayitrī) and appreciative (bhāvayitrī).
Kṣemarāja glosses the 'upsurge' that is Bhairava (Śiva Sūtra 1.5) as the flash of the supreme I-awareness.
The seers' kind of knowledge occasionally arising in ordinary people (Praśastapāda).
Apparently real: existing only while perceived and sublated by ordinary waking cognition — dream objects, the rope-snake, shell-silver.
Puruṣa, reflected in buddhi and taking on its shade, appears to have knowledge and pleasure, while buddhi, taking on the shade of consciousness, appears conscious (Vācaspati on SK 5).

The soul as reflection of God — dependent on its original, similar to it and eternally different from it; the 'adjunct' that makes it a reflection is its own nature, so the reflection is eternal (not produced by an external upādhi as in Advaita).
The universe as a reflection in the mirror of consciousness, appearing distinct yet undivided from it (TĀ 3; Paramārthasāra 12-13).
Reflection: the jīva (or Īśvara) as the reflection of consciousness in an adjunct, like the sun in water (BS 3.2.18).
Awakening: brahman 'known through each awakening' (pratibodhaviditam, Kena 2.4); the commentators interpret it variously.
Four offences to be acknowledged, concerning food.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The portion of a sāman sung by the pratihartṛ.

One of the eight 'marvels' attending the omniscient Jina, shown in his images: the aśoka tree, the rain of flowers, the divine sound, the fly-whisks, the lion-throne, the halo, the divine drum and the triple parasol.
The statement of what is to be proved (NS 1.1.33).
In the ŚS's pratīkopāsana, one's own reflected image seen first in sunlight and then in the sky.
Meditation on Brahman through a symbol (name, mind, sun, Oṃ); the symbol is not to be taken as the self (BS 4.1.4).
Reviewing and repenting of faults committed — an expiation (TS 9.22) and one of the six essential duties, performed daily, fortnightly, four-monthly and yearly.
Abstaining from what displeases the Lord; second limb of prapatti.
One of the eleven stages of lay renunciation, from right view to not accepting food prepared for oneself (Ratnakaraṇḍa); also a statue.

The discipline of individual liberation, eightfold by class (monk, nun, probationer, male and female novice, male and female lay follower, faster) and four in substance; given up by renouncing the training, death and other causes.
The code of 250 rules for monks and 348 for nuns recited at the poṣadha.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: A substitute offering (e.g. a gourd or sugarcane in place of an animal) as allowed in the Kālikā Purāṇa and later practice.
Countering harmful thoughts by reflecting on their endless fruit of suffering and ignorance (2.33–34).
Return of an effect into its cause: the subtle afflictions are abandoned by it (2.10); kaivalya is the involution of the guṇas (4.34).
A phonetic treatise of a particular Vedic school (śākhā), governing the relation of the word-by-word and continuous texts, sandhi and accent.
Cessation through discernment: disjunction (visaṃyoga) from sāsrava dharmas, obtained separately for each bond by the wisdom that discerns the truths; it is nirvāṇa.
The non-arising of further defilement and birth once the antidote has arisen; not an entity.

equivalents.note: The Kośa identifies nirvāṇa with this cessation.

definitions.definition: True seclusion as taught by Vimalakīrti: showing neither body nor mind in the three realms while acting in the world.
The four analytical knowledges of dharmas, meanings, languages and eloquence, perfected on the ninth ground.
Dissolution of the principles into their causes in reverse order, the unmanifest itself not dissolving (Tattvasamāsa 6 and commentaries).
The four reliances: on meaning not letter, dharma not person, gnosis not consciousness, definitive not provisional sūtras.
The second of the five marks; in most Purāṇic usage the secondary creation by Brahmā (and by some understood as dissolution and re-creation).
Installation and consecration of liṅga, image or temple, to be performed with a single root āgama.
Consecration of images and temples (e.g. the Hayaśīrṣa's subject).
Installation of the fixed and movable images.
Installation of the seven deities, performed only by the tantri.
Dependent origination in twelve limbs over three lives; the Vaibhāṣikas take it as 'of states' (āvasthika), each limb being the fivefold aggregates at a stage named by what predominates.
Seeing dependent origination is seeing the dharma and the Buddha (Śālistamba); what arises from conditions is unborn and empty (Anavatapta); the twelve links rest on mind (Daśabhūmika 6).

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: That of which something is the absence (the pot, for 'absence of pot'), or the first term of a relation.
Recognition of one's own self as the Lord, shown by revealing his powers (ĪPK 1.1.3); like recognizing a lover standing near (4.17).
Recognition ('this is that') as a form of mati (saṃjñā, TS 1.13) and, for Akalaṅka, an independent indirect pramāṇa.
Drawing the senses back from objects so they follow the mind, as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
Sense-withdrawal: the senses, disjoined from their objects, imitating the mind's own form (2.54), bringing supreme mastery of the senses (2.55).

Withdrawal: bringing the wandering mind back under the self's control (GS 4.1–2); withdrawing the senses while in retention and seeing all as the self (DYŚ 84–88); the sun's 'drawing in' of the moon's nectar (GŚ 55); moving breath through the eighteen marmas (YY, VS).
Withdrawal of the senses, which burns away attachments (MDh 6.72).
Withdrawal (of the senses): second limb of the Maitrī's yoga (MaiU 6.18); cf. drawing the senses into the heart (ŚU 2.8) and turning the sight inward (KU 2.1.1).
Withdrawal of the senses; five kinds, including seeing all as the Self.
In Haribhadra's correlation the limb of the sthirā view; in Hemacandra (YŚ 6) withdrawing the senses and mind from objects.
An abbreviation formed from the Māheśvara sūtras by a first sound and a final marker, naming a class of sounds (e.g. aC = the vowels).

notes: Distinct from yogic pratyāhāra (sense-withdrawal), trm:pratyahara.

definitions.definition: A formal resolve to give up something (food, activities) for a period; one of the six essential duties.
The grade of passions that prevents the great vows (TS 8.9).
The faultless contact of sense and object; sevenfold — the witness (sākṣin) and six senses (five outer and manas).
Cognition arising from sense-object contact, non-verbalizable, non-deviating, determinate (NS 1.1.4).
Arises from the contact of self, sense, mind and object (VS 3.1.13, 9.15 Candrānanda); includes yogic perception (VS 9.13).
Cognition produced by sense-object contact, indeterminate or determinate, through six contacts; also extraordinary (alaukika) perception.

Perception: the mind's activity, coloured by an external thing through the senses, that chiefly ascertains the particular; its result is the puruṣa's awareness of the activity (YBh 1.7). The perception of nirvitarkā samāpatti is the 'highest perception', the seed of testimony and inference (YBh 1.42).
Cognition arising in a person when the senses are in contact with an existing object; it grasps only what is present and so cannot know dharma (MS 1.1.4).
First an indeterminate bare awareness, then determinate cognition by universal and other features; both are perception (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
Perception: the identity of the consciousnesses delimited by the knower, the mental mode and the object; affirmative, not grasping difference (Maṇḍana).
In Jain epistemology knowledge by the soul without senses — clairvoyance, mind-reading, omniscience (TS 1.12); later also sense-perception as 'conventionally direct' (Akalaṅka).

literal: perception (as the only means of knowledge)

definitions.definition: (As reported) Perception alone is a means of knowledge; Jayanta calls this the view of the uneducated Cārvākas, and Jayarāśi overturns even perception's definition.
The knowledge realized inwardly by the noble ones, beyond words and reasoning, the goal of the Laṅkāvatāra.

cross_language.form: so so rang rig pa'i ye shes

definitions.definition: Reflective recognition, the word-natured 'grasping back' that makes a cognition determinate; the function of speech in awareness (VP 1.124).

equivalents.note: the Pratyabhijñā's vimarśa (reflexive awareness as supreme speech) develops Bhartṛhari's pratyavamarśa

definitions.definition: The demerit incurred by omitting enjoined (obligatory, occasional) acts; the seeker of release performs them to avoid it (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 110; Tantravārttika).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The adverse result which is not found in the yoga of understanding (2.40).
A cognition or presented content of the mind (1.10, 3.2, 3.19, 4.27); also 'cause' in upāya-/bhava-pratyaya (1.19–20).
Condition; four kinds: causal, immediately preceding, object and dominant conditions.

The intellectual creation of fifty kinds — five errors, twenty-eight incapacities, nine contentments, eight accomplishments — arising from the inequality of the guṇas (SK 46–51); with the liṅga creation it forms the twofold creation (SK 52).
One enlightened by an external cause without a teacher's instruction, contrasted with the one enlightened by another (buddhabodhita) (TS 10.9).
The teaching or recitation of a Vedic recension by a master, from which its name (e.g. Kāṭhaka) derives (MS 1.1.30).
The eight 'mothers' — five carefulnesses and three controls — from which all monastic conduct is born (Uttarādhyayana 24).
The 'stream': souls carried along in worldly pursuits, outside both grace and rule.
The 'invitation' at the end of the rains, where each monastic invites correction for what was seen, heard or suspected.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The beginner's stage, relying on the name and the guru's mantra.
Going forth: novice ordination with the ten precepts.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The combination for renunciation: four or more strong planets in one sign, the strongest deciding the order the native enters (BJ 15.1; BPHS 79.1–5).

literal: yogin whose wheel is in motion

definitions.definition: A practitioner in whom the wheel of practice has begun to turn (YDS).
Vedic action done with desire, bringing prosperity and equality with the gods (MDh 12.88–90); the natural activity of beings (MDh 5.56).
The undertaking of action by speech, mind and body (NS 1.1.17), good or bad (NBh 1.1.2).
The seven consciousnesses that arise from the ālaya like waves.

Rites and penances removing the stain of sin — needed by one who omits the enjoined, does the forbidden or is attached to objects (MDh 11.44); by confession, remorse, austerity, recitation and gifts (MDh 11.227).
The rite that removes sin; the Purāṇas hold the name or remembrance of the Lord to be the best expiation.
Nine (Śvetāmbara ten) forms of correcting a fault, from confession to re-initiation (TS 9.22).
Expiatory rite for faults in ritual or conduct.
Rites enjoined on the occasion of a fault or failure in performance; treated in Mīmāṃsā as occasional acts (e.g. MS 6.4).
Rites that make good lapses in ritual and observance.
Expiation for deliberate offences after surrender, which the Vaṭakalai require (or a renewed surrender) and the Teṅkalai do not regard as needed for salvation.
A mark and special quality of the self; eternal in the Lord (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Effort: Rāmdās's watchword, to be joined with devotion in both worldly and spiritual life.
The principal injunction, united with the subsidiary injunctions, that conveys the prompt, uninterrupted performance of the whole rite in a fixed sequence.
The aim with regard to which one acts (NS 1.1.24).
Love for Kṛṣṇa: bhāva grown dense, melting the heart completely and marked by intense possessiveness toward him; the supreme goal, desiring only his pleasure (as opposed to kāma).
Love for the Lord, indescribable, 'like a mute's tasting', free of guṇas and desire, ever-increasing, unbroken, subtlest, of the nature of experience (NBS 51–54).
Love of the Lord — 'the two and a half letters of prem' worth more than all books; its lane is too narrow for two.
Selfless divine love, the goal of the siddha stage, refined out of kāma.
Prem: the love-practice (prem-sādhanā) of the one who has died while alive.
The newly dead before being joined with the ancestors; one whose rites are lacking (e.g. no vṛṣotsarga) or who did great wrong remains a preta, hungry and thirsty, troubling kin.
The newly dead, not yet united with the ancestors, sustained by the first-year offerings until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.

literal: one who has gone forth; the departed

cross_language.note: hungry ghosts in Buddhist cosmology (U36)

definitions.definition: Living unwashed, unshaven and ungroomed like a poor madman (the 'preta' of the sūtra being a living man), so that caste and āśrama marks are cut off.
Arising again (NS 1.1.19); established by the eternity of the self (NS 4.1.10).
The pleasant: chosen by the fool for the sake of getting and keeping (KU 1.2.2).
Happiness; what the word 'svarga' denotes (Śabara on MS 6.1.2); what is for the person is that which gives delight (MS 4.1.2).
Fasting and spending the eighth and fourteenth days of the fortnight in religious practice as a temporary ascetic (TS 7.21); Śvetāmbara pauṣadha.
The unawakened who seize on self and on composites; 'foolish common people' are taught as no people.
The state of an ordinary person: non-possession of the noble dharmas.
The series in which the noble dharmas have not arisen.

equivalents.note: The state of an ordinary person vs the ordinary person.

definitions.definition: Cause of the usage 'separate'; in all substances.
The first pure meditation: scripture-based contemplation shifting among aspects, words and activities of a substance (TS 9.39–44).
Substance possessing smell (with colour, taste, touch); eternal as atoms, non-eternal as products; our bodies are earthy.
The Earth, mother of men (AVŚ 12.1.12), upheld by truth, order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice (12.1.1), to whom the dead are returned (RV 10.18.10).

literal: doctrine that all is due to past deeds

definitions.definition: One of the three sectarian tenets; ascribed to the Nigaṇṭhas in MN 101.
Recollecting one's many past births with their details (DN 2; MN 4); the first true knowledge.
Direct knowledge recollecting former existences; its range differs among sectarians, disciples, paccekabuddhas and Buddhas.
The person: real, neither the same as the aggregates nor different from them, designated in dependence on the present appropriated aggregates as fire on fuel; the fifth, inexpressible knowable.
A mere designation over the series of aggregates; there is no self (AK 3.18).
Not known as a real and ultimate fact (Kathāvatthu 1.1).

The only substance with form: atoms and aggregates having touch, taste, smell and colour, taking the forms of sound, darkness, light and bodies; karma itself is a subtle kind of matter (TS 5.5, 5.23–28, 8.2).

cross_language.note: Pali puggala means 'person' — a different sense

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The conventional person: 'the bearer of the burden is the person' (SN 22.22); the seven and eight noble persons (MN 70); in the ultimate sense not found (Mil 3.1.1).
A person: a conventional designation (paññatti), not an ultimate reality; the Puggalapaññatti classifies persons, and the Kathāvatthu refutes the view that the person is a real and ultimate fact.
Worship of Śiva with mantras, twofold: for oneself (in the liṅga received at initiation) and for others (in temples, for king and realm), preceded by the five purifications.
Ijyā, worship of Bhagavān, the third of the five daily periods.
Arcana of Viṣṇu in a consecrated image with Vedic mantras; the best of the means.
The daily sequence of temple pūjās performed by the śānti under the tantri's authority.
Not with flowers but the firm mind fixed on the great void (VBT 147); the liberated worships Bhairava with the substances of self-awareness (Paramārthasāra 75).
Refusing meat (Kuṟaḷ ch. 26): better than a thousand sacrifices.
Taught in the Tirumantiram's first tantra.
Refusing flesh: Paṭṭiṉattār asks what flesh-eaters will do when Yama seizes them (Tiruvēkampamālai 33).
Dying again in the other world; the Brāhmaṇas promise its conquest ('apa punarmṛtyuṃ jayati') to those who know or perform certain rites — the fire-altar, the Nāciketa fire (ŚB 10.4.3; TB 3.11.8).
Lunar mansion punarvasu: presiding deity Aditi (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Jupiter (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class movable (cara) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
(As reported) Pūraṇa denies it: giving, self-control and truthfulness bring no merit.
Auspicious karma — pleasant feeling and auspicious lifespan, body-making and status (TS 8.25); in the ultimate view merit too is a fetter, 'a golden chain' (Kundakunda).
Inhalation (HYP 2.71).
Inhalation; inwardly, 'I am Brahman' or scriptural knowledge.
Arthavāda narrating what was done or said in former times.
The 'exterior' genre of Tamil poetry — heroism, kingship, praise; the Āḻvārs turn its praise-forms to the Lord's deeds.
A class of sacred narrative lore, called with itihāsa the 'fifth Veda'; remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas and condensed by Vyāsa in every Dvāpara age into eighteen Purāṇas of four lakh verses.

The preliminary 'going before': a course of a fixed number of repetitions of a mantra (commonly counted by its syllables), with fire offering, libations, sprinkling and feeding brāhmaṇas in fixed proportions, by which the mantra is mastered before use.
The ancient Śaiva saints, above all the Tamil Nāyaṉmārs, whose lives Vīraśaiva hagiography narrates as models for the śaraṇas.
The waste of food: gives support and holds wind and fire (Su Sū 15.5).
(As reported) One of the eight 'stages of a person' in Makkhali's lists; Buddhaghosa glosses them as stages of life from the newborn onward.
(As reported) Denied by Makkhali: there is no doing by self or other, no human effort, strength or vigour.
(Prakrit purisakkāra-parakkama) Affirmed by Mahāvīra against Saddālaputta; one of the five co-causes.
Doing by oneself and by others exists, as the element of initiative shows.
The region into which the mind enters in deep sleep, where, lacking contact with the skin-sense, it produces no cognition (commentarial tradition on the Muktāvalī).

Full, complete: 'that is full, this is full; from the full the full arises; taking the full from the full, the full remains' (BAU 5.1.1); the space within the heart is full and unchanging (ChU 3.12.9).
The full Kaula consecration; those consecrated by it are Śaiva avadhūtas (Mahānirvāṇa 14.144).
The 'full consecration' of later Śrīvidyā manuals, conferring the full authority of the tradition after the preliminary initiations.
The 'form' (rūpa) level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where Satī's shoulders and neck fell; the goddess there is Pūrṇeśvarī (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.43, 18.49).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: The knowledge 'I am Śiva, I am the guru, I am the whole world' (SSM 14.38–41).
The perfect I-awareness whose essence is light and bliss, the potency of the great mantra (PH 20).

notes: Shared vocabulary with Pratyabhijñā (see brw:pratyabhijna-to-virasaiva).

definitions.definition: The reckoning of the lunar month as ending at full moon (usual in the north).

The conscious principle: neither producer nor product (SK 3); the opposite of the manifest and the unmanifest in being without guṇas, discriminating, subject, individual and conscious (SK 11); witness, isolated, neutral, seer and non-agent (SK 19); many (SK 18). Its existence is proved because aggregates are for another, etc. (SK 17). It is not truly bound or released (SK 62).

The cosmic Person, thousand-headed, who is all this, of whom one quarter is all beings and three quarters the immortal in heaven, and from whose sacrifice the world, Vedas and varṇas came (RV 10.90); the person in whom the gods dwell 'as cows in a stall' (AVŚ 11.8.32).
The seer, pure consciousness, unchanging, not self-luminous objects' owner but always knowing the mind's activities (4.18); utterly unmixed with sattva (3.35); many (2.22).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the conjunction of mind, self and body, subject-matter of Āyurveda (Ca Sū 1.47); the six dhātus (five elements and consciousness), consciousness alone, or the aggregate of twenty-four (Śā 1.16-17); 'the measure of the world' (Śā 5.3); in Suśruta the union of the five elements and the embodied one (Su Sū 1.22).

The person: the self-born person at creation (BAU 1.4.1; AU 1.1.3); the inner person in the eye or heart; in KU 1.3.11 the highest principle beyond the unmanifest; in MuU 2.1.2 the divine formless person; in ŚU 3.8-15 the great person of the Puruṣa Sūkta.

The beginningless principle that experiences pleasure and pain, seated in prakṛti and bound by attachment to the guṇas (BhG 13.19–21); the perishable and imperishable puruṣas are surpassed by the highest (15.16–18); in the Mokṣadharma the twenty-fifth principle, many according to the Sāṃkhya-Yoga thinkers, one in source according to the Nārāyaṇīya's close (12.338).
The cosmic Person with sixteen parts, source of the avatāras (BhP 1.3.1); spirit as one of the four forms of Viṣṇu (VP 1.2).
The Person with whom the sacrifice is identical (ŚB 1.3.2.1); Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa who surpassed all beings by the human sacrifice (ŚB 13.6.1.1).
The supreme Person, ruler of all, subtler than the subtle, called by many names (MDh 12.122–123).
The person, beginningless, beyond prakṛti, not touched by its qualities, like the sun reflected in water.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

equivalents.note: Both name the conscious self; Sāṃkhya's puruṣa is plural, inactive and without properties, whereas Advaita's ātman is one (with Brahman) and Nyāya's ātman bears qualities.

notes: Other lineages (e.g. Sāṃkhya) contribute very different definitions under this term; no equivalence is asserted here.

definitions.definition: Twelfth tattva: consciousness bound by māyā and the five kañcukas; the limited individual subject.
Īśvara's definition: a puruṣa distinguished from others by never having been touched by bondage (1.24, YBh 1.24).
What is done here in this life, which can overcome a weak daiva (Ca Vi 3.30-33).
Human effort, without which fate does not succeed (MBh 13.6.7); defended by Draupadī (3.28–33).
Śrī's role of intercession: she turns the soul toward the Lord and moves the Lord to forgive and receive it.

In jyotiṣa, human effort: with fate it brings success, as effort and rain together bring a harvest (Yogayātrā 1.3–4); fate is human effort of a former body (YājñSm 1.349); a well-timed undertaking succeeds even with slight effort (BS 103.60).
Mediation of Śrī (and, for the Tiruppāvai's commentators, of Nappiṉṉai): Nammāḻvār surrenders naming 'the lady who says she cannot part from him' (TVM 6.10.10).
Human effort, affirmed by Mahāvīra against Gośāla's fatalism in the argument of the potter's pots.
Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, on all of which the epic claims to contain everything (MBh 1.56.33); for Prahlāda 'puruṣārtha' as human effort is denied as a cause (12.215.15).

The purpose — experience and liberation — for which the instruments act (SK 31, 36), the liṅga plays its parts (SK 42) and prakṛti creates (SK 56); the supreme puruṣārtha is the complete cessation of the threefold suffering (SS 1.1).
The aims of human life — dharma, artha, kāma, and (as the fourth) mokṣa; Manu's settled view is that the good is the triad (MDh 2.224).
Of the three, artha is foremost since the others are rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).
The three are to be pursued in their proper ages without harming each other; each earlier is weightier (Kāmasūtra 1.2.1–14).

literal: for the sake of the person

definitions.definition: That which gives delight to a person, the desire for it being inseparable from it (MS 4.1.2); acts done for it are for the person, not for the rite.

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from the 'four aims of life' sense of puruṣārtha.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu, beyond both the perishable (souls) and the imperishable (Lakṣmī).
The Lord, beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable, who enters and sustains the three worlds (BhG 15.16–18).
Nārāyaṇa, reached by the ekāntins; those on the 'fourth path' go to him (MBh 12.336.3).
The Lord as distinct from and higher than both the bound (kṣara) and the freed (akṣara) souls (Gītā 15.16–18).
The highest person, Kṛṣṇa, above Akṣara Brahman; the goal of grace-devotion.
One of the fourteen 'former' texts, said to have been taught before the Aṅgas and contained in the Dṛṣṭivāda; known in full last by the śrutakevalin Bhadrabāhu and then gradually lost.
Portions of the second and fifth Pūrvas survive as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

Lunar mansion pūrva-bhādrapadā: presiding deity Aja Ekapād (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Jupiter (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Proṣṭhapadā.

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: The 'prior' Kaula view presented in Lakṣmīdhara's commentary on SL 34, on the Goddess as Śiva's body and the shared relation of principal and subsidiary.
Lunar mansion pūrva-phalgunī: presiding deity Bhaga (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Venus (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
The Eastern transmission; in the Kashmir–Nepal scheme usually the Kula/Trika worship of Kuleśvarī and Kuleśvara (moderate confidence).
The first, provisional answer to the doubt, stated in its strongest form before being set aside.
The preliminaries of a performance — songs, instrumental pieces and the benediction (nāndī) — offered to please the gods (NŚ 5).
The unmanifest sign of an impending disease (Mādhava Nidāna 1.5-6).
Lunar mansion pūrvāṣāḍhā: presiding deity the Waters (āpas) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Venus (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
The preliminaries to yoga: worship of teachers and gods, good conduct, austerity and non-aversion to liberation (Yogabindu).
Inference whose object's class has been seen before (e.g., fire from smoke); with śeṣavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa one of the three kinds (commentaries on SK 5).
One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.
The subtle body arising from the subtle elements and consisting of mind, ego and intellect, which confines the individual (SK 3.17).
The guide on the paths who leads the dead to the fathers (RV 10.17.3–6).
Honoring a written sūtra with flowers, incense, garlands and banners, held to exceed the worship of relics.
Grace, the Lord's nourishment (poṣaṇa) of the soul (BhP 2.10.4); the path in which grace alone, independent of means, gives loving service.
Lunar mansion puṣya: presiding deity Bṛhaspati (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Saturn (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class swift (kṣipra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Tiṣya.

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: Calcination in a pit-fire of measured cakes of dung; the basic process of mineral pharmacy.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: The uninstructed ordinary person who perceives and conceives (MN 1) and feels two darts (SN 36.6).
An ordinary person who has not reached a path.
An initiate who has received nirvāṇa-dīkṣā and seeks liberation.
Mercury, the central substance of Siddha alchemy and of the mineral medicines; recorded as a term only.

notes: Restricted subject (mercury): no preparations recorded.

definitions.definition: The true name of the supreme being and of the highest region, revealed by Soamiji; glossed in the Agra literature as Rādhā (the soul/current) and Soamī (the Lord).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Gone from the sage of steady mind (2.56); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); set with dveṣa in each sense towards its object, a waylayer (3.34).
The tāmasa opposite of dispassion; from passion of the nature of rajas comes saṃsāra (SK 45); meditation is its removal (SS 3.30); it is not quieted by enjoyment (SS 4.27).
Attachment, which follows on pleasure (2.7).
Lust, one of the three fires (SN 35.28); its destruction is part of nibbāna (SN 38.1).
Attachment to the agreeable, arising from false knowledge (NBh 1.1.2); one of the three groups of faults.
Arises from pleasure, absorption, satisfaction, the unseen and particular birth (VS 6.2.12–16 C).
Passion in which even sorrow becomes happiness for the beloved's sake.
Attachment and aversion, the 'seeds of karma' (Uttarādhyayana 32.7); in the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa, pejja and dosa, under which the four passions are classed.

cross_language.note: Kaṣāyapāhuḍa usage

definitions.definition: Kañcuka: attachment, the sense of lacking something.
A melodic entity: that particular sound adorned with notes and melodic movement which colours the minds of people (Bṛhaddeśī 280–281).

notes: Disambiguated from trm:raga (attachment, passion).

definitions.definition: Devotion that follows the rāgātmikā devotion of the Vraja residents, arising from eager longing (lobha); of two kinds, kāmānugā and sambandhānugā.
Devotion consisting of rāga — spontaneous, intense absorption in the beloved — natural to the eternal residents of Vraja.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The ancient yoga now told to Arjuna is 'the highest secret' (4.3).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The three mantras of the Śrīvaiṣṇava: the tirumantra (aṣṭākṣara), the dvaya and the carama-śloka (Gītā 18.66).
The 'secret sacrifice': the Goddess is worshipped by its sequence and pleased by secret libations (LSN 83). (Interpretations differ; summary only.)

The ascending node counted as a planet: in the epic the asura whose severed head, made immortal by the nectar, swallows sun and moon (MBh 1.17); in the siddhāntas the node (pāta) that deflects the moon (SS 2.6); for Varāhamihira not the cause of eclipses but present at them by Brahmā's boon to receive the offerings (BS 5.13–15); the Boar is born from him (BPHS 2.6); period 18 years.
A daily period of about an eighth of the daytime, falling at a different part of the day for each weekday, avoided for new undertakings (mainly South Indian practice).

notes: Classical textual basis not located; recorded as current practice.

definitions.definition: The goal served by haṭha: samādhi, the mindless, supportless state in which mind and breath are dissolved; HYP 4.3–4 lists it first among the synonyms of samādhi (with unmanī, manonmanī, amanaska, sahaja, turyā…). The DYŚ calls it the best of the four yogas, the Śiva Saṃhitā 'free of duality'; the Jyotsnā identifies it with asamprajñāta yoga, the cessation of all mental activity.
The royal yoga, the goal to which haṭha leads; synonymous with samādhi, unmanī, sahaja and the rest (HYP 4.3–4).
The fourth of the four yogas; in the Yogaśikhā the union of rajas and retas.

equivalents.standpoint: the haṭha texts' list of synonyms
equivalents.note: HYP 4.3–4 and GS 7.17 treat rājayoga and samādhi as names of one state

definitions.definition: The front teeth, at whose root the tongue is pressed in some forms of padmāsana and mahābandha (HYP 1.46, 3.22; GŚ 64; ŚS 3.73).
The duties of the king, taught by Bhīṣma in the Śāntiparvan (12.1–128) and by Rāma to Bharata (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).
'Sovereign of the king of kings': Lalitā as supreme empress, the form worshipped in South Indian Śrīvidyā temples.

literal: queen of the king of kings

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The royal sages who knew the yoga received through succession (4.2).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
A region of space, especially the atmosphere; 'there was no rajas' before creation (RV 10.129.1); the six rajāṃsi propped apart (1.164.6).
The guṇa of passion, arising from thirst and attachment, binding by attachment to action (BhG 14.7); desire and anger are born of it (3.37).
The guṇa that is stimulating and mobile (SK 13), of the nature of pain (SK 12); predominant in the middle world (SK 54); suffering is a modification of rajas (Vācaspati).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): with tamas one of the two doṣas of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21); the rājasa mind is faulty, having the part of anger (Śā 4.36); rajas and tamas bind the person to the wheel of births (Śā 1.36, 1.68); their absence is a condition of liberation (Śā 1.142).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The yogin to whom supreme happiness comes has his rajas stilled (śānta-rajas) (6.27).
The guṇa characterized as attraction and aversion; those in it go to the human state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The later guṇa sense is contributed by other units.

definitions.definition: The female generative fluid, counterpart of bindu, retained by the yoginī in the vajrolī passage (HYP 3.99–102) and identified with Śakti (SS 1.92). Not the guṇa rajas.
The royal knowledge and royal secret of ch. 9, supreme purifier, directly perceived and easy to practise (BhG 9.1–2).
A combination making the native a king or like one — by exalted planets (BJ 11), or by the relation of angle- and trine-lords (BPHS 39); distinct from rājayoga as a path of meditation.
The rope–snake: stock illustration of superimposition, sublation and substratum.
The woollen whisk ('dust-remover', ogho) with which Śvetāmbara mendicants gently sweep insects from their path and seat; the chief sign of initiation.
The eight passions among the ninety-six principles — desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, haughtiness and egoism (list recalled at low confidence).
Demonic beings who harm the rite and cause disease, driven off by Agni and the healer (RV 10.97.6).
The second tissue: gives clarity of complexion, nourishes flesh and sustains life (Su Sū 15.5); counted with the doṣas by Suśruta (Sū 21.3-4).
Bloodletting, counted by the surgical school among the purificatory therapies. Summary only.
Charm, the quality of colouring the mind with delight, lacking in the unstruck nāda and present in music (ŚR 1.2.166); cognate with rāga.
The Sants' most common name for the formless Lord who 'pervades every body' (ghaṭ ghaṭ rām) — explicitly distinguished from Rāma son of Daśaratha.
Rām as the nirguṇa object of remembrance of the 'lovers of Rām'.

cross_language.note: the Sanskrit name primarily denotes the avatāra

definitions.definition: The Vārkarī mantra, given to Tukārām in his dream-initiation and chanted by all Vārkarīs.
The name 'Rāma', greater than both the formless and the embodied Brahman, mediating between them, the one support in the Kali age and the ferrying mantra Śiva gives the dying at Kāśī.

equivalents.note: the Rāma name is one of the forms the tāraka mantra takes (Kāśī), not the whole of the tāraka doctrine

definitions.definition: Rāma's reign as the pattern of a righteous order, free of bodily, divine and elemental suffering, where all keep their dharma and love one another.
The six-syllable Rāma mantra (rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ) given at Rāmānandī initiation.

notes: Form of the initiation mantra as commonly reported; verify against Rāmānandī manuals.

definitions.definition: A verse form (caupāī stanzas closed by a sākhī) used for doctrine, especially cosmology, in the Bījak.
The pitta that colours rasa (into blood): in liver and spleen for Suśruta (Sū 21.10), in the stomach for Vāgbhaṭa (AHS Sū 12.13).

literal: sap; taste; essence; (in Rasa Śāstra) mercury

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) taste, the object of the tongue, sixfold — sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, astringent (Ca Sū 1.64-65; 26.9); (2) the first tissue (AHS Sū 1.13).
In Rasa Śāstra, mercury, 'the rasa of my body' (Rasārṇava 1.36); rasa as the means of crossing saṃsāra, identified with brahman ('raso vai saḥ', SDS Raseśvara 49).

Aesthetic relish: the stable emotion made relishable by the union of determinants, consequents and transient states, tasted by the sensitive spectator as food is tasted (NŚ 6 rasa-sūtra); eight in drama (NŚ 6.15), nine with śānta; 'twin of tasting Brahman' (SD 3.2).
The emotional flavour that notes, rāgas and dance are to evoke; the music treatises assign notes and rāgas to rasas.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The inner taste for sense-objects that remains when one abstains from them and turns away only on seeing the highest (2.59).
Quality grasped by the tongue; six tastes; in earth and water.
The essence of love tasted in the union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, located in the Sahajiyā body; the Sahajiyā reads Rūpa Gosvāmī's rasa theory as a guide to embodied practice.

notes: Homonym: in aesthetics and bhakti the relished sentiment.

definitions.definition: The first tissue, the essence of digested food: gives satisfaction and pleasure and nourishes blood (Su Sū 15.5).
Kṛṣṇa's circle dance with the gopīs on the autumn full-moon night (BhP 10.29-33).

literal: the play of the rāsa dance

definitions.definition: Mercury, which like the mind is by nature unsteady; 'bound' mercury and mind are compared in HYP 4.26–27 (an alchemical analogy; no procedure).
Abstaining from rich or savoury foods (ghee, milk, sweets, salt) (TS 9.19).
The eighteen processings of mercury required before it can be used; named in the SDS (Raseśvara 19-21) and detailed in the rasa texts. RESTRICTED: names and procedures not recorded.

notes: Homonym: saṃskāra as latent impression and as life-cycle rite.

definitions.definition: The seven obstacles to aesthetic relish listed by Abhinavagupta (lack of credibility, particularity of time and place, absorption in one's own feelings, lack of means, lack of clarity, non-predominance, doubt).
Semblance of rasa: an improper or incompatible mixture of rasas, or rasa in an unfit object.
A liṅga made of processed mercury, whose worship is praised above that of all other liṅgas (Rasārṇava 1.43; RRS 1.24, 6.19). RESTRICTED: its making is not recorded.
The hall for rasa work in a safe, righteous land, spacious and well provided with windows, with a secluded rasa-pavilion beside it (RRS 6.11-14).
The science of processing mercury and minerals for the body's stability, jīvanmukti and medicine; also rasavidyā, rasatantra (Rasārṇava 1.46; SDS Raseśvara 23).
Those who, without abandoning the body, have gained the body born of Hara and Gaurī, whose servants are the mantras (Rasahṛdaya 1.7); twenty-seven are listed in RRS 1.2-5.
Relishing: enjoying the bliss of savikalpa samādhi (or of the calm mind), which prevents going further.
Alchemy — the art (vātam) of transmuting metals and fixing mercury (iracam), in the Siddhar corpus both an outer art and a figure for perfecting the body. Summary only.

notes: 'vātam' also names the wind humour; the homonym is kept apart (see trm:vata). Restricted subject.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the branch and the means by which the healthy gain long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, lustre and strength — 'the means of obtaining the excellent rasa and other tissues' (Ca Ci 1.1.7-8; AHS Utt 39.1-2); taken by the hut-entering or the wind-and-sun mode (Ci 1.1.16); useless in an unpurified body (Su Ci 27.4; AHS Utt 39.4).
In Rasa Śāstra: rejuvenation by processed mercury and minerals (restricted), the fourth section of the Rasaratnākara 'for the aged' (Rasakhaṇḍa 1.5).
A sign: one of the twelve equal divisions of the zodiac beginning with Aries, each of nine asterism-quarters; the limbs of Kālapuruṣa; synonyms kṣetra, gṛha, ṛkṣa, bha, bhavana (BJ 1.4).

In the Jaimini system, aspect by signs: each sign aspects the sign facing it and those at its sides — movable signs the fixed (but the adjacent), fixed the movable (but the adjacent), dual signs one another (Jaimini 1.1.2–3; BPHS 8).
The empirical person, the aggregate of twenty-four, born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma, in which action, fruit, knowledge, pleasure and pain are established (Ca Śā 1.35-37, 1.53).
A devotee who contemplates the sweet, intimate love-play of Sītā and Rāma as a companion (sakhī).
A connoisseur of the pair's love (rasa) in Vṛndāvana; used of the Rādhāvallabha and Haridāsī poets.
As in the Rādhāvallabha usage: one who tastes the rasa of the nikuñja.
One of the two principal sāmans of the soma rite, forming part of the Vrātya's seat (AVŚ 15.3).
Love or attraction for Kṛṣṇa; the seed-form of the permanent emotion; in bhāva-bhakti it first appears.
Love-feeling (and, in coded usage, its bodily basis) that the practitioner must stabilize and raise into prema.
A gem: 'the fate that depends on gems is to be examined by experts', since good gems bring good to kings and bad ones harm (BS 79.1); later texts assign a gem to each planet to be worn as a remedy.
Right view, right knowledge and right conduct, which together are the path to liberation (TS 1.1); in the ultimate sense they are the self itself (YŚ 4.2; Yogaśataka 2).
The Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya saṃhitās, held to issue directly from the Lord's mouth; the Īśvara, Pārameśvara and Pādma are their explanatory expansions.

notes: Not the Buddhist or Jain 'three jewels' (different ids).

definitions.definition: Not eating at night, added as a sixth vow for mendicants and a basic rule for laity, since small beings cannot be seen in the dark.
Delighting in violence, falsehood, theft and guarding one's possessions (TS 9.35).
The Rudra-gāyatrī ('tatpuruṣāya vidmahe ...') muttered after impurity and as the chosen verse from which yoga proceeds.
Matter (wealth, substance): paired with breath as the first pair produced by Prajāpati; the moon, and all that has form or is formless (PrU 1.4-5); the southern course (1.9).
A metrical verse of praise, the unit of the Ṛgveda; the verses rest on the syllable in the highest heaven (RV 1.164.39); ṛc is speech (VS 36.1).
Magical power: in substance concentration; movement and creation; arising from cultivation, birth, spells, herbs or karma.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Exhalation, one of the three parts of breath-control (HYP 2.71).
Exhalation; inwardly, negation of the world or renunciation of objects.
Seed; desire was 'the first seed of mind' (RV 10.129.4); 'seed-placers' in 10.129.5.

Lunar mansion revatī: presiding deity Pūṣan (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Mercury (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class soft (mṛdu) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Its junction with Aśvinī is a gaṇḍānta.
A rite on the way to Paṇḍharpūr in which a horse (held to carry the saint unseen) runs in a circle round the assembled pilgrims.
Style, a special arrangement of words (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī); for Vāmana the soul of poetry (KAS 1.2.6).
A separate class of gods fit for the office of Brahmā (Vāyu is among them); only they can reach that office.
The standpoint that attends only to the present mode (TS 1.33); taken absolutely it becomes the Buddhist doctrine of momentariness.
A mantra whose division into feet depends on the sense (MS 2.1.35).
The debts with which one is born — to the seers, gods and ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5), and to men (ŚB 1.7.2.1).
The three debts to be paid before seeking liberation (MDh 6.35–37).
The three debts with which, according to scripture, a brāhmaṇa is born; urged as a bar to liberation and answered as figurative (NS 4.1.59–62; NBh).
Heaven and earth as a pair.

Lunar mansion rohiṇī: presiding deity Prajāpati (Brahmā) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord the Moon (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fixed (dhruva) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). The Moon's favourite wife in the Purāṇas.
The red (rising) sun praised as a creative supreme power in Atharvaveda book 13.
A seer of the hymns; 'a ṛṣi is so called from seeing' (Nirukta 2.11); the seers had direct perception of dharma (1.20); Vāc makes whom she loves a ṛṣi (RV 10.125.5).
One who 'saw' the hymns; Brahman the self-existent came upon them in their austerity (Nirukta 2.11); they had direct vision of dharma (Nirukta 1.20).
The seers are the breaths (ŚB 6.1.1.1; AA 2.2.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Seers whose impurities are destroyed, whose dualities are cut, who are self-restrained and devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain brahma-nirvāṇa (5.25).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A woman seer of Ṛgveda verses (e.g. Lopāmudrā, Ghoṣā, Apālā, Viśvavārā, Vāc Āmbhṛṇī), recorded in the Anukramaṇīs.
A yantra and hymn centred on 'hrīṃ' with the five supreme beings and twenty-four Jinas, worshipped for protection.

literal: what is fitting; the true course

definitions.definition: The true order that holds together the cosmos (the courses of sun, dawn, seasons and waters), the sacrifice and right conduct; guarded by Varuṇa and Mitra; born with satya from kindled tapas (RV 10.190.1); the twelve-spoked wheel of the year is 'the wheel of ṛta' (1.164.11).
The order of which food, in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, calls itself the firstborn (TB 2.8.8.1).
What is right, the order: spoken alongside truth (TU 1.1, 1.9); the right side of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); the knower is 'first-born of ṛta' (TU 3.10.6).

equivalents.note: The later tradition speaks of dharma where the Saṃhitās speak of ṛta and dharman (RV 1.164.50 calls the first sacrifices 'the first dharmas'); the scope differs (ṛta is also cosmic order).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan aṣ̌a/arta.
alt_notes: U02 adds only a Brāhmaṇa usage; the Saṃhitā concept belongs to U01.

definitions.definition: The insight arising in that clarity, which bears only truth (1.48), has the particular as its object unlike testimony and inference (1.49), and whose impression obstructs others (1.50).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the year has six seasons of two months each from Māgha — śiśira, vasanta, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemanta (AHS Sū 3.1; Ca Sū 6.4).
A season; spring, summer and autumn were ghee, fuel and oblation in the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.6).
Regimen by season: the six seasons in the 'taking' (ādāna) and 'releasing' (visarga) halves of the year, with diet and conduct to suit the strength and doṣas of each (Ca Sū 6; AHS Sū 3).
An officiating priest; the full soma rite has sixteen in four groups of four (hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahmán and their assistants).
Taste for practice itself — the sixth stage.
The fierce archer-god feared for his arrows and loved as the best physician, lord of cattle, 'auspicious' (śiva), praised in hundreds of forms in the Śatarudrīya.
The Lord of the Pāśupata Sūtra, near whom the liberated brahmin does not return and with whom he attains union; gods and ancestors are both in him.
Rudra: 'Rudra is one, they do not stand for a second' (ŚU 3.2); source of the gods, who saw Hiraṇyagarbha born (3.4); his auspicious form (3.5); in MaiU 5.2 the tamas-part of the one.
The third knot, pierced in niṣpatti, when the breath reaches Śiva's seat and flute and vīṇā sounds arise (HYP 4.76).

literal: division (of scripture) belonging to the Rudras

definitions.definition: The eighteen Siddhānta tantras from Vijaya to Vātula, revealed to eighteen Rudras; in Jayaratha's reading dominated by difference-and-non-difference.
The seed-beads born from Śiva's tears at the burning of the Triple City (SSM 7.47–48), one of the eight shields; wearing them frees brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike (7.62).
Bead from Kālāgnirudra's tears, worn with mantras.
The seed worn and used for japa by Śaivas, glorified in the Śiva Purāṇa (Vidyeśvara 25) and the Devī Bhāgavata.
The final and certain attainment of Rudra's proximity, from which no one returns.
The first aggregate: the four great elements and form derived from them (SN 12.2); also the visible object of the eye, and the fine-material sphere of the jhānas.
Matter: that which is 'molested' (ruppati) by cold, heat etc.; the third ultimate reality, twenty-eight kinds; as an object, the visible form.
Matter: the five sense faculties, five sense objects and unmanifest matter; what is subject to resistance and deterioration.
Quality grasped by sight alone; seven colours; in earth, water, fire.
The outward human form of man and woman, onto which the divine nature (svarūpa) is superimposed in practice.
The form realm: seventeen places in four dhyāna levels.
The Buddha's visible body with the thirty-two marks, by which the Tathāgata is not truly to be seen.
Lust for existence in the form realm; the sixth fetter.
Meditation on the Arhat's form in the assembly hall (YŚ 9).
Meditation on the formless, blissful Siddha (YŚ 10.1).
Consciousness of the fine-material sphere: the jhānas and their results and functionals (fifteen types).
A short aphoristic saying (from śabda, 'word') of Gorakh or another Nāth, the main form of the Gorakh Bānī.
Vernacular mantras, often ending in an oath by Gorakh or the Nāths, credited with power without the rules of Sanskrit mantras; the tradition ascribes them to Gorakhnāth.
'The all' is simply the twelve sense bases; one who would describe another all speaks beyond his domain (SN 35.23).
The Sabbatthivāda thesis that dhammas exist in the three times, refuted in the Kathāvatthu.

(1) The subtle element of sound and the quality of space (SK 22, 28). (2) The accomplishment of knowledge arising from hearing words of instruction (SK 51). (3) In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, verbal testimony = reliable instruction (SS 1.101); sound is not eternal and not sphoṭa (SS 5.57–58).
(1) Verbal testimony: the instruction of a reliable person (NS 1.1.7), of seen or unseen objects (NS 1.1.8). (2) Sound, the object of hearing and a non-eternal quality of ākāśa (NS 1.1.14, 2.2.13).
Sound: a quality of ākāśa, its mark, produced by conjunction, disjunction and sound, non-eternal (VS 2.1.24–27, 2.2.36–37 Candrānanda); verbal knowledge is inference (VS 9.19).
Verbal testimony is a statement produced by true knowledge of the meaning that causes its utterance (Tattvacintāmaṇi); sound is of two kinds, inarticulate and phonemic (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The word, defined in the Mahābhāṣya as that by which, when uttered, the understanding of the thing arises.
The Word: the guru's word that awakens the disciple, and the inner Word/sound by which the Lord is known; also the name of the song genre (śabda, pad).
Shabd, the audible life stream or sound current — the creative power of the Supreme, heard within and followed back to its source.

notes: Philosophical senses (śabda-brahman, testimony) belong to U31/U11/U12.

definitions.definition: Brahman as the Word: the Word-principle (śabdatattva) that appears as the world and permeates all cognition; its highest accessible level is paśyantī (VP 1.1, 1.123, 1.142).

The unmanifest sound arising from the dividing supreme bindu; not the word nor the meaning (both insentient) but the consciousness of all beings, which dwells in the body as kuṇḍalinī and becomes the letters (ŚT 1.11–14).
Word-brahman: of the two brahmans, sound and non-sound, one skilled in the word-brahman attains the highest (MaiU 6.22).

equivalents.note: duplicate id used by U19 for the same term; to be merged
the music treatises' nāda-brahman is described in the same words ('the consciousness of all beings') as the mantra manuals' śabda-brahman

definitions.definition: In Jainism sound is a mode of matter (TS 5.24), not eternal; linguistic sound is formed from the 'language-class' of matter.
The standpoint that distinguishes meaning by grammatical features such as tense, gender and number (TS 1.33).
Words are eternal; utterance only manifests them, and a word is recognized as the same in every utterance (MS 1.1.18–23).
Cognition of an unperceived object from words (śāstra); the Vedic word is independently valid; a human word only when the speaker is reliable and the matter within reach of other means.
Verbal testimony: the Veda, authorless and reproduced by Īśvara at each creation; the only means of knowing Brahman.
The refinement or purification of words through grammar, which is 'the attainment of the supreme self' (VP 1, verse number uncertain).
The cognition of a sentence-meaning produced by words, given expectancy, compatibility, proximity and known intention.
The unstruck sound in which one is immersed to reach the supreme Brahman (VBT 38).
The grammarians' absolute, refuted as final by Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 2).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Even one who merely wishes to know yoga passes beyond śabdabrahman (6.44); the chapter does not explain the term (commentators take it as the Veda).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A different verb, which marks a distinct rite (MS 2.2.1); first of the six means of distinguishing rites.
'Yoga preceded by the word': the path in which correct usage of words and knowledge of their nature lead to union with the Word-Brahman (Vṛtti on VP 1).
The totality of the letters, whose powers bind the unaware and grant perfection to the aware (SK 3.13-16).
The relation of word and meaning, eternal and not made by anyone (Kātyāyana's first vārttika; VP 1.23; 3.3 'fitness', yogyatā).

literal: the relation of word and meaning

definitions.definition: The principle (essence) of the Word: Bhartṛhari's name for Brahman, without beginning or end, which appears as things (VP 1.1).

literal: the word-principle / reality of the word

definitions.definition: The prompter's operation conducive to a person's engaging in action, expressed by the injunctive (liṅ) element; in the Veda it resides in the word itself.
Homogeneity: the real force of sameness by which beings belong to one class (nikāya-sabhāga).
The particular nature by which a dhamma is what it is (e.g. hardness for the earth element); dhammas are defined as bearing their own intrinsic nature.
The four samāpattis, which have an external thing as seed, are samādhi with seed (1.46, YBh 1.46).
Initiation after which the initiate must keep the observances (samaya), for those capable of them.
ŚiP 7.2.39.8-10: meditation resting on a form (with seed) and awareness of the formless self (without seed).
VP 6.7.40-42: prāṇāyāma is with a support (the gross form of the Lord as its object) or without.
Truth: the four noble truths; the seventh perfection (Bv 2); the preservation of truth (MN 95).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: A solemn declaration of truth by which a result is brought about — Aṅgulimāla's for a woman in labour (MN 86); the refrain of the Ratana Sutta.
The task regarding the third truth: cessation is to be realised (SN 56.11).
Being–consciousness–bliss: the three words indicate, by excluding their opposites, the one attributeless Brahman; they are not three attributes.
The 'true region', the fifth inner region reached by the soul on the sound current, where it meets the Sat Purush; beyond it Alakh, Agam and Anāmī.
Practices of the learned (śiṣṭa) done with no visible motive, accepted as indicating Vedic injunctions (MS 1.3.7).
Honest livelihood (kāyaka) and moral life, the fruit of which is shared (dāsōha).
The Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the entire Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇas of that character and whatever follows them.
'Oṃ namaḥ śivāya', in which Śiva who is both partless (revealed by Oṃ) and with parts (revealed by the five syllables) abides (SSM 8.17–22).
oṃ maṇipadme hūṃ, the heart of Avalokiteśvara, first taught in the Kāraṇḍavyūha.

cross_language.form: liuzi daming zhou 六字大明咒

definitions.definition: The six-limbed yoga of the Maitrī: breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, concentration, contemplative reasoning and absorption (MaiU 6.18).

notes: The Kālacakra six-branch yoga has the same name and a different list (other units).

definitions.definition: Name of the Trika scripture/tradition, placed at the top of the hierarchy of grace (TĀ 13.301).
Cat-acat: the soul's nature as neither the Real (Śiva) nor the unreal (the perishing world) but able to know and join both.

The Sāṃkhya Sūtra's account of error: what appears in error is both existent and non-existent, since it is sublated (as there) and not sublated (as real elsewhere) (SS 5.56), rejecting the rival accounts (5.52–55).
The five-faced form of Śiva (faces Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta) from whom all tantras issue; the 28 Siddhānta tantras are the limbs of his mantra-body.
Third tattva: will predominant; the inward 'nimeṣa' (ĪPK 3.1.3), 'I am this' with the 'I' prominent.
The sixfold strength of a planet — positional, directional, temporal, motional, natural and aspectual — computed to judge its power to give results (BPHS 27).
Confidence in the Tathāgata's awakening (SN 48.10), placed after examining a teacher (MN 95; MN 47); faith arises from suffering and leads to gladness (SN 12.23); the first faculty and power.
Confidence in the Triple Gem; beautiful universal; faculty and power; the wholesome counterpart of greed in the greedy temperament.

equivalents.note: same word; YS 1.20 lists śraddhā first among the five means

definitions.definition: Faith as a power unshaken by faithlessness (SN 50). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five powers.
One on the path to stream-entry who has faith and love for the Tathāgata (MN 70).
The true Dharma, twofold: scripture (āgama) and realization (adhigama), upheld by teachers and practitioners; at its last breath in a time of strong stains.
The final period ('last five hundred years') when the true dharma decays; the sūtras promise that some will still believe and keep them.

literal: the destruction of the true dharma

cross_language.form: fa miejin 法滅盡 / mofa 末法

definitions.definition: A trainee whose faith in the Tathāgata is settled (MN 70).
Faith in the Tathāgata's awakening (SN 48.10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five faculties.
Knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility and splendour, together constituting the supreme Brahman; knowledge is its very form, the other five its aspects; they are also Lakṣmī's body.

notes: Not the three guṇas of prakṛti; the AS calls Brahman 'nirguṇa' with respect to those.

definitions.definition: The self-realised teacher marked by self-knowledge, equal vision, action only from past karma, unique speech and scriptural mastery (Ātmasiddhi 10).
An initiate consecrated to master a mantra for supernatural powers and enjoyments (bubhukṣu).
In the Dāsbodh: The practitioner who takes up hearing, reflection and devotion under the guru.
The practitioner's stage, relying on bhāva.
The pitta in the heart that accomplishes desired aims through intellect, intelligence and self-regard (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.13-14).
Devotion as practice, performed with the senses, whose aim is the manifestation of the eternally perfect bhāva in the heart.
The four means: discrimination of eternal and non-eternal, dispassion toward enjoyments here and hereafter, the six virtues beginning with calm, and longing for liberation.
Discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues and longing for liberation.
The woman partner of the Sahajiyā (and Bāul) practitioner, regarded as Rādhā and often as the guru of the practice; recorded without details (restricted context).

Viveka (purity of food), vimoka (freedom from desire), abhyāsa (practice), kriyā (ritual duties), kalyāṇa (virtues), anavasāda (no dejection), anuddharṣa (no excessive elation) — the aids to meditation listed by the Vākyakāra.
