In Jainism twelvefold — six external (fasting, eating less, restricting alms, giving up tasty food, lonely seat, bodily mortification) and six internal (expiation, humility, service, study, abandonment, meditation) — which both stops and sheds karma (TS 9.3, 9.19–20).

cross_language.note: the Buddhist texts reassess tapas

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

equivalents.note: same word; Jain and Brahmanical traditions value tapas as purifying

definitions.definition: Suffering from oneself (body and mind), from other beings, and from divine/natural powers (VP 6.5.1-6).

The second Mahāvidyā; Akṣobhya is her Bhairava because he drank the poison without agitation (Toḍala 1.4-6); the Toḍala makes her the Fish avatāra; linked with Mahācīna and the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).

cross_language.note: the Buddhist saviour goddess Tārā; the Hindu tantras themselves place Tārā worship in Mahācīna with the Buddha

definitions.definition: Second view: like cow-dung fire; observance (niyama); no anxiety; desire to know (YDS).
Knowledge born of discrimination as arising from one's own intuition, not from instruction (3.54, YBh 3.54); also a name of intuition (YBh 3.33).
(1) The light between the brows and the yoga of targets that carries across saṃsāra; (2) the mantra Rudra gives the dying at Avimukta (Oṃ, the Rāma mantra or the Nārāyaṇa mantra).
What saves (carries across), which those confused by Āgamas, Vedas and logic do not know (HYP 4.40); in the Yoga Upaniṣads a form of rājayoga.
The Rāma name as the ferrying mantra Śiva gives those who die at Kāśī.
The beginningless, unalterable gradation of souls in nature, knowledge, bliss and office, from the lowest to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Lakṣmī above and Viṣṇu infinitely above; it continues in liberation.
Reasoned consideration of what fits, about a thing whose nature is unknown (NS 1.1.40); neither a means of knowledge nor included among them, but their helper (NBh 1.1.1).
Superimposition of the pervader through superimposing the pervaded ('if there were no fire there would be no smoke'); classed as a non-valid cognition that assists (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Reasoning: 'this understanding is not to be gained by reasoning' (KU 1.2.9); yet in MaiU 6.18 and 6.20 tarka is a limb of yoga, contemplative reasoning by which brahman is seen.
In Jain logic the knowledge of invariable concomitance (cintā, TS 1.13), an independent indirect pramāṇa.
In the Amṛtanāda's six limbs, reasoning not opposed to the āgamas.
Reasoning, unstable when unsupported by scripture: what is inferred by the skilled is refuted by the more skilled (VP 1.34).
The kapha in the head that nourishes the senses (AHS Sū 12.17).
Libation that satisfies the deity; the Goddess is 'gratified by libation into the bindu' (LSN 178) and 'by secret libations' (LSN 83).
The water-offering to the ancestors (and gods and seers), the daily sacrifice to the ancestors (MDh 3.70).
Being happy in his happiness — the mark that distinguishes the gopīs' love from a paramour's (NBS 24).
'You are that' (ChU 6.8.7): the teaching sentence whose word-meanings, purified by exclusive-non-exclusive implication, indicate the identity of the inner self and Brahman.

literal: defining mark standing on the bank

definitions.definition: Incidental definition: Brahman as the cause of the world's origin etc., pointing to it as the crow points out the house.
The marginal power: the souls, 'on the border' between the internal and external powers, able to turn to either.
The Buddha's term for himself and for the liberated one, who cannot be described as existing, not existing, both or neither after death, being deep like the ocean (MN 72; SN 22.86).
'One who has not gone anywhere and has not come from anywhere' (Vajracchedikā 29); a synonym of true suchness; he knows the world's suchness through the perfection of wisdom.
Epithet of the Buddha; the Kathāvatthu rejects views that he did not really live in the human world or that Buddhas stand in all directions.

literal: the one thus gone / thus come

definitions.definition: The ten powers of knowledge by which the Tathāgata roars the lion's roar (MN 12).
The buddha present in every being, covered by adventitious defilements — the dharmakāya not yet freed; empty of stains, not empty of qualities; what saṃsāra and nirvāṇa depend on.
In the Laṅkāvatāra, taught to remove the fear of no-self and meaning emptiness, not a tīrthika self; identified with the ālayavijñāna.

literal: embryo / womb / matrix of the Tathāgata

cross_language.form: de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po

definitions.definition: The way things really are, unaltered: the suchness of the Tathāgata and of all dharmas is one undivided suchness; 'Tathāgata' is a synonym of true suchness.
Suchness with stains (samalā tathatā) is the tathāgatagarbha, suchness without stains the dharmakāya; in the Awakening of Faith 'mind as suchness' is the one mind's unborn aspect.

cross_language.note: in SN 12.20 of dependent origination

definitions.definition: The intended import of a text, known by the marks (opening and close, repetition, novelty, result, praise, reasoning); the 'great purport' of all scripture is Viṣṇu's supremacy.
The speaker's intention, knowledge of which is a condition of verbal cognition (Tātparyavāda).

The intended sense of a passage, settled by the rules of interpretation; the determinants listed in Vedānta manuals as six marks (upakrama–upasaṃhāra, abhyāsa, apūrvatā, phala, arthavāda, upapatti) draw on Mīmāṃsā rules.
Purport: Dhanika and others hold that rasa and implied senses are conveyed by the purport of the sentence, making a separate power of suggestion unnecessary.
The six marks of a text's purport — opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise, demonstration — by which hearing determines that the Upaniṣads teach the non-dual Brahman.
Balance, keeping the associated states even; a beautiful universal, the factor that becomes the divine abiding of equanimity.
'Their happiness': the sakhī's joy lies only in the pair's joy, never in her own union.
Whatever is real, i.e. not superimposed (anāropita) and an object of valid knowledge; twofold, independent (Viṣṇu) and dependent (everything else).

Each of the twenty-five principles: mūlaprakṛti, mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra, manas, the five sense capacities, the five action capacities, the five subtle elements, the five gross elements, and puruṣa (SK 3, 22; SS 1.61). Knowledge of them liberates.
A principle of the Sāṃkhya enumeration: twenty-four together with prakṛti, the twenty-fifth beyond them (MBh 12.294.42); listed in the field of BhG 13.5.
The thirty-six principles, which are the waves and bubbles of Śiva as the ocean of consciousness (SSM 1.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Knowing the Lord's birth and action 'in truth' (tattvataḥ) frees from rebirth (4.9); the knower of reality (tattvavit) thinks 'I do nothing' (5.8); established in the happiness of yoga one does not waver from reality (6.21); truth-seeing knowers teach (4.34).
One of the seven (or nine) realities whose true understanding and acceptance is right view (TS 1.2, 1.4).
(1) Reality, to which the mind is joined and dissolves (HYP 4.59). (2) In the svara science, the five elements present in the flow of breath (Śiva Svarodaya).
One of the thirty-six levels of manifestation from Śiva to earth (Paramārthasāra 11; PH 7).
Tamil tattuvam: the principles of the embodied person, counted in the Siddha tradition as ninety-six; realization burns them away (Aḻukaṇṇi 36).
A principle or level of reality in the ascending scale of 36 from earth to Śiva; the lower 31 (or so) are products of māyā, the pure five of bindu.
Tattuvam: 36 tattvas (24 ātma, 7 vidyā, 5 śiva), elaborated to 96 in the Tamil lists.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The circle in which the participants realise 'all is Brahman' (Mahānirvāṇa 8.208).
(As reported) The principles are the four elements; Jayarāśi: the sūtra states them only to reflect worldly belief, and not even they stand examination.
The fifth concentration: seeing oneself as the pure, omniscient self, like a Siddha (YŚ 7).

The repeated contemplation of the principles from which the liberating knowledge arises (SK 64); described by Vācaspati as long, reverent, uninterrupted meditative cultivation after hearing and reasoning, and by the Sāṃkhya Sūtra as renouncing each with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

equivalents.note: Vācaspati's description of tattvābhyāsa (long, reverent, uninterrupted) echoes Yoga's definition of firm practice (YS 1.14); Sāṃkhya's practice has the principles as its content.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The seers of truth (tattvadarśibhiḥ) have seen the conclusion (anta) about the real and the unreal (2.16). (The knower of truth at 3.28 is called tattvavit: trm:tattvavid.)
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The knowers who see the truth and will teach knowledge to one who approaches with prostration, questioning and service (4.34).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the true nature of the categories — in the science of the self, of the self and the rest (NBh 1.1.1); it removes false knowledge (NS 1.1.2, 4.2.35) and arises from the practice of samādhi (NS 4.2.38).
Knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the categories, arising from dharma (Praśastapāda).
Knowledge of reality, which Abhinavagupta makes the stable emotion of śānta: it is the self itself (Abhinavabhāratī).
The presence of the memory of truth from which all the means of liberation proceed; 'the one path shown by the liberated' (Ca Śā 1.146-150).
The three real categories: cit (souls), acit (insentient matter) and Īśvara (the Lord).
The three realities: cit, acit and Īśvara, established by scripture (Daśaślokī 7).
The adherents' own name for Madhva's system: the doctrine that what is known through valid means is real (tattva = not superimposed), above all the reality of difference.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The knower of the truth about the division of guṇas and actions, who is not attached (3.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the yoked knower of reality (tattvavit) thinks 'I do nothing at all' (5.8).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Jayarāśi's thesis that no principle can be established, since no means of knowledge can be defined.
Austerity: bearing pain and not harming others (Kuṟaḷ ch. 27).
In the Isibhāsiyāiṃ's chapter of Maṅkhaliputta, the steadfast one who is not moved and does not turn into this or that state, and so saves himself and others from saṃsāra.
Substance with hot touch and colour; bodies of fire in Āditya's world; includes gold (mineral fire).

Heat, radiance: the first emanation of being, which produced water (ChU 6.2.3); its finest part is speech (6.5.4); in dying breath goes into heat (6.8.6); in deep sleep the mind is overcome by tejas (PrU 4.6).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) the fire element, the person's heat (Ca Śā 5.5); (2) 'essence' — ojas is the supreme tejas of the tissues (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); (3) listed with ojas, the fires and the prāṇas among what depends on the body's fire (Ca Ci 15.3).

notes: The grouping 'ojas, tejas and prāṇa' as a doctrinal triad is not found as such in the classical texts checked; Ca Ci 15.3 lists them among things dependent on agni.

definitions.definition: (Jain report) A destructive fiery power gained by severe austerity; Gosāla learnt its method from Mahāvīra and used it to burn two monks and against Mahāvīra.
A supernormal fiery power (labdhi) of ascetics; Mahāvīra's cool power (śītaleśyā) counters it.
The Śvetāmbara order founded by Ācārya Bhikṣu (1760); the name is explained as 'the path of thirteen' (after the first thirteen monks or laymen) or as 'your path, O Lord' (terā = 'yours').
Also the name of an unconnected 17th-c. Digambara reform (against the bhaṭṭārakas and fresh offerings), contrasted with the Bīsapantha.

Recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents, attained on the night of awakening (MN 4; MN 36) — the Buddhist re-definition of the brahmin's 'three Vedas' (DN 13; AN 3.58).
The third hindrance, fed by discontent, lethargy and sleepiness after meals and starved by arousal and exertion (SN 46.51; AN 7.61).
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.

Impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha) and not-self (anattā): 'all formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are not-self' (AN 3.136; Dhp 277–279); the term tilakkhaṇa itself is commentarial.
The first of Lakṣmī's five acts, the concealing power by which souls are bound.
Śiva's concealing power (rodha-śakti), called a bond by figure because it impels the bonds until the soul is ripe.
Tirōtāyi / tirōtam: fifth of the five malas; 'na' of the five letters.
Concealment, the fourth cosmic act, done as Īśvarī (LSN 64).
A holy place of pilgrimage and bathing; the virtues are inner tīrthas and the purest mind the supreme tīrtha; devotees are living tīrthas.
A sacred ford; Vidura calls the self a river with sacred fords whose water is truth, in which one is purified (MBh 5.40.19).
Pilgrim place; the Sants deny that bathing at tīrthas purifies — the true Gaṅgā is in a pure mind.
The pilgrimage is within: 'the original Mecca is in this human body'.
The Pāśupata teachers of the line from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara saluted daily; Jain doxographers list eighteen.
Variant of tīrthaṅkara, the ford-making Jina (used in the Digambara Tattvārthasūtra 6.24).

A 'ford-maker': an omniscient Jina who, after attaining kevala, teaches the dharma and founds the fourfold community (the 'ford' across saṃsāra); twenty-four appear in each half of the time-cycle, by the ripening of the tīrthaṅkara-nāma-karma bound in an earlier life.
The Śvetāmbaras include a woman, Mallī, among the Tīrthaṅkaras of this era.
All Tīrthaṅkaras are male; the Tīrthaṅkara does not eat after omniscience.
An omniscient who establishes the fourfold community and teaches the path in a given age; twenty-four in each half-cycle.

cross_language.note: variant form used e.g. in Tattvārthasūtra 6.24

equivalents.note: the same word in its variant form; the Pāśupata use of 'tīrthakara' for their own teachers is a different referent

definitions.definition: The auspicious body-making karma that makes a soul a founder of the teaching-ford, bound through sixteen causes (TS 6.24, 8.11).
Śrī — the Goddess inseparable from the Lord; also the prefix 'sacred' (tiru-) before names of places, works and parts of the Lord.
The Lord with Śrī (Tiru) — Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa as the Āḻvārs name him; supreme, dark-hued, bearing discus and conch, with Śrī on his chest.

literal: the great one with Śrī; the sacred dark one

equivalents.note: the Āḻvārs use Tirumāl and Nāraṇaṉ of the same Lord

definitions.definition: 'Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya', the eight-syllable root mantra, teaching the soul's exclusive belonging to the Lord and its prayer for service.
'Sacred word/speech': a sequence of hymns, usually in decads, as in Periya Tirumoḻi, Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi, Nācciyār Tirumoḻi; Tiruvāymoḻi is 'the sacred word of the mouth'.
The Lord's sacred feet — the Āḻvārs' constant object of refuge, service and contemplation ('his radiant feet that end sorrow', TVM 1.1.1).
All beings other than gods, hell-beings and humans — one-sensed beings, insects, animals (TS 4.27).
Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, three times (Khp 1); first used as ordination (Vin Mv 1.12).
The 'third eye' or eye centre behind and between the eyebrows, where the scattered attention is gathered by simran and the inner journey begins.

equivalents.note: Located at the brow like the ājñā cakra, but Sant Mat places it above the six lower cakras as the door out of the body.

definitions.definition: The lunar day: the time in which the moon gains 12° on the sun; thirty make a lunar month; each has a presiding deity and belongs to one of five classes (SS 1.13; MC 1.3–4).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to endure (titikṣasva) the impermanent sense-contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain (2.14).
Enduring the transient contacts that give pleasure and pain (BhG 2.14).
Forbearance: enduring heat and cold, pleasure and pain and all afflictions without retaliation or lament.
Title given in the Pali canon to each of the six famous teachers as founder of a religious 'ford'.
(Jain) tīrthaṅkara: a Jina who founds the fourfold community; Gosāla claimed to be the last of this age (as reported in Bhagavatī 15).
Siddha therapeutic massage and manipulation, practised in several kinds.
Worship with joined palms; adoration and bowing ('toḻutu eḻu', 'worship and rise', TVM 1.1.1).

equivalents.note: toḻutal includes the gesture and attitude of worship, not only prostration

definitions.definition: The ninety-six principles that make up the embodied person in the Siddha tradition (see cpt:ninety-six-tattvas).
Service to Śiva and his devotees; the Nāyaṉmārs are 'toṇṭar', servants.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The domain of the Vedas (traiguṇya-viṣayāḥ vedāḥ, 2.45).
The three guṇas taken together, of which prakṛti and the manifest consist (SK 14; Tattvasamāsa 4).
The domain of the three guṇas, which is the Vedas' domain; Arjuna is told to be free of it (BhG 2.45).
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ and Svar - the region dissolved in each occasional dissolution and within which the hells lie.
A soul with two to five senses, able to move of its own will (TS 2.12, 2.14).
The central vertical column of the universe, one rajju wide, outside which mobile beings do not live.
Gazing without blinking at a small target until tears fall; one of the six acts, and in the GS a way to śāmbhavī.
The three Vedas (Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman) as the knowledge of the śrauta rite; the Atharvaveda's place beside them was debated.
The second age, in which sacrifice (yajña) is the principal means.
One who has laid down the rods of speech, mind and body (MDh 12.10); outwardly, a renouncer carrying three staves.
Renouncer with the triple staff (Vaiṣṇava mark); inwardly, restraint of speech, body and mind.
The tenth, three-part mudrā of Śrīvidyā worship; the Goddess is 'lady of the trikhaṇḍā' (LSN 180).
The central downward triangle of the Śrīcakra, the eighth enclosure, seat of Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī and Bhagamālinī (in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the unmanifest, mahat and ahaṃkāra).
The 5th and 9th houses (with the 1st), the most auspicious houses; lords of angles and trines together make royal yogas (BPHS 39).
What the yogin sees in the stage of paricaya: the 'three peaks' of his karma (SS 3.61).
The second inner region ('three prominences'), seat of Brahm/the universal mind and source of the Veda, sounding like thunder or drum; the causal region.
In Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants, the meeting place between the brows (trikuṭī) where Gaṅgā, Yamunā and Sarasvatī meet.
The 'triple peak' between the brows where the three channels meet (Hindi Nāth and Sant usage).
The three aims (inner, outer, middle) of the yogī's attention (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The one Lord as Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva for creation, maintenance and destruction (VP 1.2.66); in Śākta Purāṇas the three receive their power from the Goddess.
Naturelessness of characteristic, of arising and ultimate naturelessness — the intent of 'all dharmas lack own-being'.

cross_language.form: ngo bo nyid med pa gsum

definitions.definition: The Lord's transcendent three quarters beyond māyā.
The three horizontal lines of ash on the forehead and body; the SSM's qualified guru is eager to wear it (6.1–6).
Three horizontal lines of ash, each with its correspondences.

The Goddess as she who is prior (purā) to every triad — abodes, principles, seats, liṅgas, letters — the fusion of light and self-awareness (Amṛtānanda on YH 1.6); she 'whose city is threefold' (triangle, circle and square; the three-part mantra) in Bhāskararāya's gloss.
She who existed before the three lights (Naṭanānanda's Cidvallī on Kāmakalāvilāsa 2).

literal: she of the three cities / prior to the three

definitions.definition: 'The beauty of the three cities': the Goddess of Śrīvidyā; as Mahātripurasundarī the queen of Mahākāmeśa (LSN 57).
As a Mahāvidyā, worshipped with the five-faced Śiva as her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.7-9) and matched with Paraśurāma (10.10); her full cult is Śrīvidyā (U23).

literal: beautiful one of the three cities

definitions.definition: The triad of knower, known and knowing, all manifested by every cognition, which is self-luminous (tripuṭī-pratyakṣa).
'True in three': the one for whom devotion alone is greatest (NBS 81); read as true in body, speech and mind, or in the three times.
The metre of four eleven-syllable lines, the commonest of the Ṛgveda.
A Vedic metre of 44 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
Āyurveda as knowledge of cause (hetu), sign (liṅga) and remedy (auṣadha), for the healthy and the sick; eternal (Ca Sū 1.24).
The imagined, dependent and perfected natures (the Saṃdhinirmocana's 'three characteristics').

cross_language.form: ngo bo nyid gsum / mtshan nyid gsum

definitions.definition: Dharma, artha and kāma, of which dharma is the root (MBh 18.5.49); each to be pursued at its time (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).
Dharma, artha and kāma taken together (MDh 2.224); later texts add mokṣa to make the caturvarga.
The confluence of the three channels (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā — Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī), which mahābandha brings about (HYP 3.24).
Making threefold: being made each of heat, water and food threefold (ChU 6.3.3-4); the later Vedānta name for the teaching (the text says 'trivṛt').

The vehicles of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas; for the Lotus and Śrīmālā a skillful means leading to the one vehicle, for the Saṃdhinirmocana and Laṅkāvatāra matched to fixed lineages of beings.
The third, 'beyond the highest' (parātpara) liṅga of the SSM's triad, after the gross iṣṭaliṅga and the subtle prāṇaliṅga.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): craving consisting of desire and aversion arises from pleasure and pain and is again their cause, grasping the seats of feeling (Ca Śā 1.134-135); the ignorant takes it from objects as the silkworm its deadly threads (Śā 1.96).
Thirst from which, with attachment, rajas arises (BhG 14.7).
Craving, the eighth limb of dependent origination: desire for pleasures and sexual union.

cross_language.note: cognate; defined in the Buddhist units

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The god (Rudra) of the verse 'we worship Tryambaka … may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12; TS 1.8.6; VS 3.60).
The 'three-eyed' Śiva of the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya verse (RV 7.59.12), whose mantra, with added seed-syllables, is repeated for protection from death and disease.

literal: triad; the mote in a sunbeam

definitions.definition: The product of (three) dyads, the smallest visible substance — the mote seen in a sunbeam (later manuals).

notes: The 'three dyads' formula is from later manuals (recalled).

definitions.definition: Wandering ascetic practice in forests and mountains, with alms-round, umbrella-tent (klot) and forest dwelling.
The wandering forest life of the kammaṭṭhāna monks.

The seventh sign (Libra), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the bladder (lower belly) of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by Venus; movable; of the air triplicity (later texts); odd, male and cruel (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: jūka (BJ 1.8); dignities: Saturn exalted (20°); Sun in fall (BJ 1.13).
The first great gift: gold (or other goods) equal to the donor's weight.
The necklace of tuḷsī (basil) beads put on at initiation into the Vārkarī way; its wearer (māḷkarī) vows vegetarianism, abstinence, the Ekādaśī fast and the name.
'Sleeping without sleeping': the yogic sleep of Śiva-yoga, in which the senses are withdrawn but awareness stays (Pattirakiriyār 1–2).

equivalents.note: both name a sleep-like state with awareness; texts and traditions differ

definitions.definition: Renunciation (Kuṟaḷ ch. 35): cutting 'I' and 'mine'.
Renunciation: Paṭṭiṉattār ranks the renouncer far above the giver and the renouncer-in-mind higher still (Tiruvēkampamālai 1).
Renunciation: in the Nālaṭiyār the wise one's giving up of attachment on seeing the body's impurity and the world's transience.
The form of Viṣṇu at the dvādaśānta, attained by the liberated and occasionally seen by the fully concentrated with direct vision; it gives the liberated their knowledge and activity.
The fourth quarter of speech, the only one humans speak; the other three are hidden (RV 1.164.45).
The fourth, the Lord in whom one abides beyond the intellect's states of waking, dream and sleep, of which the jīva is the witness.
The fourth: not a fourth state beside waking, dream and sleep but the self that pervades and transcends them, non-dual, peaceful, auspicious; the Lord able to end all sorrow (GK 1.10).
The fourth state beyond waking, dream and sleep; the Goddess is 'turyā' (LSN 63); in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the fourth state is the prostration of inner worship.
The fourth: beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; neither inward- nor outward-knowing, the stilling of the world, non-dual (MāU 7, 12, where the word is caturtha); turya in MaiU 6.19 and 7.11.
The fourth state beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; placed between the brows (Triśikhi) or at the head.

notes: The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's turīya (the fourth state) is contributed by U03; any link between the two is interpretive and not asserted here.

definitions.definition: (1) A fifth state beyond turīya, located at the brahmarandhra; (2) the name of the highest renouncer who lives like a cow, naked, the body as a corpse.
The state beyond the fourth, reached by firmness in the fourth; the Goddess is 'devoid of all states' (Bhāskararāya on LSN 63).
The fourth state, whose enjoyment arises amid the three (Śiva Sūtra 1.7) and which is to be poured like oil into them (3.20).
The fourth abode in which emission, maintenance, withdrawal and the three states shine without covering it (Paramārthasāra 34-35).
The fourth state, a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the place between the brows where mind dissolves and time does not exist (4.48).

equivalents.note: the Māṇḍūkya's fourth; the Kashmir Śaivas add turyātīta and require the fourth to pervade the three

definitions.definition: Seventh stage: with no difference perceived, abiding solely in one's own nature; the turya state of those liberated while living.
Seventh stage: no difference; one's own nature.

equivalents.note: the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha itself calls the seventh stage the turya state of the jīvanmukta (3.118.16); turyagā names the stage, turīya the state

literal: the one gone to the fourth

definitions.definition: The state beyond the fourth, the domain of those liberated without a body (videhamukta), lying beyond the seventh stage.
Turīyātītam: the fifth state beyond the fourth, in the Siddhānta account of the five avasthās.
The state beyond the fourth, in which the fourth pervades all states completely (Tantrāloka 10; Kṣemarāja).

Nine contentments (SK 50): four internal — resting content with nature, with outward means (such as the triple staff and water-pot), with time, or with luck — and five external, from abstaining from objects for seeing their faults; they do not bring liberation and, with error and incapacity, are the curb on accomplishment (SK 51).
The messenger poem: the love-sick heroine sends birds, clouds or the wind as messengers to the Lord.
The divine craftsman who shapes forms and grants long life (RV 10.18.6).

Relinquishing the fruit of all actions (BhG 18.2), threefold according to the guṇas (18.7–9); the embodied cannot give up all action, and so the one who gives up the fruit is the relinquisher (18.11); one of the 'three horses of Brahman' (MBh 11.7.19; 5.43.14).
The eighth virtue: giving up, including giving knowledge and other gifts (TS 9.6).
The soul at the stages of bhakta and māheśvara, in the vacana and manual scheme correlated with the gross body and the iṣṭaliṅga.
A renunciant Rāmānandī ascetic, as distinct from the householder and the rasik.
One who contacts the formless liberations with the body and has destroyed the effluents by wisdom (MN 70; DN 15).
One who touches the eight liberations with the body and whose taints are destroyed by wisdom.
The twofold character of Brahman in all scripture: opposition to all that is defiling and possession of infinite auspicious qualities.
The Sanskrit Upaniṣads and the Tamil Prabandham (above all the Tiruvāymoḻi) as one Vedānta of equal authority.
Exaltation: the sign and degree where a planet is most exalted — Sun Aries 10°, Moon Taurus 3°, Mars Capricorn 28°, Mercury Virgo 15°, Jupiter Cancer 5°, Venus Pisces 27°, Saturn Libra 20° (BJ 1.13).
The first āṇava support: the breath contemplated in its movement (MVT 2.21; TĀ 5).
The view that the self is annihilated at death (DN 1; SN 44.10).
(As reported) Ajita's doctrine that fool and wise alike are annihilated at the breaking of the body.
One of the extremes: seven grounds for asserting the annihilation of an existing being, from the four-element self to the self of the highest formless sphere.
The remainder of the sacrifice, praised as the ground in which name and form and all the world rest (AVŚ 11.7).
The familiar instance possessing the property to be proved, or its opposite (NS 1.1.36–37).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the throat.
The vital air that leads upward, operating up to the head; its mastery gives non-adherence to water, mud and thorns and departure at death at will (3.39, YBh 3.39).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu seated in the chest, moving in nose, navel and throat, governing speech, effort, energy, strength, complexion and memory (AHS Sū 12.5-6).
The up-breath, which through one channel leads upward at death — to a world of merit, of evil or of humans (PrU 3.7); identified with heat (PrU 3.9).
The breath in the throat (SS 3.7).
The breath in the throat.
The up-breath, named with the other breaths in some Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa lists (low confidence for particular Saṃhitā loci).

checks.note: Located in the Śaunaka AV: 'vyānodānau vāṅ manaḥ' (AVŚ 11.8.4, 26) — the low-confidence Saṃhitā locus now exists.

definitions.definition: A state of the afflictions (2.4): Operating on an object (YBh 2.4).
Puruṣa, indifferent, which appears as agent through conjunction (SK 20); on knowledge it is the indifferent onlooker (SK 66).
Indifference to what opposes the Lord: acting in the world and in the rites only as is favourable to him (NBS 9, 11).
The raised (high) accent.

literal: knowledge of contemplating rise and fall

definitions.definition: Insight seeing the arising and passing of formations; in its tender form beset by the imperfections.
Naming the things to be examined — the first activity of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
Restlessness as the ninth fetter and part of the fourth hindrance.
Agitation of mind; a universal unwholesome factor; a fetter abandoned only by arahantship.
The fourth hindrance, fed by unsettledness of mind and starved by peace of mind (SN 46.51).
A non-returner whose mind is not bound to sensual pleasures (Thig 1.12).
The abdominal lock by which prāṇa 'flies up' suṣumnā; best of the locks, giving liberation naturally when firm (HYP 3.55–60).
The abdominal lock between genitals and navel, 'the lion to the elephant of death' (GŚ 35).
The priest who sings the sāmans.
The central portion of a sāman, sung by the udgātṛ.
The loud chant of the Sāman singer, venerated as Om and as breath (ChU 1.1-1.12; BAU 1.3).
'The upsurge is Bhairava' (Śiva Sūtra 1.5).
The mental image of the object perceived as clearly with eyes closed as with eyes open, still showing the device's faults.
The fierce form of Tārā whose five-syllable mantra perfected Buddha and Vasiṣṭha (Tārā Tantra 1.3-4).
The accomplishment of reflecting on 'what is true, what is highest, what is the final good' until the difference of puruṣa and pradhāna is known (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).
The adaptation of a base melody to new verses in the order of the rites.
Adapting transferred mantras, chants and purificatory acts to the ectype, e.g. replacing 'to Agni' by 'to Sūrya' (adhyāya 9).
The secret (rahasya) song-book applying forest melodies to ritual verse-groups.
'Upstream': going against the current, the direction of Bāul practice, as the fish swims upstream.
The retention with breath drawn through both nostrils so that it sounds from throat to heart, held and released through the left.
The letter 'u', which in the Tirumūla ñāṉam is supreme consciousness (ciṟparam), paired with akāram.
(Jain report) Five kinds of denier — staff, rope, thief, partial and total — who cut off the doctrine of the soul, rebirth, compassion, or everything.

notes: Etymology uncertain (utkala / utkaṭa); the gloss 'one who cuts off' follows the chapter's own use of vocchedaṃ / chedaṃ vadati.

definitions.definition: Fate, the ordained outcome of former deeds (Kuṟaḷ ch. 38), mightier than any device.
Upside-down speech: paradoxical riddles (the well upside down in the sky, the woman enjoyed by two) used by the Nāths and after them by Kabīr to point to reversed practice.
'Upside-down speech': riddling songs of impossible images (the lion grazing cows, the son born before the mother) whose inversion points to the reversal of ordinary perception.

equivalents.note: Both are coded, paradoxical registers; the Sant form is a genre of songs, the Buddhist/Bāul form a language of double meanings.

definitions.definition: The seven degrees of inner exhilaration in the Kula rite — ārambha, taruṇa, yauvana, prauḍha, tadanta, unmanā, anavastha (Kulārṇava 8.4); the first five are 'waking', unmanā is 'dream', the equal state is 'deep sleep' (8.94-95). The Kulārṇava's chapters are also called ullāsas.
'Reverse practice': turning the downward, outward flow (of desire and bodily substance) back upward and inward; recorded here as a doctrine only (restricted).
The Sahajiyā reversal by which kāma is turned into prema.
Reversed practice: turning the downward flows (breath, bindu, nectar, mind) upward — the viparīta-karaṇa of the Sanskrit texts (GŚ 59).

equivalents.note: Both describe an upward reversal of the vital substance; the Bāul form is a couple's practice and is framed devotionally.

definitions.definition: The ascetic livelihood of gleaning grain left in the fields; the gleaner's gift outweighs a horse sacrifice (MBh 14.92–93) and a gleaning sage attains the highest (12.340–353).
Derangement of mind, fivefold (from each doṣa, all three, and exogenous); the exogenous kind is caused by prajñāparādha and treated by the divine therapies (Ca Ni 7.10-17).
The last and timeless phase in the pronunciation of the mantra's final sound, beyond samanā (Varivasyārahasya).
The sixth ullāsa, called 'dream' (Kulārṇava 8.94).
The final, 'beyond-mind' phase in the subtle utterance of Oṃ, where sound dissolves into the supreme.

equivalents.note: the haṭha unmanī is the mind-free state of samādhi; the Kaula unmanā is a named stage of ullāsa

definitions.definition: The state in which the mind is transcended; it cannot arise while the channels are impure (HYP 2.4); a synonym of samādhi (4.3); through it duality is not perceived (4.61) and the body becomes like a log (4.106).
The mind-less state beyond mind, in which one is not roused even by drums (KJN 14.83–85); a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.3).
The mind 'beyond mind' by which one is liberated here (KJN 13.5); the fourth mind beyond the guṇas (Jñānakārikā 2.8).
The state in which the mind has dissolved; 'unmanībhāva'; beyond merit and sin.
The 'no-mind' state beyond the mind, a Nāth term used by Kabīr for absorption in the Lord.

equivalents.note: listed as synonyms in HYP 4.3
listed as synonyms in HYP 4.3–4
Both name the mind-less state; amanaska is the later part of tāraka-yoga, unmanī the state reached by nāda.

definitions.definition: The state beyond mind described by Hemacandra from experience, reached by effortless indifference (YŚ 12).
The madman's guise the ascetic adopts, wandering alone so that people call him mad and foolish.
The opening-out of spanda: that from which a new thought arises in one absorbed in one thought (SK 3.9); with nimeṣa, the pulse of creation and dissolution (1.1).
Īśvara is the outward unmeṣa, Sadāśiva the inward nimeṣa (ĪPK 3.1.3).
Two modes of absorption: inward, eyes-closed absorption and outward absorption in which the world is seen as consciousness; 'again and again there is merging' (Śiva Sūtra 3.45, Kṣemarāja).

notes: Pairing of the two samādhis follows Kṣemarāja's commentaries (low confidence on details).

definitions.definition: A service offered to the deity; the Goddess is 'rich in sixty-four services' (LSN 58); the Kalpasūtra lists them (PKS 4.5); the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad interiorizes them.
Concentration in the neighbourhood of absorption, with the hindrances suppressed and the counterpart sign present.
The 'increasing' houses, 3rd, 6th, 10th and 11th, where malefics do good (BJ 1.15).
The twenty-four kinds of matter dependent on the great elements.
Four kinds: clinging to sensual pleasures, views, rules and observances, and a doctrine of self (SN 12.2; MN 11); also the 'fuel' by which a fire burns, used of the aggregates.
Clinging: to sense pleasures, views, rules and observances, and a doctrine of self.
The second daily period: gathering flowers and other materials for worship.
Grasping; as the ninth limb, running about to obtain pleasures; as defilement group, four kinds.
The material cause of the world: māyā (and bindu for the pure universe) — never Śiva.
The aggregates as affected by the effluents and subject to clinging (SN 22.48); in brief, they are suffering (SN 56.11) and identity (sakkāya) (MN 44).
Designation in dependence: the person is designated taking the aggregates as basis, as fire taking fuel.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The truth-seeing knowers 'will instruct' (upadekṣyanti) knowledge to one who approaches rightly (4.34).
In MS 1.1.5, the (Vedic) instruction that is the means of knowing dharma.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

literal: grasping; craving as the basis of suffering

definitions.definition: The supreme cause giving suffering and the seats of suffering; its total renunciation removes all suffering (Ca Śā 1.95).
A fault of disposition; the life-stages yield merit according to its absence (VS 6.2.3–5 C).

cross_language.note: Pali upadhi, 'substratum (of rebirth)'

definitions.definition: Secondary products of the tissues: from rasa breast-milk and menstrual blood, from blood tendons and vessels, from flesh muscle-fat and the six layers of skin, from fat ligaments and joints (Ca Ci 15.17).

notes: Ref from the local Devanāgarī e-text of Ca Ci 15; the term 'upadhātu' itself is the later commentarial name.

definitions.definition: What pervades the probandum without pervading the probans (e.g. contact with wet fuel when smoke is inferred from fire); its presence makes the reason unestablished as to pervasion.
Limiting adjunct: something that makes a thing appear with characteristics not its own without changing it (the red flower near the crystal; the pot delimiting space; body and mind for the self).
The Advaita notion that the soul is Brahman limited by adjuncts, refuted in the Upādhikhaṇḍana: ignorance cannot belong to the all-knower, and adjuncts cannot account for it.
A limiting adjunct — body, senses, intellect — that really delimits Brahman as the individual soul; real, not imagined, and removed only at liberation after death.
(As reported) A hidden extra condition that can never be ruled out, so no concomitance is certain.
The acquisitions (aggregates, sensual objects, defilements) on which suffering depends (Ud 3.10); their relinquishing is nibbāna.

notes: Advaita also uses upādhi but holds the adjuncts to be products of avidyā (not ultimately real); Bhāskara insists they are real — same word, different status.

definitions.definition: The monk who teaches the scriptures, fourth of the five supreme beings.
Preceptor: the senior monk (at least ten years ordained) who sponsors an ordination and under whom the new monk lives in dependence.
One who teaches a part of the Veda or its limbs for a living (MDh 2.141).
The supreme person in the body as witness (BhG 13.22).
The fourth portion of a five-part sāman, sung by the udgātṛ.

A subsidiary scripture attached to one of the 28 mūlāgamas; the Kāmika calls them upabheda ('sub-divisions') and lists 206 by the counts it gives (the usual traditional total is 207); the Kiraṇa says a division within the divisions is an upabheda.

Secondary points treated as minor planets — Dhūma, Vyatīpāta, Pariveṣa, Indracāpa and Upaketu computed from the sun, and Gulika/Māndi and others from the divisions of the day — whose placement is judged with the planets (BPHS 25).
The six-limbed offering: laughter, song, dance, the ḍuṇḍuṅ sound, prostration and muttering.
The sixteen defilements of mind (MN 7); the adventitious defilements of the luminous mind (AN 1.51); the imperfections of concentration (MN 128).
Secondary defilement: defiled mental factors other than the root defilements, including the envelopments and the six stains.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The beginning of a passage; its relative strength against the conclusion (upasaṃhāra) is argued by Appayya Dīkṣita in the Upakramaparākrama.
Establishing what is to be established through similarity to the well known (NS 1.1.6).
Yields knowledge of the name–named relation from cognition of similarity (the gavaya example).
Not a separate means; included in inference (Praśastapāda).
Similarity producing knowledge of an unperceived object: seeing a gavaya one cognizes the similarity in the remembered cow (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Comparison: knowing the similarity of a remembered thing to one now perceived (the cow is like the gavaya).
Whispered repetition, lips moving slightly, barely audible; a hundred times better.
Restating the subject as 'so' or 'not so' with reference to the example (NS 1.1.38).
Initiation of the student by the teacher (AVŚ 11.5.3, 'upanayamāna').
Initiation in which the boy gives himself to studentship and the teacher, 'becoming pregnant', brings him to birth with the Sāvitrī (ŚB 11.5.4).
The sacrament of initiation at 8, 11 or 12 years for the three classes — the second birth (MDh 2.36, 2.169; ĀpDh 1.1.1.9).
A 'subsidiary limb': one of twelve aṅga-external canonical texts, each paired with an Aṅga (Aupapātika with the Ācārāṅga, and so on).

The supporting condition in the series from suffering through faith, gladness, rapture, tranquillity, happiness, concentration, knowledge and vision, disenchantment and dispassion to liberation and the knowledge of destruction (SN 12.23).

Secret teaching, hidden connection or name: 'its upaniṣad is the real behind the real' (BAU 2.1.20); the upaniṣad of the asuras (ChU 8.8.4); 'we have told you the upaniṣad about brahman' (Kena 4.7); what is done with the upaniṣad is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10).
Knowledge of Brahman, so called because it loosens and destroys the seeds of saṃsāra and leads to Brahman; secondarily the texts.
Strong-dependence condition: earlier states, persons, climate, food and lodging as powerful supports for later states.
The ārūḍha of the twelfth house, judged for marriage and spouse in the Jaimini system (BPHS 30).
The birth of gods and hell-beings, arising in a birth-place without parents (TS 2.31, 2.34).
A lesser seat added to the lists of the major pīṭhas (Pīṭhanirṇaya and Bengali lists).
A Purāṇa outside the eighteen, said to have been told by sages or Vyāsa's disciples; the Kūrma lists eighteen; any Purāṇa taught apart from the eighteen has issued from them (Matsya 53.64).
The apparent coloring of puruṣa by buddhi's modifications, through which agency seems to belong to it (SS 1.164); not real coloring like the red flower's on a crystal but misidentification (SS 6.28).
Withdrawal: the mind's not leaning on external things (VC 23); defined by the Tattvabodha as performance of one's own dharma, and by others as renunciation of works.
The ascent (stages 8–11) by suppressing the deluding karma, from which the soul falls back.
Full ordination as bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī by a formal act of motion and three proclamations before a quorum (ten, or five in border lands).

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: Worship of Hari with the qualities appropriate to one's fitness — Brahmā with all qualities, humans as bliss, knower and the ever-existing Self.
The 'knowledge' the Upaniṣads enjoin for liberation: repeated, continuous meditation on Brahman, which, when it becomes loving and vivid, is bhakti.
Veneration, meditation: venerating X as brahman (ChU 7; BAU 4.1); 'one should venerate it as the self' (BAU 1.4.7); 'not this that people venerate here' (Kena 1.5).

Meditation/worship: sustained mental activity directed to a prescribed object (the qualified Brahman, a symbol), an act that can be enjoined; purifies and steadies the mind and leads to the Brahma-world.
Meditation on a thing as something else ('let one meditate on the Real as Brahman'), by which one becomes what one meditates on (ŚB 10.6.3).
The eleventh guṇasthāna: delusion wholly subsided but not destroyed — one falls back from here.
What the powers are within samādhi, because they oppose seeing (3.37, YBh 3.37).

Obstacle-powers that arise after the gross obstacles are overcome: in MkP longings for rewards and five states (prātibha, śrāvaṇa, daiva, bhrama, āvarta); in LiP/ŚiP six siddhis (pratibhā, śravaṇa, vārtā, darśana, āsvāda, vedanā).
An affliction inflicted by gods, humans or animals on a meditating ascetic, to be borne with equanimity; Mahāvīra's twelve years were full of them, and Pārśva's attacker was Kamaṭha.
The agreeable effect of medicine, food or conduct used contrary to the cause or the disease; it is sātmya (Mādhava Nidāna 1.8-9).
The three supports of the body — food, sleep and continence — by which, rightly used, it continues strong for its full span (Ca Sū 11.35); 'as a house by its pillars' (AHS Sū 7.52).
The one-day-and-night fast discipline in eight limbs taken by a lay person from another in the morning until the next sunrise.
Fasting as part of a vow.
The means to liberation; the five in Arthapañcaka are karma, jñāna, bhakti, prapatti and the teacher's regard.
The means to immersion: anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava; liberation is one whatever the means (TĀ 1.165-170).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Yoga can be attained through the proper means by one whose self is controlled and who strives (6.36).
Residence, observance, muttering-and-meditation, constant remembrance of Rudra, and grace.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The buddhas' and bodhisattvas' skill in adapting the teaching and their conduct to beings' capacities — teaching three vehicles for one, showing parinirvāṇa though the Buddha's life is immeasurable, living as a householder; joined with wisdom it keeps the bodhisattva from both saṃsāra and premature nirvāṇa.

cross_language.form: fangbian 方便 / shanqiao fangbian 善巧方便

equivalents.note: general Sanskrit 'means'; in Śaiva usage the four means (upāya) of practice

definitions.definition: Samādhi arising from means (faith etc.), that of yogins (1.20, YBh 1.19–20).
The defining mark of the soul: its activity of knowing and perceiving — eight kinds of knowledge-activity and four of perception-activity (TS 2.8–9).

Equanimity: the fourth brahmavihāra (abandoning aversion, MN 62), the seventh factor of awakening, the purity of the fourth jhāna; equanimity based on unity abandons that based on diversity (MN 137); the tenth perfection (Bv 2).

equivalents.note: same word; YS 1.33 lists it among the four attitudes

definitions.definition: Looking on with equanimity at the concentrated mind (MN 118). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.

Equanimity, disregard cultivated toward the non-virtuous, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Vyāsa: equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation and yields no strength (YBh 3.23).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: The goal: the Lord (with Śrī) himself and eternal service to him.

literal: goal, what is to be attained

definitions.definition: The heavens of the celestial-vehicle gods, rising to the Sarvārthasiddhi vehicle, above which is the abode of the liberated.
The Upper transmission, declared highest and the direct means to liberation (Kulārṇava 3.15-19).
The upright forehead mark of the Vaiṣṇava, made with gopīcandana clay; praised as purifying and required for rites to bear fruit.
Vaiṣṇava vertical mark of gopīcandana.
The vertical forehead mark of white clay with the central line (śrīcūrṇa) for Śrī; U-shaped among the Vaṭakalai, Y-shaped with a line down the nose among the Teṅkalai.
One whose seed flows upward — a sign of the nectar-filled yogī's body (GŚ 65; KJN 14.57).
One of the marks of a great man; the Buddha's ray from it lights up worlds before great teachings.

literal: the tuft (of hair) between the brows

definitions.definition: The melting of the heart in love — the 'wick' of Pūtattāḻvār's lamp and the state of the love-sick heroine.

notes: Cf. Madhusūdana's definition of bhakti as the mind melted (druta) by the Lord's qualities (tea:bhaktirasayana:1.3).

definitions.definition: The Dawn, ever returning while generations of mortals pass (RV 1.113.11).
Bodily heat, which with vitality and consciousness leaves the body at death (MN 43; SN 22.95).
The first root of penetration, with the four truths in sixteen aspects as object — the sign that the fire of the noble path is near.
The body (also uṭampu, kāyam, tēkam): for the Siddhars both a leaking pot of filth to be seen through (Aḻukaṇṇi 8; Paṭṭiṉattār) and the Lord's temple to be preserved and perfected (TM 724–725).
The knower's departure from the body through the crown channel, when the tip of the heart lights up, aided by the grace of Hari in the heart.
Departure from the body at death, undertaken at will by one who has mastered udāna (3.39, YBh 3.39).
The departure of the living being from the body at death; for the yogin a controlled departure through the crown.
The triple mark of every existent (TS 5.30): a thing persists as substance while its modes arise and pass away.

A portent: 'a change of nature' — produced by the gods' displeasure at men's misconduct, it announces coming calamity and is to be countered by pacification (BS 45.1–3); heavenly, atmospheric or earthly.

cross_language.note: among the low arts in DN 1.21

definitions.definition: An injunction that conveys only the form of the act, e.g. 'he offers the Agnihotra'.
The half of the time-wheel in which conditions improve through six periods (TS 3.27).
The annual temple festival (mahotsava) with flag-hoisting and processions.
The annual festival conducted by the tantri.
Livelihood of the second stage: food cast away or given out of pity or curiosity.
The highest, pure devotion: favourable cultivation of Kṛṣṇa, free from other desires and uncovered by knowledge, works and the like.
The first of the ten virtues: forgiveness and patience under provocation (TS 9.6).
The strongest joint-structure of the body, required for meditation of the highest kind (TS 9.27); held to be unavailable in the present age.
Lunar mansion uttara-bhādrapadā: presiding deity Ahirbudhnya (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Saturn (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fixed (dhruva) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
The 'later' Kaula view, in which there is no Śiva-principle apart from the Śakti-principle and she alone is worshipped (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 23, 35).
Lunar mansion uttara-phalgunī: presiding deity Aryaman (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord the Sun (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fixed (dhruva) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
Sins before the attainment of knowledge or surrender, which are destroyed, and those after it, which do not cling (if unintentional).
The Northern transmission: the cults of Kālī (Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, Guhyakālī) and the Krama.
Lunar mansion uttarāṣāḍhā: presiding deity the All-gods (viśvedevāḥ) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord the Sun (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fixed (dhruva) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
The six months of the northern course, part of the bright path (BhG 8.24); Bhīṣma holds his breath until it comes (MBh 6.114.89–98).

In jyotiṣa, the sun's northern course; Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa places the northward turning of sun and moon at the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā in Māgha (VJ r.6); in later calendars it is marked by Makara-saṃkrānti.
Jhāna, knowledge and vision, the paths and fruits; falsely claiming one entails defeat (Vin Pār 4).
(As reported) 'There is no exertion, action, strength, energy, human effort' — Gosāla's formula in the Jain canon.
Temperature (the fire element) as one of the four originators of matter.

Speech as goddess and power: she proclaims herself queen and self of all (RV 10.125); four quarters of her, three hidden (1.164.45); she revealed herself to some like a bride (10.71.4); the gods begot her and all animals speak her (8.100.11).
Speech as Prajāpati's own and second, sent forth to pervade all (PB 20.14.2); yoked with mind to carry the sacrifice (ŚB 1.4.4.7); speech as consecration (KB 7.1).
The object of grammar and phonetics; in the Mahābhāṣya the 'great god' who enters mortals, identity with whom is the aim of grammar.
Speech as the consciousness of beings, within and without, moving them to all activity; when it departs a being is like a log (VP 1, from memory).

equivalents.note: Bhartṛhari's 'Brahman as word' is a later philosophy of sound that draws on the Vedic exaltation of Vāc; the Saṃhitās do not use the term.

definitions.definition: A short rhythmic Kannada prose-poem spoken from experience, usually closing with the author's signature name for the Lord; the scripture of the śaraṇa strand.

A 'recitation' — an assembly of monks to collect and fix the scripture: at Pāṭaliputra after the famine, at Mathurā under Skandila (and at Valabhī under Nāgārjuna), and at Valabhī under Devarddhigaṇi, where the canon was written down.
An author of vacanas.
'A verbal handle': the modification is a verbal handle, a name; the reality is clay (ChU 6.1.4).
'A matter of speech': the Chāndogya's description of modifications as mere names (the clay alone being real), the basis of the non-difference of effect from cause (BS 2.1.14).
Audible repetition with correct tones and clear syllables; ten times better than ritual sacrifice.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): disputation with another based on the science, of two kinds, jalpa and vitaṇḍā (Ca Vi 8.28).

Debate in which both sides prove and refute with the means of knowledge and tarka, without contradicting tenets, using the five members (NS 1.2.1); undertaken with teachers, pupils and seekers of the good (NS 4.2.48).
Debate aimed only at ascertaining the truth, as between teacher and disciple.

notes: Homonym in Rasa Śāstra: 'vāda' = alchemy (dhātuvāda).

definitions.definition: The first section of the mantra, 'born of speech'; the Goddess's face (LSN 35).

The eight goddesses of speech (Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, Kaulinī) of the eight-cornered enclosure, composers of the Lalitā Sahasranāma; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire and the three qualities.
The word-nature of awareness: eternal, it makes recognition (pratyavamarśa) possible; without it light would not illumine (VP 1.124).
A follower of the Vibhāṣā — those who 'live by' or 'know' the Vibhāṣā; the Kashmiri orthodoxy whose system the Kośa mostly presents.
Devotion by rule: practice impelled by the command of scripture, where spontaneous attraction (rāga) is not yet present.
A brahmin following the Sūtra of Vikhanas; the Vaikhānasa Sūtra is held to be the first and best of sūtras and 'Vikhanas' to denote Nārāyaṇa.

notes: In Dharmaśāstra the word also names a class of forest hermits.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta and Aniruddha, the five forms invoked in Vaikhānasa worship.

equivalents.note: both are sets of divine forms for worship; the Vaikhānasas do not present theirs as vyūhas

definitions.definition: Articulated, audible speech, produced when breath strikes the places of articulation, whose letters are grasped by the hearer (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); for Nāgeśa, speech in the throat and mouth.
Spoken speech coming forth through the palate.
The body of gods and hell-beings, which can change size and form; also gained by some ascetics as an attainment (TS 2.36, 2.46–47).
Ahaṃkāra in its sāttvika aspect, from which the eleven organs proceed (SK 25).
The eternal realm of the Lord, made of pure sattva, the goal of the freed.
The fourth order, dwelling in heavens one above another (TS 4.16–19).
(Jain report) The 'assembly' of those who hold that discipline or reverence (vinaya) alone leads to the good: 32 kinds — veneration of eight objects by mind, speech, body and gifts.

Dispassion: the consciousness of mastery of one free of thirst for seen and scriptural objects (1.15); the higher is freedom from thirst for the guṇas (1.16); dispassion even toward the highest powers leads to kaivalya (3.50).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23); by itself it leads to absorption into prakṛti (SK 45), not to liberation; Gauḍapāda distinguishes external dispassion (from seeing the faults of objects) and internal (seeing even pradhāna as like a dream). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra makes it a support of meditation (3.36).
Dispassion, which with practice restrains the mind (BhG 6.35); dispassion toward sense-objects is a mark of knowledge (13.8).
Freedom from attachment; the supreme dispassion by which the upasarga-powers are renounced (LiP 1.9.52-56).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Together with practice, the means by which the restless mind is held (6.35).
Dispassion toward the enjoyment of results of action in this world and the next.
In Jainism detachment cultivated by contemplating the world and the body (TS 7.12); threefold — born of suffering, of delusion and of knowledge, only the last true (Adhyātmasāra).
Dispassion, the condition of renunciation ('the very day one becomes dispassionate'); the oil of the lamp of knowledge (Dakṣiṇāmūrti).

cross_language.note: Buddhist dispassion

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: In the Avataṃsaka the Buddha as he is seen in the dharmadhātu, his body filling all worlds; in the Brahmajāla sūtra the buddha on the lotus-throne.
Narsinh Mehta's 'true Vaiṣṇava': one who knows others' pain, helps without pride, speaks ill of none and is free of greed, deceit, lust and anger.
The second mode: devotion to Viṣṇu with vegetarian purity.
In the Yoga Upaniṣads the inner target held with the outward unblinking gaze — the same definition the HYP gives for śāmbhavī.

equivalents.note: Defined in identical terms (antarlakṣya, bahirdṛṣṭi, nimeṣonmeṣa-varjitā).

definitions.definition: 'Common to all men': the self conceived as the cosmos with sky as head etc. (ChU 5.11-18); the first quarter, waking (MāU 3); the digestive fire within a person (BAU 5.9.1).
The fire of digestion that the Lord becomes in living bodies (BhG 15.14); the fire within whose seven tongues are the senses, mind and intellect (Anugītā 14.20).
The terrible river on the road to Yama, a hundred yojanas wide and full of pus and blood, crossed easily by those who gave the Vaitaraṇī cow; also one of the hells of BhP 5.26.
Service to teachers, ascetics, novices, the sick and the community (TS 9.24).

The branch of virilization: that which gives offspring and delight and keeps semen fruitful into age, for the continuity of lineage here and endlessness hereafter (Ca Ci 1.1.9-12; Su Sū 1.8). Summary only.
'Making adamantine': the practice in the bone-circle by which 'a man becomes like a thunderbolt' and the body has no dissolution (KJN 15, 'paramavajrīkaraṇa').
The channel within suṣumnā, enclosing citriṇī (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa).
A mudrā for retaining and drawing up bindu (and rajas), with the variants sahajolī and amarolī (HYP 3.83–103; DYŚ 137–143). RESTRICTED: summary only.
A seal for drawing up and preserving bindu, in the context of which the HYP states that death comes by the fall of bindu (HYP 3.83–89); restricted, summary only.
The diamond-like concentration: the uninterrupted path of the ninth grade at the peak of existence, which destroys the last defilement.
Speech: one of the vital functions contending with breath (BAU 1.3; ChU 5.1); fire becoming speech entered the mouth (AU 1.2.4); in the inner agnihotra speech is offered into breath (KauU 2.5).
Retrogression; a retrograde planet is counted strong for longevity (BJ 7.2) and is a name of Mars (BJ 2.2).
Oblique, striking expression; for Bhāmaha the basis of all figures, for Kuntaka the life of poetry.
A sentence is one when it has a single purpose and its parts need each other (MS 2.1.46); as the third means of subsidiarity, joint utterance (samabhivyāhāra) of subsidiary and principal words.
The sentence, for the grammarians the primary indivisible unit of meaning (vākya-sphoṭa); Bhartṛhari lists eight rival definitions (VP 2.1–2).
A group of words (Tarkasaṅgraha); Vedic sentences are valid as spoken by the Lord, worldly ones when spoken by a reliable person.
The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by understanding (VS 6.1.1).
Taking one utterance as several sentences, a fault to be avoided in interpretation (MS 2.1.47; Śabara on 1.1.1).
The meaning of the whole sentence, conveyed by the word-meanings (Bhāṭṭa) or by words expressing meanings already connected (Prābhākara).
The meaning of the sentence, grasped as a flash of pratibhā distinct from the word-meanings (VP 2.143).
The remainder of the passage, which settles a doubtful meaning (MS 1.4.29).
The young goddess (Bālā), the Siddhars' Śakti worshipped at the root with three syllables; identified with Maṉōṉmaṇi.
The eleven supplementary hymns printed as RV 8.49–59.
Scriptures of the left/northern stream centred on Tumburu and his four sisters (e.g. Vīṇāśikha).
The left-hand conduct, contrasted with the right; Lakṣmīdhara assigns it to those not eligible for the Vedic way.
The fifth mode: 'left-hand' worship with the Kaula substances, reserved for the vīra (summary only).
Therapeutic emesis, the chief remedy for kapha (AHS Sū 1.25).
The genealogies of gods, sages and kings - the third mark of a Purāṇa.
The narratives of the kings of the solar and lunar dynasties - the fifth mark of a Purāṇa.
The forest-hermit, entered when one sees wrinkles, grey hair and grandchildren (MDh 6.2).
Bowing to and praising the Lord, the sixth form of devotion.
Formal veneration of the teacher; one of the six essential duties.
Bowing, adoration with joined palms (Tamil toḻutal): 'O mind, worship his feet and rise' (TVM 1.1.1).
The 'utterance' of a saint — his or her collected words, treated as scripture by the panth.
The four classes (khattiya, brāhmaṇa, vessa, sudda), which arose from occupations (DN 27) and are all capable of purity (MN 93).

equivalents.note: same word; its basis (birth versus conduct) is disputed

definitions.definition: The weekday, named for the planet ruling its first hour in the sequence Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn; each weekday suits certain classes of asterism and action (MC 1.4, 2.2–8).
Lalitā's general (Daṇḍanāthā, Daṇḍinī) on the Kiricakra chariot who slays Viśukra (LSN 26-30); her worship is the seventh section of the Kalpasūtra; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad she is 'the father'.
A protective vidyā associated with Mahāvīra, given to Śvetāmbara monks at certain stages (low confidence on details).

A division of each sign into equal parts, each ruled by a planet, forming a separate chart: six in Varāhamihira (sign, horā, drekkāṇa, navāṃśa, twelfth, thirtieth: BJ 1.9), sixteen in Parāśara (BPHS 6.2–4).
A grouping of material particles by fineness; the karmic class (kārmaṇa-vargaṇā) is the matter drawn in and bound as karma.
A planet or ascendant occupying the same sign in the birth chart and the navāṃśa — the first navāṃśa of movable, the middle of fixed and the last of dual signs — held to give good results (BJ 1.14).

The regular walking pilgrimage to Paṇḍharpūr, above all for the Āṣāḍhī and Kārtikī ekādaśīs, made in singing companies (diṇḍī) behind the saints' palanquins; keeping it for life is what makes one a Vārkarī.
One who keeps the vārī to Paṇḍharpūr; a member of the Vārkarī sampradāya, marked by the tuḷsī necklace, vegetarianism, the Ekādaśī fast and the name.

Vital points of the body where life-breath concentrates; injury to them harms or kills and pressure on them heals. The Siddha tradition counts 108 (12 'striking' paṭu varmam and 96 'touching' toṭu varmam) and ascribes the lore to Agastya.

equivalents.note: Āyurveda's 107 marmas: overlapping idea, different counts and uses

definitions.definition: A phoneme — sixty-three or sixty-four, declared by Svayambhū (PŚ 3); the first topic of phonetics (TU 1.2).
Each of the four social classes — brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra — with their duties (MDh 1.31, 1.88–91; 10.4); stated by the tradition as created from the Person's mouth, arms, thighs and feet.
In the Brāhmaṇas the classes are correlated with metres, gods, chants and animals (TS 7.1.1.4–6) and with the three Vedas (TB 3.12.9.2).

The four classes, created by the Lord according to guṇa and action (BhG 4.13), their duties arising from their nature (18.41–44); Bhṛgu teaches that the whole world was of Brahman and came to varṇa-division by actions (MBh 12.181.10); conduct makes the brāhmaṇa (3.177.16).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.13: the fourfold class order (cāturvarṇya), created by the Lord according to the division of qualities (guṇa) and actions (karma).
The eternal letters are the word: 'gauḥ' is g, au and ḥ (Upavarṣa); meaning is conveyed by the letters through their impressions, without a sphoṭa.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The social orders whose mixture (varṇa-saṅkara) Arjuna fears (1.41).
Letter or sound as object of contemplation (VBT 30, 40, 81, 90) and as an āṇava support (MVT 2.21).
The letter: for the grammarians not a real part of the word, which is partless (VP 1.73).
The letters as the manifestation of śabda-brahman through kuṇḍalinī (ŚT 1.14); gathered as the fifty mātṛkās.

notes: Homonym: phoneme (Vedāṅga) and social class (Dharmaśāstra) kept as separate definitions.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument it arises when the women of a family are corrupted after adharma prevails (1.41), leads the family and its destroyers to hell (1.42) and uproots the jāti- and kula-dharmas (1.43); Kṛṣṇa says that if he did not act he would be the maker of saṅkara (3.24).
The mixture of varṇas that Arjuna fears will follow the ruin of families (BhG 1.41) and that the Lord says would follow if he did not act (3.24).
The three-month rains retreat.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The annual chart cast for the sun's return to its natal longitude, with its own year-lord, muntha and sahamas (Tājikanīlakaṇṭhī, Varṣatantra).
The ongoing persistence-in-change of each thing, assisted by time (TS 5.22).
Sovereign guardian of ṛta and the vows, all-seeing judge who binds with fetters and forgives (RV 7.86–89; AVŚ 4.16).
Visualising rain that washes away the remaining ash (YŚ 7).

A technical term for the disciple's eight faculties of learning while living with the teacher (grasping, retaining, inferring, rejecting, understanding, speaking, service, right application); the first means.
One is an outcaste by deeds, not by birth (Snp 1.7).

Latent tendency: the grasping of an object through firm conception without reflection; one of the two seeds of mind; impure vāsanās bind to rebirth, pure ones (friendliness and the like) are to be cultivated before all are given up; bondage is bondage to vāsanā.

Latent tendencies from past experience that manifest only when suited to ripening karma (4.8), continuous across births (4.9), beginningless because the will to be is eternal (4.10), and ceasing when cause, result, substrate and support cease (4.11).
One of the two causes of mind (with breath): if either is destroyed both are (HYP 4.22); laya is forgetting objects when vāsanās no longer arise (4.34).

Latent tendency: the impressions of past experience and action that incline the mind; the three vāsanās (world, scripture-learning, body) obstruct knowledge; their destruction is a discipline of the jīvanmukta.
Impressions of past experience; the material from which dreams are really produced (dreams are therefore not false).
Latent tendency that sustains mind; pure or impure; its destruction (vāsanā-kṣaya) with dissolution of mind and knowledge gives jīvanmukti.
Exhaustion of latent tendencies; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha equates it with liberation ('mokṣaḥ syād vāsanākṣayaḥ').
Destruction of latent tendencies, practised with knowledge and mind-dissolution for the stable freedom of the jīvanmukta.
The hotṛ's exclamation at the moment of offering.
The five masteries of a jhāna: adverting, attaining, resolving, emerging, reviewing.

The breath treated as a horse to be mastered: the Siddhar breath-yoga (vāci yōkam) that stills and turns the breath inward and is held to perfect the body and lengthen life (summary; see prc:vasi-yoga).

cross_language.note: horse

equivalents.note: vāci is the breath as the object of mastery

definitions.definition: The defining mark of lower dispassion (1.15); in Vācaspati the fourth of four stages of dispassion.

The 'site-man': a being who obstructed heaven and earth, pinned face-down by the gods who stay where they seized him, and made by the Creator into the god-filled figure laid over every site (BS 52.2–3).

literal: son of Vasudeva; the indwelling god

definitions.definition: Name of Kṛṣṇa; 'Vāsudeva is all' is the realization of the rare great soul (BhG 7.19); 'among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva' (10.37).
The supreme of the fourfold form, the knower of the field without guṇas, dwelling of all, entered by the liberated (MBh 12.326.38; 12.332.17).
The supreme Lord and first vyūha, full of all six qualities.

equivalents.note: the Nārāyaṇīya identifies Vāsudeva as the knower of the field

definitions.definition: One of the nine half-world-conquerors of each half-cycle, always paired with an elder brother baladeva and opposed by a prativāsudeva whom he kills; Lakṣmaṇa and Kṛṣṇa are the eighth and ninth. Because of the violence of their lives vāsudevas go to hell, though Kṛṣṇa will be a future Tīrthaṅkara.

cross_language.note: Digambara usage

definitions.definition: The doṣa of movement: dry, cold, light, subtle, mobile, clear and rough (Ca Sū 1.59); fivefold as prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna and apāna; unprovoked it upholds the body's structure, impels all movement and guides the mind, and in the world upholds the earth and drives the seasons (Ca Sū 12.8); chief seat the colon (AHS Sū 12.1).
Tamil vaḷi or vātam: the wind humour, first of the three (Kuṟaḷ 941 names the three 'beginning with vaḷi'); built of air and ether; in Siddha pulse-reading the strongest beat.

equivalents.note: vāta is vāyu as a bodily doṣa; Āyurveda uses vāyu, anila, māruta, samīraṇa as synonyms

definitions.definition: The easier mode of rasāyana, taken without withdrawing from ordinary life (Ca Ci 1.1.16; 1.4.28).
The Lord's love that overlooks — or, for the Teṅkalai, relishes — the faults of the dependent, like a cow's for its calf.
Parental love: love for Kṛṣṇa as one's child, as of Yaśodā and Nanda.
The three rounds of dependent origination: of defilement, of kamma and of result.
The physical base of consciousness: the five sense organs and the heart-base.
Truthfulness: speech that harms no one (Kuṟaḷ ch. 30).

equivalents.note: defined by the Kuṟaḷ by its harmlessness

definitions.definition: The deity Vāyu, highest soul, giver of liberation by Viṣṇu's permission, whose three avatāras are Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva.
The breath as wind: ten vāyus move in the channels as the living soul's vehicles (GŚ 23–25; SS 3.4–8); when the wind moves the mind moves (HYP 2.2).
Substance with touch and without colour, inferred from touch; within the body it is breath.
The Wind, 'the breath of the gods, germ of the world', whose sounds are heard, not his form (RV 10.168.4).
In the Siddha ninety-six principles, the ten vital winds (Tamil vāyu, with Tamil names pirāṇaṉ, apāṉaṉ, viyāṉaṉ, utāṉaṉ, camāṉaṉ, nākaṉ, kūrmaṉ, kirukaraṉ, tēvatattaṉ, taṉañcayaṉ).
The authorless (apauruṣeya), beginningless body of sentences, the sole means of knowing dharma; it comprises injunction, mantra, name, prohibition and arthavāda.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who delight in the words of the Veda and say there is nothing else proclaim a flowery speech aimed at heaven, enjoyment and power (2.42–44); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain (2.45); for a knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well in a flood (2.46).
The first mode: Vedic ritual conduct.
Learning the Veda from a teacher by the injunction 'one's own Veda is to be studied'; every such study presupposes a teacher's study, without first beginning (ŚV vākya 366).
Pleasant, painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of the six kinds of contact (SN 12.2); the second aggregate; the uninstructed adds a 'second dart' of mental pain (SN 36.6).
Feeling: the experiencing of the object's flavour as pleasant, painful or neutral (bodily or mental); a universal mental factor and an aggregate.
Bodily sensation, observed objectively as the meeting-point of mind and matter; reaction to it with craving or aversion generates saṅkhāras (Goenka).
Feeling, the aggregate of experience; pleasant, painful or neutral.

Knowing pleasant, painful and neutral feelings, worldly and unworldly (MN 10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four establishments of mindfulness.
Each of the six auxiliary sciences — śikṣā, kalpa, vyākaraṇa, nirukta, chandas, jyotiṣa — pictured as the Veda's nose, hands, mouth, ear, feet and eye (PŚ 41–42).
Karma producing pleasant and unpleasant feeling (TS 8.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who delight in vedavāda say 'there is nothing else' and proclaim flowery speech offering heaven, power and rebirth as fruit of works (2.42–43).
The rarest initiation, in which the guru's power pierces the disciple's centres; rare is the guru who can give it (Kulārṇava 13.79; 14.66).
The altar ground strewn with grass between the fires.

Natural urges (of urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, belching, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, breath after exertion) which must not be suppressed; and the urges of greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, envy, passion and rash acts which must be restrained (Ca Sū 7.3-4, 7.26-29; AHS Sū 4.1, 4.24).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The surge arising from desire and anger which the yoked, happy person withstands before release from the body (5.23).
The impression that keeps a moving thing moving (Tarkasaṅgraha; VS 5.1.17 C on the arrow).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The Tathāgata's four grounds of fearlessness (MN 12).

The open, empty space — the supreme as boundless void-expanse beyond the crown; 'for those who hold the open space to be the truth, what need of a title-deed?' (Kuṭampai 1); Kaṭuveḷi speaks of 'the open space of pure Vedānta'.

equivalents.note: space as image of the supreme
the Siddhar 'void' is not the Buddhist emptiness; resemblance only

definitions.definition: The quality that destroys conjunction.
Self-designation of the Theravāda of the Mahāvihāra as 'those who analyse'.
The teaching of those who distinguish: some of the past exists (unripened karma) and some does not.
'Option, extensive commentary': the great commentaries on the Jñānaprasthāna, above all the Mahāvibhāṣā.
The Lord's descents; the Ahirbudhnya counts thirty-nine, beginning with Padmanābha.
The Lord's descents (avatāra) — principal ones like Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in bodies of pure sattva taken by his will, and secondary ones by empowerment of souls — for the protection of the good.
The excitants of rasa: the object and substratum (ālambana: Kṛṣṇa and his devotees) and the stimuli (uddīpana: his qualities, flute, dress, places).
Determinant: the cause of an emotion in drama or poetry — its object and support (ālambana) and its excitants (uddīpana) (NŚ 6–7).

literal: that which causes to be felt
notes: Disambiguated from trm:vibhava (Pāñcarātra 'vibhava', the Lord's descents); U16's aesthetic use of trm:vibhava belongs here.

definitions.definition: Craving for annihilation, the third craving (SN 56.11); those repelled by becoming who delight in non-becoming 'overreach' (Iti 49).
Separated parts: the souls, parts of his marginal power.

The Lord's manifestations in the best of every class — Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, the sun among lights, Oṃ among words, japa among sacrifices, Kapila among the perfected — all sprung from a fragment of his splendour (BhG ch. 10).
Holy ash, one of the eight shields; called vibhūti because it causes prosperity (SSM 7.4–5).
The powers treated in the third pāda (Vibhūti-pāda) that arise from saṃyama.
One of the five names of sacred ash.
Sacred ash from the dhūnī, smeared on the body and given as blessing; in the common legend Gorakh is born from Matsyendra's ash.
Ash of the cremation ground smeared on the body.

notes: In yoga texts vibhūti also means yogic power; the Gītā's sense is the Lord's glory.

definitions.definition: Inquiry: discriminating reflection, guided by scripture and the wise, into what one is and what the world is; the second gatekeeper and the lamp by which the real is seen.
